Project $\vec A$ onto the axes: $\vec A = A_x\hat x + A_y\hat y + A_z\hat z$, with unit vectors ("x roof") along the positive axes. Its magnitude is $|\vec A| = \sqrt{A_x^{2} + A_y^{2} + A_z^{2}}$.
$\vec A = 3\hat x - 5\hat y + 6\hat z$ has $|\vec A| = \sqrt{70}$, and its angle $\theta$ to the $z$-axis satisfies $\cos\theta = 6/\sqrt{70}$.

$\vec A\cdot\vec B = A_xB_x + A_yB_y + A_zB_z = |\vec A||\vec B|\cos\theta$ — a SCALAR. Positive, zero or negative; zero when the vectors are perpendicular. It will return as work: positive and negative.

$\vec A \times \vec B$ by the three-row determinant with $\hat x, \hat y, \hat z$ on top — or geometrically, magnitude $|\vec A||\vec B|\sin\theta$, perpendicular to both. Zero when they are parallel.

Turn $\vec A$ into $\vec B$ through the smaller angle, as a corkscrew — demonstrated in a potato. Clockwise as seen by you drives it away: into the board. So $\vec A \times \vec B = -\vec B \times \vec A$, unlike the dot product.
Axes must satisfy $\hat x \times \hat y = +\hat z$. Draw them the other way and every torque and angular momentum later comes out with the wrong sign.

$\vec r(t) = x(t)\hat x + y(t)\hat y + z(t)\hat z$, so $\vec v = \dot x\hat x + \dot y\hat y + \dot z\hat z$ and $\vec a = \ddot x\hat x + \ddot y\hat y + \ddot z\hat z$. A three-dimensional motion is three one-dimensional motions, each governed by the familiar constant-acceleration equations.

Launched at speed $v_0$ and angle $\alpha$: horizontally, $v_x = v_0\cos\alpha$ forever, since there is no horizontal acceleration. Vertically, $v_y = v_0\sin\alpha - gt$. The horizontal motion does not know what the vertical one is doing.

beats.t: The cart and the golf ball
beats.d: A cart fires a golf ball straight up while rolling. The ball keeps the cart's horizontal velocity, so it stays above the cart and lands back on it. 'Physics works.'

phys100.0.3.worked: Faced with motion in two or three dimensions, resolve everything — initial velocity, acceleration — along perpendicular axes, and solve each axis as a separate one-dimensional problem with its own constant acceleration.
phys100.0.3.watch: Using a left-handed set of axes. With $\hat x \times \hat y = -\hat z$, every cross product later in the course flips sign.

checks.q: The cross product $\vec A \times \vec B$ is zero when:
opts: The vectors are perpendicular
The vectors are parallel or antiparallel
The vectors have equal length
Never
checks.expl: Its magnitude is $|\vec A||\vec B|\sin\theta$, zero at 0° and 180°. The DOT product is the one that vanishes for perpendicular vectors.

checks.q: The magnitude of $\vec A = 3\hat x - 5\hat y + 6\hat z$, to three decimal places, is:
The angle between that vector and the positive $z$-axis, in degrees to two decimal places, is:
checks.expl: $\cos\theta = A_z/|\vec A| = 6/\sqrt{70}$, so $\theta = 44.18°$.

phys100.0.4.takeaway: A projectile is a constant-velocity motion sideways and a constant-acceleration motion vertically, and from those two alone come the parabola, the maximum height, the range $v_0^{2}\sin2\alpha/g$ — and the monkey that cannot escape.

beats.d: $x = v_0\cos\alpha\,t$ and $y = v_0\sin\alpha\,t - \tfrac12gt^{2}$. Eliminate $t$: $y = x\tan\alpha - \frac{g\,x^{2}}{2v_0^{2}\cos^{2}\alpha}$ — a constant times $x$ minus a constant times $x^{2}$.
Where $v_y = v_0\sin\alpha - gt = 0$: at $t = v_0\sin\alpha/g$, and height $h = \frac{(v_0\sin\alpha)^{2}}{2g}$. Larger with faster launch and steeper angle; larger on the Moon.
The parabola is symmetric, so the flight takes twice as long as the climb: $\frac{2v_0\sin\alpha}{g}$. Multiply by $v_0\cos\alpha$: range $= \frac{v_0^{2}\sin2\alpha}{g}$, largest at 45°.
Double the launch speed and the ball stays up twice as long AND moves sideways twice as fast: four times the range.

Fire the spring gun straight up: it rises $3.07$ m, estimated against a 3 m mark, but repeated shots differed by up to 15 cm, so allow 5%. Then $v_0^{2} = 2gh = 60.2$ m²/s², and only $v_0^{2}$ is needed.
Prediction $60.2/9.8 = 6.14 \pm 0.31$ m. A one-degree error in the angle changes $\sin 2\alpha$ by $0.06\%$ at the flat top of the sine curve — negligible. The ball lands inside the band.
$\sin 60°$ sits on the steep part of the sine curve: one degree changes it by 2%. Total uncertainty about 7%, so $5.3 \pm 0.37$ m. It lands in the band again — 'hit the jackpot'.
$\sin 120° = \sin 60°$, so the range is the same, but the flight takes LONGER: the horizontal component $v_0\cos60°$ is smaller, and horizontal speed is what sets how long the trip takes.

A hunter aims straight at a monkey in a tree; the monkey lets go the instant the gun fires. Without gravity the ball would travel the straight line to it. With gravity the ball falls $\tfrac12gt^{2}$ below that line — exactly as far as the monkey has fallen in the same time.
Faster or slower, the ball meets the monkey — higher up or lower down. Only the AIM matters, and a very slow ball simply reaches the ground first.

In a frame falling freely with $g$, gravity disappears: the ball flies straight at the monkey at speed $v_0$ and arrives after $\sqrt{D^{2} + h^{2}}/v_0$. From the lecture hall it is $D/(v_0\cos\alpha)$ — the same time, as it must be.
A toy monkey on an electromagnet, a golf-ball gun, and Lewin in hunting costume. The ball hits.

phys100.0.4.worked: For any projectile question, write the horizontal and vertical equations separately, find the time from whichever axis pins it down, and substitute that time into the other axis.
phys100.0.4.watch: Assuming equal range means equal flight time. Launches at 30° and 60° land in the same spot, but the steeper one stays in the air longer.

checks.q: The hunter aims directly at the monkey, which drops at the instant of firing. The ball hits the monkey:
opts: Only for one particular launch speed
For any launch speed high enough to reach it before it lands
Never, because gravity pulls the ball below the aim
Only if fired horizontally
checks.expl: Ball and monkey fall the same $\tfrac12gt^{2}$ below the aim line in the same time, so the aim alone decides it.

checks.q: With $v_0^{2} = 60.172$ m²/s² and $g = 9.8$ m/s², the range at 45°, in metres to two decimal places, is:
checks.expl: $v_0^{2}\sin 90°/g = 60.172/9.8 = 6.14$ m — the maximum possible range.

checks.q: The same launch at 30°, in metres to two decimal places, lands at:
checks.expl: $60.172\sin60°/9.8 = 5.32$ m. A launch at 60° lands in the same place, after a longer flight.

phys100.0.5.takeaway: Going round a circle at constant speed still means accelerating — toward the centre, with magnitude $v^{2}/r = \omega^{2}r$ — and something must push or pull to supply it; remove that push and the object flies off along the tangent, not in a spiral.

beats.d: $T$ is the time for one revolution; $f = 1/T$ in hertz; $\omega = 2\pi/T$ in radians per second. And the speed is $v = 2\pi r/T = \omega r$.

The speed is constant but the velocity's direction keeps changing, so there must be an acceleration: $a_c = v^{2}/r = \omega^{2}r$, always pointing to the CENTRE. He leaves the derivation to the book.
Blades at 10 cm turning at 600 rpm: $f = 10$ Hz, $\omega \approx 63$ rad/s, $v \approx 6.3$ m/s, $a_c \approx 400$ m/s² — forty times $g$.
With $\omega$ fixed, $a_c = \omega^{2}r$ GROWS with distance from the axis. Writing $v^{2}/r$ tempts you to think the reverse, but $v$ itself grows with $r$.
On a turntable, a seat bolted down pushes on your back, or a bar you hold pulls you inward. No free lunch: the acceleration needs a cause. Next lecture calls it a force.
A ball circling on a string, cut at the bottom of the circle: it flies straight up, stops and falls back. Not the spiral that intuition suggests — just the velocity it had, continued.

From each planet's orbital period and mean distance, compute $\omega^{2}R$. On log–log paper the points lie on a line of slope $-2$: Mercury, 100 times closer than Pluto, has 10,000 times the centripetal acceleration. Gravity falls off as $1/R^{2}$.

beats.t: A marble in a spinning tube
beats.d: Nothing in a smooth tube can push the marble inward, so it keeps its velocity and drifts to the end. That is a centrifuge — and his grandmother drying lettuce in a colander swung round her head.
Hung from a string you feel a pull up; standing, a push up. Either way you perceive gravity OPPOSITE the push or pull. Swung round in a circle, the pull points inward — so your 'down' points outward.

A 100 m wheel with $\omega^{2}R \approx 10$ m/s² needs $\omega \approx 0.3$ rad/s, a turn every 20 seconds, rim speed about 30 m/s. 'Down' is outward everywhere, zero at the hub. Walking into a spoke means climbing a wall; walking out of the hub means falling down a shaft.

3600 rpm at 15 cm: about 20,000 m/s², some 2000 $g$. Fine silver chloride particles that stayed suspended for hours sink to the side in seconds; the glass itself must survive being 2000 times heavier.

beats.t: A bucket of water, upside down
beats.d: At the top of a vertical circle of radius 1 m, you need $v^{2}/R \gt g$, so $v \gt 3.2$ m/s — a revolution in under 2 seconds. Then the string still pulls, 'gravity' for the water points up to the ceiling, and the water stays in.

phys100.0.5.worked: For anything moving in a circle, first write $a_c = \omega^{2}r$ toward the centre, then ask which real push or pull supplies it. If nothing can, the object leaves along the tangent.
phys100.0.5.watch: Thinking centripetal acceleration falls with radius on a rotating body. At fixed $\omega$ it is $\omega^{2}r$ and grows outward; the hub feels nothing.

checks.q: A ball whirled on a string in a horizontal circle has its string cut. It then moves:
opts: Outward along the radius
In a spiral away from the centre
Along the tangent to the circle at that instant
Toward the centre
checks.expl: With the pull removed there is no centripetal acceleration; it keeps the velocity it had, which is tangent to the circle.

checks.q: Vacuum-cleaner blades 10 cm from the axis turn at 600 rpm. Their centripetal acceleration, in m/s² to one decimal place, is:
checks.expl: $\omega = 2\pi \times 10 = 62.8$ rad/s, so $\omega^{2}r = 394.8$ m/s² — about 40 $g$.

checks.q: A space station of radius 100 m must give $\omega^{2}R = 10$ m/s² at its rim. The time for one revolution, in seconds to two decimal places, is:
checks.expl: $\omega = \sqrt{10/100} = 0.316$ rad/s, so $T = 2\pi/\omega = 19.87$ s.

phys100.0.6.takeaway: Newton's three laws: without a net force velocity stays constant; $\vec F = m\vec a$ defines force; and every force comes with an equal and opposite force on the other body — none provable, all believed because every measurement agrees with them.

beats.d: Galileo's law of inertia: a body at rest stays at rest, and a body in motion keeps its velocity along a straight line, unless acted on by an external force. Everyday experience denies it — friction, air drag and gravity always intervene.
Accelerate yourself toward the class and the class seems to accelerate toward you, yet nobody feels a push. The first law fails in an accelerating frame.

No: the Earth spins (at the equator $\omega^{2}R \approx 0.034$ m/s², about 300 times less than $g$), orbits the Sun (five times less again), and so on. Small enough that the lecture hall is a good inertial frame in practice.

Stretch a spring by a fixed amount and it pulls with the same strength on any mass. Experimentally $m_1a_1 = m_2a_2$. That product is FORCE: $\vec F = m\vec a$, in newtons, kg·m/s². The acceleration points along the force.
Is this circular, if masses are measured with gravity? No: two identical pieces of cheese have twice the mass of one — count the atoms. Relative mass needs no force.

Everything here falls with the same $g$, so the gravitational force is $mg$, proportional to mass. A half-kilogram ball at rest in the hand: gravity pulls down with about 5 N, the hand pushes up with 5 N.
$F = ma$ says nothing about velocity, so it holds for anything slow compared with light. Near the speed of light, special relativity takes over.
If one body exerts a force on another, the other exerts an equal and opposite force on the first: action equals minus reaction. Always — moving, accelerating or at rest.

20 N pushes a 5 kg block against a 15 kg block. The pair accelerates at 1 m/s². Isolate the 15 kg block: it needs 15 N, supplied by the first block. Isolate the 5 kg block: 20 N in, 15 N back from the second block. The contact forces are equal and opposite.

A garden hose snaking backward. A balloon let go — a rocket. A gun's recoil. Hero's steam engine spinning as jets leave it; a soda can with slanted holes doing the same. Walking pushes the floor back so the floor pushes you forward; on ice you cannot.
An apple falling 100 m pulls the Earth with the same 5 N. The Earth accelerates at about $8\times10^{-25}$ m/s² and moves some $10^{-23}$ m before they meet — real, and unmeasurable.

A block hangs by a string with another hanging below it. Pull the lower one and which breaks? Slowly, the upper one — it carries the weight plus your pull. Yanked, the lower one: the block's inertia means it has barely moved before the lower string fails, so the upper string never feels the pull. Lewin leaves the class to think it through.

phys100.0.6.worked: For a system of bodies, find the acceleration of the whole first, then isolate each body, draw only the forces ON it, and apply $F = ma$ to that body alone. Contact forces appear in equal and opposite pairs.
phys100.0.6.watch: Putting both members of a third-law pair on the same body. Action and reaction act on DIFFERENT bodies, so they never cancel each other.

checks.q: Action and reaction forces never cancel because:
opts: One is always larger
They act on different bodies
They act at different times
Only one of them is real
checks.expl: The pair consists of the force of A on B and the force of B on A. To cancel, forces must act on the same body.

checks.q: A 4 kg mass hangs from two strings at 60° and 45° to the horizontal ($g = 10$). The tension in the 60° string, in newtons to two decimal places, is:
checks.expl: Resolving horizontally and vertically, $T_1 = 2mg/(1 + \sqrt3) = 29.28$ N.

checks.q: And the tension in the 45° string, in newtons to two decimal places, is:
checks.expl: $T_2 = T_1/\sqrt2 = 20.71$ N. Lewin's spring scales read roughly 30 and 20.

phys100.0.7.takeaway: Your WEIGHT is the push or pull that supports you — what a bathroom scale reads — not the gravitational force $mg$. Accelerate up and you weigh more; accelerate down and you weigh less; fall freely and you weigh nothing, though gravity has not changed at all.

beats.d: Standing on a bathroom scale, gravity pulls with $mg$ and the scale pushes up with $F_s$. That push IS your weight. At rest it equals $mg$.
Accelerating up at $a$: $F_s - mg = ma$, so $F_s = m(a + g)$. At 5 m/s² you weigh one and a half times as much; at 30 m/s², four times. Seeing is believing: that is your weight.
Accelerating down: $F_s = m(g - a)$. Cut the cable and $a = g$: the scale reads zero. You are WEIGHTLESS — like an astronaut in orbit, except the elevator eventually hits the ground.
Free fall means the ONLY forces on you are gravitational. No floor, seat or string is pushing or pulling.
Hanging from a spring scale, the tension is your weight: $T = m(a + g)$ when accelerating up, zero in free fall.

Masses $m_1 \lt m_2$ over a frictionless pulley on a massless string. The tension is the same on both sides — a massless string with different tensions at its ends would have infinite acceleration — so both masses have the SAME weight.

$T - m_1g = m_1a$ and $m_2g - T = m_2a$ give $a = \frac{m_2 - m_1}{m_1 + m_2}g$ and $T = \frac{2m_1m_2}{m_1 + m_2}g$. Equal masses: no acceleration, $T = mg$. One mass zero: the other falls freely and $T = 0$.
With 1.1 kg and 1.25 kg, $a \approx g/16$ and both weigh $1.17g$ newtons: the lighter one, accelerating up, has gained weight; the heavier one, accelerating down, has lost it.

At the bottom of a swing, $T = m(a_c + g)$: heavier. At the top, $T = m(a_c - g)$: lighter, and weightless when $a_c = g$ exactly. If $a_c \lt g$ the tension would be negative — meaning the bucket never gets there.

Half a second of weightlessness from a 1 m table: a gallon of water floats above the hands. Then the bill: hitting the floor at about 5 m/s and stopping in 0.2 s is 25 m/s² upward — about three and a half times normal weight.
Professor Trumper's scale with a 10 ms response: a 14.5 lb load drops to zero in free fall, spikes to three or four times its weight on the cushion, bounces into weightlessness again, and settles.

The KC-135 cuts power at 45° and 425 mph and flies a free-fall parabola for about 30 seconds: everyone weightless. Then about double weight as it pulls out. 'Zero gravity' is a misnomer: gravity is fully present — the weight is zero.

phys100.0.7.worked: To find the reading on any scale, isolate the body, write $F = ma$ with the scale's force and $mg$, and solve for the scale's force. Up-acceleration adds to $g$, down-acceleration subtracts.
phys100.0.7.watch: Calling a weightless astronaut 'free of gravity'. Gravity acts on them almost as strongly as on the ground; they are weightless because nothing pushes back.

checks.q: In a freely falling elevator, a bathroom scale under your feet reads zero because:
opts: Gravity has switched off
Nothing needs to push on you — only gravity acts, so your weight is zero
Your mass has become zero
The scale is broken by the fall
checks.expl: Weight is the supporting force. In free fall gravity alone acts and the floor pushes with nothing.

checks.q: An Atwood machine has 1.1 kg and 1.25 kg masses ($g = 10$). Its acceleration, in m/s² to three decimal places, is:
The string tension in that machine, in newtons to two decimal places, is:
checks.expl: $T = \frac{2 \times 1.1 \times 1.25}{2.35}\times10 = 11.70$ N — the weight of BOTH masses, $1.17g$.

phys100.0.8.takeaway: Friction grows to match whatever push it must resist, up to a maximum $\mu N$ — and that maximum is, surprisingly, independent of the mass and of the contact area; only the pair of materials matters.

beats.d: Push gently on a block and it does not move: friction grows to match. Push harder and it grows further, until it reaches a MAXIMUM, $F_f^{\max} = \mu N$, and you win. $N$ is the normal force, equal to $mg$ on a level floor.
$\mu_s$ is for breaking the block loose; $\mu_k$, smaller, is for keeping it sliding. Starting motion is harder than sustaining it.

On an incline at $\alpha$, resolve gravity into $mg\cos\alpha$ into the surface (balanced by $N$) and $mg\sin\alpha$ down the slope. At the angle where it just slips, $mg\sin\alpha = \mu_s mg\cos\alpha$, so $\mu_s = \tan\alpha$.

The mass cancels. A plastic bin empty and a bin loaded with five times its mass slid at 21.0° and 21.2°. A parked truck and a small car start to slide on the same slope, about 45° for rubber on concrete.

Two wooden blocks, one resting on a face four times larger than the other: they slid within two-tenths of a degree. Wider tyres do not grip better by this law — so why do race cars use them? An assignment question.

beats.t: An incline with a hanging mass
beats.d: Block $m_1$ on a slope tied over a pulley to hanging $m_2$. The trouble: you do not know in advance whether it will move up, move down, or stay put — and friction points DIFFERENTLY in each case.

It accelerates uphill if $m_2g \gt m_1g\sin\alpha + \mu_s m_1g\cos\alpha$. Downhill if $m_2g \lt m_1g\sin\alpha - \mu_s m_1g\cos\alpha$. Otherwise it does not move at all, and static friction takes whatever value balances it.

$m_1 = 1$ kg, $m_2 = 2$ kg, $\alpha = 30°$, $\mu_s = 0.5$, $\mu_k = 0.4$, $g = 10$. Since $20 \gt 5 + 4.33$, it goes uphill — and once moving, KINETIC friction applies and the tension falls below $m_2g$, because $m_2$ is now accelerating down and losing weight.
The acceleration must come out positive in the direction you established, and the tension must be less than 20 N. If not, there is an error.
With $m_2 = 0.4$ kg: neither condition holds, so $a = 0$. Gravity pulls 5 N downhill, the string 4 N uphill, and static friction supplies exactly 1 N uphill.
Water between tyre and dusty road can make friction almost vanish: hydroplaning. His pan lid, scraping when dry, spun freely once water collected in the rim.
Hovercraft, air tracks and a dry-ice puck all float on a thin gas film, reducing friction to almost nothing — the air track will serve for collision experiments later.

phys100.0.8.worked: With friction in play, first decide which way the system would move, test each direction against the maximum static friction, and only then write the equations — with kinetic friction if it moves, and whatever friction is needed if it does not.
phys100.0.8.watch: Assuming friction always equals $\mu N$. That is only its maximum; until slipping, static friction is exactly what equilibrium requires, and may even point the other way.

checks.q: Two blocks of the same material but different masses sit on an incline that is slowly raised. They start to slide:
opts: The heavier first
The lighter first
At the same angle, since $\mu_s = \tan\alpha$ does not involve the mass
Only if their contact areas match
checks.expl: Both $mg\sin\alpha$ and the maximum friction $\mu_s mg\cos\alpha$ scale with $m$; the mass cancels.

checks.q: With $m_1 = 1$ kg on a 30° slope, $m_2 = 2$ kg hanging, $\mu_k = 0.4$ and $g = 10$, the acceleration once moving, in m/s² to two decimal places, is:
checks.expl: $a = \frac{20 - 5 - 0.4\times10\cos30°}{3} = 3.85$ m/s² uphill.

checks.q: A 0.361 kg box on a 20° incline starts moving uphill when 0.270 kg hangs from it. The static friction coefficient, to three decimal places, is:
checks.expl: $\mu_s = \frac{m_2 - m_1\sin20°}{m_1\cos20°} = 0.432$ — larger than the $\tan20° = 0.364$ from the tilt test, since wood grain differs with direction.

phys100.0.9.takeaway: A revision sheet for the first exam: scaling, vectors, one-dimensional motion read off a graph, projectiles as two independent motions, and uniform circular motion — each worked with numbers.

beats.d: The first five lectures and the first two assignments. The fundamental equations will NOT be given — they have to be part of your world.

Resisting crushing requires $d \propto \ell^{3/2}$; the data say $d \propto \ell$. What nature actually guards against is BUCKLING — bones bowing and snapping — and that requirement scales $d$ with $\ell$.

$\vec A = 3\hat x$, $\vec B = 2\hat x + 2\hat y$: by components, $3 \times 2 = 6$ at once. By $|\vec A||\vec B|\cos\theta = 3 \times 2\sqrt2 \times \cos45° = 6$ too — but slower. Choose the method the question makes easy.
$|\vec A \times \vec B| = |\vec A||\vec B|\sin\theta$, perpendicular to both, direction by the right-hand corkscrew, and $\vec A \times \vec B = -\vec B \times \vec A$.

$x(t)$ over four seconds: a parabola from 6 to 3 m, a straight line to $-3$ m, a flat second, a straight line back to 6 m. Parabola means constant acceleration ($-6$ m/s²); straight lines mean constant velocity ($-6$, 0, $+9$ m/s); at the corners $v$ and $a$ are undefined.
Start and end at $x = 6$: average velocity 0. Distance travelled $3 + 6 + 0 + 9 = 18$ m in 4 s: average speed 4.5 m/s. Signs appear only in velocity.

$x = x_0 + v_{0x}t$ and $v_x = v_{0x}$ forever. $y = y_0 + v_{0y}t - \tfrac12gt^{2}$, $v_y = v_{0y} - gt$, $a_y = -g$ — with the minus because 'up' was chosen positive, not because gravity points down.

189 m/s at 45°: both components 133 m/s. Top when $v_y = 0$: $t = 13.3$ s, $h \approx 884$ m. Back to start height after 26.6 s, 3.5 km downrange, with $v_y = -133$ m/s — the same speed at the mirror angle.
$f = 1/T$, $\omega = 2\pi/T$, $v = \omega r$, $a_c = v^{2}/r = \omega^{2}r$ toward the centre.

15 m arm, 24 rpm: $T = 2.5$ s, $\omega \approx 2.5$ rad/s, $v \approx 38$ m/s (85 mph), $a_c \approx 95$ m/s² — nearly 10 $g$, with the direction changing all the while. Most of us faint near 6 $g$. A 747 takeoff is only about 2 m/s².

Slide your fingers together under a metre stick: they move alternately, never together. The finger nearer the centre carries more of the weight, so more friction; the other slides until IT is nearer, and they swap. Friction's maximum is $\mu N$, and $N$ is shifting.

phys100.0.9.worked: On any problem, draw the axes and choose which way is positive before writing a single equation. Every sign afterwards follows from that choice — and the final answer's sign is a check on it.
phys100.0.9.watch: Putting a minus sign on $g$ because 'gravity points down'. The sign comes from your axis; choose 'down' as positive and the acceleration is $+g$.

checks.q: An object goes from $x = 6$ m to 3, to $-3$, stays, and returns to 6 m in 4 s. Its average speed and average velocity are:
opts: 4.5 m/s and 4.5 m/s
4.5 m/s and 0
0 and 4.5 m/s
1.5 m/s and 0
checks.expl: Distance $3 + 6 + 0 + 9 = 18$ m over 4 s; displacement zero.

checks.q: The KC-135 enters its parabola with a vertical speed of 133 m/s ($g = 10$). The height it gains, in metres to the nearest metre, is:
NASA's centrifuge has a 15 m arm and turns once every 2.5 s. The centripetal acceleration, in m/s² to one decimal place, is:
checks.expl: $\omega = 2\pi/2.5 = 2.51$ rad/s, so $\omega^{2}r = 94.7$ m/s² — almost 10 $g$.

phys100.0.10.takeaway: A force that pulls back in proportion to the displacement, $F = -kx$, gives simple harmonic motion: $x = A\cos(\omega t + \varphi)$ with $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$ — and a period that does not depend on how far you pull it.

beats.d: Stretch or compress a spring by $x$ and it pushes back with $F = -kx$. The minus sign is the whole story: the force always points back toward equilibrium. It holds only until the spring is overstretched.
Hang masses on the spring and plot the extension: a straight line. Each kilogram added stretched Lewin's spring about 13 cm, so $k = \Delta(mg)/\Delta x$ — the slope, not a single reading.

$m\ddot x = -kx$, so $\ddot x + \tfrac km x = 0$. The solution is $x = A\cos(\omega t + \varphi)$ with $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$ and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$. $A$ and $\varphi$ come from the starting conditions; $T$ does not.
$k = 10$ N/m, $m = 0.1$ kg, released from $x = 0$ at $-3$ m/s: $\omega = 10$ rad/s, $T = 0.628$ s, and the starting conditions fix $A = v_0/\omega = 0.3$ m and $\varphi = \pi/2$.

beats.t: The glider on the air track
beats.d: 186 g on two springs: ten oscillations took 15.16 s, and 15.13 s from a larger amplitude — the same within error. Double the mass to 372 g: the prediction is $\sqrt2 \times 15.15 = 21.42$ s; measured 21.36 s.

The restoring force is $-mg\sin\theta$. Only for small angles, where $\sin\theta \approx \theta$, is it proportional to the displacement, and then $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\ell/g}$ — no mass in it. A 1 m pendulum ticks with a period of about 2 s.

A 5 m pendulum, $T = 4.57 \pm 0.02$ s predicted. Ten swings: 45.70 s at 5°, 45.75 s at 10°, and 45.6 s with Lewin himself sitting on the bob — mass does not matter, as long as he keeps his body in the shape of the ball.

phys100.0.10.worked: For any system that oscillates, write $m\ddot x$ as minus a constant times $x$. Whatever multiplies $x$ after dividing by $m$ is $\omega^{2}$, and the period is $2\pi/\omega$ — read off the equation, not solved again.
phys100.0.10.watch: Using $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\ell/g}$ for large swings. It rests on $\sin\theta \approx \theta$; at large angles the period grows and the motion is no longer simple harmonic.

checks.q: A 0.1 kg mass on a spring with $k = 10$ N/m. Its period, in seconds to three decimal places, is:
checks.expl: $\omega = \sqrt{10/0.1} = 10$ rad/s, so $T = 2\pi/10 = 0.628$ s, whatever the amplitude.

checks.q: The glider's mass is doubled from 186 g to 372 g. Its period:
opts: doubles
grows by $\sqrt2$
halves
is unchanged
checks.expl: $T \propto \sqrt m$: $15.15 \times \sqrt2 = 21.42$ s predicted, 21.36 s measured.

checks.q: Lewin sits on the bob of the 5 m pendulum. The period:
opts: grows, because the mass is larger
shrinks, because the mass is larger
stays the same, because $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\ell/g}$ has no mass in it
doubles
checks.expl: The mass cancels. Ten swings took 45.6 s with him on it, against 45.70 s without — the same within the error, provided he does not change the length by sitting up.

phys100.0.11.takeaway: Work is force times displacement, $W = \int \vec F \cdot d\vec r$, and it equals the change in kinetic energy. For a conservative force like gravity the work depends only on the endpoints, so mechanical energy $K + U$ is conserved.

beats.d: $W = \int \vec F \cdot d\vec r$, a scalar measured in joules. The work–energy theorem: the work done by the net force is $\Delta K = \tfrac12 mv_B^{2} - \tfrac12 mv_A^{2}$. Lifting 15 kg by 1 m costs about 150 J.

Going from A to B, gravity does $-mg(y_B - y_A)$ of work, whatever the path — straight up, a zig-zag, a loop. Only the height difference counts. Friction is not conservative: the longer the path, the more work it takes.
When only conservative forces do work, $K + U$ is constant. An object released from height $h$ has $v^{2} = 2g(h - y)$ at height $y$ — no matter what track it came down.

At the top of a loop of radius $R$ the track can only push down, so the minimum speed there satisfies $mg = mv^{2}/R$. With $v^{2} = 2g(h - 2R)$, the ball needs $h \ge 2.5R$. Release it from lower and it falls off.
$F = GMm/r^{2}$, $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$. At the Earth's surface this is $mg$, so $g = GM/R^{2}$. Far away the potential energy is $U = -GMm/r$: zero at infinity, negative everywhere else.

beats.t: The bowling ball to the chin
beats.d: A heavy pendulum released from his chin swings across the room and back. Mechanical energy is conserved, so it cannot come back higher than it started — as long as he does not push it. Lewin stands still, and trusts the physics.

phys100.0.11.worked: For a speed at the end of a track, skip the forces: write $mgh_A + \tfrac12mv_A^{2} = mgh_B + \tfrac12mv_B^{2}$ and solve. Forces are only needed where a CONDITION matters — like the track still pushing at the top of the loop.
phys100.0.11.watch: Taking $h = 2R$ for the loop because 'the ball has to reach the top'. Reaching the top with zero speed means falling off before it gets there; it has to arrive with $v^{2} = gR$ to spare.

checks.q: A ball rolls without friction into a vertical loop of radius $R$. The minimum release height, in units of $R$ to one decimal place, is:
checks.expl: At the top $v^{2} \ge gR$, and $v^{2} = 2g(h - 2R)$, so $2(h - 2R) \ge R$ and $h \ge 2.5R$.

checks.q: With $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$, $M = 5.97 \times 10^{24}$ kg and $R = 6.37 \times 10^{6}$ m, the gravitational acceleration at the Earth's surface, in m/s² to two decimal places, is:
An object slides from A to B once straight down and once along a long zig-zag, both frictionless. The work gravity does:
opts: is larger on the zig-zag
is larger straight down
is the same both ways
is zero both ways
checks.expl: Gravity is conservative: its work is $-mg\,\Delta y$ and depends only on the endpoints.

phys100.0.12.takeaway: Drag on a sphere has two parts, $F = C_1 r v + C_2 r^{2} v^{2}$: viscous at low speed, pressure at high speed. When drag equals weight the object stops accelerating, and that terminal speed scales as $r^{2}$ in the first regime and $\sqrt r$ in the second.

beats.d: $|F| = C_1 r v + C_2 r^{2} v^{2}$. $C_1$ comes from viscosity, $C_2$ from pushing the fluid out of the way. The two are equal at the critical speed $v_c = C_1/(C_2 r)$; well below it the first term rules (regime 1), well above it the second (regime 2).
The object speeds up until drag balances $mg$. In regime 1, $v_t = mg/(C_1 r)$; for a sphere $m \propto r^{3}$, so $v_t \propto r^{2}$. In regime 2, $v_t = \sqrt{mg/(C_2 r^{2})} \propto \sqrt r$.

Steel balls of several sizes fall through Karo syrup — deep in regime 1. They reach 99% of terminal speed within about 9 ms. Plot the fall time against $1/d^{2}$: a straight line, exactly as $v_t \propto r^{2}$ demands.
For air, $C_1 \approx 3.1 \times 10^{-4}$ and $C_2 \approx 0.85$. The critical speed for anything the size of a pebble is tiny, so almost everything that falls in air is in regime 2.
34 g, radius 0.35 m: $v_t = \sqrt{mg/(C_2 r^{2})} \approx 1.8$ m/s, so a 3 m drop should take about 2 s rather than the 0.8 s of free fall. It took 2.0 s.

A 1 cm pebble dropped from 475 m would hit at about 225 mph without air; with air, about 75 mph. A skydiver's terminal speed is about 150 mph. Even an apple dropped from a few metres arrives some 2 ms late.

With drag the path is no longer a parabola: it comes down more steeply than it went up. Lewin's puzzle — is the rise or the fall longer? Drag opposes the motion both ways, so it adds to gravity going up and subtracts from it coming down. The fall takes longer.

phys100.0.12.worked: Before using a drag formula, decide which regime you are in by comparing the speed with $v_c = C_1/(C_2 r)$. Then keep only the dominant term — the terminal speed follows from setting it equal to $mg$.
phys100.0.12.watch: Assuming heavier objects always fall faster. In regime 2, $v_t \propto \sqrt{m}/r$, so what matters is the mass per unit of cross-section, not the mass — a big light balloon drifts down while a small pebble drops.

checks.q: A balloon of mass 34 g and radius 0.35 m falls in regime 2 with $C_2 = 0.85$ ($g = 9.8$). Its terminal speed, in m/s to two decimal places, is:
In regime 1 (viscous), doubling the radius of a steel sphere multiplies its terminal speed by:
opts: $\sqrt2$
checks.expl: $v_t = mg/(C_1 r)$ with $m \propto r^{3}$, so $v_t \propto r^{2}$: a factor of 4.

checks.q: A ball thrown straight up in air, with drag. Compared with the time going up, the time coming down is:
opts: shorter
the same
longer
zero
checks.expl: Going up, drag and gravity both slow it; coming down, drag works against gravity. The net downward acceleration is smaller, so the fall takes longer.

phys100.0.13.takeaway: Force is minus the slope of the potential, $F = -dU/dx$. Near any minimum of $U$ the potential is a parabola, so small motions about a stable equilibrium are simple harmonic — and energy conservation gives the period without drawing a single force.

beats.d: For a conservative force, $F = -dU/dx$. Where $dU/dx = 0$ there is equilibrium: stable at a minimum of $U$ ($U'' > 0$), unstable at a maximum ($U'' \lt 0$). A marble in a bowl against a marble on a dome.

$\tfrac12 mv^{2} + \tfrac12 kx^{2}$ is constant. Differentiate with respect to time: $m v\dot v + kx\dot x = 0$, so $\ddot x + \tfrac km x = 0$ — the same equation as from Newton, with no force diagram.

beats.t: An object on a circular track
beats.d: Its height is $R(1 - \cos\theta)$, so $U = mgR(1 - \cos\theta) \approx \tfrac12 mgR\theta^{2}$ for small angles. Energy conservation gives $\ddot\theta + \tfrac gR\theta = 0$ and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{R/g}$ — the pendulum again.

The normal force of the track, like the tension in a pendulum string, is always perpendicular to the motion. It does no work, so it never enters the energy equation — which is why the track and the string give the same period.

beats.t: The air track bent into a circle
beats.d: Radius $115 \pm 5$ m, swung only about 1.2°: predicted $T = 21.5 \pm 0.5$ s. Three oscillations took 64.05 s, so $T = 21.35$ s — inside the error.

A ball rolling in a curved track of radius 85 cm: predicted 1.85 s, measured 2.27 s from ten oscillations. Friction cannot explain it, since it hardly damps. Lewin leaves it open; the answer is that the ball also ROTATES, so some of its energy goes into spinning and it moves more slowly than a sliding object would.

phys100.0.13.worked: To find the period of any small oscillation: write the energy, expand $U$ to second order around the minimum, and read off $\omega^{2} = U''/m$ (or the angular equivalent). One derivative, no force diagram.
phys100.0.13.watch: Treating a rolling ball as a sliding block. Rolling stores kinetic energy in rotation as well as in translation, so the same drop in $U$ buys less speed — and the period comes out longer than $2\pi\sqrt{R/g}$.

checks.q: An air-track glider oscillates on a circular track of radius 115 m ($g = 9.8$), with small amplitude. Its period, in seconds to one decimal place, is:
checks.expl: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{R/g} = 2\pi\sqrt{115/9.8} = 21.5$ s. Lewin measured 21.35 s.

checks.q: A point where $dU/dx = 0$ and $d^{2}U/dx^{2} \gt 0$ is:
opts: an unstable equilibrium
a stable equilibrium
not an equilibrium
a point of maximum force
checks.expl: Zero slope means zero force; positive curvature means $U$ is a minimum, so a small displacement produces a force pulling back.

checks.q: A ball ROLLING in a curved track oscillates more slowly than $2\pi\sqrt{R/g}$ predicts, mainly because:
opts: friction damps it
part of its kinetic energy is rotational
the normal force does work
the track radius was measured wrongly
checks.expl: The same loss of $U$ is shared between translation and rotation, so the ball moves more slowly and the period is longer.

phys100.0.14.takeaway: To escape the Earth, total energy must reach zero: $v_{esc} = \sqrt{2GM/R}$, about 11.2 km/s. A circular orbit needs $\sqrt{GM/r}$, exactly $\sqrt2$ less. Then power, $P = \vec F \cdot \vec v$, and how little of our energy use is muscle.

beats.d: $E = \tfrac12 mv^{2} - GMm/r$ is conserved. To just reach infinity with nothing left, $E = 0$: $v_{esc} = \sqrt{2GM/R} \approx 11.2$ km/s, about 25,000 mph. $E \ge 0$ is an unbound orbit; $E \lt 0$ is bound.
Gravity supplies the centripetal force: $GMm/r^{2} = mv^{2}/r$, so $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$ and $T = 2\pi r^{3/2}/\sqrt{GM}$. Know $r$ and the period follows, and the other way round.

The shuttle at 400 km altitude ($r \approx 6800$ km): about 90 minutes and 8 km/s. The Moon: 27.5 days at 1 km/s. The Earth around the Sun: a year at 30 km/s. Jupiter, five times further out: $5^{3/2} \approx 12$ years.
The period and radius of Sputnik's orbit were easy to find — 96 minutes. Its mass was not: orbital motion does not depend on the satellite's mass, which is exactly what the Americans wanted to know.
At any radius, escape speed is $\sqrt2$ times orbital speed: $8 \times \sqrt2 \approx 11.2$. And in a circular orbit $K = \tfrac12 GMm/r$, so $E = \tfrac12 U = -K$: always negative.

$P = dW/dt = \vec F \cdot \vec v$, in watts. On a bike in regime 2, drag $\propto v^{2}$, so $P \propto v^{3}$: 10 mph takes about 15 W, 25 mph about $2.5^{3} \approx 15$ times more, some 230 W. It is the road's friction that pushes you forward.

One calorie heats 1 g of water 1 °C and is 4.2 J (Joule's paddle wheel). Your body radiates about 100 W, $10^{7}$ J a day — 2,000 food Calories. Climbing three floors five times is only 35,000 J; climbing 5,000 feet is $10^{6}$ J, and then you do need to eat more.

Heating a bath takes about $2 \times 10^{7}$ J — a volunteer could not even keep six 20 W bulbs lit. The world uses about $4 \times 10^{20}$ J a year; sunlight brings 1,400 W/m². Fossil fuel is being burned a million times faster than it forms; fusion of the oceans' deuterium would last billions of years.

phys100.0.14.worked: For any orbit question, set gravity equal to $mv^{2}/r$ first; $v$ and $T$ follow. For escape, set the total energy to zero. The two answers always differ by $\sqrt2$, which is a quick check.
phys100.0.14.watch: Thinking a heavier satellite needs a different speed. The satellite's mass cancels on both sides of $GMm/r^{2} = mv^{2}/r$ — which is exactly why Sputnik's orbit gave away nothing about the rocket.

checks.q: With $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$, $M = 5.97 \times 10^{24}$ kg and $R = 6.37 \times 10^{6}$ m, the escape speed from the Earth's surface, in km/s to one decimal place, is:
With the same constants, the period of a circular orbit of radius 6800 km, in minutes to the nearest minute, is:
checks.expl: $T = 2\pi r^{3/2}/\sqrt{GM} = 5583$ s, which is 93 minutes — Lewin's 'about an hour and a half'.

checks.q: A cyclist in regime 2 speeds up from 10 to 25 mph. The power needed grows by a factor of about:
checks.expl: Drag $\propto v^{2}$ and $P = Fv \propto v^{3}$: $2.5^{3} = 15.6$.

phys100.0.15.takeaway: Momentum $\vec p = m\vec v$ obeys $d\vec p_{tot}/dt = \vec F_{ext}$: the internal forces cancel in pairs, so with no net external force the total momentum cannot change — however much kinetic energy is destroyed, and however wildly the parts move.

beats.t: Force is the rate of change of momentum
beats.d: $F = ma = d(mv)/dt = dp/dt$. For a system, add them up: every internal pair $F_{ij} = -F_{ji}$ cancels by Newton's third law, and only the external forces are left. Zero net external force, and $\vec p_{tot}$ is conserved.
1 kg at 5 m/s catches 2 kg at 3 m/s and they stick: $11 = 3v'$, so $v' = 11/3$ m/s. Kinetic energy goes from 21.5 J to 20.2 J — lost to heat in the collision.
Now the 2 kg comes the other way: total momentum $5 - 6 = -1$, so $v' = -1/3$ m/s. The kinetic energy before is still 21.5 J; after, 0.17 J. Nearly all of it is gone — the momentum is not.
5 kg at 1 m/s meets 1 kg at 5 m/s: total momentum zero. They stick and stand still. All the kinetic energy is gone; the momentum was zero before and is zero after.
A block at rest blows apart: momentum zero before, so $m_1v_1' = m_2v_2'$ after, in opposite directions. Kinetic energy APPEARS, from the chemistry. Momentum does not care.
Two cars pushed apart by a spring. Equal masses (244 g): 219 and 223 ms to cross 10 cm. 244 g against 488 g: 193 and 406 ms — twice the mass, half the speed, within the 2.5% error.

$M\vec r_{cm} = \sum m_i\vec r_i$. Differentiate: $\vec p_{tot} = M\vec v_{cm}$, and again: $\vec F_{ext} = M\vec a_{cm}$. The centre of mass moves as if all the mass and all the external force were at that one point.

Two cars joined by a spring jerk about wildly, but under UV light only the centre-of-mass marker is visible — and it glides at constant speed. A thrown squash racquet tumbles, but its centre of mass traces a clean parabola.

phys100.0.15.worked: For any collision, write the total momentum before and put it equal to the total after — with signs for direction in one dimension, by components in two. Only then look at energy, and expect it NOT to be conserved unless you are told so.
phys100.0.15.watch: Treating momentum and kinetic energy as interchangeable. Kinetic energy can be destroyed (collisions) or created (explosions); momentum cannot, as long as the net external force is zero.

checks.q: 1 kg at $+5$ m/s and 2 kg at $-3$ m/s collide head on and stick. The kinetic energy left afterwards, in joules to two decimal places, is:
checks.expl: $v' = (5 - 6)/3 = -1/3$ m/s, so $K = \tfrac12 \cdot 3 \cdot \tfrac19 = 0.17$ J, out of 21.5 J before.

checks.q: Masses $m$ at $(0, 0)$, $2m$ at $(\ell, 0)$ and $m$ at $(\ell/2, \sqrt3\ell/2)$. The $x$-coordinate of the centre of mass, in units of $\ell$ to three decimal places, is:
A block at rest explodes into two pieces. Afterwards:
opts: momentum and kinetic energy are both conserved
momentum is conserved; kinetic energy increased
kinetic energy is conserved; momentum increased
neither is conserved
checks.expl: The explosion is internal, so the total momentum stays zero. The kinetic energy came from the chemistry.

phys100.0.16.takeaway: Momentum gives one equation; for a second you need to know what happens to the kinetic energy. In an elastic collision none is lost — and in the centre-of-mass frame each object simply bounces back with its speed unchanged.

beats.d: $K_{before} + Q = K_{after}$. $Q > 0$: superelastic (an explosion, a released spring). $Q = 0$: elastic. $Q \lt 0$: inelastic, the loss going to heat. With momentum and $Q$, both final velocities follow.
$v_1' = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}v_1$, $v_2' = \dfrac{2m_1}{m_1 + m_2}v_1$. $v_2'$ is always forward; $v_1'$ can reverse.

Bowling ball into ping-pong ball: the bowling ball carries on unaffected and the ping-pong ball leaves at $2v_1$. Ping-pong ball into bowling ball: it bounces straight back. Equal masses: the first stops dead and the second takes over its velocity — Newton's cradle.

Springs on the cars make the collision nearly elastic. Equal masses: 194 and 196 ms. One onto twice its mass: 123, 375 and 186 ms, against predictions of $-\tfrac13v_1$ and $+\tfrac23v_1$ — within about 2%.

A tennis ball bounces elastically off a wall: the wall takes momentum $2mv$ but no kinetic energy. Lewin leaves it for a sleepless night. The resolution: the wall's $p = 2mv$ with an enormous $M$ means a speed $2mv/M$ and a kinetic energy $p^{2}/2M$, which goes to zero as $M$ grows.

Move with $v_{cm} = (m_1v_1 + m_2v_2)/(m_1 + m_2)$. There the total momentum is zero before and after, whatever the collision. If it is elastic, $u_1' = -u_1$ and $u_2' = -u_2$: the velocities simply reverse. Transform back by adding $v_{cm}$.

beats.t: The most heat there can be
beats.d: In a completely inelastic collision, everything stops in the CM frame, so all the CM-frame kinetic energy becomes heat: $\tfrac12\dfrac{m_1m_2}{m_1 + m_2}v_1^{2}$. The same number comes out of the lab-frame calculation. Putty on a wall: all of $\tfrac12m_1v_1^{2}$.
Two balls in, two out; three in, three out; five on three, five out. Momentum and energy together force it — Lewin invites anyone to prove it analytically.

phys100.0.16.worked: For an elastic collision, go to the centre-of-mass frame: subtract $v_{cm}$, reverse every velocity, add $v_{cm}$ back. Three lines, no quadratic equation.
phys100.0.16.watch: Conserving kinetic energy in a collision that makes objects stick. Sticking means completely inelastic: use momentum alone, and the kinetic energy afterwards will be less.

checks.q: A 1 kg cart at 6 m/s hits a 2 kg cart at rest, elastically. The speed of the 2 kg cart afterwards, in m/s, is:
checks.expl: $v_2' = 2m_1v_1/(m_1 + m_2) = 12/3 = 4$ m/s; the 1 kg cart bounces back at 2 m/s.

checks.q: The same carts collide and STICK. The heat produced, in joules, is:
checks.expl: $\tfrac12\dfrac{m_1m_2}{m_1 + m_2}v_1^{2} = \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac23 \cdot 36 = 12$ J, out of 18 J.

checks.q: A billiard ball hits an identical ball at rest, head on and elastically. Afterwards:
opts: both move at $v/2$
the first stops; the second moves at $v$
the first bounces back at $v$
both stop
checks.expl: With $m_1 = m_2$, $v_1' = 0$ and $v_2' = v_1$ — Newton's cradle.

phys100.0.17.takeaway: An impulse $\int F\,dt$ is a change of momentum. That idea measures a bullet's speed with a pendulum, puts forces of hundreds of newtons into a bouncing ball, and — as a steady stream of expelled mass — drives a rocket: $\Delta v = -u\ln(m_f/m_i) - gt$.

beats.d: The bullet sticks in a heavy block: $mv = (m + M)v'$. The block swings up: $v' = \sqrt{2gh}$. But $h$ is tiny — 0.6 mm at 2° — so measure the sideways swing $x$ instead: $h \approx x^{2}/2L$ and $v = \dfrac{m + M}{m}x\sqrt{g/L}$.

Bullet 2 g, block 3.2 kg, $L = 1.13$ m: $v \approx 4.7 \times 10^{3}x$. The wiper stopped at 5.2 cm: 244 m/s, give or take 15% — just under the speed of sound. 99.94% of the bullet's kinetic energy became heat in the block.

$\vec J = \int_0^{\Delta t}\vec F\,dt = \vec p_f - \vec p_i$. A 0.1 kg ball hits the floor at 5.5 m/s and bounces back: $J = 2mv = 1.1$ kg·m/s. In a 2 ms contact that is an average 550 N — 550 times its weight.
A ball that sticks gets half the impulse, but over a shorter contact, so the average force is about the same. High-speed film: contact lasts only a few milliseconds.
Dropped together, the tennis ball on top flies far higher than it was dropped from — the basketball rebounds into it. Lewin leaves the height for the problem set.

Throw tomatoes at a wall at $v$ and it feels $F = v\,dm/dt$; the thrower feels the same force back. A rocket expels gas at $u$ relative to itself: thrust $= u\,dm/dt$. Saturn: 2.5 km/s at 15,000 kg/s, about $3.5 \times 10^{7}$ N.

Momentum over $\Delta t$: $m\,dv = u\,dm$. Integrate: $v_f - v_i = -u\ln(m_f/m_i) - gt$ for a vertical launch. With $u = 1000$ m/s, $m_f/m_i = 0.1$, 100 s burn: $2303 - 1000 \approx 1.3$ km/s. In orbit, or without gravity, the $gt$ term is not there.

The same burn always gives the same $\Delta v$. From rest, 100 m/s gives $\tfrac12m \cdot 10^{4}$. From 1000 m/s, the same burn gives $\tfrac12m(1100^{2} - 1000^{2})$ — twenty times more kinetic energy.

phys100.0.17.worked: When a force acts briefly and violently, do not try to follow it: find the momentum change and divide by the contact time. When mass is being expelled, write the momentum of rocket AND exhaust before and after a small $dt$.
phys100.0.17.watch: Measuring the pendulum's rise $h$ directly. At a few degrees it is a fraction of a millimetre; the horizontal swing is centimetres, and $h \approx x^{2}/2L$ turns one into the other.

checks.q: A 2 g bullet sticks in a 3.2 kg pendulum block of length 1.13 m, which swings out sideways 5.2 cm ($g = 9.8$). The bullet's speed, in m/s to the nearest whole number, is:
checks.expl: $v = \dfrac{3.202}{0.002} \times 0.052 \times \sqrt{9.8/1.13} = 1601 \times 0.052 \times 2.945 = 245$ m/s. Lewin, rounding the constant to $4.7 \times 10^{3}$, got 244.

checks.q: A rocket is launched vertically ($g = 10$) with exhaust speed 1000 m/s and burns for 100 s until $m_f/m_i = 0.1$. Its final speed, in km/s to one decimal place, is:
A rocket fires the same burn once from rest and once already moving at 1000 m/s. The second burn gives:
opts: the same $\Delta v$ and the same $\Delta K$
the same $\Delta v$ but far more $\Delta K$
a smaller $\Delta v$
a larger $\Delta v$
checks.expl: The burn fixes $\Delta v$. Kinetic energy grows with $v^{2}$, so the same $\Delta v$ at high speed is worth much more energy — here 20 times.

phys100.0.18.takeaway: A revision sheet for the second exam: the work-energy theorem (always) against conservation of mechanical energy (conservative forces only), then the pendulum and the spring, orbital energy, drag in syrup, and a completely inelastic collision.

beats.d: Work-energy: $W_{A\to B} = K_B - K_A$ holds with ANY forces, friction included. Conservation of $K + U$ holds only when every force doing work is conservative.
Free-body diagram: $mg$, $N$, friction. Tilt until it just slips: $\mu_s = \tan\theta$. Once sliding, $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)$.

beats.t: Speed at the bottom, two ways
beats.d: By kinematics, $v_B = \sqrt{2al}$. By work-energy, $mgl\sin\theta - \mu_kmgl\cos\theta = \tfrac12mv_B^{2}$ — the same answer, and Lewin's preferred route.

$\ell = 1$ m, started at 5° with 0.3 m/s. Rise to the starting point: $h_1 = \ell(1 - \cos5°) = 3.8$ mm. Extra rise from the speed: $h_2 = v_B^{2}/2g = 4.5$ mm. Then $\cos\theta_{max} = 1 - (h_1 + h_2)/\ell$: $\theta_{max} \approx 7.4°$. The tension does no work.

$\theta = \theta_{max}\cos(\omega t + \varphi)$. The starting angle gives $\cos\varphi$ (two roots); the starting angular speed $v/\ell$ gives $\sin\varphi$ (two roots); the one they share is the answer: $\varphi \approx -0.82$ rad. Not much physics, but it must be consistent.
The same approach: $\tfrac12mv_B^{2} + \tfrac12kx_B^{2} = \tfrac12kx_{max}^{2}$ gives the amplitude.

$v = \sqrt{GM_\odot/R} \approx 30$ km/s. $K = -\tfrac12U$, $E = \tfrac12U = -K \approx -2.7 \times 10^{33}$ J. To leave the solar system, add $K$: double the kinetic energy, so multiply the speed by $\sqrt2$ — about 42 km/s.

$C_1 \approx 160$, $C_2 \approx 1.2 \times 10^{3}$. For a quarter-inch ball bearing the critical speed is about 100 mph and the actual terminal speed about 2 cm/s, so drop the $v^{2}$ term: $v_t = mg/(C_1r)$. Measuring $v_t$ is how $C_1$ was found — and it drifts with temperature.

beats.t: The top that will not stop
beats.d: Lewin's tiny top keeps spinning through the whole lecture, as if friction were suspended. He tells the class to forget it until after the exam.

phys100.0.18.worked: Before writing an equation, list the forces that do work. All conservative: conserve $K + U$. Any friction: use the work-energy theorem with friction's work as $-f\ell$. The pendulum's tension and the incline's normal force do no work, so they never appear.
phys100.0.18.watch: Conserving mechanical energy on a rough incline. Friction turns kinetic energy into heat; only the work-energy theorem, with friction's negative work included, gives the right speed.

checks.q: A block slides from rest 2 m down a 30° incline with $\mu_k = 0.2$ ($g = 9.8$). Its speed at the bottom, in m/s to two decimal places, is:
A 1 m pendulum at 5° is given 0.3 m/s outward ($g = 9.8$). Its maximum angle, in degrees to one decimal place, is:
The Earth orbits at 30 km/s. The speed it would need to escape the Sun from its orbit is about:
opts: 30 km/s
42 km/s
60 km/s
checks.expl: $E = -K$, so escape needs double the kinetic energy: $\sqrt2 \times 30 \approx 42$ km/s.

phys100.0.19.takeaway: A rotating body stores kinetic energy $\tfrac12I\omega^{2}$, where $I = \sum m_ir_i^{2}$ depends on the shape AND the axis. The parallel- and perpendicular-axis theorems extend a table of moments of inertia — and put numbers on flywheels, the Earth and a pulsar.

beats.d: $v = \omega R$, tangential acceleration $\alpha R$ with $\alpha = \ddot\theta$ — not to be confused with the centripetal acceleration. Swap $x \to \theta$, $v \to \omega$, $a \to \alpha$ and the old equations hold: $\theta = \theta_0 + \omega_0t + \tfrac12\alpha t^{2}$.
Each piece has $\tfrac12m_i\omega^{2}r_i^{2}$; $\omega$ is the same for all of them. Sum: $K = \tfrac12I\omega^{2}$ with $I = \sum m_ir_i^{2}$. Mass becomes moment of inertia.
Disk about its perpendicular central axis: $\tfrac12MR^{2}$. Solid sphere: $\tfrac25MR^{2}$. Rod about its centre: $\tfrac1{12}M\ell^{2}$. Look them up; the axis is part of the answer.
About any axis parallel to one through the centre of mass, a distance $d$ away: $I = I_{cm} + Md^{2}$. Always larger than about the centre.
For a THIN plate only: $I_z = I_x + I_y$, with $x$ and $y$ in the plate and $z$ perpendicular to it.

A 1000 kg car creeping down 500 m of mountain road at 4 m/s arrives with 8000 J; gravity did 5 million J of work, all burned in the brakes. A 200 kg, 0.5 m-radius disk ($I = 25$) could hold it at $\omega \approx 632$ rad/s, about 100 revolutions per second.
Two 85-ton flywheels at about 6 Hz store some 200 million J each, poured into magnetic fields in five seconds and taken back afterwards.

The Sun's spin holds about $10^{36}$ J — at its output that lasts about 125 years, so it is not the Sun's power. The Crab Pulsar: 1.5 solar masses, 10 km radius, a 33 ms period, and a period growing 36.4 ns a day. That loss of $\tfrac12I\omega^{2}$ is $6 \times 10^{31}$ W — exactly what it radiates.

phys100.0.19.worked: For an axis that is not in the table, start from the centre-of-mass value and add $Md^{2}$. For a thin plate spinning perpendicular to itself, add the two in-plane values.
phys100.0.19.watch: Quoting a moment of inertia without its axis. A disk about its perpendicular axis ($\tfrac12MR^{2}$) and about a diameter ($\tfrac14MR^{2}$) differ by a factor of two.

checks.q: A 200 kg disk of radius 0.5 m must store $5 \times 10^{6}$ J spinning about its central axis. The angular velocity needed, in rad/s to the nearest whole number, is:
checks.expl: $I = \tfrac12 \cdot 200 \cdot 0.25 = 25$, so $\omega = \sqrt{2 \times 5 \times 10^{6}/25} = 632$ rad/s.

checks.q: A 2 kg uniform disk of radius 0.5 m spins about an axis perpendicular to it through a point on its rim. Its moment of inertia, in kg·m² to two decimal places, is:
checks.expl: $I = \tfrac12MR^{2} + MR^{2} = 0.25 + 0.5 = 0.75$ kg·m², by the parallel-axis theorem.

checks.q: The Crab Pulsar's rotation is slowing. The energy it loses:
opts: is far less than it radiates
matches the power it radiates, about $6 \times 10^{31}$ W
goes into speeding up the nebula's filaments only
cannot be computed without its mass
checks.expl: The drop in $\tfrac12I\omega^{2}$ each second equals the observed x-ray, gamma-ray and jet output: it is powered by its spin.

phys100.0.20.takeaway: Angular momentum $\vec L = \vec r \times \vec p$ depends on the point you measure from; torque $\vec\tau = \vec r \times \vec F$ changes it. With no net external torque it is conserved — which is why a skater spins up, and why a collapsing star becomes a millisecond pulsar.

beats.d: $\vec L_Q = \vec r_Q \times m\vec v$, magnitude $mvr\sin\theta$. Measure from a point on the line of motion and $L = 0$; from the other side it points the other way. Unlike momentum, $L$ depends on the origin you choose.
The Earth circling the Sun: the velocity turns all the time, but about the Sun $L = mrv$ never changes. About any other point it does.
$d\vec L_Q/dt = \vec r_Q \times \vec F = \vec\tau_Q$. Gravity points straight at the Sun, so its torque about the Sun is zero — the reason $L$ is conserved about that one point.

A disk spinning about its centre of mass: $L = \sum m_ir_i^{2}\omega = I_{cm}\omega$. For rotation about the centre of mass it is the same about EVERY point — an intrinsic spin, like the Earth's, separate from its orbital angular momentum.

On a turntable holding two 1.8 kg weights: body as a 75 kg cylinder of radius 0.2 m gives $I \approx 1.5$; arms out at 0.9 m adds $2 \times 1.8 \times 0.81$, to about 4.4. Pulling in cuts $I$ threefold, so $\omega$ triples — no torque, $I\omega$ fixed. Lewin got very dizzy.

Internal forces come in equal and opposite pairs along the line joining them, so their torques cancel. With no net EXTERNAL torque, the total angular momentum is conserved, whatever collides or explodes inside.

When the nuclear fuel runs out: a white dwarf (Earth-sized, ~$10^{6}$ g/cm³), a neutron star (10 km, ~1.5 solar masses, ~$10^{14}$ g/cm³) or a black hole. Collapsing the Sun to 10 km would release about $10^{46}$ J — a hundred times its whole lifetime's output, in seconds.

Radius down by ~$10^{5}$, $I$ down by ~$10^{10}$, so $\omega$ up by $10^{10}$: a 100-day rotation becomes about a millisecond. Pulsars were found in 1967 by Jocelyn Bell — who did not share the 1974 Nobel Prize. The Crab's supernova was seen by Chinese astronomers on 4 July 1054.

phys100.0.20.worked: Before using conservation of angular momentum, name the point and check that the net external torque about THAT point is zero. Then $I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2$.
phys100.0.20.watch: Talking about 'the' angular momentum of a moving particle. Without a named origin it is undefined; only spin about the centre of mass is the same from every point.

checks.q: Lewin models himself as a 75 kg cylinder of radius 0.2 m, and holds 1.8 kg at 0.9 m in each hand. Pulling his arms in, his angular velocity grows by a factor of (two decimal places):
checks.expl: $I_{in} = \tfrac12 \cdot 75 \cdot 0.04 = 1.5$, $I_{out} = 1.5 + 2 \cdot 1.8 \cdot 0.81 = 4.416$; $L$ fixed, so $\omega$ grows by $4.416/1.5 = 2.94$.

checks.q: The Earth's angular momentum is conserved about the Sun but not about another point because:
opts: the Earth's speed changes
gravity points through the Sun, so its torque about the Sun is zero
the Earth spins
there is no force on the Earth
checks.expl: $\vec\tau = \vec r \times \vec F$ vanishes when $\vec F$ is along $\vec r$ — true only for $\vec r$ measured from the Sun.

checks.q: A star's radius shrinks by a factor of $10^{5}$ with no mass lost and no external torque. Its rotation rate:
opts: rises by $10^{5}$
rises by $10^{10}$
is unchanged
falls by $10^{10}$
checks.expl: $I \propto MR^{2}$ falls by $10^{10}$, so $\omega$ rises by $10^{10}$ to keep $I\omega$ fixed.

phys100.0.21.takeaway: Choose the origin that makes the torque easy: about a fixed pivot, forces at the pivot drop out. That turns a swinging ruler or a hula hoop into $\tau = I\alpha$, a simple harmonic oscillator, and a period you can predict to half a percent.

beats.d: $\vec L = \vec r \times \vec p$; $\vec\tau = \vec r \times \vec F$; $\vec\tau = d\vec L/dt$ (and $I\alpha$ for a fixed axis); no net external torque means $\vec L$ conserved; spin about the centre of mass, $L = I_{cm}\omega$, is the same about every point.
Often $L$ is conserved about one point and changes about another, and both descriptions are correct. That is exactly what makes angular momentum feel unintuitive.

A rod forced to spin about a point P off its centre: $L_P = (\tfrac1{12}M\ell^{2} + Md^{2})\omega$. The pin must push on the rod — the centripetal forces no longer balance — but that force passes through P, so about P there is no torque.

An impulse $J$ a distance $d$ from the centre: the centre of mass moves off at $J/M$ whatever $d$ is, and the rod rotates about its centre of mass. The spin grows with $d$; hit it at the middle and it only translates. Take torques about C, or about a point on the line of the blow, where $L$ stays zero.
Take torques about the pivot: $-Mgb\sin\theta = I_P\ddot\theta$. For small angles $\ddot\theta + \dfrac{Mgb}{I_P}\theta = 0$, so $T = 2\pi\sqrt{I_P/Mgb}$ — the mass cancels, since $I_P$ contains it.
Pivot 0.40 m from the centre: $I_P = \tfrac1{12}M\ell^{2} + Mb^{2}$ gives $T = 2\pi\sqrt{(\ell^{2}/12 + b^{2})/gb} = 1.565 \pm 0.01$ s. Ten swings: 15.71 s.
Hung from a point on its rim: $I_P = MR^{2} + MR^{2} = 2MR^{2}$, so $T = 2\pi\sqrt{2R/g}$ — the same as a simple pendulum of length $2R$. $R = 0.40$ m: predicted 1.795 s, measured 1.807 s.
Spin a certain piece of plastic one way and it slows, stops and spins back the other way. Friction stops things; it does not reverse them. Lewin leaves it for the class to think about.

phys100.0.21.worked: For anything swinging on a pin: torque about the pin, $I$ about the pin by the parallel-axis theorem, small-angle approximation, and read $\omega^{2} = Mgb/I_P$ off the equation.
phys100.0.21.watch: Putting the rod's length into the pendulum formula as if it were a string. For a physical pendulum the 'length' is $I_P/Mb$, set by the whole mass distribution, not by any one dimension.

checks.q: A metre stick swings from a pin 0.40 m from its centre ($g = 9.8$). Its small-angle period, in seconds to two decimal places, is:
checks.expl: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{(1/12 + 0.16)/(9.8 \times 0.4)} = 1.57$ s. Lewin measured 15.71 s for ten swings.

checks.q: A hoop of radius 0.40 m hangs on a pin at its rim ($g = 9.8$). Its small-angle period, in seconds to two decimal places, is:
A rod on frictionless ice is struck with impulse $J$ near one end rather than at its centre. The speed of its centre of mass is:
opts: larger
smaller
the same, $J/M$
zero
checks.expl: The centre of mass obeys $F = Ma$ whatever the point of impact; only the spin depends on where it is hit.

phys100.0.22.takeaway: Bound orbits are ellipses, and their energy and period depend only on the semimajor axis: $E = -GMm/2a$, $T^{2} = 4\pi^{2}a^{3}/GM$. Energy fixes $a$; angular momentum about the central body fixes where perigee and apogee are.

beats.d: Orbits are ellipses with the Sun at a focus. Equal areas in equal times — angular momentum in disguise. $T^{2} \propto a^{3}$: Kepler's table for six planets gives a constant, and it leads to Newton's inverse square.
Every circular formula survives with $R \to a$: $E = -GMm/2a$ and $T^{2} = 4\pi^{2}a^{3}/GM$. So orbits with the same semimajor axis have the same energy and the same period, however elongated.

Given $r_0 = 9000$ km, $v_0 = 9.0$ km/s and 120° between them around the Earth: energy gives $a \approx 50{,}000$ km (escape speed there is 9.4 km/s, so this is nearly unbound), and $T \approx 31$ hours.

Angular momentum about the Earth: $mv_0r_0\sin\varphi_0 = mv_Pr_P$. With energy that is a quadratic whose two roots are perigee and apogee: $r_P \approx 6600$ km at 10.7 km/s — only 200 km up — and $r_A \approx 93{,}000$ km at 0.75 km/s.
Fire forward at a point: more energy, larger $a$, longer period — the orbit swells on the far side. Fire backward: smaller $a$, shorter period. The burn point stays on the new orbit.

Peter and Mary share a 7000 km orbit (7.55 km/s, 97 min), 5% apart. To reach Mary, the sandwich needs a period of 92 min: $a = R(1 - f)^{2/3} = 6765$ km, so Peter throws it BACKWARD at about 0.13 km/s — 300 mph.
Let Mary pass the throw point $n_a$ times and the sandwich $n_s$ times: $a = R\big((n_a - f)/n_s\big)^{2/3}$. Some choices crash into the Earth; throw hard enough forward and the sandwich escapes.

phys100.0.22.worked: For any orbit from initial conditions: energy gives $a$ at once; $a$ gives $T$; angular momentum about the central mass plus energy give the perigee and apogee as the two roots of one quadratic.
phys100.0.22.watch: Throwing toward something ahead of you in orbit. A forward throw raises the orbit and LENGTHENS its period, so the sandwich falls behind; to catch up you throw backward.

checks.q: Around the Earth ($GM = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6 \times 10^{24}$), an object at 9000 km moves at 9.0 km/s at 120° to the radius. Its orbital period, in hours to the nearest hour, is:
checks.expl: $E/m = \tfrac12v_0^{2} - GM/r_0$ gives $a \approx 50{,}400$ km, and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{a^{3}/GM} \approx 31$ h.

checks.q: Peter and Mary orbit at 7000 km, Mary 5% of an orbit ahead. The throw speed (sandwich minus Peter), in m/s to the nearest whole number, is:
checks.expl: $a = 7000 \times 0.95^{2/3} = 6765$ km; vis-viva gives $v_s = 7428$ m/s against $v_a = 7561$ m/s, so $-133$ m/s — thrown backward.

checks.q: Two orbits have the same semimajor axis; one is a circle, the other a long thin ellipse. Their periods are:
opts: longer for the ellipse
shorter for the ellipse
the same
impossible to compare
checks.expl: $T^{2} = 4\pi^{2}a^{3}/GM$ contains only $a$.

phys100.0.23.takeaway: Motion toward or away from you shifts frequency: $\lambda'/\lambda = 1 - (v/c)\cos\theta$. In binary stars the shifting spectral lines give orbital speeds, radii and periods — then, through Kepler's third law, masses, and the evidence for neutron stars and black holes.

beats.d: A 4000 Hz fork moved at 1 m/s changes by 0.3% (1 part in 340): about 4012 Hz approaching, 3988 Hz receding. Swing a source in a circle and the pitch rises and falls sinusoidally.
$f'_{max}/f$ gives the orbital speed; the time between peaks gives the period; together, $2\pi R = vT$ gives the radius.

For $v \ll c$: $f' = f(1 + \tfrac vc\cos\theta)$, only the radial component counts. Wavelengths: $\lambda' = \lambda(1 - \tfrac vc\cos\theta)$. Approaching — blue shift; receding — red shift. Only the relative motion matters.

Star spectra carry dark lines identifying their elements — helium was found in the Sun's spectrum before it was found on Earth. $\lambda'/\lambda = 1.00333$ for every line means a radial velocity of $-100$ km/s: receding.

Half the stars are binaries. Measure both stars' Doppler curves: $v_1, r_1, v_2, r_2$ and $T$. Kepler's third law gives $m_1 + m_2$; $m_1r_1 = m_2r_2$ splits it. From Doppler shifts alone, the masses.

A normal star spills matter onto a neutron star through the inner Lagrangian point, forming an accretion disk. Falling in, matter reaches $\sqrt{2GM/R} \approx 0.7c$; ten grams release a Hiroshima bomb. At $10^{14}$ kg/s that is ~5000 Suns, at ten million kelvin — x-rays.

Matter channelled to the magnetic poles makes hot spots; rotation makes x-ray pulses (Hercules X-1: 1.24 s), and eclipses give the orbit. Pulse-timing Doppler plus optical Doppler give both masses — neutron stars come out near 1.4 solar masses, Chandrasekhar's limit.

Escape speed equals $c$ at $R = 2GM/c^{2}$ — the event horizon: 1 cm for the Earth, 3 km for the Sun. Nothing gets out; hot matter just outside still shines. Cygnus X-1: donor about 30 solar masses, so the unseen compact object is ~15 — far above 3, a black hole.

phys100.0.23.worked: Turn a wavelength ratio straight into a radial velocity: $v_r = c(1 - \lambda'/\lambda)$, negative for receding. Only the line-of-sight component is ever measured.
phys100.0.23.watch: Reading the Doppler velocity as the star's full speed. It is only $v\cos\theta$, the component along the line of sight; motion across the sky shifts nothing.

checks.q: Matter falls from far away onto a neutron star of mass $3 \times 10^{30}$ kg and radius 10 km ($G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$, $c = 3 \times 10^{8}$). Its impact speed as a fraction of $c$, to two decimal places, is:
checks.expl: $v = \sqrt{2GM/R} = \sqrt{4.0 \times 10^{16}} = 2.0 \times 10^{8}$ m/s, about $0.67c$.

checks.q: The event horizon radius of a black hole of mass $2 \times 10^{30}$ kg ($G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$, $c = 3 \times 10^{8}$), in km to two decimal places, is:
Every absorption line of a star has $\lambda'/\lambda = 1.00333$. The star is:
opts: approaching at 100 km/s
receding at 100 km/s
receding at 1000 km/s
moving across the sky
checks.expl: Longer wavelength means red shift: $v_r = -0.00333c \approx -100$ km/s.

phys100.0.24.takeaway: A rolling object's acceleration down a slope, $a = \dfrac{g\sin\beta}{1 + I/MR^{2}}$, depends only on its shape. And torque on a spinning wheel does not tip it over: the spin angular momentum chases the torque, and the wheel precesses.

beats.d: No slipping: one turn moves the centre $2\pi R$, so $v = \omega R$ and $a = \alpha R$. Friction is what makes it roll, and it can be well below its maximum.
Torque about the centre: $RF_f = I\alpha = Ia/R$. Newton for the centre of mass: $Ma = Mg\sin\beta - F_f$. Eliminate $F_f$: $a = g\sin\beta/(1 + I/MR^{2})$.

Solid cylinder, $I = \tfrac12MR^{2}$: $a = \tfrac23g\sin\beta$ — no mass, radius or length left. Brass against aluminium, thin against thick: dead heats. A hollow cylinder, $I \approx MR^{2}$: $a = \tfrac12g\sin\beta$, and it loses every time.

In space, torque a still wheel and it starts to turn about the torque's axis. But torque a SPINNING wheel and $\Delta\vec L = \vec\tau\Delta t$ adds sideways to a large $\vec L$: the axis swings toward the torque. The rule: spin angular momentum chases the torque.
Sitting on a turntable holding a spinning wheel and tilting it, Lewin starts to rotate; stop torquing and it stops. Keep torquing and it keeps going — precession.

Hang a spinning wheel from one end of its axle: gravity's torque $rMg$ is horizontal, perpendicular to $\vec L$, and swings around with it. The wheel does not fall; it precesses at $\omega_p = \tau/L = rMg/I\omega_s$. The rope holds $Mg$, so there is no net force — only torque.

$r = 0.17$ m, $R = 0.29$ m, all mass at the rim, spinning at 5 Hz: $\omega_p = rg/(\omega_sR^{2})$, a period of about 10 s. Add weight to the axle and it precesses faster; reverse the spin and it goes the other way.

Spin stabilises: a rolling coin, a top, a bicycle wheel. A gyroscope in three gimbals feels no torque, so its axis stays fixed while the aircraft turns around it — an inertial guidance system. And a suitcase with a spinning wheel inside behaves very oddly at the airport.

phys100.0.24.worked: For any rolling race, compute $I/MR^{2}$ and nothing else: the smaller it is, the faster the object. Solid sphere $\tfrac25$ beats solid cylinder $\tfrac12$ beats hoop 1.
phys100.0.24.watch: Expecting a torqued gyroscope to tip in the direction you push. $\Delta\vec L$ is along $\vec\tau$, which is perpendicular to the push, so the axis swings sideways.

checks.q: A solid cylinder rolls without slipping from rest 1 m down a 10° slope ($g = 9.8$). The time, in seconds to two decimal places, is:
checks.expl: $a = \tfrac23 g\sin10° = 1.134$ m/s², so $t = \sqrt{2/1.134} = 1.33$ s — whatever its mass or size.

checks.q: A bicycle wheel (all mass at $R = 0.29$ m) spins at 5 Hz, hung from a point 0.17 m along its axle ($g = 9.8$). Its precession period, in seconds to one decimal place, is:
A heavy brass solid cylinder races a light hollow cylinder of the same radius down a slope. Which wins?
opts: the brass one, because it is heavier
the hollow one, because it is lighter
the brass one, because $I/MR^{2}$ is smaller
it is a tie
checks.expl: Only $I/MR^{2}$ matters: $\tfrac12$ for the solid, about 1 for the hollow. Mass has nothing to do with it.

phys100.0.25.takeaway: Static equilibrium needs BOTH the net force and the net torque to be zero. That decides when a ladder slips, how a few turns of rope around a post hold a huge load, and why anything hanging freely settles with its centre of mass below the pivot.

beats.d: Two equal, opposite forces not on the same line: the net force is zero, but a torque $bF$ turns the object. Equilibrium needs $\sum\vec F = 0$ and $\sum\vec\tau = 0$ about ANY point.

Smooth wall, friction $\mu$ at the floor, angle $\alpha$ to the floor. Forces: $N_Q = Mg$, $N_P = F_f$. Take torques about the foot — two forces vanish. Result: $F_f = \tfrac12Mg\cot\alpha$, and no slipping needs $\tan\alpha \ge 1/2\mu$. $\mu = 0.5$: 45°; $\mu = 0.25$: about 63°.

Set the ladder exactly at the critical angle and climb. At the bottom it becomes MORE stable — the extra weight raises the maximum friction at once. Climbing raises the friction needed; it slips once you pass the middle, $d > \ell/2$. Demonstrated with 4 kg on a model ladder.
When the rope is about to slip, $T_2/T_1 = e^{\mu\theta}$ — independent of the post's radius. With $\mu = 0.2$: three turns give about 40, six turns about 2000. Five kilograms can hold ten tonnes.
To raise the load the friction reverses: you would need $e^{\mu\theta}$ times MORE. Sailors use it to hold and let out, never to hoist. With twelve turns, the rope's own weight held 30 kg of lead.

About a pivot, the only torque is from gravity at the centre of mass; it vanishes when the two are on a vertical line. Below the pivot: stable. Above: unstable. Hang an object from two points, draw both verticals: where they cross is the centre of mass.

beats.t: Centre of mass below the support
beats.d: A pencil with a pocket knife jammed in balances on a fingertip; a hammer on a stiff wire hangs from its end. A rope walker carrying long poles with weights ten metres down has the centre of mass below the rope — and the class's model walker crossed the lecture hall.

phys100.0.25.worked: In a statics problem, take torques about the point where the most unknown forces act — they drop out. Then the force balances finish the job.
phys100.0.25.watch: Stopping at $\sum\vec F = 0$. A couple has zero net force and still spins the object; the torque condition is a separate equation.

checks.q: A uniform ladder leans on a frictionless wall; the floor has $\mu = 0.25$. The smallest angle to the floor at which it does not slip, in degrees to one decimal place, is:
checks.expl: $\tan\alpha \ge 1/2\mu = 2$, so $\alpha \ge 63.4°$.

checks.q: A rope is wrapped three full turns around a post with $\mu = 0.2$. The largest ratio of loads it can hold, to the nearest whole number, is:
A ladder is set exactly at its slipping angle, and a person steps onto the lowest rung. The ladder:
opts: slips at once
becomes more stable
is unaffected
slips only if the person is heavy
checks.expl: The extra weight raises the floor's normal force, so the maximum friction rises; the friction needed only rises once the person climbs. It slips after they pass the middle.

phys100.0.26.takeaway: A rod stretches like a spring: $F/A = Y\,\Delta\ell/\ell$, stress equals Young's modulus times strain. Past the elastic limit it deforms for good, flows, and breaks — and Young's modulus also sets the speed of sound, $v = \sqrt{Y/\rho}$.

beats.d: Double the force, double the stretch. Two springs in series stretch twice as far; two side by side, half as far. So a rod's $\Delta\ell \propto F\ell/A$, and $F/A = Y\,\Delta\ell/\ell$: stress (a pressure, N/m²) equals Young's modulus times strain (dimensionless).
A steel rod 1 cm thick and 1 m long carrying 500 kg stretches about 0.3 mm — invisible. Nylon, with $Y$ some 55 times smaller, stretches 1.7 cm. Aluminium would be close to breaking.

Linear at first (Hooke), then bending over to the elastic limit, past which the rod no longer returns to its length. Then plastic flow — stretching with almost no extra stress — then necking, a local pinch where $F/A'$ rises, and fracture at the ultimate tensile strength.

36 cm of copper wire, cross-section $2 \times 10^{-7}$ m². A mirror on a lever turns its stretch into a laser spot moved 425 times as far across the room. Loaded half a kilogram at a time: linear to about 2.5 kg; permanent stretch from about 1.5 kg; 400 cm of spot movement at 6 kg; broken at 8 kg.

At 2 kg the spot moved 20 cm: $Y \approx 7.7 \times 10^{10}$ N/m², against a table value of $11 \times 10^{10}$. Breaking at 8 kg: about $4 \times 10^{8}$ N/m². At the end of the Hooke region the wire had stretched only 0.13%.
In the linear region $F = -(YA/\ell)\Delta\ell$, so $k = YA/\ell$. A kilogram on the copper wire would oscillate vertically at around 40 Hz.
$v = \sqrt{Y/\rho}$: stiffer means faster. In magnesium, about 5 km/s. A 1.22 m magnesium bar rings at $v/2\ell \approx 2100$ Hz — and it did.

A block hangs between two identical strings. Pull slowly and the top string breaks (it carries $F + Mg$). Jerk and the bottom breaks: the top string can only break once it has stretched, and the block's inertia does not give it the time.

phys100.0.26.worked: To find a stretch: compute the stress $F/A$, compare it with the tensile strength to make sure it will not break, then $\Delta\ell = (F/A)\,\ell/Y$.
phys100.0.26.watch: Using $Y$ beyond the elastic limit. Young's modulus describes only the straight first part of the curve; after that the stretch grows far faster than the stress.

checks.q: A steel rod ($Y = 20 \times 10^{10}$ N/m²), 1 m long with radius 0.5 cm, carries 5000 N. Its stretch, in millimetres to two decimal places, is:
A 1 kg mass hangs on a copper wire ($Y = 11 \times 10^{10}$ N/m², $A = 2 \times 10^{-7}$ m², $\ell = 0.36$ m). Its vertical oscillation frequency, in Hz to the nearest whole number, is:
checks.expl: $k = YA/\ell = 6.1 \times 10^{4}$ N/m, so $f = \sqrt{k/m}/2\pi = 39$ Hz.

checks.q: Past the elastic limit, a wire's load is removed. It:
opts: returns to its original length
stays permanently longer
gets shorter than it began
breaks
checks.expl: Beyond the elastic limit the deformation is permanent; the curve comes back down to a nonzero strain.

phys100.0.27.takeaway: Pressure in a fluid is transmitted undiminished (Pascal), and gravity adds $\rho g h$ with depth. We live under an ocean of air pressing at about $10^{5}$ Pa — enough to crush a can and hold a 10 m column of water — and our lungs can fight only a tenth of it.

beats.d: $P = F/A$, in pascals. A scalar: the force a static fluid exerts on any surface is perpendicular to it, or the fluid would flow.

Without gravity the pressure is the same everywhere in an enclosed fluid. So $F_1/A_1 = F_2/A_2$: 10 kg on a small piston balances 1000 kg on one 100 times larger. No free lunch — the small piston moves 100 times as far.
Balance a thin horizontal slab: $dP/dy = -\rho g$. Liquids are nearly incompressible, so $P_1 - P_2 = \rho g(y_2 - y_1)$ — the pressure depends only on depth, not on the vessel's shape.
A bullet through a paint can full of air leaves two holes. Through a can filled to the brim with water, the pressure spike is transmitted everywhere and the lid blows off.
A 1 cm² column of air up to space weighs about 1 kg: roughly $10^{5}$ Pa, one atmosphere. Your hand carries 150 kg of it — balanced by 150 kg pushing up.
Pull a liquid-filled tube up until the top goes empty: $P_{atm} = \rho gh$. Torricelli's mercury: 76 cm, $1.01 \times 10^{5}$ Pa. Water needs about 10 m. Every 10 m of water adds one atmosphere.
Drebbel's 1620s submarine went 5 m down: half an atmosphere of overpressure. Pump the air out of a paint can and the atmosphere crushes it — 375 kg of force on the front face alone at full vacuum.
