A manometer measures what the lungs can do: about 1 m of water, a tenth of an atmosphere, blowing or sucking. So you cannot snorkel much deeper than a metre. Yet Lewin drank cranberry juice up a 5 m tube — a puzzle he leaves open: it was not done with his lungs.

phys100.0.27.worked: To find the pressure at a depth, add up the layers above: $P = P_{atm} + \rho g h$. For a barometer, set the top pressure to zero and read $P_{atm} = \rho g h$.
phys100.0.27.watch: Thinking a wider vessel gives more pressure at the bottom. Pressure depends only on the depth below the surface; the shape and the total weight of liquid do not enter.

checks.q: Mercury ($\rho = 13.6 \times 10^{3}$ kg/m³) stands 0.76 m in a barometer ($g = 9.8$). The atmospheric pressure, in units of $10^{5}$ Pa to two decimal places, is:
The same pressure holds up a column of water ($\rho = 1000$). Its height, in metres to one decimal place, is:
checks.expl: $h = 1.013 \times 10^{5}/(1000 \times 9.8) = 10.3$ m — 13.6 times the mercury column.

checks.q: A hydraulic jack has pistons of area ratio 100. Pushing the small piston down 1 m raises the large one:
opts: 1 m
1 cm
10 cm
checks.expl: The volume pushed out equals the volume moved in: $A_1d_1 = A_2d_2$, so the large piston moves $1/100$ as far. Work in equals work out.

phys100.0.28.takeaway: A body in a fluid is pushed up by the weight of the fluid it displaces (Archimedes). That decides floating and sinking, gives densities without cutting anything, and explains stability. Moving fluids trade pressure for speed: $\tfrac12\rho v^{2} + \rho gy + P$ is constant (Bernoulli).

beats.d: A floating cylinder: the pressure below exceeds the pressure above by $\rho_{fl}gh$, so the net upward force is $\rho_{fl}gAh$ — the weight of the displaced fluid. That is Archimedes' principle, for any shape.

Weigh it in air, then in water. The loss of weight is the weight of the displaced water, so $W/\text{loss} = \rho_{crown}/\rho_{water}$. Density found without damage — the same method measures body fat.
Floating means $V_{under}/V = \rho_{ice}/\rho_{water} = 0.92$: 92% below the surface — the tip of the iceberg. An object floats if its density is below the fluid's, whatever its shape.

Throw a rock from a boat into a pool: does the water level rise, fall or stay? Lewin leaves it. In the boat, the rock displaces its WEIGHT of water; on the bottom, only its VOLUME. Rock is denser than water, so the level falls.
Gravity acts at the centre of mass, buoyancy at the centre of the displaced fluid. Tilt the body: with its centre of mass low, the torque rights it; high, it capsizes. Ships carry their weight low.

A balloon rises only if its gas is less dense than air — necessary, not sufficient. In a closed car that accelerates, an apple on a string swings back but a helium balloon swings FORWARD: the air is thrown back, raising the pressure behind.
Energy per unit volume: $\tfrac12\rho v^{2} + \rho gy + P = $ const. In a level pipe that narrows, the fluid speeds up and the pressure DROPS — the opposite of instinct.

A siphon empties a tank at $v = \sqrt{2gh}$, like a pebble falling $h$ — as long as the hump is under 10 m. Blow hard through a funnel and the ball stays put: fast air, low pressure. An air jet holds a ball steady for the same reason.

phys100.0.28.worked: For floating or weighing problems: buoyant force $= \rho_{fluid}\,V_{submerged}\,g$, set equal to the weight (floating) or subtracted from it (weighing). For flow: pick two points on a streamline and equate Bernoulli's three terms.
phys100.0.28.watch: Expecting high pressure where the fluid moves fast. In steady flow at one height, faster means LOWER pressure — which is why the ping-pong ball will not blow out of the funnel.

checks.q: A crown weighs 10.00 N in air and 9.48 N submerged in water. Its density relative to water, to one decimal place, is:
checks.expl: The loss, 0.52 N, is the weight of the displaced water, so $\rho/\rho_w = 10/0.52 = 19.2$ — gold is 19.3.

checks.q: A siphon's outlet is 0.8 m below the water surface in the tank ($g = 9.8$). The outflow speed, in m/s to two decimal places, is:
checks.expl: Bernoulli between surface and outlet, both at atmospheric pressure: $v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{15.68} = 3.96$ m/s.

checks.q: You throw a rock out of a boat into a swimming pool. The pool's water level:
opts: rises
falls
stays the same
depends on the rock's size
checks.expl: Aboard, the rock displaces its weight of water; underwater, only its volume, which is less because it is denser than water.

phys100.0.29.takeaway: A revision sheet for the third exam: collisions, the Atwood machine with a massive pulley, the physical pendulum, an elliptical orbit from its launch, Doppler shift, and a ball rolling down a slope — each set up the same way, with forces, torques and the conservation laws.

beats.d: Completely inelastic: momentum alone gives $v'$, and kinetic energy is always lost. Elastic: momentum plus kinetic energy. Equal masses with one at rest: square the momentum equation, compare, and $v_1' = 0$, $v_2' = v_1$ — Newton's cradle.

Free-body diagrams for both masses and the pulley. No slip: $a = \alpha R$. Three equations: $T_1 - m_1g = m_1a$, $m_2g - T_2 = m_2a$, $(T_2 - T_1)R = \tfrac12MR^{2}\,a/R$. Check the result: $m_2g > T_2 > T_1 > m_1g$, and $a = 0$ when $m_1 = m_2$.

Torque about the pivot: $-\tfrac12\ell Mg\sin\theta = I_P\ddot\theta$, with $I_P = \tfrac13M\ell^{2}$ by parallel axes. Small angles: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{2\ell/3g}$. The two omegas — angular velocity and angular frequency — are different things.

Launched at 20° to the vertical from the surface, reaching $5R$ at its farthest. Angular momentum about the centre: $mv_0R\sin20° = mv_A \cdot 5R$. Energy: $\tfrac12v_0^{2} - GM/R = \tfrac12v_A^{2} - GM/5R$. Two equations, two unknowns; $E = -GMm/2a$ gives $a$.

$f' = f(1 + \tfrac vc\cos\theta)$ and $\lambda' = \lambda(1 - \tfrac vc\cos\theta)$ for light; for sound, a moving source and $v_{sound} = 340$ m/s. Swing a 1500 Hz source at 3.4 m/s and it rises and falls by 1%.

Torque about the centre gives $F_fR = I\alpha$; Newton gives $Mg\sin\beta - F_f = Ma$. Solid sphere: $a = \tfrac57g\sin\beta$, $F_f = \tfrac27Mg\sin\beta$. Less than a slider's $g\sin\beta$, because some energy goes into spin.
Pure roll needs $F_f \le \mu_sMg\cos\beta$, so $\mu_s \ge \tfrac27\tan\beta$. Too steep a slope, and it slips as well as rolls.
The ball in the 85 cm track took about 2.3 s against 1.85 s predicted: rolling shares the energy with rotation, so it moves more slowly than a slider — exactly what the rolling analysis says.

phys100.0.29.worked: Every rotational problem: a free-body diagram for each object, Newton for each centre of mass, torque about a well-chosen point for each rotating body, and a no-slip link between $a$ and $\alpha$. Count equations against unknowns before solving.
phys100.0.29.watch: Taking both rope tensions equal around a massive pulley. If the pulley has rotational inertia, the tensions MUST differ; that difference is what spins it.

checks.q: An Atwood machine has 1 kg and 2 kg on a rope over a solid-disk pulley of mass 2 kg, without slipping ($g = 9.8$). The acceleration, in m/s² to two decimal places, is:
A uniform rod 0.372 m long swings from one end ($g = 9.8$). Its small-angle period, in seconds to two decimal places, is:
checks.expl: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{2\ell/3g} = 2\pi\sqrt{0.248/9.8} = 1.00$ s — designed that way in the next lecture.

checks.q: A solid sphere rolls without slipping down a 20° slope. The least static friction coefficient that allows this, to three decimal places, is:
checks.expl: $\mu_s \ge \tfrac27\tan20° = \tfrac27 \times 0.364 = 0.104$.

phys100.0.30.takeaway: Any body swinging about a pivot has $T = 2\pi\sqrt{I_P/Mgb}$. A rod, a ring, a disk and a simple pendulum can all be built to beat in time. The same energy method gives the period of liquid sloshing in a U-tube, and a torsion pendulum is a spring for angles.

beats.d: Torque about the pivot: $-bMg\sin\theta = I_P\ddot\theta$. Small angles: $\ddot\theta + (bMg/I_P)\theta = 0$, so $T = 2\pi\sqrt{I_P/bMg}$. $I_P$ always carries an $M$, so the mass drops out.

Rod from its end: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{2L/3g}$. Simple pendulum: $2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$. Ring from its rim: $2\pi\sqrt{2R/g}$. Disk from its rim: $2\pi\sqrt{3R/2g}$. Equal periods need $L = 1.5\,l$, ring diameter $= l$, disk diameter $= \tfrac43 l$.
A 37.2 cm rod should swing in $1.00 \pm 0.005$ s; ten swings took 9.92 s. Rod, ring, disk and pendulum released together stay in step for a good while.

Raise one side by $y$: the whole column moves at $\dot y$, and a slab of mass $A\rho y$ has been lifted $y$. Energy $\tfrac12A\ell\rho\dot y^{2} + A\rho gy^{2}$ is constant; differentiate: $\ddot y + (2g/\ell)y = 0$, $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\ell/2g}$ — a pendulum of length $\ell/2$.
$\ell \approx 72$ cm: predicted 1.204 s, measured 1.22 s. Lewin expected it slightly long — damping lengthens the period, and the averaged length of the bend is not quite the right one.

Twisting a wire gives a restoring torque $-\kappa\theta$, the analogue of $-kx$. So $T = 2\pi\sqrt{I/\kappa}$, with no small-angle approximation needed. Thicker wire, larger $\kappa$; longer wire, smaller.

A 2.5 m piano wire with two 200 g masses 30 cm out: $I \approx 0.036$, $\kappa \approx 4 \times 10^{-4}$, $T \approx 60$ s. Half-periods for one turn, three turns and TEN turns of twist: 28.8, 28.5 and 29.2 s — the period does not care.

phys100.0.30.worked: For any oscillator, write the energy as $\tfrac12(\text{inertia})\dot q^{2} + \tfrac12(\text{stiffness})q^{2}$ and read $\omega^{2}$ = stiffness / inertia — the U-tube, the torsion wire and the spring are the same equation.
phys100.0.30.watch: Assuming a bigger or heavier physical pendulum always swings more slowly. Only the geometry through $I_P/Mb$ matters: a 37 cm rod and a 25 cm simple pendulum have the same period.

checks.q: Water fills 0.72 m of a uniform U-tube ($g = 9.8$). The period of its sloshing, in seconds to two decimal places, is:
checks.expl: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\ell/2g} = 2\pi\sqrt{0.72/19.6} = 1.20$ s. Lewin measured 1.22 s.

checks.q: A torsion pendulum has $I = 0.036$ kg·m² and $\kappa = 4 \times 10^{-4}$ N·m/rad. Its period, in seconds to the nearest whole number, is:
A ring hung from its rim swings with the same period as a simple pendulum whose length equals the ring's:
opts: radius
diameter
circumference
radius times 1.5
checks.expl: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{2R/g}$, a pendulum of length $2R$.

phys100.0.31.takeaway: Drive an oscillator at a frequency of your choosing and, once the transient dies, it follows you with amplitude $\dfrac{F_0/m}{\omega_0^{2} - \omega^{2}}$. Near its natural frequency the response explodes — resonance, the physics of violins, organ pipes, shattered wineglasses and the Tacoma Narrows Bridge.

beats.d: $m\ddot x = -kx + F_0\cos\omega t$. In the steady state the mass moves at the DRIVER's frequency; trying $x = A\cos\omega t$ gives $A = \dfrac{F_0/m}{\omega_0^{2} - \omega^{2}}$ with $\omega_0^{2} = k/m$.

Slow driving: $A = F_0/k$, in phase. Fast: $A \to 0$, and 180° out of phase. At $\omega = \omega_0$ the amplitude would be infinite; damping caps it, and the less damping, the narrower and taller the peak. The air-track cart showed all three.
Two coupled masses have two resonant frequencies, three have three. A string is effectively infinitely many coupled oscillators — and has infinitely many.

Shake a string: at $f_1$ it bulges in one loop; at $f_2 = 2f_1$ a node appears in the middle; at $f_3$ two nodes. $f_n = nf_1$, and $f_1$ is set by length, tension and mass. A violinist changes the length with a finger; a bow drives it at all frequencies, and the string keeps only the ones it likes.

In a pipe the air itself resonates. Closed–closed or open–open: $f_n = nv/2L$, so 25 cm gives 680 Hz, 1 m gives 170 Hz. Organ pipes of different lengths; flute holes change the length; a slide trombone played 'Jingle Bells'.

Car rattles that come and go with speed, your arms when shaken, the wineglass rubbed with a wet finger at about 470 Hz. Driven at that frequency with a loud enough tone, the glass shattered on camera.
Opened 1 July 1940, nicknamed 'Galloping Gertie' for its ripples. On 7 November a 40 mph wind — a broad spectrum of frequencies — found a twisting mode, and the bridge tore itself apart.
Sound travels about 2.7 times faster in helium, so the same vocal tract resonates at far higher frequencies. Lewin's voice went squeaky — at some risk, since helium carries no oxygen.

phys100.0.31.worked: Near resonance, compute the natural frequency first: for a spring $\sqrt{k/m}$, for a string or pipe $f_n = nv/2L$. A driver close to any of these produces large motion; far from all of them, very little.
phys100.0.31.watch: Thinking a large force is needed for large motion. At resonance a small periodic force, applied at the right frequency, builds an enormous amplitude — which is how a 40 mph wind destroyed a bridge.

checks.q: A 0.1 kg mass on a spring with $k = 10$ N/m is driven by $F = 0.5\cos(5t)$ N. The steady-state amplitude, in centimetres to two decimal places, is:
A string's first harmonic is 100 Hz. Its third harmonic is:
opts: 133 Hz
300 Hz
900 Hz
33 Hz
checks.expl: $f_n = nf_1$: 300 Hz, with two nodes between the ends.

checks.q: An organ pipe open at both ends is made twice as long. Its fundamental frequency:
opts: doubles
halves
is unchanged
quadruples
checks.expl: $f_1 = v/2L$: doubling $L$ halves the frequency — long pipes for low notes.

phys100.0.32.takeaway: Heat most things and they grow: $\Delta L = \alpha L\,\Delta T$, and for volume $\beta = 3\alpha$. Small as the numbers are, they bend bimetal strips into thermostats, drive mercury up a thermometer — and water, alone, shrinks as it warms from 0 to 4 °C.

beats.d: Any thermometric property — length, gas pressure, resistance — can define a scale. Celsius (1742): melting ice 0, boiling water 100. Fahrenheit: $F = \tfrac95C + 32$, so 20 °C is 68 °F and $-40$ is the same on both. Kelvin starts at absolute zero, $-273.15$ °C, with Celsius-sized degrees.

$\Delta L = \alpha L\,\Delta T$. In units of $10^{-6}$ per °C: brass 19, copper 17, steel about 12, Pyrex 3.3, Invar 0.9 — Invar won Guillaume the 1920 Nobel Prize, because precise clocks need parts that do not grow.
A kilometre of steel rail from $-15$ to $+35$ °C grows about 60 cm. So rails have gaps you can hear, bridges have expansion joints, and on a very hot day a rail with no room buckles sideways.

Bond copper to Invar: the copper grows more and the strip curls. Ten centimetres, 100 °C: a length difference of only 0.16 mm, but a bend of about 4 mm. Thermostats, pilot-light safety valves, coffee makers and dial thermometers all run on this.
$(L + \Delta L)^{3} \approx L^{3}(1 + 3\Delta L/L)$, so $\Delta V = 3\alpha V\Delta T$: $\beta = 3\alpha$. For liquids the tables give $\beta$ directly — mercury, $18 \times 10^{-5}$ per °C.

1 cm³ of mercury warmed 10 °C grows 0.0018 cm³; forced up a capillary of radius 0.1 mm it rises 5.7 cm — about 6 mm per degree. The glass grows too, but eighteen times less. Heat one too far and it bursts.
A brass ball that just passes through a brass ring will not pass once the ball alone is heated; as they share heat, it drops through. Heat both and it always passes. The reverse is shrink fitting.

From 0 to 4 °C water SHRINKS as it warms, so it is densest at 4 °C and sinks: ponds freeze from the top and fish survive. Ice is 8% less dense than water — pipes burst, icebergs float, and the ice cubes stay on top of Lewin's cider.

phys100.0.32.worked: For any expansion problem: multiply the coefficient by the original size and the temperature change. For a mismatch (a bimetal, a ring, a gap), what matters is the DIFFERENCE between the two coefficients.
phys100.0.32.watch: Using $\alpha$ for a volume change. Volume grows three times as fast as length: $\beta = 3\alpha$ for solids, and liquids are quoted by $\beta$ alone.

checks.q: A 1000 m steel rail ($\alpha = 12 \times 10^{-6}$ per °C) warms from $-15$ °C to $+35$ °C. It grows, in centimetres to the nearest whole number, by:
checks.expl: $\Delta L = 12 \times 10^{-6} \times 1000 \times 50 = 0.6$ m.

checks.q: 1 cm³ of mercury ($\beta = 18 \times 10^{-5}$ per °C) warms 10 °C and rises into a capillary of radius 0.1 mm. The rise, in centimetres to one decimal place, is:
checks.expl: $\Delta V = 1.8 \times 10^{-3}$ cm³ spread over $\pi(0.01)^{2} = 3.14 \times 10^{-4}$ cm², so $h = 5.7$ cm.

checks.q: A pond cools in winter. The water at the bottom stays near:
opts: the air temperature
checks.expl: Water is densest at 4 °C, so that water sinks; colder water floats above it and freezes at the top.

phys100.0.33.takeaway: For a gas, $PV = nRT$ — and the mass of the molecules does not appear. So at one temperature every gas has the same $mv^{2}$, a mole of anything fills 24 litres at room conditions, and an isothermal atmosphere thins as $e^{-h/8\,\text{km}}$.

beats.d: $PV = nRT$, $R = 8.3$ J/K, $T$ in kelvin, $n$ in moles. A mole is $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ molecules (Avogadro), weighing $A$ grams: carbon-12 12 g, helium 4 g, O₂ 32 g. One nucleon is about $1.66 \times 10^{-27}$ kg.
One mole at one atmosphere and 293 K: $V = RT/P \approx 24$ litres, whatever the gas. Oxygen deviates by only 0.1%; even at 20 atmospheres, 2%.

Pressure comes from momentum delivered to the wall: $2mv$ per hit, with a hit rate $\propto v$, so $P \propto mv^{2}$. Same $P$, $V$, $T$ and $n$ for helium and oxygen means the same $mv^{2}$: oxygen about 480 m/s, helium $\sqrt8$ times faster.
$PV = NkT$ with $N$ molecules and $k = R/N_A = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}$ J/K.

A sealed copper sphere of air moved from melting ice to boiling water: $P_2 = P_1 \times 373/273 = 1.37$ atm, so an overpressure gauge should read $0.37 \times 15 \approx 5.4$ psi. It crept to 5 psi, and dropped to zero when the valve opened.

Squeeze a gas at fixed temperature: $P$ rises until liquid forms, then stays put until all of it has condensed. The CO₂ extinguisher: 100 moles in 2.3 litres would need 1000 atmospheres as gas, so it is liquid and vapour together, held at about 60 atmospheres — the coexistence line.

$dP/dy = -\rho g$ with $\rho = Pm/kT$ gives $P = P_0e^{-h/H_0}$, $H_0 = kT/mg \approx 8$ km. Everest: a third of an atmosphere; at 2400 m water boils at 92 °C; at 30 km, 20 °C water boils — shown in a bell jar.

A can filled with steam and sealed collapses as it cools: vapour at 20 °C is only 17 mm of mercury. Balloons in liquid nitrogen should shrink to a quarter of their volume but go almost flat — the air itself liquefies. And tennis balls hiss when opened: Lewin leaves the why for the weekend.

phys100.0.33.worked: For a sealed gas changing state, write $P_1V_1/T_1 = P_2V_2/T_2$ with temperatures in kelvin, cancel whatever is held fixed, and solve. Gauges read the pressure above atmospheric, so subtract 1 atm at the end.
phys100.0.33.watch: Using Celsius in the gas law. $T$ must be absolute: heating from 0 to 100 °C raises the pressure by 373/273, not by 'infinity' or by 100/0.

checks.q: One mole of gas at $1.03 \times 10^{5}$ Pa and 293 K ($R = 8.3$). Its volume, in litres to one decimal place, is:
A sealed rigid sphere at 1 atm and 273 K is heated to 373 K. An overpressure gauge (1 atm = 15 psi) reads, in psi to one decimal place:
checks.expl: $P_2 = 373/273 = 1.366$ atm; the gauge shows the 0.366 atm above atmospheric, $\times 15 = 5.5$ psi. Lewin saw 5.

checks.q: In an isothermal atmosphere with scale height 7.99 km, the pressure at 8.9 km (Everest), as a fraction of sea level to two decimal places, is:
checks.expl: $e^{-8.9/7.99} = 0.33$ — about a third of an atmosphere.

phys100.0.34.takeaway: On the scale of atoms, classical physics fails: electrons sit only in discrete energy levels, light and matter are both waves and particles ($\lambda = h/p$), and position and momentum cannot both be sharp — $\Delta p\,\Delta x \gtrsim \hbar$.

beats.d: An atom is $10^{-10}$ m across; its nucleus (Rutherford, 1911) is 100,000 times smaller. Blow the atom up to the lecture hall and the proton is a grain of sand. Classically the electron should spiral into it in a fraction of a second.

Electrons exist only in discrete orbits, never between. The same rule would quantise a planet's orbit or a bouncing ball's height — but the steps there are immeasurably small. Quantum effects matter only for the very small.

An electron falling to an inner orbit emits a photon of energy $E = hf = hc/\lambda$, $h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34}$ J·s. Bigger jumps, shorter wavelengths. Through a grating, helium and neon lamps show sharp coloured lines — the energy levels made visible.

Newton said particles, Huygens waves; Young's 1801 experiment seemed to settle it for waves. Quantum mechanics says both, depending on the experiment. De Broglie (1923): matter too has $\lambda = h/p$. A baseball's is absurdly small; an electron at 1000 m/s has one near red light's.
'The very concept of exact position of an object and its exact momentum, together, have no meaning in nature.' $\Delta p\,\Delta x \gtrsim \hbar \approx 10^{-34}$ J·s.
In Gamow's dream $\hbar = 1$: a 1 kg ball penned in a 30 cm triangle must move at least ~3 m/s — it rattles about. With the real $\hbar$ the uncertainty is $3 \times 10^{-34}$ m/s: nothing.
Confine an electron to $10^{-10}$ m and its speed is uncertain by about $10^{6}$ m/s — a third of a percent of $c$. It moves because it is confined.

Narrow a slit on a laser beam and the spot narrows — until, near 0.1 mm, it spreads: knowing $x$ better makes $p_x$ uncertain, spreading the beam by $\theta \approx \Delta p/p$. At 0.01 mm the streak was a metre wide. One photon a day would build the same pattern; only probabilities are predicted. 'God does not throw dice' — Einstein; He does, within Heisenberg's rules.

phys100.0.34.worked: To see whether quantum effects matter, compute $\hbar/(m\,\Delta x)$. If that velocity is negligible next to the motion you care about, classical physics is fine; if not, it is not.
phys100.0.34.watch: Thinking the uncertainty principle is about clumsy instruments. It is a property of nature: an exactly known position and momentum together do not exist, however good the measurement.

checks.q: An electron ($m = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}$ kg) moves at 1000 m/s ($h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34}$ J·s). Its de Broglie wavelength, in nanometres to the nearest whole number, is:
checks.expl: $\lambda = h/mv = 6.6 \times 10^{-34}/9.11 \times 10^{-28} = 7.24 \times 10^{-7}$ m — red light.

checks.q: In Gamow's dream world ($\hbar = 1$), a 1 kg ball is confined to 0.3 m. The least speed uncertainty, in m/s to two decimal places, is:
checks.expl: $\Delta v \gtrsim \hbar/(m\Delta x) = 1/0.3 = 3.33$ m/s — the ball cannot sit still.

checks.q: A laser passes through a slit that is made narrower and narrower. Past a certain width, the spot on the far wall:
opts: keeps shrinking
spreads out wider
vanishes
stays the same size
checks.expl: Pinning down $x$ makes $p_x$ uncertain, so the light fans out at an angle of about $\Delta p/p$ — wider as the slit narrows.

phys100.0.35.takeaway: Lewin's own research story: how x-ray astronomy began, why he flew telescopes on enormous balloons to the top of the atmosphere, and how x-ray binaries — and thermonuclear bursts on neutron stars — came to be understood.

beats.d: A Dutch PhD in nuclear physics, he came in January 1966 for a one-year postdoc in Bruno Rossi's x-ray group — and never left.
X-rays are absorbed by air, so x-ray astronomy must be done above the atmosphere. V-2 rockets found solar x-rays in 1948 — only $10^{-7}$ of the Sun's output.

In 1962 Rossi, Giacconi and Gursky looked for x-rays from beyond the solar system with detectors a billion times too insensitive to see a Sun-like star — and found Sco X-1, with x-rays a thousand times its optical light. What could such an object be?

Rockets give five minutes above the air; balloons give hours, even days, at the cost of 0.3% of the atmosphere left overhead. Million-dollar telescopes, two years to build; polyethylene balloons thinner than cigarette paper, 500 feet across, rising to 140,000 feet from Texas and Alice Springs.

Calm dawns, a launch truck manoeuvring under the rising bubble, radio commands to drop ballast or cut the parachute free before the ocean or a flight zone — then days of recovery in the Australian desert. Twice the balloon burst in the cold tropopause and the payload fell free.

Five new sources, doubling the known sky; flares tripling in ten minutes, which five-minute rockets could never see; and GX 1+4 pulsing every 2.3 minutes — later understood as a spinning neutron star.

A normal star feeds a neutron star through an accretion disk; matter hits at about a third of the speed of light and heats the surface to $10^{7}$–$10^{8}$ K — x-rays. A marshmallow dropped on a neutron star releases a Hiroshima bomb. Pulses from magnetic poles, eclipses behind the donor.

In 1975–76, with MIT's SAS-3 satellite, x-ray bursts turned out to be thermonuclear flashes — helium fusing to carbon in a runaway on the neutron star's surface. In 1978 an optical flash was caught with an x-ray burst, delayed by about two seconds: the disk is light-seconds across.

phys100.0.35.worked: The method in every step of this story: find what is surprising in the data (x-ray/optical ratio, flares, periods, delays), then ask what physical system could produce exactly that.
phys100.0.35.watch: Taking the newspaper's version — that balloons fly 'to be closer to the stars'. They fly to get above the air that absorbs the x-rays.

checks.q: X-ray telescopes must fly on balloons, rockets or satellites because:
opts: they must be closer to the stars
the atmosphere absorbs x-rays
the telescopes are too heavy for the ground
the Sun blocks x-rays by day
checks.expl: Air absorbs x-rays; at 140,000 feet only about 0.3% of the atmosphere remains overhead.

checks.q: What made Sco X-1 so different from the Sun?
opts: it was brighter in optical light
its x-ray power was about 1000 times its optical power
it was a planet
it was inside the solar system
checks.expl: The Sun emits $10^{-7}$ of its power in x-rays; Sco X-1 emits most of its power as x-rays — an accreting neutron star.

checks.q: An optical flash arrived about 2 s after an x-ray burst from the same source. This measured:
opts: the neutron star's radius
the size of the accretion disk, about two light-seconds
the distance to the source
the donor star's mass
checks.expl: The x-rays heat the disk, which glows in optical light; the extra path to the disk and back shows up as the delay.

phys100.0.36.takeaway: Lewin's last lecture, 'For the Love of Physics': the course in miniature — a pendulum whose period ignores amplitude and mass, a wrecking ball that stops at his chin, the blue sky and the red sunset made in a bucket — and his one piece of advice: you have to love it.

beats.d: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$: no amplitude, no mass. The 15.5 kg bob on 5.21 m: predicted $4.58 \pm 0.02$ s. Ten swings: 45.7 s at 5°, 45.7 s at 10°, 45.9 s with Lewin himself on the bob, stretched flat to keep the length.

$mgh$ becomes $\tfrac12mv^{2}$ and back. A dropped ball can never bounce higher than it started, or we would have free energy. A pendulum loses almost nothing, so it returns almost exactly to its release point.

Released gently against a glass plate, the ball stops short; given a slight push, it smashes the glass. Then Lewin puts his chin where the glass was, releases from rest, and closes his eyes. 'Physics works, and I'm still alive.'

Particles smaller than about 0.1 micron scatter blue far more than red: power $\propto 1/\lambda^{4}$, and blue's wavelength is about 1.5 times shorter, so $1.5^{4} \approx 5$. Cigarette smoke glows blue; exhaled after water condenses on it, the drops exceed 0.5 micron (Mie scattering) and the smoke is white.

The sky is blue from sunlight scattered off tiny particles and air-density fluctuations. Clouds are white: their drops scatter all colours equally. At sunset the long path strips out all but the red — and pollution and volcanic dust make sunsets more beautiful.
Sulfuric acid into sodium thiosulfate precipitates tiny sulfur particles: the side glows blue, the transmitted beam turns orange, then red. Seen at 90°, the blue light is polarised.
After some 800 lectures in 26-100, he leaves in his own private rocket.

Each lecture took 40–60 hours, dry-run three times in an empty room, the last at 5:30 on the morning of the lecture. Advice to a would-be physicist: you have to love it — and if you hate it, you had a bad teacher. Physics is his life; art history is his love.

phys100.0.36.worked: Lewin's habit in every demonstration: state the prediction and its uncertainty BEFORE measuring, then check whether the result lies within it. A number without its error is not a measurement.
phys100.0.36.watch: Thinking a heavier pendulum or a wider swing must change the period. Within small angles, neither appears in $2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ — and 45.7, 45.7 and 45.9 s agree within the timing error.

checks.q: A pendulum of length 5.21 m ($g = 9.8$). Its period, in seconds to two decimal places, is:
checks.expl: $2\pi\sqrt{5.21/9.8} = 4.58$ s. Lewin measured 45.7 s for ten swings.

checks.q: Clouds are white while the sky is blue because cloud drops:
opts: are colder
are larger than about half a micron, so they scatter all colours equally
absorb blue light
are made of ice
checks.expl: Mie scattering from large drops treats all wavelengths alike; Rayleigh scattering from tiny particles favours blue.

checks.q: Lewin releases the wrecking ball from rest at his chin. It cannot hit him on the return because:
opts: air drag stops it
energy is conserved, so it cannot rise above its release point
the string stretches
the period is too long
checks.expl: With no push, $mgh$ at release is all it has; it can come back at most to the same height — slightly less, after air drag.

math210.0.0.takeaway: Calculus should run scalar → vector → matrix, and a derivative is best seen as a LINEARIZATION: $df = f'(x)\,dx$, with $f'(x)$ a linear operator acting on the small change. For matrices this is not a trivial generalisation — $d(X^{2}) = X\,dX + dX\,X$, not $2X\,dX$.

beats.t: Why a course on matrix calculus
beats.d: 18.01 is scalars, 18.02 is vectors, and the sequence stops — yet machine learning, statistics and engineering optimisation all need gradients of functions of matrices. Topology-optimised aircraft wings put a whole physics simulation inside an optimisation loop.

It is neither symbolic differentiation (Mathematica) nor numerical finite differences — something else, closer to compiler technology. Using it well means knowing what is under the hood: forward versus reverse mode, vector–Jacobian products, and when it fails.

Near a point, pretend the function is linear: $\delta y \approx f'(x)\,\delta x$. Written $df = f'(x)\,dx$ with $dx$ kept on the RIGHT — because soon $dx$ will be a vector or a matrix, and you cannot divide by a vector.
$x^{2}$ at 3: nudging $x$ by $\delta x$ changes $x^{2}$ by $6\,\delta x$ plus higher order. Think of $dx$ as 0.0001 on a computer — small enough, in context.

Scalar or vector or matrix in, scalar or vector or matrix out. Vector in, scalar out (a loss function) gives a gradient with the SAME shape as the input — for $x^{T}x$, $\nabla f = 2x$ while $f'(x) = 2x^{T}$, a row vector, so that $df = 2x^{T}dx$ is a scalar. Vector to vector gives an $m \times n$ Jacobian; higher cases need more than 2-D arrays.

$d(X^{2}) = X\,dX + dX\,X$: matrices do not commute, so neither order is preferred and both appear. Checked in Julia on a 3×3 matrix with a tiny random $dX$: $(X + dX)^{2} - X^{2}$ matches $X\,dX + dX\,X$, and $2X\,dX$ does not.

$d(AB) = dA\,B + A\,dB$ for any compatible products — keep $A$ on the left and $B$ on the right. For $x^{T}x$: $dx^{T}x + x^{T}dx = 2x^{T}dx$, allowed only because a dot product is a scalar and $u^{T}v = v^{T}u$.

A function $\mathbb R^{n} \to \mathbb R^{m}$ has an $m \times n$ Jacobian — a first derivative. A scalar function of a vector, like $x^{T}Ax$, has a Hessian matrix — a second derivative, better thought of as a quadratic form.

math210.0.0.worked: To find a derivative holistically: perturb the input by $dx$, expand, keep only the terms linear in $dx$, and read off the linear operator. Then check it numerically: $f(x + dx) - f(x)$ against $f'(x)\,dx$ for a small random $dx$.
math210.0.0.watch: Writing $d(X^{2}) = 2X\,dX$ by analogy with scalars. It is only right when $dX$ commutes with $X$; in general both orders, $X\,dX + dX\,X$, are needed.

checks.q: $f(x) = x^{T}x$ at $x = (3, 4)$, nudged by $dx = (0.001, 0.002)$. The linearized change $2x^{T}dx$, to three decimal places, is:
checks.expl: $2(3 \times 0.001 + 4 \times 0.002) = 0.022$. The true change is 25.022005 − 25; the difference is second order.

checks.q: For a square matrix $X$, the differential of $X^{2}$ is:
opts: $X\,dX + dX\,X$
checks.expl: The product rule with order kept: $d(XX) = dX\,X + X\,dX$. It reduces to $2X\,dX$ only when $X$ and $dX$ commute.

checks.q: A loss function takes a vector of $n$ parameters to one number. Its gradient is:
opts: a scalar
a vector the same shape as the input
an $n \times n$ matrix
a row vector with $m$ entries
checks.expl: The gradient of a scalar function always has the input's shape; the derivative $f' = (\nabla f)^{T}$ is the row vector that acts on $dx$.

math210.0.1.takeaway: Johnson's precise version: the derivative is the linear operator $f'(x)$ with $f(x + \delta x) - f(x) = f'(x)\,\delta x + o(\delta x)$. Linear operators live on any vector space, so this definition works for vectors, matrices and even functions — and for a scalar of a vector it DEFINES the gradient, $df = \nabla f \cdot dx$.

beats.d: $f(x + \delta x) = f(x) + f'(x)\,\delta x + o(\delta x)$, where little-o means anything that vanishes faster than $\delta x$. This is not a Taylor series — a function need not have one — it is the definition of a derivative.
Switching $\delta$ to $d$ just means: drop the higher-order terms. $df = f(x + dx) - f(x) = f'(x)\,dx$. The derivative is $f'$; the differential is $df$. They are different objects.

On a vector space (anything you can add and scale), $L$ is linear if $L(v_1 + v_2) = Lv_1 + Lv_2$ and $L(\alpha v) = \alpha Lv$. Multiplying by a scalar or a matrix is linear; so are differentiation and integration of functions, and even $f(x) \mapsto f(x^{2})$.
$v \mapsto 2v + 1$ has a straight-line graph but fails the test: $3v \mapsto 6v + 1$, not $6v + 3$. Such maps are called affine.

$df = f'(x)\,dx$ must turn a vector into a scalar, and the only linear way to do that is a dot product with some vector. That vector is the gradient: $df = \nabla f \cdot dx$, so $f' = (\nabla f)^{T}$.

With $A$ constant and not assumed symmetric: expand $(x + dx)^{T}A(x + dx)$, drop $dx^{T}A\,dx$, and transpose the scalar $dx^{T}Ax$ into $x^{T}A^{T}dx$. So $df = x^{T}(A + A^{T})\,dx$ and $\nabla f = (A + A^{T})x$.
If $f: \mathbb R^{n} \to \mathbb R^{m}$, then $f'(x)$ is a linear map from $n$ components to $m$ — expressible as an $m \times n$ matrix, the Jacobian. You do not have to write the matrix down.

math210.0.1.worked: For a scalar function of a vector: compute $df$, rearrange it into (something)$^{T}dx$ — transposing scalar terms freely — and that something is the gradient.
math210.0.1.watch: Calling a function 'linear' because its graph is a line. $2v + 1$ is affine: it fails $L(\alpha v) = \alpha L(v)$, and derivatives are linear operators in the strict sense.

checks.q: $f(x) = x^{T}Ax$ with $A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\ 0 & 3\end{pmatrix}$. The second component of $\nabla f$ at $x = (1, 1)$ is:
checks.expl: $\nabla f = (A + A^{T})x = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 2\\ 2 & 6\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix} = (4, 8)$.

checks.q: Which map is linear in the sense of linear algebra?
opts: $v \mapsto 2v + 1$
$f(x) \mapsto f(x^{2})$ on functions
$v \mapsto v^{2}$
$v \mapsto |v|$
checks.expl: Substituting $x^{2}$ into a function respects sums and scalar multiples of the FUNCTION. The others fail additivity or scaling.

checks.q: For a scalar function of a vector, $f'(x)$ is best described as:
opts: a column vector, the gradient
a row vector, the transpose of the gradient
a scalar
the Hessian
checks.expl: $f'(x)$ acts on $dx$ to give a scalar $df$, so it is a row vector: $f' = (\nabla f)^{T}$.

math210.0.2.takeaway: A nonlinear map is locally linear, and its Jacobian is that local linear map. The sum, product and chain rules all carry over — keeping order. And the order you multiply the chain rule's Jacobians is not a detail: right-to-left is forward mode, left-to-right is reverse mode, and for one output and many inputs reverse mode wins by a factor of $n$.

beats.d: Rotating a picture of Philip the corgi is a linear map of $\mathbb R^{2}$ — his ears move on a circle. A hyperbolic rotation is also linear — his eyes move on a hyperbola. A nonlinear shear or warp bends squares into curves; its 2×2 Jacobian changes from point to point, but in a tiny patch squares still become parallelograms.

$df = J\,dx$ with $J_{ij} = \partial f_i/\partial x_j$: rows are outputs, columns are inputs. For the determinant used in change of variables the transpose does not matter; as a linear operator it matters a lot.
$f(x) = Ax$: $d(Ax) = A\,dx$, so $f' = A$ everywhere — constant, as the slope of $3x$ is constant. Note that $dA$ there is the $m \times n$ ZERO matrix.

$d(g + h) = dg + dh$. $d(gh) = dg\,h + g\,dh$ for any product obeying the distributive law, with $dg\,dh$ dropped as second order — and you may not write $f' = g'h + gh'$, since $dx$ cannot always be moved past $h$. Re-derived: $\nabla(x^{T}Ax) = (A + A^{T})x$.

$f(x) = g(h(x))$: $f'(x) = g'(h(x))\,h'(x)$, a composition of linear operators — $h'$ first. For $\mathbb R^{n} \to \mathbb R^{p} \to \mathbb R^{m}$ it is an $m \times p$ times a $p \times n$ matrix; the other order does not even conform.

$f = a(b(c(x)))$: $f' = a'b'c'$. Multiplying an $m \times q$ by a $q \times p$ matrix costs about $mpq$ operations. Right-to-left, $a'(b'c')$, is forward mode; left-to-right, $(a'b')c'$, is reverse mode.

Optimisation and machine learning: $m = 1$ (a loss), $n$ huge. Reverse mode is a row vector times matrices, $n^{2}$ each; forward mode multiplies matrices first, $n^{3}$. Reverse mode — also called backpropagation or adjoint differentiation — costs about as much as evaluating $f$ once.
Asked for $\frac{d}{dx}\sin(x^{2})$, nearly everyone writes the cosine first, working from the output inward — reverse mode, done by instinct.

math210.0.2.worked: Before multiplying a chain of Jacobians, write each one's shape. With a scalar output, start from the left (a row vector) and keep every intermediate product a row vector: that is backpropagation.
math210.0.2.watch: Multiplying the chain rule's Jacobians right to left when the output is a single number. The answer is identical, but the cost is $n^{3}$ instead of $n^{2}$ — a factor of $n$, a billion for a large network.

checks.q: $f(x_1, x_2) = (x_1^{2}x_2,\ x_1 + x_2^{3})$. The determinant of its Jacobian at $(1, 2)$ is:
checks.expl: $J = \begin{pmatrix}2x_1x_2 & x_1^{2}\\ 1 & 3x_2^{2}\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 1\\ 1 & 12\end{pmatrix}$, determinant $48 - 1 = 47$.

checks.q: A scalar loss depends on $n$ parameters through two $n \times n$ Jacobian stages. Evaluating $a'b'c'$ left to right (reverse mode) costs about:
checks.expl: Row vector times matrix is $n^{2}$, and every intermediate stays a row vector. Right to left forms a matrix–matrix product, $n^{3}$.

checks.q: In the Jacobian $J_{ij} = \partial f_i/\partial x_j$, the columns correspond to:
opts: the outputs
the inputs
the second derivatives
the eigenvalues
checks.expl: $df = J\,dx$: each column multiplies one component of $dx$, one input.

math210.0.3.takeaway: Inputs and outputs can themselves be matrices. The product rule gives $d(A^{3}) = dA\,A^{2} + A\,dA\,A + A^{2}dA$ — which cannot be simplified — and differentiating $A^{-1}A = I$ gives $d(A^{-1}) = -A^{-1}\,dA\,A^{-1}$, the matrix version of $-dA/A^{2}$.

beats.d: A vector space is anything you can add and scale, so matrices qualify. Matrix to matrix: $A^{-1}$, $A^{3}$, the $U$ of Gaussian elimination. Matrix to scalar: the determinant, the trace, the largest singular value.

$A^{3} = AAA$, so $d(A^{3}) = dA\,A^{2} + A\,dA\,A + A^{2}dA$ — three terms, one for each factor perturbed. It equals $3A^{2}dA$ only if $dA$ commutes with $A$. This linear operator is not 'some matrix times $dA$'.
You can stack the $n^{2}$ entries of $dA$ into a column and write an $n^{2} \times n^{2}$ Jacobian. Edelman dislikes it as much as indices — it hides the structure.
$A^{-1}A = I$ for every $A$, so its differential is zero. Product rule: $d(A^{-1})\,A + A^{-1}dA = 0$. Multiply by $A^{-1}$ on the right: $d(A^{-1}) = -A^{-1}\,dA\,A^{-1}$.
Engineering problems solve linear systems; optimising their results means differentiating through a matrix inverse. Doing it entry by entry with Cramer's rule would be madness even at 2×2.

For the symbolic 2×2 matrix $\begin{pmatrix}p & r\\ q & s\end{pmatrix}$, vec of $X^{2}$ is four functions of four variables and its 4×4 Jacobian can be printed. Numerically, $(M + E)^{2} - M^{2}$ matches $ME + EM$ to first order.

The Kronecker product $A \otimes B$ — every entry of $A$ times the whole of $B$ — is the notation that turns operators like $dA \mapsto M\,dA + dA\,M$ back into explicit Jacobian matrices when needed.

math210.0.3.worked: To differentiate a matrix function you cannot expand directly, differentiate an IDENTITY it satisfies ($A^{-1}A = I$, $Q^{T}Q = I$, $L U = A$) and solve for the unknown differential.
math210.0.3.watch: Writing $d(A^{-1}) = -A^{-2}dA$. The two inverses must sit on either side of $dA$: $-A^{-1}\,dA\,A^{-1}$.

checks.q: $A = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1\\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ is perturbed in the direction $dA = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 0\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$. The (1,1) entry of $d(A^{-1}) = -A^{-1}dA\,A^{-1}$ is:
checks.expl: $A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}0.5 & -0.5\\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$; $dA\,A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 0\\ 0.5 & -0.5\end{pmatrix}$; $-A^{-1}$ times that has (1,1) entry $-(0.5 \times 0 + (-0.5)(0.5)) = 0.25$.

checks.q: The differential of $A^{3}$ is:
checks.expl: One term for each factor of $AAA$ perturbed, order preserved.

checks.q: How is $d(A^{-1})$ derived most easily?
opts: from Cramer's rule entry by entry
by differentiating $A^{-1}A = I$ with the product rule
by a Taylor series of $1/A$
it cannot be done in closed form
checks.expl: $d(A^{-1})A + A^{-1}dA = 0$, then multiply by $A^{-1}$ on the right.

math210.0.4.takeaway: The Kronecker product lets you write a matrix-to-matrix derivative as an explicit Jacobian without ever forming it: $(A \otimes B)\,\mathrm{vec}(C) = \mathrm{vec}(BCA^{T})$. With it, $d(X^{2}) = (I \otimes X + X^{T} \otimes I)\,\mathrm{vec}(dX)$ — and matrix factorizations such as LU and eigendecompositions become functions with Jacobians too.

beats.d: Gradient of $\|x\|$: with $r = \|x\|$, $r^{2} = x^{T}x$, so $2r\,dr = 2x^{T}dx$ and $\nabla r = x/r$. The index-by-index way works too; this is the 'grown-up' way.

The 4×4 Jacobian of the matrix square at $M$ carries the same information as the operator $E \mapsto ME + EM$. That operator is linear in $E$ — even though $M^{2}$ is not linear in $M$ — and nobody needs to build the matrix.
$A \otimes B$ places $a_{ij}B$ in block $(i, j)$ — every product of an entry of $A$ with an entry of $B$, in a fixed order. Julia happily does it with symbols, or pizza and pandas.
$(A \otimes B)\,\mathrm{vec}(C) = \mathrm{vec}(BCA^{T})$. Mnemonic: $B$ sits next to $C$ on the left; $A$ goes around to the right and gets transposed for it.

$(A \otimes B)^{T} = A^{T} \otimes B^{T}$ and $(A \otimes B)^{-1} = A^{-1} \otimes B^{-1}$ — same order, unlike ordinary products. For $n \times n$ $A$ and $m \times m$ $B$: $\det(A \otimes B) = (\det A)^{m}(\det B)^{n}$; trace is the product of traces; eigenvalues are the products of eigenvalues.

$d(X^{2}) = X\,dX\,I + I\,dX\,X$, so the Jacobian is $I \otimes X + X^{T} \otimes I$. $d(X^{3})$ gives $I \otimes X^{2} + X^{T} \otimes X + (X^{T})^{2} \otimes I$. A student caught a live bug here: the test $E$ happened to commute with $M$ — choose random perturbations.

$A = LU$ with $L$ unit lower triangular: $n(n - 1)/2$ numbers in $L$ and $n(n + 1)/2$ in $U$, $n^{2}$ in all. So LU maps $n^{2}$ numbers to $n^{2}$ numbers and has a Jacobian. $dA = dL\,U + L\,dU$, with the perturbations restricted to triangular shapes.

A traceless symmetric 2×2 matrix written through its eigenvectors (angle $\theta/2$) and eigenvalues $\pm r$ is exactly Cartesian-to-polar coordinates, with Jacobian determinant $r$. The full 2×2 symmetric problem is $\mathbb R^{3} \to \mathbb R^{3}$ with Jacobian determinant $\lambda_1 - \lambda_2$ — eigenvalue repulsion.

math210.0.4.worked: To turn $dY = \sum_k A_k\,dX\,B_k$ into an explicit Jacobian, replace each term by $B_k^{T} \otimes A_k$ and add them. Test the result against a finite difference with a RANDOM perturbation.
math210.0.4.watch: Checking a matrix derivative with a perturbation that commutes with $X$ — a multiple of $X$ or of $I$. Wrong formulas pass that test; only a generic random perturbation catches them.

checks.q: $A$ is 2×2 with $\det A = 3$, $B$ is 3×3 with $\det B = 3$. Then $\det(A \otimes B)$ is:
checks.expl: $(\det A)^{3}(\det B)^{2} = 27 \times 9 = 243$ — each determinant raised to the OTHER matrix's size.

checks.q: The gradient of $\|x\|$ at $x = (3, 4)$ has first component:
checks.expl: $\nabla\|x\| = x/\|x\| = (3, 4)/5$, first component 0.6.

checks.q: $(A \otimes B)\,\mathrm{vec}(C)$ equals:
opts: $\mathrm{vec}(ACB)$
$\mathrm{vec}(BCA^{T})$
$\mathrm{vec}(A^{T}CB)$
$\mathrm{vec}(CAB)$
checks.expl: $B$ stays beside $C$ on the left; $A$ comes around to the right, transposed.

math210.0.5.takeaway: Finite differences are a poor way to compute derivatives but the best way to CHECK them. The error of $f(x + \delta x) - f(x)$ against $f'(x)\,\delta x$ falls linearly with $\delta x$ (truncation) until floating-point roundoff takes over; a step near $\sqrt{\varepsilon} \approx 10^{-8}$ times $x$ balances the two.

beats.d: Automatic differentiation is reliable, but it fails on external libraries, on parts of a language, and wastes effort differentiating the ERROR of iterative solvers. So you often hand-derive one piece — a custom chain rule — and hand derivations are error-prone.
$f(x + \delta x) - f(x) \approx f'(x)\,\delta x$ — written without dividing, so $\delta x$ can be a matrix. Forward difference; the backward one uses $x - \delta x$ (unrelated to backward-mode AD).
$f(A) = A^{2}$ with random 4×4 $A$ and $dA$ of size $10^{-8}$: the difference matches $A\,dA + dA\,A$ to about eight digits, while $2A\,dA$ is off by about 60%.

'Small' always means small COMPARED TO something: use $\|\text{approx} - \text{exact}\|/\|\text{exact}\|$. For matrices the Frobenius norm $\|A\|_F = \sqrt{\sum a_{ij}^{2}} = \sqrt{\mathrm{tr}(A^{T}A)}$ does the job.
$f(x + \delta x) = f(x) + f'(x)\,\delta x + O(\delta x^{2})$, so the relative error is $O(\|\delta x\|)$: first-order accuracy, a straight line of slope 1 on a log–log plot.

Double precision keeps about 15–16 digits. Make $\delta x$ tiny and $f(x + \delta x)$ and $f(x)$ agree in most digits, so subtracting them cancels them — catastrophic cancellation. $1 + 10^{-100}$ is exactly 1 on a computer; $\sin(1 + 10^{-13}) - \sin 1$ keeps only about four digits.

Machine epsilon $\varepsilon = 2^{-52} \approx 2.2 \times 10^{-16}$. Rule of thumb: $|\delta x| \approx \sqrt{\varepsilon}\,|x| \approx 10^{-8}|x|$ — about half the digits — where truncation and roundoff errors balance. Both the matrix and the $\sin$ plots turn up there.

math210.0.5.worked: To test a hand-derived derivative: random input, random direction, $\delta x$ about $10^{-8}$ of the input's size; compare $f(x + \delta x) - f(x)$ with $f'(x)[\delta x]$ by relative error. Around $10^{-8}$ is a pass; order 1 means a bug.
math210.0.5.watch: Making $\delta x$ as small as possible to get a better check. Below about $10^{-8}$ relative, roundoff dominates and the error grows again; at $10^{-100}$ the difference is exactly zero.

checks.q: Double-precision machine epsilon is $2^{-52}$. Its square root, the rule-of-thumb relative step, in units of $10^{-8}$ to two decimal places, is:
Forward differences for $\sin$ at $x = 1$: in the truncation regime, the relative error divided by $h$ tends to $\tfrac12\tan 1$. To two decimal places that is:
checks.expl: Error $\approx \tfrac12|f''|h = \tfrac12\sin(1)h$; relative to $\cos 1$ that is $\tfrac12\tan(1)\,h = 0.78h$.

checks.q: Shrinking $\delta x$ from $10^{-8}$ to $10^{-13}$ makes a forward-difference check:
opts: more accurate, as the math predicts
less accurate, because of catastrophic cancellation
exactly correct
unchanged
checks.expl: Past the sweet spot, the subtraction of two nearly equal floating-point numbers loses most of the significant digits.

math210.0.6.takeaway: A gradient needs an inner product. Pick one on your vector space — for matrices, the Frobenius product $A \cdot B = \mathrm{tr}(A^{T}B)$ — and the gradient of any scalar function is whatever you dot with $dA$ to get $df$. So $\nabla\|A\|_F = A/\|A\|_F$ and $\nabla_A(x^{T}Ay) = xy^{T}$.

beats.d: Centered differences, $[f(x + \delta x) - f(x - \delta x)]/2$, cancel the even Taylor terms: error $O(\delta x^{2})$, second-order accurate, with the sweet spot near $10^{-5}$. Higher orders and Richardson extrapolation go further.

Each finite difference gives the derivative in ONE direction. A gradient with a million components needs a million evaluations of $f$ — hopeless for training a network, fine as a spot check in a few random directions.
Any rule $x \cdot y$ that is symmetric, linear, and positive ($x \cdot x > 0$ unless $x = 0$). A vector space with one is a Hilbert space. Its norm is $\|x\| = \sqrt{x \cdot x}$.

For a scalar $f$ on a Hilbert space, $f'(x)$ is a linear form, and every linear form is a dot product with some vector (the Riesz representation theorem). That vector is $\nabla f$: $df = \nabla f \cdot dx$, always shaped like $x$.

Weighted: $x^{T}Wy$ with $W$ symmetric positive definite — useful when components have different uncertainties or different units (metres, seconds, kilograms). A different inner product gives a different gradient.

The obvious product multiplies entries and adds: $A \cdot B = \sum a_{ij}b_{ij} = \mathrm{vec}(A)^{T}\mathrm{vec}(B) = \mathrm{tr}(A^{T}B)$ — each diagonal entry of $A^{T}B$ is a column of $A$ dotted with a column of $B$. Its norm is the Frobenius norm.

$d\sqrt{\mathrm{tr}(A^{T}A)} = \dfrac{\mathrm{tr}(dA^{T}A + A^{T}dA)}{2\|A\|}$, and $\mathrm{tr}(B) = \mathrm{tr}(B^{T})$ merges the terms: $df = \dfrac{A}{\|A\|} \cdot dA$. The same answer as $\nabla\|x\| = x/\|x\|$ — it is the same norm.

$df = x^{T}dA\,y$, a scalar, so equal to its trace; the cyclic property $\mathrm{tr}(AB) = \mathrm{tr}(BA)$ moves $y$ round: $\mathrm{tr}(yx^{T}dA) = (xy^{T}) \cdot dA$. So $\nabla_A = xy^{T}$ — the matrix of partials $\partial f/\partial a_{ij}$, without computing any. Coming soon: $\nabla\det A = \det(A)\,A^{-T}$.

math210.0.6.worked: For a scalar function of a matrix: compute $df$, wrap it in a trace (it is a scalar), then use $\mathrm{tr}(B) = \mathrm{tr}(B^{T})$ and cyclic swaps until it reads $\mathrm{tr}(G^{T}dA)$. Then $\nabla f = G$.
math210.0.6.watch: Rearranging a trace freely. Only CYCLIC moves are allowed, $\mathrm{tr}(ABC) = \mathrm{tr}(CAB)$; swapping two factors in a longer product is not.

checks.q: $f(A) = x^{T}Ay$ with $x = (1, 2)$ and $y = (3, 1, 2)$. The entry $\partial f/\partial a_{21}$ of the gradient is:
checks.expl: $\nabla_A f = xy^{T}$, whose (2,1) entry is $x_2y_1 = 2 \times 3 = 6$.

checks.q: The Frobenius inner product of $A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\ 3 & 4\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, $\mathrm{tr}(A^{T}B)$, is:
checks.expl: It is the sum of entrywise products: $0 + 2 + 3 + 0 = 5$.

checks.q: Centered differences are more accurate than forward differences for the same step because:
opts: they use a smaller step
the even-order Taylor terms cancel, leaving $O(\delta x^{2})$ error
they avoid roundoff completely
they evaluate $f$ only once
checks.expl: The symmetric difference cancels the $\delta x^{2}$ term of the expansion, so the error starts at the next order.

math210.0.7.takeaway: Derivatives drive Newton's method (linearize, solve, repeat) and optimisation (go downhill along $-\nabla f$). When $f$ depends on parameters through the solution of $Ax = b$ or $g(x, p) = 0$, the adjoint method gets the whole gradient for ONE extra solve with the transposed system — reverse mode, backpropagation, by another name.

beats.d: Linearize $f(x + \delta x) \approx f(x) + f'(x)\,\delta x$, set it to zero, step: $x \leftarrow x - f(x)/f'(x)$. Near a root the number of correct digits doubles each step.
The same with the Jacobian: solve $f'(x)\,\delta x = -f(x)$, a linear system each step. $n$ equations in $n$ unknowns; start close, or it can wander — the Newton fractals.

For a scalar loss, $-\nabla f$ is the steepest-descent direction. Then the hard parts: how far to step (line search, backtracking, trust regions), constraints, zig-zagging in long valleys (momentum, conjugate gradients, BFGS, Adam). Most practitioners take an algorithm off the shelf and spend their effort on the formulation.
Parameters $p$ (shape, materials) feed a physical model, $A(p)\,x = b$; its solution $x$ feeds an objective $f(x)$. A topology-optimised chair came out of letting every voxel be metal or air.

$df = f'(x)\,dx = -f'(x)\,A^{-1}\,dA\,x$. Multiply LEFT to right: $v^{T} = f'(x)A^{-1}$ means solving $A^{T}v = \nabla f$ — one adjoint solve. Then $\partial f/\partial p_k = -v^{T}\,(\partial A/\partial p_k)\,x$: just a dot product per parameter.

Right to left needs $A^{-1}(\partial A/\partial p_k)x$ for every $k$ — one big solve per parameter. So do finite differences. Forward mode suits few inputs and many outputs; reverse mode suits many inputs and one output.
If $x$ solves $g(p, x) = 0$: $g_p\,dp + g_x\,dx = 0$ gives $dx = -g_x^{-1}g_p\,dp$ (the implicit function theorem). The adjoint equation uses the transposed Newton Jacobian, $g_x^{T}v = \nabla f$.

Differentiated naively, automatic differentiation propagates derivatives through every Newton iteration — differentiating the solver's ERROR. Tell it the step solves $g = 0$ and one linear solve suffices; the same goes for code in libraries it cannot see.

math210.0.7.worked: For $f(x(p))$ with $A(p)x = b$: solve $Ax = b$, then solve $A^{T}v = \nabla_x f$, then $\partial f/\partial p_k = -v^{T}(\partial A/\partial p_k)x$. Two solves, however many parameters.
math210.0.7.watch: Computing $dx/dp$ for each parameter and then applying $f'$. That is forward mode — one solve PER parameter — when the adjoint gets all of them for one extra solve.

checks.q: Newton's method on $f(x) = x^{2} - 2$ from $x_0 = 1$. After two steps, $x_2$ to four decimal places is:
$A(p) = \begin{pmatrix}2 + p & 1\\ 1 & 3\end{pmatrix}$, $Ax = (1, 0)$, $f = x_1$. At $p = 0$, $df/dp = -v^{T}(\partial A/\partial p)\,x$ equals (two decimals):
checks.expl: $x = (3/5, -1/5)$; $A^{T}v = (1, 0)$ gives $v = (3/5, -1/5)$; $\partial A/\partial p$ has a single 1 in the corner, so $df/dp = -v_1x_1 = -9/25$.

checks.q: With a million parameters and one objective, the adjoint method needs:
opts: a million solves
two solves (forward and adjoint) and cheap dot products
a million finite differences
the full Jacobian matrix
checks.expl: One forward solve, one transposed solve, then a dot product per parameter.

math210.0.8.takeaway: A derivative needs a NORM (to say what 'small' means), which is why the setting is a Banach space. The gradient of the determinant is the cofactor matrix, $\nabla\det A = \det(A)\,A^{-T}$, so $d\det A = \det A\,\mathrm{tr}(A^{-1}dA)$ and $d\log\det A = \mathrm{tr}(A^{-1}dA)$.

beats.t: The norm we swept under the rug
beats.d: $o(\delta x)$ means $\|\text{remainder}\|/\|\delta x\| \to 0$: you need a norm on both input and output even to define a derivative. A normed vector space is a Banach space; an inner product supplies a norm for free.
$\nabla\det A = \mathrm{cofactor}(A) = \mathrm{adj}(A)^{T} = \det(A)\,(A^{-1})^{T}$. For 2×2 the adjugate swaps the diagonal and negates the off-diagonal.
A random $A$, a small random $dA$: $\det(A + dA) - \det A$ matches $\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{adj}(A)\,dA)$ — and both ForwardDiff and Zygote return the cofactor matrix as the gradient.

Expand along row $i$: $\det A = \sum_j a_{ij}C_{ij}$, and no cofactor $C_{ij}$ contains $a_{ij}$. So $\det A$ is affine in each entry with slope $C_{ij}$. A 3×3 example with one symbolic entry gave $13a + \dots$, and 13 is its minor.
$\det(I + dA) = 1 + \mathrm{tr}(dA) + \dots$ — the second coefficient of the characteristic polynomial. Then $\det(A + dA) = \det A\,\det(I + A^{-1}dA)$, giving $\det A\,\mathrm{tr}(A^{-1}dA)$.
$d\log\det A = \mathrm{tr}(A^{-1}dA)$ — the logarithmic derivative, which turns up all over mathematics (and in Newton's $f/f'$).

In floating point, singular versus nonsingular is a spectrum; conditioning, measured by singular values, is the useful notion. Nor are eigenvalues found from characteristic polynomials: the QR algorithm factors $A = QR$, forms $RQ$, and repeats.

math210.0.8.worked: For any function built from a determinant, use $d\det A = \det A\,\mathrm{tr}(A^{-1}dA)$, or $d\log\det A = \mathrm{tr}(A^{-1}dA)$ when a log is present, then read off the gradient with the Frobenius product: $\mathrm{tr}(G^{T}dA)$ means $\nabla = G$.
math210.0.8.watch: Forgetting the transpose. $d\det A = \det A\,\mathrm{tr}(A^{-1}dA)$, so the GRADIENT is $\det(A)\,A^{-T}$, not $\det(A)\,A^{-1}$ — they differ whenever $A$ is not symmetric.

checks.q: $A = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1\\ 1 & 3\end{pmatrix}$. The derivative of $\log\det A$ with respect to the entry $a_{11}$ is:
checks.expl: $\partial\log\det A/\partial a_{ij} = (A^{-T})_{ij}$; $A^{-1} = \tfrac15\begin{pmatrix}3 & -1\\ -1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$, so $3/5 = 0.6$.

checks.q: $\nabla\det A$ equals:
opts: $\det(A)\,A^{-T}$, the cofactor matrix
$\mathrm{tr}(A)\,I$
$\det(A)\,A$
checks.expl: By the Laplace expansion each entry's slope is its cofactor; in matrix form that is $\det(A)(A^{-1})^{T}$.

checks.q: In practice, eigenvalues are computed by:
opts: finding roots of the characteristic polynomial
the QR algorithm: factor, reverse to RQ, repeat
Cramer's rule
the determinant of $A - \lambda I$ on a grid of $\lambda$
checks.expl: Characteristic polynomials are numerically poor; iterated QR factorizations reveal the eigenvalues.

math210.0.9.takeaway: Forward-mode automatic differentiation is neither symbolic nor finite differences. Carry a pair — value and derivative — through every operation, with the sum and quotient rules taught to the arithmetic, and an unmodified program returns its exact derivative. Written $a + b\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon^{2} = 0$, these are dual numbers.

beats.d: Edelman assumed it was a symbolic table of derivatives, or finite differences with a well-chosen step. It is neither — and that is what makes it surprising.

Start with $t = 1$; repeat $t \leftarrow (t + x/t)/2$, averaging a guess that is too small with one too large. Ten steps match the built-in square root. Each iterate is a rational function of $x$ — the fifth is a degree-16 over degree-15 polynomial — that nobody ever writes out.

Define a type $D$ holding (value, derivative). Teach it $+$ (add both parts) and $/$ (value divided; derivative by the quotient rule, $(v\,du - u\,dv)/v^{2}$), and how to promote an ordinary number $c$ to $(c, 0)$.
Feed the UNCHANGED Babylonian code $D(49, 1)$: out comes $(7, 0.0714\ldots)$ — $\sqrt{49}$ and $1/(2\sqrt{49}) = 1/14$. No formula for the derivative of a square root was given anywhere.

It is exactly what differentiating every line by hand does: $t' = 1/2$, then $t' \leftarrow (t' + (t - x t')/t^{2})/2$ alongside each update. The pair carries that second iteration automatically — and it converges to $1/(2\sqrt x)$ as the first converges to $\sqrt x$.

Write $(a, b)$ as $a + b\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon^{2} = 0$: a first-order expansion. Then $(a + b\varepsilon)(c + d\varepsilon) = ac + (ad + bc)\varepsilon$ — the product rule — and $1/(1 + \varepsilon) = 1 - \varepsilon$, $(1 + \varepsilon)^{5} = 1 + 5\varepsilon$. All numerical, though it looks symbolic.

Every program bottoms out in $+ - \times \div$, so those four rules suffice in principle (in practice $\sin$ and friends get their own rules). Julia compiles the derivative code into short, efficient assembler.

math210.0.9.worked: To differentiate a program in forward mode: seed the input as (value, 1), make every operation update the derivative by its own rule, and read the derivative off the output. Constants enter as (value, 0).
math210.0.9.watch: Thinking forward-mode AD approximates. There is no step size and no truncation error: it computes the exact derivative of the program as written, to floating-point accuracy.

checks.q: Running the Babylonian square root on the dual number $49 + 1\varepsilon$ returns a derivative part of (four decimal places):
With $\varepsilon^{2} = 0$, the dual number $(1 + \varepsilon)^{5}$ has $\varepsilon$-coefficient:
checks.expl: Only the linear term of the binomial expansion survives: $1 + 5\varepsilon$ — the derivative of $x^{5}$ at 1.

checks.q: Dividing dual numbers $(u, u')/(v, v')$ gives derivative part:
checks.expl: The quotient rule, applied at a point: denominator times derivative of numerator, minus numerator times derivative of denominator, over the denominator squared.

math210.0.10.takeaway: Draw a program as a directed acyclic graph with each edge labelled by its one-step derivative. The derivative of an output with respect to an input is the SUM over paths of the PRODUCT of edge labels. Accumulate those path products from the inputs and you have forward mode; from the output, reverse mode.

beats.d: $a = \sin x$, $b = a/y$, $z = b + x$. By hand: $z = \sin(x)/y + x$, so $\partial z/\partial x = \cos(x)/y + 1$ and $\partial z/\partial y = -\sin(x)/y^{2}$.
Nodes are variables; edges carry one-step derivatives: $x \to a$ with $\cos x$; $a \to b$ with $1/y$; $y \to b$ with $-a/y^{2}$; $b \to z$ with 1; and $x \to z$ with 1.
From $x$ to $z$ there are two paths: $x \to a \to b \to z$ contributes $1 \cdot (1/y) \cdot \cos x$, and $x \to z$ contributes 1. Their sum is $\cos(x)/y + 1$. For $y$: one path, $-a/y^{2}$.

Walk each path from input to output (forward) or from output to input (reverse). With scalars the order is irrelevant; with matrices on the edges, associativity still allows either order — even middle-outward — as long as products stay in order.

Carry (value, path-product) through the graph: a node $f$ turns $(x, p)$ into $(f(x), f'(x)\,p)$. Start with $(x, 1)$ — the empty path product is 1, as the empty sum is 0. A constant sends everything to $(c, 0)$.

At a node with several inputs, $z = f(a, b)$ receives $(a, p)$ and $(b, q)$ and passes on $p\,\partial f/\partial a + q\,\partial f/\partial b$. For $a + b$ the partials are 1 and 1; for $ab$ they are $b$ and $a$.

math210.0.10.worked: To differentiate any composition: draw the graph, label each edge with its local derivative, then sum the path products from input to output. Every chain rule you know is a special case.
math210.0.10.watch: Forgetting a path. Where a variable reaches the output by two routes — $x$ goes into $a$ and also straight into $z$ — both products must be ADDED; dropping one loses a term.

checks.q: For $z = \sin(x)/y + x$, the value of $\partial z/\partial x$ at $x = 0$, $y = 2$ is:
checks.expl: Two paths: $\cos(0)/2 = 0.5$ through $a$ and $b$, plus 1 directly.

checks.q: For the same program, $\partial z/\partial y$ at $x = \pi/2$, $y = 2$ is:
In forward mode, the input node is seeded with path product:
opts: 0, the empty sum
1, the empty product
the input value
$\varepsilon$
checks.expl: A path of length zero multiplies no edges, so its product is the multiplicative identity, 1.

math210.0.11.takeaway: To differentiate the solution of an ODE with respect to many parameters, add a Lagrange multiplier $\lambda(t)$, integrate by parts, and choose $\lambda$ to kill the unknown sensitivities. $\lambda$ solves a linear adjoint ODE BACKWARDS in time, and the gradient becomes an integral — one forward solve, one backward solve, however many parameters.

beats.d: $u' = f(u, p, t)$, $u(t_0) = u_0$. Higher-order equations become first-order systems (height and velocity for a falling ball). With no closed form, discretize: explicit Euler, $u_{n+1} = u_n + \Delta t\,f(u_n)$ — a forward difference.

How does the solution respond to the parameters — for fitting reaction rates, control, design? Two families: discretize-then-differentiate (run AD through the solver) or differentiate-then-discretize (continuous sensitivities), each with forward and adjoint modes.
$z(T) = z_0 + v_0T - \tfrac12gT^{2}$, so $\partial z(T)/\partial g = -\tfrac12T^{2}$. The question is how to get such derivatives without a closed form.
$G(p) = \int_{t_0}^{T} g(u, p, t)\,dt$, e.g. squared mismatch with data. Add $\int \lambda^{T}(f - u')\,dt$, which is zero for any $\lambda(t)$ because $u$ solves the ODE.

Differentiating brings in $s = du/dp$, the hard term. Integrate $\lambda^{T}s'$ by parts and group every $s$ term: they vanish if $\lambda' = -f_u^{T}\lambda - g_u^{T}$ with $\lambda(T) = 0$ — and $s(t_0) = 0$ kills the other boundary term.

Solve for $u(t)$ forward; solve the adjoint ODE for $\lambda(t)$ backward from $T$; then $dG/dp = \int (g_p + \lambda^{T}f_p)\,dt$. Like $A^{T}v$ for linear systems: the adjoint problem is linear and the same size.

Storing $u(t)$ at every time can be prohibitive for large systems. Re-solve $u$ backwards alongside $\lambda$ — but that can be unstable, so use checkpoints. And the final integral is itself an ODE, $w' = g_p + \lambda^{T}f_p$, solved in lockstep.
If $G$ is a sum over measurement times rather than an integral, integrate backwards between them and add a jump to $\lambda$ at each measurement.

math210.0.11.worked: For $dG/dp$ with $G = \int g(u, p)\,dt$ and $u' = f(u, p)$: solve forward for $u$; solve $\lambda' = -f_u^{T}\lambda - g_u^{T}$ backward from $\lambda(T) = 0$; integrate $g_p + \lambda^{T}f_p$. The cost does not grow with the number of parameters.
math210.0.11.watch: Running the adjoint ODE forwards. Its condition is set at the FINAL time, $\lambda(T) = 0$, so it must be integrated from $T$ back to $t_0$.

checks.q: A ball falls under gravity for $T = 2$ s. The sensitivity of its final height to $g$, $\partial z(T)/\partial g$, is:
checks.expl: $z(T) = z_0 + v_0T - \tfrac12gT^{2}$, so the derivative is $-\tfrac12T^{2} = -2$.

checks.q: The adjoint variable $\lambda(t)$ has the same size as:
opts: the parameter vector $p$
the state $u(t)$
a scalar
the Jacobian $f_u$
checks.expl: It multiplies $f - u'$, a state-sized vector, so it is a column vector with one entry per state component.

checks.q: Adding $\int\lambda^{T}(f - u')\,dt$ to the cost is allowed because:
opts: $\lambda$ is zero
the integrand is zero along any solution of the ODE
it is a small error
integration by parts removes it
checks.expl: $u' = f$ along the solution, so the added term is identically zero for any choice of $\lambda(t)$ — which is then chosen to cancel the sensitivities.

math210.0.12.takeaway: Functions are vectors too, so a functional $f(u) = \int F(u, u', x)\,dx$ has a derivative defined exactly as before: linearize $f(u + du) - f(u)$. With the inner product $\langle u, v\rangle = \int uv\,dx$ and one integration by parts, the gradient is $F_u - (F_{u'})'$. Setting it to zero gives the Euler–Lagrange equation.

beats.d: You can add functions and scale them, so they form a vector space. Linear operators, dot products, orthogonality and eigenfunctions all carry over. The one caution is that functions can misbehave (blow up, or oscillate infinitely fast), so we implicitly stay among functions whose integrals exist.

$f(u) = \int_0^1 \sin(u(x))\,dx$ takes a function and returns a number. Perturb it by a small function $du(x)$. At each $x$ this is ordinary 18.01 linearization, $\sin(u + du) \approx \sin u + \cos u\,du$. So $df = \int_0^1 \cos(u(x))\,du(x)\,dx$, which is plainly linear in $du$.

beats.t: The gradient needs a dot product
beats.d: The obvious inner product multiplies the 'components' (the values at each $x$) and adds them up: $\langle u, v\rangle = \int_0^1 u(x)v(x)\,dx$. Its norm is what says a change is small. Then $df = \langle \nabla f, du\rangle$ gives $\nabla f = \cos u(x)$. In this setting it is often called a Fréchet derivative, but it is just the derivative.

$f(u) = \int_0^1 \sqrt{1 + u'(x)^{2}}\,dx$ is the length of the curve. Expanding the square root to first order gives $df = \int \frac{u'}{\sqrt{1 + u'^{2}}}\,du'\,dx$. That is linear, but in $du'$ rather than $du$, so it is not yet a dot product with $du$.

Moving the derivative off $du$ leaves a boundary term $\left[\frac{u'}{\sqrt{1+u'^{2}}}\,du\right]_0^1$ minus $\int \left(\frac{u'}{\sqrt{1+u'^{2}}}\right)'du\,dx$. Fixing the endpoints allows only perturbations with $du(0) = du(1) = 0$, so the boundary term vanishes and $\nabla f = -\left(u'/\sqrt{1+u'^{2}}\right)'$.

At a minimum the gradient is zero. The quotient rule (after a student caught a slip on the board) collapses it to $u''/(1 + u'^{2})^{3/2} = 0$, so $u'' = 0$: a straight line. Nothing new, but this time derived rather than assumed.

Take $f(u) = \int_a^b F(u, u', x)\,dx$, where $F_u$ and $F_{u'}$ are the derivatives of $F$ in its first and second slots. Then $df = \int (F_u\,du + F_{u'}\,du')\,dx$. Integrate by parts and drop the boundary term to get $\nabla f = F_u - (F_{u'})' = 0$, a second-order ODE for $u$.

The principle of least action uses it to give Newton's laws in any coordinates, and optimal control uses it too. In the brachistochrone problem, the frictionless ramp that gets a mass down fastest turns out to be a cycloid: the curve traced by a point on a rolling wheel. The classical name is calculus of variations, but it is the same derivative on a new vector space.

math210.0.12.worked: To minimize $\int F(u, u', x)\,dx$ with fixed ends: write $F_u\,du + F_{u'}\,du'$ and integrate the second term by parts. The boundary term dies because $du = 0$ at the ends. Then set what multiplies $du$ to zero: $F_u - \frac{d}{dx}F_{u'} = 0$.
math210.0.12.watch: Reading $\int F_{u'}\,du'\,dx$ as the gradient. It is linear in $du'$, not $du$, and becomes a dot product with $du$ only after integrating by parts. Even then, the boundary term vanishes only because the endpoints are held fixed.

checks.q: $f(u) = \int_0^1 \sin(u(x))\,dx$ at $u(x) = x$. Perturb $u$ by the constant function $du(x) = \varepsilon$. The rate $df/\varepsilon$ is (two decimals):
checks.expl: $df = \int_0^1 \cos(x)\,\varepsilon\,dx = \varepsilon\sin 1$, so the rate is $\sin 1 \approx 0.84$.

checks.q: The straight line from $(0, 0)$ to $(1, 1)$ has length $\sqrt2 \approx 1.41$. The parabola $u = x^{2}$ between the same points has length (two decimals):
checks.expl: $\int_0^1\sqrt{1 + 4x^{2}}\,dx = \tfrac{\sqrt5}{2} + \tfrac14\sinh^{-1}2 \approx 1.48$. It is longer, as the Euler–Lagrange result says any curve other than the line must be.

checks.q: In the arc-length derivation, the boundary term $\left[\frac{u'}{\sqrt{1+u'^{2}}}\,du\right]_0^1$ disappears because:
opts: $u'$ is zero at the ends
the endpoints are fixed, so every allowed perturbation has $du(0) = du(1) = 0$
the integrand is odd
it is second order in $du$
checks.expl: We only compare curves with the same endpoints, so every admissible $du$ vanishes there.

math210.0.13.takeaway: A random function $X(p)$ returns a random variable. Differencing samples taken independently does not work, because the difference never shrinks. The useful derivative comes from samples that SHARE their randomness: write $X(p) = x(p, \omega)$ with $\omega$ drawn from a fixed distribution, and differentiate at fixed $\omega$. This is the reparameterization trick, and its average is $\frac{d}{dp}E[X(p)]$, until the function jumps, as discrete ones do.

beats.d: Guest lecturer Gaurav Arya starts with $f(A) = A^{2}$ and answers two questions separately. How does the output change? $(A + dA)^{2} - A^{2} = dA\,A + A\,dA + dA^{2}$. Which terms can be neglected? Here, $dA^{2}$. Both questions become non-trivial when the output is random.

$X(p)$ is a family of random variables indexed by a real number $p$. Examples are a Bernoulli that returns 1 with probability $p$, and an exponential with scale $p$ (samples of order $p$, larger values exponentially unlikely). Every call returns a different number.

Because what we optimize is an average. A variational autoencoder's loss is an expectation; a stochastic model of reacting molecules, with exponential waiting times, is fitted to data. Sampling is easy, but the exact expectation often is not: a five-line random walk is easy to simulate and hard to average analytically. The goal is a new program $\tilde X(p)$ whose average is $\frac{d}{dp}E[X(p)]$, an unbiased gradient estimator.

$dX(\varepsilon) = X(p + \varepsilon) - X(p)$ is a random variable, but subtracting two random variables needs their JOINT distribution. Two fair coins differ half the time if independent, and never if they are the same coin. Sampled independently, $dX$ stays huge as $\varepsilon \to 0$: values around $10^{7}$ that, divided by $\varepsilon$, average to 1 only in theory.

Put all the randomness in a sample space $\Omega$ whose distribution does not depend on $p$. Then $X(p)$ is a deterministic map $\omega \mapsto x(p, \omega)$. With $\omega$ uniform on $(0, 1)$, which is the computer's rand, an exponential of scale $p$ is $x = -p\log(1 - \omega)$.

Use the SAME $\omega$ for $p$ and for $p + \varepsilon$. Now $dX$ is of size $\varepsilon$ at every $\omega$, and $\delta(\omega) = \lim dX/\varepsilon$ exists pointwise. For the exponential, $\delta = -\log(1 - \omega)$. Its average is 1, which equals $\frac{d}{dp}E[X]$ since $E[X] = p$.

Because $x(p, \omega)$ is an ordinary deterministic function, the chain rule just works: $Y = X^{2}$ has pathwise derivative $2X\delta$. The class noticed that the live demo drew fresh random numbers for $X$ and $\delta$. They must come from the same $\omega$.

A Bernoulli is a step: it returns 1 if $\omega \gt 1 - p$. Nudging $p$ moves the step, so almost every $\omega$ sees no change and $\delta = 0$, yet $\frac{d}{dp}E[X] = 1$. The missing piece is a jump of size 1 that happens with probability of order $\varepsilon$, so the limit and the expectation can no longer be swapped. Arya's stochastic triples fix this: like dual numbers with a third slot, they carry the value, the derivative, and a possible jump with its probability.

math210.0.13.worked: To differentiate $E[f(X(p))]$: write the sampler as a deterministic function of $p$ and a random input that does not depend on $p$, $X = x(p, \omega)$. Differentiate $f(x(p, \omega))$ in $p$ at fixed $\omega$ with the ordinary chain rule, then average over $\omega$. This works when $x$ is continuous in $p$.
math210.0.13.watch: Estimating $[X(p + \varepsilon) - X(p)]/\varepsilon$ from two independent runs. It is unbiased in principle and useless in practice: the noise does not shrink with $\varepsilon$, so the variance grows like $1/\varepsilon^{2}$.

checks.q: $X$ is exponential with scale $p$, sampled as $X = -p\log(1 - \omega)$. The pathwise derivative of $Y = X^{2}$ is $2X\delta$, with $\delta = -\log(1 - \omega)$ from the same $\omega$. At $p = 3$, its average (which equals $\frac{d}{dp}E[Y]$) is:
checks.expl: $E[Y] = E[X^{2}] = 2p^{2}$ for an exponential of scale $p$, so the derivative is $4p = 12$. Directly: $E[2X\delta] = 2p\,E[\delta^{2}] = 2p \cdot 2 = 12$.

checks.q: Differencing two independent samples, one of $X(p + \varepsilon)$ and one of $X(p)$, fails because:
opts: it is biased
the difference does not shrink as $\varepsilon \to 0$, so dividing by $\varepsilon$ gives enormous variance
random variables cannot be subtracted
the exponential has no mean
checks.expl: The average is right but the noise of two unrelated samples swamps the signal. Sharing $\omega$ makes the difference proportional to $\varepsilon$.

checks.q: A Bernoulli$(p)$ is written as $1$ if $\omega \gt 1 - p$. At fixed $\omega$ its pathwise derivative is 0 almost everywhere, yet $\frac{d}{dp}E[X] = 1$. What does the pathwise derivative miss?
opts: a rounding error
rare jumps of size 1, with probability of order $\varepsilon$, where the step moves past $\omega$
the variance of $\omega$
a factor of $p$
checks.expl: The change is not small everywhere; it is large on a small set. That is why discrete randomness needs something beyond the reparameterization trick.

math210.0.14.takeaway: The second derivative is the derivative of the derivative: $f''(x)[dx', dx] = f'(x + dx')[dx] - f'(x)[dx]$. It takes TWO small changes and is linear in each (a bilinear form), and it is always symmetric. For $f: \mathbb{R}^{n} \to \mathbb{R}$ it is $dx'^{T}H\,dx$, with $H$ the symmetric Hessian. Its job is the quadratic approximation behind Newton's method.

beats.d: $f'(x)$ is a linear operator, so $f'(x + dx') - f'(x)$ is a difference of linear operators. That is itself a linear operator, acting on $dx$. Linear operators form a vector space, which is exactly why matrices add and scale entrywise: those rules are what make $(L_1 + L_2)v = L_1v + L_2v$.
So $f''(x)$ takes two vectors: $dx'$, the change in WHERE the derivative is taken, and $dx$, the change the derivative acts on. It is linear in each separately, not jointly: $B(2u, 3v) = 6B(u, v)$.

A general bilinear form need not be symmetric; its two arguments need not even live in the same space. But writing out the definitions gives $f''(x)[dx', dx] = f(x + dx' + dx) - f(x + dx') - f(x + dx) + f(x)$, which treats $dx$ and $dx'$ identically. Equality of mixed partials from 18.02 is a special case.

For scalar $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$, $f'(x) = (\nabla f)^{T}$. The only bilinear map from two column vectors to a scalar is $dx'^{T}H\,dx$, and symmetry forces $H = H^{T}$. Differentiating $\nabla f$ row by row gives $H_{ij} = \partial^{2}f/\partial x_i\,\partial x_j$: the Hessian is the Jacobian of the gradient.

Start from $d\det A = \det A\,\mathrm{tr}(A^{-1}dA)$ and differentiate again with $dA$ held fixed, using the product rule and $d(A^{-1}) = -A^{-1}dA'\,A^{-1}$. The result is $f''(A)[dA', dA] = \det A\,[\mathrm{tr}(A^{-1}dA')\,\mathrm{tr}(A^{-1}dA) - \mathrm{tr}(A^{-1}dA'\,A^{-1}dA)]$, symmetric by the cyclic property of the trace. As a Hessian it would be $n^{2} \times n^{2}$ acting on $\mathrm{vec}(dA)$: possible, but unnatural.

$f(x + \delta x) \approx f(x) + f'(x)\delta x + \tfrac12 f''(x)[\delta x, \delta x]$. The $\tfrac12$ is there because $\delta x$ appears twice, as in a Taylor series: differentiate the model twice and you must get back $f''$.

To optimize, fit a quadratic and step to its minimum; with constraints linearized as well, this is sequential quadratic programming. Equivalently, find a root of $\nabla f$ by linearizing it. That is Newton's method, with the Hessian as the Jacobian.

The Hessian is $n \times n$, so for a neural network it cannot even be stored.
