Hence quasi-Newton methods, which approximate it: BFGS (named for four people who found it independently in the same year) and Newton–Krylov methods. Hessian-vector products $H\,dx$ stay cheap even when $H$ itself is not.

math210.0.14.worked: To get a second derivative of a matrix function: take the first-derivative formula, hold the first perturbation $dA$ fixed, perturb $A$ by a second $dA'$, and differentiate with the ordinary rules. The result, linear in both $dA$ and $dA'$, is the bilinear form. Check its symmetry with the cyclic property of the trace.
math210.0.14.watch: Dropping the $\tfrac12$ in the quadratic model. $f''[\delta x, \delta x]$ is quadratic in $\delta x$, so without the half the model's second derivative is $2f''$, and Newton steps come out half the right length.

checks.q: $f(A) = \det A$ at $A = I$, with both perturbations $dA = dA' = E = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\ 3 & 4\end{pmatrix}$. The second derivative $f''(I)[E, E]$ is:
checks.expl: At $A = I$ the formula is $\mathrm{tr}(E)^{2} - \mathrm{tr}(E^{2}) = 25 - 29 = -4$. Indeed $\det(I + tE) = 1 + 5t - 2t^{2}$.

checks.q: $f(x, y) = x^{2}y$ at $(1, 1)$, with step $\delta = (0.1, 0.1)$. The quadratic approximation $f + \nabla f^{T}\delta + \tfrac12\delta^{T}H\delta$ gives (two decimals):
checks.expl: $\nabla f = (2, 1)$ contributes $0.3$. $H = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 2\\ 2 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ contributes $\tfrac12(0.06) = 0.03$. Total $1.33$, against the true $1.1^{3} = 1.331$.

checks.q: Why is $f''(x)[dx', dx] = f''(x)[dx, dx']$?
opts: every bilinear form is symmetric
expanded, it is $f(x + dx + dx') - f(x + dx) - f(x + dx') + f(x)$, which treats the two changes alike
because $H$ is diagonal
only for polynomials
checks.expl: Most bilinear forms are not symmetric. This one is, because writing out the definition of the derivative twice puts $dx$ and $dx'$ in interchangeable positions.

checks.q: Full Newton's method is impractical for a neural network with $10^{9}$ parameters because:
opts: Hessians do not exist for neural networks
the Hessian has $10^{18}$ entries, too many even to store
the gradient is too expensive
Newton only works in one dimension
checks.expl: Hence quasi-Newton approximations such as BFGS, and methods that need only Hessian-vector products.

math210.0.15.takeaway: Constrained quantities have constrained perturbations: on the sphere $x^{T}dx = 0$, and for an orthogonal $Q$, $Q^{T}dQ$ is antisymmetric. Differentiate $S = Q\Lambda Q^{T}$ and take the diagonal: that gives the Hellmann–Feynman result $d\lambda_i = q_i^{T}\,dS\,q_i$. The off-diagonal entries give the eigenvectors, and break down when eigenvalues collide.

beats.d: If $x^{T}x = 1$, differentiating gives $dx^{T}x + x^{T}dx = 2x^{T}dx = 0$. The only allowed changes are tangent, orthogonal to $x$. Edelman checks it on the circle $x = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ and numerically at a random point on the sphere. That point comes from normalizing a standard normal vector, whose distribution is rotation-invariant; normalizing a uniform rand vector does not give a uniform point.

Describing the circle by $x$, two coordinates plus a constraint, is extrinsic. Describing it by the single angle $\theta$ is intrinsic. Pure mathematicians came to prefer intrinsic coordinates; Edelman thinks extrinsic ones are better for computation.

For $x^{T}Ax$ with $A$ symmetric, insert the projection $I - xx^{T}$ to restrict $dx$ to the tangent plane. The gradient becomes the ordinary gradient projected onto that plane, pushed back onto the sphere's tangent space. The same holds for any function on the sphere.

$Q^{T}Q = I$ gives $Q^{T}dQ + dQ^{T}Q = 0$: $Q^{T}dQ$ plus its transpose is zero, so it is antisymmetric. The notebook showed it first: a numerical $Q^{T}dQ$ with a near-zero diagonal and mirrored entries of opposite sign.

2×2 rotations have one parameter; 3×3 have three (roll, pitch and yaw). In general the count is $n(n-1)/2$: $n^{2}$ entries minus the $n(n+1)/2$ constraints in $Q^{T}Q = I$. Counting through QR, the symmetric eigendecomposition or the SVD gives the same answer.

The product rule gives three terms. Rotate them by $Q^{T}(\cdot)Q$: $Q^{T}dS\,Q = Q^{T}dQ\,\Lambda - \Lambda\,Q^{T}dQ + d\Lambda$. Edelman checks this numerically on a random symmetric 5×5 matrix and a perturbation of it.

Take the diagonal. $Q^{T}dQ$ is antisymmetric, so its diagonal is zero, and multiplying by the diagonal $\Lambda$ keeps it zero. What remains is $d\lambda_i = q_i^{T}\,dS\,q_i$, which physicists call first-order perturbation theory. Johnson adds that it holds even for a non-symmetric $dS$, which is how small losses are added to a lossless system.

The off-diagonal entries give the change in the eigenvectors, divided by $\lambda_j - \lambda_i$. When two eigenvalues are equal, it is no longer differentiable. Carrying on, first-order eigenvectors give second-order eigenvalues. For an inequality constraint such as positive semidefinite, parametrize instead: such matrices usually came from a $B^{T}B$ anyway.

math210.0.15.worked: To differentiate an eigenvalue of a symmetric $S(p)$: find its unit eigenvector $q$ and compute $d\lambda/dp = q^{T}(dS/dp)\,q$. You do not need the derivative of the eigenvector, as long as $\lambda$ is not repeated.
math210.0.15.watch: Allowing any $dQ$ for an orthogonal matrix. Only perturbations with $Q^{T}dQ$ antisymmetric stay on the orthogonal group. The others step off it, just as a radial $dx$ steps off the sphere.

checks.q: $S = \begin{pmatrix}3 & 1\\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$. As the entry $s_{11}$ increases, the largest eigenvalue changes at the rate $q^{T}E_{11}q = q_1^{2}$, which is (two decimals):
checks.expl: $\lambda = 2 + \sqrt2$ with eigenvector proportional to $(1, \sqrt2 - 1)$, so $q_1^{2} = 1/(4 - 2\sqrt2) \approx 0.85$.

checks.q: The orthogonal $4 \times 4$ matrices form a set of dimension:
checks.expl: $n(n-1)/2 = 6$: sixteen entries minus the ten independent constraints in $Q^{T}Q = I$.

checks.q: Differentiating $Q^{T}Q = I$ shows that a perturbation of an orthogonal matrix must make $Q^{T}dQ$:
opts: zero
symmetric
antisymmetric
diagonal
checks.expl: $Q^{T}dQ + (Q^{T}dQ)^{T} = 0$ is the definition of antisymmetric. On the sphere the same step gave $x^{T}dx = 0$.

checks.q: The derivative of the eigenvectors breaks down when:
opts: $S$ is singular
two eigenvalues coincide, because the formula divides by $\lambda_j - \lambda_i$
$dS$ is not symmetric
$n \gt 3$
checks.expl: Hellmann–Feynman for the eigenvalues needs no division. The eigenvector formula does, and a repeated eigenvalue makes the eigenvectors non-unique.

math210.0.16.takeaway: A program is a directed acyclic graph with one-step partial derivatives on its edges, and every derivative is the sum over paths of the product of edge weights. Forward mode accumulates those products from the inputs and needs no stored graph. Reverse mode records the graph on a forward pass, then accumulates backwards from the output, sharing work along the way. Its cost scales with the number of outputs, which is why machine learning, with a single loss, uses it.

beats.d: Take $a = \sin x$, $b = a/y$, $z = b + x$. $\partial z/\partial x = 1$ is the one-step derivative, pretending $b$ does not depend on $x$; $dz/dx = \cos(x)/y + 1$ is the whole truth. The graph carries the partials on its edges. A program's graph is always a DAG, because each step needs its inputs first.

$dz/dx$ is the sum, over all paths from $x$ to $z$, of the product of the edge weights. This is the chain rule, but the graph shows that the order of multiplication is yours to choose. On a computer every weight is a floating-point number, never a finite difference.

Every arithmetic program reduces to $+$, $-$, $\times$ and $\div$. Their partials are $\pm1$; $a_2$ and $a_1$; and $1/a_2$ and $-a_1/a_2^{2}$: the sum, product and quotient rules restated. In practice, libraries add known rules (ChainRules.jl), so $\sin$ comes with $\cos$. Code that calls out to a Fortran library breaks this unless someone writes a rule for it.

At node $b$, knowing $da_i/dx$ for every input $a_i$: $db/dx = \sum_i \frac{\partial b}{\partial a_i}\frac{da_i}{dx}$. The products are carried along as the program executes, so no graph is stored. This is why operator overloading with dual numbers works.

Now look at the nodes $b_i$ that $a$ feeds: $dz/da = \sum_i \frac{dz}{db_i}\frac{\partial b_i}{\partial a}$, starting from $dz/dz = 1$. The sum can be built one edge at a time, adding into an accumulator $\bar a$. For $b = a_1 + a_2$: $\bar a_1 \leftarrow \bar a_1 + \bar b$ and $\bar a_2 \leftarrow \bar a_2 + \bar b$. For $b = a_1a_2$: $\bar a_1 \leftarrow \bar a_1 + a_2\bar b$ and $\bar a_2 \leftarrow \bar a_2 + a_1\bar b$. Programs run forwards, so reverse mode must first run forward to compute every value and record the graph. Mathematically the two modes are mirror images; the asymmetry comes from the computer.

Johnson: forward mode costs the function times the number of inputs; reverse mode costs it times the number of outputs. With many of both, it is expensive either way. Edelman's graph has sources $a$ and $b$ feeding $c$, which feeds $d$. Forward mode computes $acd$ and $bcd$ separately: four multiplies. Reverse mode forms $cd$ once and reuses it: three. This is dynamic programming, and the same reason a row vector times a Jacobian beats a Jacobian times a Jacobian.

$z = 2xy + (x - 1)^{2}$ at $x = 3$, $y = 5$. Forward pass: 6, 30, 2, 4, then $z = 34$. Reverse pass: the sum passes 1 to both branches. The product $6 \cdot 5$ sends 5 and 6. The product $2 \cdot x$ sends 15 and 10. The square sends $2 \cdot 2 = 4$, and the subtraction adds 4 to $x$ and $-4$ to the constant. Since $x$ is one variable in storage, its contributions accumulate: $\nabla z = (14, 6)$.

When AD fails, or is wasteful (for example, differentiating the error of an approximate integral), you supply the rule yourself. That is a Jacobian-vector product (frule, pushforward) for forward mode, or a vector-Jacobian product (rrule, pullback) for reverse mode. Complex numbers need care too: $|z|^{2} = zz^{*}$ is not complex-differentiable, yet $df = z^{*}dz + z\,dz^{*}$. CR (Wirtinger) calculus handles this by treating $z$ and $z^{*}$ as two variables.

math210.0.16.worked: Reverse mode by hand: run forward and write down every intermediate value. Set the output's adjoint to 1. Then walk the operations backwards. For each one, add (edge weight × adjoint of its output) into the adjoint of each input: the weight is $1$ for a sum and the OTHER factor for a product. A variable used twice collects from both uses.
math210.0.16.watch: Overwriting instead of accumulating. A variable that feeds two operations, like $x$ in both $2x$ and $x - 1$, must SUM its contributions. Assigning the second one discards the first path, which here gives 4 or 10 instead of 14.

checks.expl: $x$ collects 10 through $2x$ and 4 through $(x - 1)^{2}$: $2y + 2(x - 1) = 10 + 4 = 14$.

checks.q: For the same $z$ and point, $\partial z/\partial y$ =
checks.expl: $2x = 6$: the product node sends the other factor, $2x$, back to $y$.

checks.q: Ten sources each feed node $c$, which feeds the output $d$, and every edge has a weight. Computing the ten path products $a_i\,c\,d$ one source at a time takes 20 multiplies. Reverse mode, reusing $cd$, takes:
checks.expl: One multiply for $cd$, then one per source: $1 + 10 = 11$. With one output and many inputs, reverse mode shares everything downstream.

checks.q: Reverse mode, unlike forward mode, must store the computational graph because:
opts: it uses more memory by design
programs execute forwards, so the values and edge weights must be recorded before the backward sweep
it uses finite differences
it handles only scalars
checks.expl: Forward mode can ride along with execution. Reverse mode needs the whole forward computation first.

math210.1.0.takeaway: Training a linear classifier needs two things. The first is a LOSS that scores how bad a weight matrix $W$ is: the multiclass SVM's hinge loss or softmax's $-\log$ probability, plus a regularization penalty that prefers simpler $W$. The second is OPTIMIZATION to find a good $W$: follow the negative gradient, computed analytically, checked numerically, and estimated on minibatches.

beats.d: The scores are $s = f(x, W) = Wx$. There are three training images (a cat, a car, a frog), and a $W$ that scores the cat image 3.2 for cat, 5.1 for car and $-1.7$ for frog. A loss $L_i(f(x_i, W), y_i)$ for each example, averaged over the dataset, turns 'this $W$ is bad' into a number.

$L_i = \sum_{j \ne y_i}\max(0,\, s_j - s_{y_i} + 1)$. The correct score must beat every other score by a margin of 1, and the shape is a hinge. The three images give losses of 2.9, 0 and 12.9, which average to 5.27.

Jiggle the car image's scores and its loss stays 0, because it already clears the margin. The minimum is 0 and the maximum is infinite. At initialization, scores near 0 give $C - 1$, a debugging check at the first iteration. Summing over $j = y_i$ as well adds 1. Using a mean instead of a sum only rescales. Squaring the hinge gives a DIFFERENT classifier.

If $W$ gets zero loss, so does $2W$. So far the loss only asks the model to fit the TRAINING data, which invites overfitting: a wiggly curve through every point where a simple line would generalize. The fix is $L = \frac1N\sum_i L_i + \lambda R(W)$, Occam's razor as a soft penalty, with $\lambda$ a hyperparameter to cross-validate. L2 (weight decay) is the most common, L1 encourages sparsity, and elastic net mixes the two. With $x = (1, 1, 1, 1)$, both $w_1 = (1, 0, 0, 0)$ and $w_2 = (\tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac14)$ give the same score, and L2 prefers $w_2$, which spreads influence across the input.

Treat the scores as unnormalized log probabilities: $P(k \mid x) = e^{s_k}/\sum_j e^{s_j}$ and $L_i = -\log P(y_i \mid x_i)$. For the cat, exponentiate to 24.5, 164.0 and 0.18, then normalize to 0.13, 0.87 and 0.00. The loss is $-\ln 0.13 \approx 2.04$. The minimum is 0 and the maximum infinite, neither reachable with finite scores. At initialization the loss is $\log C$. The SVM stops caring once the margin is met, whereas softmax always wants more probability on the correct class. In practice the two perform similarly.

Optimization is walking downhill in a valley you cannot see. Random search reached 15% on CIFAR-10, against 10% for chance and about 95% for the state of the art. Better is to feel the slope. The gradient, the vector of partial derivatives, points uphill, and the slope in any direction is its dot product with that unit vector. Finite differences, one coordinate at a time, are slow and approximate; calculus gives the analytic gradient, exact and fast. Keep the numerical gradient as a GRADIENT CHECK on a scaled-down problem.

Initialize $W$, then repeatedly step against the gradient. The step size (learning rate) is the first hyperparameter to set. The full loss is an average over $N$ examples (1.3 million for ImageNet), and so is its gradient. So estimate it on a minibatch of 32, 64 or 128: this is stochastic gradient descent. Momentum and Adam are refinements to come.

Before ConvNets, the standard approach was to compute features and feed them to a linear classifier: a colour histogram, histograms of oriented gradients over 8×8 cells, or a bag of visual words found by k-means. A transform to polar coordinates can make rings of points linearly separable. ConvNets learn the features from the pixels instead of fixing them in advance.

math210.1.0.worked: Sanity-check a new classifier at iteration 0. With small random weights, the loss should be about $C - 1$ for the SVM, or $\log C$ for softmax (2.30 for ten classes). Then compare the analytic gradient with a finite-difference one on a small problem before training.
math210.1.0.watch: Training with the numerical gradient. It is right for gradient checking and hopeless for training: it needs one loss evaluation per parameter per step, and is still only approximate.

checks.q: $x = (1, 1, 1, 1)$. The weights $w_1 = (1, 0, 0, 0)$ and $w_2 = (0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25)$ give the same score. L2 regularization prefers:

math210.1.1.takeaway: Four choices decide whether a network can train at all. Use ReLU, not sigmoid. Zero-centre the data. Scale the initial weights by the fan-in (Xavier, with a factor of 2 for ReLU). Add batch normalization. Then babysit the run: check the initial loss, overfit a tiny subset, set the learning rate first, and search hyperparameters at random, on a log scale, from coarse to fine.

beats.d: $\sigma(x) = 1/(1 + e^{-x})$ squashes to $[0, 1]$, which made it popular as a neuron's firing rate. First, saturated neurons kill the gradient: at $x = \pm10$ the local gradient is almost 0, and the chain rule multiplies whatever comes from upstream by it. Second, its outputs are not zero-centred: if a neuron's inputs are all positive, every weight gradient has the sign of the upstream gradient, so updates can only move in two quadrants and must zigzag. Third, $\exp$ is mildly expensive.

tanh is zero-centred but still saturates. ReLU, $\max(0, x)$, does not saturate for positive inputs, costs almost nothing, and converged about six times faster in AlexNet (2012). But it is not zero-centred, and its negative half is dead: a ReLU knocked off the data cloud, by bad initialization or more often by too high a learning rate, never fires or updates again, and 10–20% of a trained network can be dead. Leaky ReLU gives the negative side a small slope, PReLU learns that slope, and ELU saturates gently for negative inputs. Maxout, $\max(w_1^{T}x + b_1, w_2^{T}x + b_2)$, neither saturates nor dies, but doubles the parameters. Rule: use ReLU, try the variants, never sigmoid.

Zero-centre the data, for the same reason as above; general machine learning also normalizes, or uses PCA and whitening. For images, subtract the mean image (32×32×3 for CIFAR) or a per-channel mean (as VGG does), computed once on the training set and applied unchanged at test time. It only fixes the first layer.

With $W = 0$, every neuron computes the same thing, gets the same gradient and makes the same update: nothing breaks the symmetry. Small random weights ($0.01 \times$ Gaussian) work for small networks. But in a 10-layer, 500-unit tanh network the activations shrink toward zero layer by layer, so the weight gradients (proportional to the inputs) vanish too. With standard deviation 1 instead, every tanh saturates at $\pm1$ and the gradients are zero again.

Glorot (2010) chose the scale so that output variance equals input variance: $W = \text{randn}/\sqrt{n_{\text{in}}}$. Fewer inputs call for larger weights. The derivation assumes linear activations, and a ReLU zeroes half its inputs, which halves the variance and makes the activations collapse. Divide by $\sqrt{n_{\text{in}}/2}$ instead. In papers this can be the difference between a network training and nothing happening.

If unit Gaussian activations are wanted, force them: for each dimension, $\hat x = (x - \mu_B)/\sqrt{\sigma_B^{2} + \varepsilon}$ over the minibatch. For conv layers there is one mean and variance per activation map, shared across the batch and all spatial locations. It is differentiable, and goes after the fully connected or conv layer. A learned scale and shift, $y = \gamma\hat x + \beta$, lets the network undo it, or choose how much tanh saturation it wants. Gradients flow better, training tolerates more learning rates and initializations, and it regularizes slightly, because each output now depends on the rest of the batch. At test time, use running averages from training.

Check that the initial loss is right: $\ln 10 \approx 2.3$ for ten-class softmax. Turn on regularization and check that the loss rises. Overfit a tiny subset with no regularization, and the loss should reach 0. Then find the learning rate. At $10^{-6}$ the loss barely moves, though accuracy can jump to 20% as diffuse probabilities tilt the right way. At $10^{6}$ the loss becomes NaN. The useful range is roughly $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-3}$.

Go coarse to fine: run a few epochs over wide ranges, and abandon any run whose cost exceeds three times the original. Sample on a log scale, because the learning rate acts multiplicatively. Distrust a best value at the edge of the range. Random search beats grid search, because performance usually depends on a few parameters, and random samples try more distinct values of each. Diagnostics: a big train–validation gap means more regularization; no gap means more capacity; the ratio of update size to weight size should be about $10^{-3}$.

math210.1.1.worked: Before a long run: check the initial loss ($\ln C$ for softmax), check that regularization raises it, and overfit twenty examples to zero loss. Then sweep the learning rate on a log scale for a few epochs and zoom in, making sure the best values sit inside the range, not at its edge.
math210.1.1.watch: Initializing every weight to zero. Every neuron then computes the same output, receives the same gradient and makes the same update, forever. Random initialization breaks the symmetry, and its scale has to match the fan-in.

checks.q: The local gradient of the sigmoid, $\sigma'(x)$, at $x = 0$ is (two decimals):
checks.expl: $\sigma' = \sigma(1 - \sigma) = \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac12$. This is its LARGEST value, so every sigmoid layer shrinks the backward signal by at least a factor of 4, and near $x = \pm10$ it is about $5 \times 10^{-5}$.

checks.q: A ReLU layer with 500 inputs, initialized so the variance is preserved (He: Xavier with the factor of 2). The weight standard deviation is (three decimals):
checks.expl: $\sqrt{2/500} \approx 0.063$. A ReLU passes half the variance of a zero-mean input, $E[\max(0, z)^{2}] = \tfrac12\mathrm{Var}(z)$, so the weights need twice the Xavier variance.

checks.q: Batch normalization of one feature over the minibatch $(1, 2, 3, 6)$. The normalized value of the 6, with $\varepsilon$ negligible, is (two decimals):
Why does random search beat grid search for hyperparameters?
opts: it is cheaper per trial
performance usually depends strongly on few of them, and random samples try many more distinct values of each
grid search cannot use a log scale
random search always finds the optimum
checks.expl: A 3×3 grid tries only three learning rates. Nine random trials try nine.

math210.1.2.takeaway: Plain SGD zigzags across badly conditioned valleys, crawls near saddle points, and wanders with noisy gradients. Momentum adds velocity. AdaGrad and RMSProp divide each coordinate's step by a running size of its gradient. Adam does both, with bias correction, and is the default. Optimizers reduce TRAINING error; regularization (dropout, data augmentation, batch norm), ensembles and transfer learning close the gap to test error.

beats.d: A loss shaped like a taco shell, steep one way and shallow the other, has a bad condition number: the ratio of the Hessian's largest to smallest singular value. SGD zigzags across it and crawls along it, and with millions of parameters some ratio is almost certainly large. Where the gradient is zero it stops. In high dimensions saddle points are everywhere and true local minima are rare, and near a saddle the slope is tiny, so progress is slow. Minibatch noise makes it meander. Full-batch gradient descent fixes none of this.

Keep a velocity: $v \leftarrow \rho v + \nabla f$, $x \leftarrow x - \alpha v$, with friction $\rho \approx 0.9$ and $v$ starting at 0. Like a ball rolling downhill, it carries through local minima and saddles; zigzags cancel while speed builds along the shallow direction; and the noise averages out. The velocity is an exponentially weighted average of past gradients. Nesterov evaluates the gradient where the velocity is about to take you, and a change of variables puts it back at the current point. It overshoots less. Momentum may also skip sharp minima, which could be a feature: flat minima probably generalize better.

AdaGrad adds each squared gradient to a running sum and divides the step by its square root, plus $10^{-7}$ so it never divides by zero. Coordinates with small gradients speed up and steep ones slow down. But the sum only grows, so steps shrink forever: fine for convex problems, bad near saddle points. RMSProp makes the sum leaky, $s \leftarrow 0.99s + 0.01g^{2}$, a kind of momentum over squared gradients.

Adam combines a first moment (momentum) and a second moment (RMSProp) and steps by $m/\sqrt{v}$. Both start at zero, so early steps divide by an almost-zero $v$ and can be huge. Bias correction divides by $1 - \beta^{t}$. With $\beta_1 = 0.9$, $\beta_2 = 0.999$ and a learning rate of $10^{-3}$ or $5 \times 10^{-4}$, it is a great starting point for almost any architecture. It rescales each coordinate axis separately, so it cannot fix a valley that runs diagonally to the axes.

Decay the learning rate: in steps (the sudden drops in ResNet loss curves), exponentially, or as $1/t$. Decay is more common with SGD+momentum than with Adam, and it is a second-order hyperparameter: train without it first, then look at the curve. Newton's step, $x - H^{-1}\nabla f$, jumps to the minimum of a quadratic model and needs no learning rate, but $H$ is $N \times N$ for $N = 10^{8}$. Quasi-Newton methods like L-BFGS approximate it. They suit full-batch, noise-free problems such as style transfer, not stochastic training.

Training ten models and averaging their predictions reliably gains a couple of percent. Snapshots from one run, taken at the lows of a cyclic learning rate, or Polyak averaging of the weights, are cheaper versions of the same idea. Dropout zeroes a random subset of activations on every forward pass. It keeps neurons from co-adapting (no single 'ear' or 'furry' feature can carry the decision) and trains an exponentially large ensemble of subnetworks that share weights. At test time, remove the randomness: multiply by the keep probability $p$, or divide by $p$ during training (inverted dropout). Training takes longer.

beats.t: Noise in training, averaged at test
beats.d: The general pattern: add randomness during training, then marginalize it out at test. Dropout is one example. Batch normalization is another: an example's normalization depends on its batch during training and on fixed statistics at test. Data augmentation uses random flips, random crops (tested on 10 fixed crops), and colour jitter. DropConnect zeroes weights instead of activations; fractional max pooling uses random pooling regions; stochastic depth drops whole layers. Use batch norm by default, and add dropout if the network overfits.

It busts the myth that a CNN needs huge data. Train on ImageNet. Replace the last layer (4096×1000 becomes 4096×C), freeze everything else, and train a linear classifier. With more data, fine-tune more layers at a lower learning rate. Data unlike ImageNet (X-rays, say) needs more re-initialization. It is the norm, not the exception: every framework ships a model zoo.

math210.1.2.worked: A default that works for most new problems: Adam with $\beta_1 = 0.9$, $\beta_2 = 0.999$ and a learning rate of $10^{-3}$ or $5 \times 10^{-4}$. Put batch normalization in the network. Add dropout only once the validation curve shows overfitting. Start from a pretrained model if your dataset is small.
math210.1.2.watch: Forgetting to rescale dropout at test time. With keep probability $\tfrac12$, a neuron saw half its inputs on average during training. Run it on all of them and every activation doubles. Multiply by $p$ at test time, or divide by $p$ during training.

checks.q: Momentum with $\rho = 0.9$, starting from $v = 0$, under a gradient that stays constant at $g$. The velocity approaches what multiple of $g$?
checks.expl: The steady state satisfies $v = 0.9v + g$, so $v = g/(1 - \rho) = 10g$. On a long gentle slope, momentum steps ten times further than SGD.

checks.q: Adam with $\beta_1 = 0.9$, $\beta_2 = 0.999$ and NO bias correction. On step 1, $m/\sqrt{v}$ equals what multiple of $\mathrm{sign}(g)$ ($\varepsilon$ ignored; two decimals)?
checks.expl: $m = 0.1g$ and $v = 0.001g^{2}$, so $m/\sqrt v = 0.1/\sqrt{0.001} \approx 3.16$. Bias correction divides by $1 - 0.9$ and $1 - 0.999$, which brings it back to 1.

checks.q: A neuron $a = w_1x + w_2y$ with $w_1 = 2$, $x = 3$, $w_2 = 1$, $y = 4$, trained with dropout that keeps each input with probability $\tfrac12$. Its expected output during training is:
checks.expl: Average over the four masks: $(0 + 6 + 4 + 10)/4 = 5$, half the test-time value of 10. That is why test outputs are multiplied by $p$.

checks.q: In a network with $10^{8}$ parameters, the points where SGD most often stalls are:
opts: sharp local minima
saddle points, where some directions go up and others go down
global minima
points of infinite gradient
checks.expl: A local minimum needs every one of $10^{8}$ directions to curve upward, which is rare. A saddle only needs a mix, which is almost everywhere. Momentum helps carry through.

math210.1.3.takeaway: On a quadratic, gradient descent splits into independent eigen-directions, each shrinking by $|1 - \alpha\lambda_i|$, so the condition number $\kappa = \lambda_n/\lambda_1$ sets the pace: at best $(\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1)$ per step. Momentum turns each direction into a damped oscillator, and with the right $\alpha$ and $\beta$ the rate becomes $(\sqrt\kappa - 1)/(\sqrt\kappa + 1)$. That is a square-root speedup, and no first-order method can beat it.

beats.d: Gradient descent: $w^{k+1} = w^{k} - \alpha\nabla f(w^{k})$. Momentum adds a memory: $z^{k+1} = \beta z^{k} + \nabla f(w^{k})$, $w^{k+1} = w^{k} - \alpha z^{k+1}$. The usual story is a ball rolling downhill, but the article sets out to show exactly why it helps: a quadratic speedup on many functions.

Take $f(w) = \tfrac12 w^{T}Aw - b^{T}w$ with $A = Q\,\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_i)\,Q^{T}$. In eigen-coordinates $x = Q^{T}(w - w^{*})$ the iteration decouples: $x_i^{k} = (1 - \alpha\lambda_i)^{k}x_i^{0}$. The error is a sum of eigen-components, each decaying at its own rate. The large-$\lambda$ ones go first, which is why loss curves drop fast and then crawl.

Convergence needs $0 \lt \alpha\lambda_i \lt 2$ for every $i$, so $\alpha \lt 2/\lambda_n$. The overall rate is $\max_i |1 - \alpha\lambda_i|$, which depends only on the two extreme eigenvalues. It is minimized by $\alpha = 2/(\lambda_1 + \lambda_n)$, where the rate is $(\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1)$. When $\kappa$ is large, that is barely below 1.

Fitting a polynomial by gradient descent makes the eigenvectors concrete. The eigenfeatures with large eigenvalues are smooth and fitted early. Those with small eigenvalues are wiggly and fitted late, if ever. Stopping early therefore acts as a regularizer: it never reaches the directions that overfit.

Per eigen-direction, momentum is a 2×2 linear recurrence, and its rate is the larger magnitude of that matrix's two eigenvalues. It converges for $0 \lt \alpha\lambda \lt 2 + 2\beta$, a wider range than plain descent. As $\beta$ varies, the path ripples, decreases monotonically, or oscillates. Critical damping, at $\beta = (1 - \sqrt{\alpha\lambda})^{2}$, is the fastest.

Tune for the extreme eigenvalues: $\alpha = \left(2/(\sqrt{\lambda_1} + \sqrt{\lambda_n})\right)^{2}$ and $\beta = \left((\sqrt\kappa - 1)/(\sqrt\kappa + 1)\right)^{2}$. The rate becomes $(\sqrt\kappa - 1)/(\sqrt\kappa + 1)$, so the number of iterations scales like $\sqrt\kappa$ instead of $\kappa$. For $\kappa = 100$ the rate falls from 0.98 to 0.82 per step.

Spread colour along a graph by penalizing differences between neighbours: a quadratic built on the graph Laplacian. Information travels one edge per step, and the condition number grows with the graph's size, like $n^{2}$ for a path. Momentum spreads the information visibly faster.

beats.t: The limits of descent, and noise
beats.d: Nesterov's lower bound: on a badly conditioned 'convex Rosenbrock' function, no first-order method can beat $(\sqrt\kappa - 1)/(\sqrt\kappa + 1)$, so momentum is optimal in that sense. With stochastic gradients, the error has a transient phase, which momentum speeds up, and a fine-tuning phase dominated by noise, which momentum does not remove. The optimal $\beta$ found on a quadratic is a guide, not a guarantee, for a neural network.

math210.1.3.worked: To reason about a step size: find (or estimate) the extreme eigenvalues of the Hessian. Plain descent is stable only for $\alpha \lt 2/\lambda_{\max}$, and its best rate is $(\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1)$. With momentum, use $\beta \approx ((\sqrt\kappa - 1)/(\sqrt\kappa + 1))^{2}$. Needing $\sqrt\kappa$ iterations instead of $\kappa$ is the whole gain.
math210.1.3.watch: Reading the early drop of the loss as convergence. The large-eigenvalue components vanish first. The small-eigenvalue ones, which set the rate, have hardly started.

checks.q: Gradient descent on $f = \tfrac12(x^{2} + 100y^{2})$, so $\kappa = 100$. With the best fixed step size, the error shrinks per step by a factor of (two decimals):
The same function with optimally tuned momentum. The per-step rate is (two decimals):
checks.expl: $(\sqrt{100} - 1)/(\sqrt{100} + 1) = 9/11 \approx 0.82$. Reducing the error a thousandfold takes about 35 steps instead of about 350.

checks.q: On $f = \tfrac12(x^{2} + 100y^{2})$, the largest step size for which plain gradient descent still converges is (supremum, two decimals):
checks.expl: The $y$ component is multiplied by $1 - 100\alpha$ each step, which needs $|1 - 100\alpha| \lt 1$, so $\alpha \lt 2/100$. The steepest direction sets the limit.

checks.q: Early in gradient descent the loss falls quickly, then crawls. Why?
opts: the learning rate decays automatically
components along large-eigenvalue directions vanish fast; the small-eigenvalue ones decay at $|1 - \alpha\lambda_1|$, close to 1
the gradient becomes noisy
the function stops being quadratic
checks.expl: Each eigen-component has its own rate. The slow ones dominate once the fast ones have gone.

math210.1.4.takeaway: A field guide to the update rules. Gradient descent comes in batch, stochastic and mini-batch variants. Momentum and Nesterov add velocity. Adagrad, Adadelta, RMSprop, Adam, AdaMax and Nadam adapt the learning rate for each parameter. Around them sit practical tricks: shuffling, curriculum learning, batch normalization, early stopping and gradient noise. Adaptive methods suit sparse data; Adam is a sound default; well-tuned SGD with a schedule remains competitive.

beats.d: Batch gradient descent uses the whole dataset for each update: it converges to the global minimum on convex problems, but is slow and cannot learn online. SGD updates on one example at a time: fast and noisy, and the noise can jump into better basins; with a decaying learning rate it behaves like batch descent. Mini-batch, with 50 to 256 examples, cuts the variance and uses fast matrix operations. It is what 'SGD' usually means.

The learning rate is hard to choose. Predefined schedules cannot adapt to the data. One rate for all parameters is wrong for sparse features, which want larger updates when they finally appear. And saddle points, not local minima, are the real obstacle in high dimensions (Dauphin et al.).

Momentum: $v_t = \gamma v_{t-1} + \eta\nabla J(\theta)$, $\theta \leftarrow \theta - v_t$, with $\gamma \approx 0.9$. It builds speed where gradients agree and damps where they flip. Nesterov takes the gradient at the look-ahead point $\theta - \gamma v_{t-1}$, correcting before it overshoots, which helped RNNs.

Adagrad divides each parameter's rate by the root of its accumulated squared gradients, $\theta_i \leftarrow \theta_i - \eta g_i/\sqrt{G_{ii} + \epsilon}$. Rare features get large steps, which is good for sparse data (it trained GloVe), but the accumulator only grows, so learning eventually stops. Adadelta keeps a decaying average instead, $E[g^{2}]_t = \gamma E[g^{2}]_{t-1} + (1 - \gamma)g_t^{2}$, and replaces $\eta$ with the RMS of recent updates, so it needs no learning rate. RMSprop, from Hinton's lecture notes, is the same decaying average with $\gamma = 0.9$ and $\eta = 0.001$.

Adam keeps decaying averages of $g$ and $g^{2}$ ($\beta_1 = 0.9$, $\beta_2 = 0.999$, $\epsilon = 10^{-8}$). Both start at zero and are biased toward it, so it divides by $1 - \beta^{t}$. It behaves like a heavy ball with friction. AdaMax replaces the $\ell_2$ scaling with $\ell_\infty$: $u_t = \max(\beta_2u_{t-1}, |g_t|)$. Nadam is Adam with a Nesterov look-ahead.

On the Beale function and at a saddle point, the adaptive methods head the right way at once. Momentum and NAG overshoot like a rolling ball, with NAG correcting sooner. At the saddle, SGD barely escapes. For sparse inputs, use an adaptive method. RMSprop, Adadelta and Adam behave alike, with Adam's bias correction giving it a slight edge. Plain SGD with an annealing schedule often works but is slower, more sensitive to initialization, and prone to stalling at saddles.

Hogwild! lets processors update shared memory without locks, which is safe when updates are sparse. Downpour SGD (DistBelief) runs model replicas against a parameter server. There are delay-tolerant algorithms, TensorFlow's distributed runtime, and elastic averaging SGD, which lets workers drift from a centre variable to explore.

Shuffle every epoch, or use curriculum learning (easy examples first, mixed with random ones). Batch normalization permits higher learning rates. Early stopping on validation error is what Hinton called a 'beautiful free lunch'. Gradient noise, Gaussian with annealed variance $\eta/(1 + t)^{\gamma}$, helps very deep networks train.

math210.1.4.worked: Choosing an optimizer: with sparse features, pick an adaptive method (Adagrad family or Adam). Otherwise start with Adam at its default settings. If you have the time to tune, SGD with momentum and a learning-rate schedule can match or beat it. Always shuffle, and keep early stopping on.
math210.1.4.watch: Leaving Adagrad running indefinitely. Its denominator is a sum of squares that never shrinks, so the effective learning rate decays like $1/\sqrt t$ and training quietly stops. That is the flaw Adadelta, RMSprop and Adam were designed to fix.

checks.q: Adagrad sees the same gradient on every step. Ignoring $\epsilon$, its step at $t = 100$ is what fraction of its first step?
checks.expl: The accumulator is $t g^{2}$, so the step is $\eta g/\sqrt{t g^{2}} = \eta/\sqrt t$: one tenth at $t = 100$.

checks.q: A decaying average $E[g^{2}]$ starts at 0 with $\gamma = 0.9$, and every gradient is 1. After 10 steps it equals (two decimals):
checks.expl: $E_t = 0.9E_{t-1} + 0.1$ gives $1 - 0.9^{10} \approx 0.65$, still biased toward its zero start. That is why Adam divides by $1 - \beta^{t}$.

checks.q: For a model whose input features are very sparse, the overview recommends:
opts: plain SGD with a fixed rate
an adaptive learning-rate method
batch gradient descent
momentum without an adaptive rate
checks.expl: Adaptive methods give rarely seen features larger updates, with no tuning of per-feature rates.

checks.q: Adadelta needs no global learning rate because:
opts: it uses second derivatives
it replaces $\eta$ with the RMS of recent parameter updates, which also fixes the units
it fixes $\eta = 1$
it normalizes the weights
checks.expl: The ratio $\mathrm{RMS}[\Delta\theta]_{t-1}/\mathrm{RMS}[g]_t$ has the units of $\theta$ per unit gradient, so it acts as a self-scaled learning rate.

math210.1.5.takeaway: A set is convex if it contains every segment between its points. A function is convex if its graph lies below every chord, or equivalently above every tangent plane, which is why a zero gradient means a GLOBAL minimum. Rather than checking the definition every time, build convex things from known examples using operations that preserve convexity.

beats.d: $C$ is convex if $\theta x_1 + (1 - \theta)x_2 \in C$ for all $x_1, x_2 \in C$ and $\theta \in [0, 1]$. Affine sets contain whole lines, cones contain every ray through their points, and the convex hull is the smallest convex set containing given points. Standard examples are hyperplanes $\{a^{T}x = b\}$, halfspaces, Euclidean balls, ellipsoids, norm balls and norm cones, polyhedra $\{Ax \preceq b,\ Cx = d\}$, simplexes, and the cone of positive semidefinite matrices.

Intersections (of any number of sets), affine images and preimages, the perspective map $(x, t) \mapsto x/t$, and linear-fractional maps all keep a set convex. Proving convexity usually means writing the set as one of these built from known pieces.

A proper cone $K$ defines an order: $x \preceq_K y$ means $y - x \in K$ (for example, componentwise order, or $A \preceq B$ for matrices). Its dual cone is $K^{*} = \{y : y^{T}x \ge 0 \text{ for all } x \in K\}$. The nonnegative orthant and the PSD cone are self-dual. Minimum and minimal elements behave differently under a partial order.

Two disjoint convex sets can be separated by a hyperplane, $a^{T}x \le b$ on one side and $\ge b$ on the other. At every boundary point of a convex set there is a supporting hyperplane. These geometric facts underlie duality and optimality conditions.

$f$ is convex if its domain is convex and $f(	heta x + (1 - 	heta)y) \le 	heta f(x) + (1 - 	heta)f(y)$. First-order condition: $f(y) \ge f(x) + 
abla f(x)^{T}(y - x)$. The tangent is a GLOBAL underestimator, so $
abla f(x) = 0$ means a global minimum. Second-order condition: $
abla^{2}f \succeq 0$. The epigraph is a convex set, sublevel sets are convex, and Jensen's inequality gives $f(E x) \le E f(x)$.

Convex: $e^{ax}$; $x^{a}$ on $x \gt 0$ for $a \ge 1$ or $a \le 0$; $|x|^{p}$ for $p \ge 1$; $-\log x$; $x\log x$; every norm; $\max_i x_i$; the quadratic-over-linear $x^{2}/y$ for $y \gt 0$; and log-sum-exp, $\log\sum e^{x_i}$, a smooth max whose gradient is the softmax. Concave: the geometric mean, and $\log\det X$ on positive definite matrices.

Nonnegative weighted sums, composition with an affine map, pointwise maximum or supremum (so the largest eigenvalue is convex), the composition rules (a convex, nondecreasing $h$ of a convex $g$ is convex), minimization over some of the variables, and the perspective $t f(x/t)$ all preserve convexity.

The conjugate $f^{*}(y) = \sup_x\,(y^{T}x - f(x))$ is always convex, being a supremum of affine functions. Fenchel's inequality: $f(x) + f^{*}(y) \ge x^{T}y$. Example: $\tfrac12x^{T}Qx$ has conjugate $\tfrac12y^{T}Q^{-1}y$. Weaker notions: quasiconvex functions (convex sublevel sets) and log-concave functions (Gaussian densities; closed under products and marginalization).

math210.1.5.worked: To prove a function is convex, avoid the definition. Assemble the function from the catalogue (norms, $-\log$, log-sum-exp, quadratics with PSD matrices) using the operations that preserve convexity (sums, affine substitution, maxima, the composition rules). If that fails, check whether the Hessian is positive semidefinite.
math210.1.5.watch: Taking the minimum of convex functions, or the union of convex sets. Maxima and intersections preserve convexity; minima and unions do not. $\min(x^{2}, (x - 2)^{2})$ has two separate valleys.

checks.q: $x$ is 0 or 2 with probability $\tfrac12$ each, and $f(x) = e^{x}$. The Jensen gap $E f(x) - f(E x)$ is (two decimals):
checks.expl: $E f = (1 + e^{2})/2 \approx 4.19$ and $f(E x) = e \approx 2.72$. The gap is about $1.48$, positive as Jensen requires for convex $f$.

checks.q: The conjugate of $f(x) = -\log x$ is $f^{*}(y) = \sup_{x \gt 0}(yx + \log x)$. At $y = -2$ it equals (two decimals):
checks.expl: The supremum is at $x = -1/y = \tfrac12$: $-1 + \log\tfrac12 = -1 - \log 2 \approx -1.69$. In general $f^{*}(y) = -1 - \log(-y)$ for $y \lt 0$.

checks.q: For a differentiable convex $f$, $\nabla f(x^{*}) = 0$ implies:
opts: $x^{*}$ is a local minimum only
$x^{*}$ is a global minimum, because the tangent plane at $x^{*}$ lies below $f$ everywhere
$x^{*}$ is a saddle point
nothing without the Hessian
checks.expl: The first-order condition gives $f(y) \ge f(x^{*}) + 0$ for every $y$.

checks.q: Which operation does NOT preserve convexity?
opts: pointwise maximum of convex functions
intersection of convex sets
pointwise minimum of convex functions
composition with an affine map
checks.expl: $\min(x^{2}, (x - 2)^{2})$ is not convex: its chord from 0 to 2 lies below the graph at 1.

math210.2.0.takeaway: Shannon's problem is reliable communication over an unreliable channel. Instead of buying better physics, wrap the channel in an encoder that adds redundancy and a decoder that uses inference to remove the noise. Repetition codes lower the error only by driving the rate toward zero. Shannon proved that below the channel's capacity (0.53 for a binary symmetric channel that flips 10% of bits), the error can be made as small as you like at a fixed rate.

beats.d: Voice to ear through air. Eye to brain. DNA copied into each of $10^{13}$ cells. An antenna talking to a Mars rover. A phone line. A disk drive, which carries a message from one place to the same place at a later time. In every one of them, what is received is not quite what was sent.

Either improve the physics (better insulation, cooling, a better magnetic film), or accept the lousy channel and build systems around it. The source $s$ goes through an encoder, which we design to add redundancy, to give the transmission $t$. The channel adds noise, and we receive $r$. The decoder, which we also design, infers the noise and the source and outputs a guess $\hat s$.

A bit goes in and a bit comes out, flipped with probability $f$ (say 0.1). A 10,000-bit file on such a disk has $1000 \pm 30$ bits flipped: the binomial mean is $Nf$, the variance $Nf(1 - f) = 900$, and the standard deviation 30. The binomial distribution is nearly all the mathematics the course needs. How small must $f$ be? Five years at 1 GB per day is about $10^{13}$ bits. A 1% chance of any error at all needs about $10^{-15}$; a thousand happy customers need $10^{-18}$, which is the industry's standard.

$R_3$ sends each bit three times. Decode by majority vote, and justify it with the rules of probability: the product rule, the sum rule, and so Bayes' theorem. For $r = 011$ with equal priors, $P(s = 1 \mid r) = 1 - f$: the likelihood favours the hypothesis that needs the fewest flips. The decoder fails on two or more flips, $3f^{2}(1 - f) + f^{3} \approx 3f^{2}$, at rate $\tfrac13$. Reaching $10^{-15}$ needs about 61 repetitions: 61 disk drives in the box.

Four source bits go in three overlapping circles, and three parity bits make each circle's parity even: 1000 encodes to 1000101. To decode, write what was received into the circles. The syndrome is the pattern of unhappy circles; flip the one bit that is inside every unhappy circle and outside every happy one. It corrects any single flip. Two flips make it add a third error. Rate $\tfrac47$; block error about $21f^{2}$ and bit error about $9f^{2}$ for small $f$.

Conventional wisdom drew the boundary between achievable and unachievable (rate, error) pairs through the origin: vanishing error seemed to need vanishing rate. Shannon proved the boundary meets the rate axis at a positive value, the capacity $C$. For the binary symmetric channel, $C = 1 - H_2(f)$ with $H_2(f) = f\log_2\frac1f + (1 - f)\log_2\frac1{1 - f}$.

For $f = 0.1$, $C \approx 0.53 \gt \tfrac12$. So a rate-$\tfrac12$ system — two drives in the box — has encoders and decoders achieving $10^{-15}$, or $10^{-18}$, or $10^{-60}$. That is the noisy-channel coding theorem, and proving it is the heart of the course.

First data compression, then modelling, inference and neural networks. The puzzle to think about: twelve balls, one heavier or lighter than the rest, and a balance. Find the odd ball, and whether it is heavy or light, in as few weighings as possible.

math210.2.0.worked: To decode any code on a binary symmetric channel with $f \lt \tfrac12$: the posterior of each candidate message is proportional to $f^{d}(1 - f)^{N - d}$, where $d$ is the number of flips it would need. So choose the codeword closest in Hamming distance to what was received. For $R_3$ that is the majority vote; for the Hamming code, the syndrome points at the single most likely flip.
math210.2.0.watch: Thinking reliability must cost rate without limit. Repetition codes do trade them off that way, but Shannon's theorem says any rate below $C$ can reach any error target. Repetition is just a very poor code.

checks.q: The repetition code $R_3$ with majority vote on a binary symmetric channel with $f = 0.1$. The probability that a decoded bit is wrong is (three decimals):
checks.expl: It fails when two or three of the three copies flip: $3f^{2}(1 - f) + f^{3} = 0.027 + 0.001 = 0.028$.

checks.q: The capacity of the binary symmetric channel with $f = 0.1$, $C = 1 - H_2(0.1)$, is (two decimals):
checks.expl: $H_2(0.1) = 0.1\log_2 10 + 0.9\log_2\frac{10}{9} \approx 0.469$, so $C \approx 0.53$ bits per channel use.

checks.q: The (7, 4) Hamming code with syndrome decoding at $f = 0.1$. The exact probability that a block is decoded wrongly is (two decimals):
checks.expl: The decoder succeeds only with zero or one flip: $1 - 0.9^{7} - 7(0.1)(0.9)^{6} \approx 0.15$. The $21f^{2}$ estimate (0.21) is only good for small $f$.

checks.q: Majority vote is the right decoder for $R_3$ because:
opts: it is the simplest rule
with equal priors, the posterior favours the source bit whose transmission needs the fewest flips to explain what was received
it guarantees zero error
the channel is symmetric, so any rule works
checks.expl: Each flip multiplies the likelihood by $f/(1 - f) \lt 1$, so fewer flips means a more probable explanation.

math210.2.1.takeaway: Real sources are redundant, so compress first (source coding), then add the right redundancy for the channel. Shannon measures the information in an outcome as $\log_2(1/p)$ bits: zero for a certainty, large for a surprise, and additive for independent events. Its average, the entropy $H(X) = \sum p\log_2(1/p)$, measures a whole ensemble. It turns the weighing puzzle into a recipe: choose the weighing whose outcome has maximum entropy.

beats.d: A passage of Jane Austen's Emma with a third of its letters erased can still be read aloud. So the full system is: compress, encode for the channel, send, decode, decompress. Source coding comes first, channel coding second.

An ensemble $X$ is a random variable $x$, an alphabet $\mathcal A_X = \{a_1, \ldots, a_I\}$, and probabilities $p_i \ge 0$ that sum to 1. The bent coin is the toy example: 0 with probability 0.9 and 1 with probability 0.1. Toss it a thousand times. How much information is there, how should it be compressed, and what is the smallest possible file?

$h(x) = \log_2\frac1{P(x)}$ bits. A certain outcome carries 0 bits and a 50/50 outcome 1 bit. The bent coin's tail carries 0.15 bits and its head 3.3 bits. Shannon's claim is that this is both the right measure of information and the compressed length to aspire to.

It is additive for independent variables: if $P(x, y) = P(x)P(y)$, then $h(x, y) = h(x) + h(y)$. Being told the coin landed tails and it is not raining is worth the same as being told each separately. And it is biggest for improbable outcomes.
$H(X) = \sum_x P(x)\log_2\frac1{P(x)}$, the average information content, in bits. It is maximized by the uniform distribution: to share out cake as fairly as possible, make the pieces equal.

With 12 balls, one odd, there are 24 equally likely hypotheses. The entropy of each possible first weighing's outcome: 6 v 6 gives 1 bit (it never balances); 5 v 5, 1.48; 4 v 4, $\log_2 3 = 1.58$; 3 v 3, 1.5; 2 v 2, 1.25; 1 v 1, 0.82. Shannon's advice is 4 against 4, which is what most of the room chose after thinking hard.

Say the left side went down. That leaves four possibly-heavy balls, four possibly-light ones, and four known good. Weighing four good against the four possibly-light gives $(\tfrac12, \tfrac12, 0)$: 1 bit. The popular choice gives $(\tfrac48, \tfrac28, \tfrac28)$: 1.5 bits. A weighing splitting the eight hypotheses 3, 3, 2 is closer to uniform, at 1.56 bits. Keep choosing the most informative weighing and you finish in three.

The information has to be relevant: staring at television static is maximally informative and useless. And the greedy choice is only a rule of thumb, since an informative first move can lead into a dead end. For this puzzle it works. Next time's puzzle, the bent-coin lottery: which tickets buy a 99% chance of winning, and how many are there?

math210.2.1.worked: To pick the most informative experiment: list its possible outcomes, work out each one's probability by counting the equally likely hypotheses it covers, and compute the entropy. Choose the experiment with the largest entropy, aiming for outcome probabilities as close to uniform as possible.
math210.2.1.watch: Choosing a weighing because it could be decisive. Six against six seems bold, but it always tips, so it tells you only which side: 1 bit. Four against four has three equally likely outcomes, and that is where the information is.

checks.q: The bent coin lands heads with probability 0.1. The Shannon information content of seeing a head is (two decimals):
checks.expl: $\log_2(1/0.1) = \log_2 10 \approx 3.32$ bits. A tail, with probability 0.9, is worth only 0.15 bits.

checks.q: The entropy of that bent coin, $H_2(0.1)$, is (two decimals):
checks.expl: $0.1 \times 3.32 + 0.9 \times 0.152 \approx 0.47$ bits per toss, so a thousand tosses should compress to about 470 bits.

checks.q: Twelve balls, one odd (heavy or light, 24 equal hypotheses). The entropy of the outcome of weighing four against four is (three decimals):
checks.expl: Left down, balanced, and right down each cover 8 of the 24 hypotheses, so the entropy is $\log_2 3 \approx 1.585$ bits, the largest of any first weighing.

checks.q: Choosing the experiment with the largest entropy can mislead when:
opts: the probabilities are uniform
the information gained is irrelevant to the question, or a greedy first move leads into a dead end
there are only three outcomes
entropy is measured in bits
checks.expl: TV static has enormous entropy and tells you nothing about the odd ball. Maximizing entropy is a guide, not a theorem.

math210.2.2.takeaway: Three games support Shannon's measure. In 63, six yes/no questions, each worth one bit, identify a number from 0 to 63. In submarine, the information contents of every miss and the final hit always add up to $\log_2 64 = 6$ bits. In the bent-coin lottery, the tickets needed for a 99% chance of winning number about $2^{NH}$. That is the source coding theorem: N outcomes compress to about $NH$ bits.

beats.d: Ask 'is $x \ge 32$?', then '$x \bmod 32 \ge 16$?', and so on down. The answers 101010 spell 42 in binary. Each answer was 50/50, worth one bit, so six questions collect six bits, and the string of answers is itself an encoding of $x$. In general, giving each of $S$ outcomes a unique fixed-length binary name (MacKay labelling his underwear) takes $\lceil\log_2 S\rceil$ bits.
Splitting the remaining possibilities exactly in half maximizes the expected information of each question. 'Is it prime?' gives an unequal split, and on average you learn less.

One submarine is hidden in 64 squares. The first miss had probability $\tfrac{63}{64}$, so it is worth $\log_2\tfrac{64}{63} \approx 0.0227$ bits; the next miss $\log_2\tfrac{63}{62}$; and so on. Thirty-two misses add up to exactly 1 bit, like asking 'is it in this half?'. The final hit brings a burst (4.3 bits in the demo), and the running total telescopes to $\log_2 64 = 6$ bits, whenever the hit comes.

Toss a coin with $f = 0.1$ a thousand times, and the winning ticket is that exact string. If you may buy only one ticket, buy the all-zeros one: it is the single most probable. In a run with $N = 20$ it won 10 times, while the 'typical-looking' tickets with two scattered ones never won.

Buy tickets in order of probability: every ticket with 0 ones, then 1, then 2, and so on up to $r_{\max}$. The number of ones has mean $Nf = 100$ and standard deviation $\sqrt{Nf(1 - f)} = \sqrt{90} \approx 9.5$, so $r_{\max} \approx 123$, about 2.3 standard deviations up, is needed.

That is $\sum_{r \le 123}\binom{1000}{r}$ tickets, dominated by the last term. Using $\log_2\binom{N}{r} \approx N H_2(r/N)$, $\binom{1000}{100} \approx 2^{469}$, and the whole purchase is about $2^{530}$. In general it is $2^{NH_2(f) + O(\sqrt N)}$: the fluctuations grow only like $\sqrt N$.

Write a 530-bit name on the back of every ticket. To compress a coin-toss file, find its ticket and send the name; to decompress, look the name up. It works 99% of the time, and a little more $\sqrt N$ pushes that higher. So $N$ outcomes compress to about $NH$ bits. That is the source coding theorem, proved by counting the typical set: the strings with about $Nf$ ones. Chapter 4 has the general proof.

$2^{500}$ tickets is more than the number of electrons in the universe. Practical compressors come next. The project: invent a compressor and decompressor for 10,000 tosses of a coin with $P(1) = 0.01$, and measure how well they work.

math210.2.2.worked: To estimate how far a source can be compressed: the typical outcomes of $N$ draws number about $2^{NH}$ and are roughly equally probable, so naming them takes about $NH$ bits. For a bent coin, $H = H_2(f)$, and the typical strings are those with about $Nf$ ones, give or take $\sqrt{Nf(1 - f)}$.
math210.2.2.watch: Confusing the most probable outcome with a typical one. The all-zeros string is the likeliest single ticket, but almost every actual draw has about 100 ones. The typical set is where the probability mass lies, even though each of its members is individually unlikely.

checks.q: Submarine on 64 squares: the first 32 shots all miss. The total Shannon information gained is (bits):
checks.expl: $\log_2\tfrac{64}{63} + \log_2\tfrac{63}{62} + \cdots + \log_2\tfrac{33}{32}$ telescopes to $\log_2 2 = 1$: exactly the answer to 'is it in the first half?'.

checks.q: A thousand tosses of a coin with $P(1) = 0.1$. The standard deviation of the number of ones is (two decimals):
checks.expl: $\sqrt{Nf(1 - f)} = \sqrt{90} \approx 9.49$, which is why the typical set is '100 give or take a few tens'.

checks.q: In the game of 63 extended to the numbers 0 to 999, the number of yes/no questions that always suffices is:
Forced to buy one ticket in the bent-coin lottery ($f = 0.1$, $N = 1000$), the best choice is:
opts: a string with exactly 100 ones spread out
the all-zeros string
the all-ones string
any string; they are equally likely
checks.expl: Each extra one multiplies the probability by $0.1/0.9$, so all-zeros is the single most probable string, even though the actual outcome will almost surely have about 100 ones.

math210.2.3.takeaway: A symbol code gives each symbol a binary codeword and concatenates them without punctuation. To be uniquely decodable, its codeword lengths must satisfy the Kraft inequality $\sum 2^{-l_i} \le 1$, a fixed budget: shortening one codeword forces others to lengthen. The expected length is then at least the entropy, reaching it exactly when $l_i = \log_2(1/p_i)$. Prefix codes are easy to decode, and the Huffman algorithm builds an optimal one, always within one bit of $H$.

beats.d: The typical-set proof needed a bag of $2^{500}$ tickets. Symbol codes are practical: a map $c: \mathcal A_X \to \{0, 1\}^{+}$ from each symbol to a binary string. A file is encoded by concatenating its codewords with no punctuation, so the receiver has to work out where the boundaries fall.

The code must be uniquely decodable: distinct strings must have distinct encodings, always, not just 99.9% of the time. It should ideally be easy to decode. And it should have small expected length, $L(C, X) = \sum_i p_i l_i$.

Take $a, b, c, d$ with probabilities $\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac18$, so $H = 1.75$ bits. Fixed four-bit codewords give $L = 4$. Dropping their trailing zeros (1, 01, 001, 0001) still lets the receiver punctuate, and gives $L = 1.875$. A code with lengths 1, 2, 3, 2 reaches $L = 1.625$, below the entropy. Too good to be true: two different strings share an encoding.

The code 1, 01, 001, 000 has lengths 1, 2, 3, 3, equal to the information contents, so $L = H = 1.75$. No codeword is a prefix of another, so the receiver decodes as it reads, walking down a binary tree. Reversing every codeword gives a code that is still uniquely decodable, but not prefix-free, so the receiver may have to wait arbitrarily long to decode.

'Give the shortest codewords to the most probable symbols' has the right spirit, but it is not an algorithm. With four probabilities all essentially $\tfrac14$, the lengths 1, 2, 3, 3 give 2.25 bits, while 00, 01, 10, 11 give 2. Shorten one codeword and others must grow, like squeezing one finger of a water-filled glove.

A codeword of length $l$ costs $2^{-l}$ from a budget of 1. Any uniquely decodable code satisfies $\sum_i 2^{-l_i} \le 1$, the Kraft inequality. The 1, 2, 3, 2 code spends 1.125, so it could never have worked, and no search for a counterexample was needed. A complete code spends exactly 1.

Define implicit probabilities $q_i = 2^{-l_i}/z$, where $z = \sum 2^{-l_i} \le 1$. Then $L = H(X) + D_{KL}(p\,\|\,q) + \log_2\frac1z$. Gibbs' inequality gives $D_{KL} \ge 0$, so $L \ge H$, with equality exactly when $l_i = \log_2(1/p_i)$. Those are rarely integers, but an optimal symbol code always achieves $H \le L \lt H + 1$.

Build the tree from its leaves: merge the two least probable symbols into one whose probability is their sum, and repeat until one remains. Label the branches 0 and 1, and read each codeword from the root outward. The result is an optimal prefix code.

math210.2.3.worked: To build a Huffman code: list the probabilities, repeatedly merge the two smallest, and record the merges as a binary tree. A symbol's codeword length is its depth in the tree. Check the result: $\sum 2^{-l_i} = 1$, and $H \le L \lt H + 1$.
math210.2.3.watch: Celebrating an expected length below the entropy. It means the code is not uniquely decodable, and the Kraft sum will exceed 1. Check that sum before hunting for a pair of strings with the same encoding.

checks.q: A proposed code for four symbols has codeword lengths 1, 2, 3 and 2. Its Kraft sum $\sum 2^{-l_i}$ is:
checks.expl: $\tfrac12 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac18 + \tfrac14 = 1.125 \gt 1$, so no uniquely decodable code has these lengths.

checks.q: Probabilities $\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac18$ coded with four two-bit codewords, so $L = 2$ against $H = 1.75$. The gap, $D_{KL}(p\,\|\,q)$ with $q$ uniform, is (bits):
checks.expl: $\sum p\log_2(p/q) = \tfrac12(1) + \tfrac14(0) + \tfrac18(-1) + \tfrac18(-1) = 0.25$. The code's implicit probabilities are uniform, and the mismatch costs exactly the KL divergence.

checks.q: The optimal symbol code for probabilities $0.25, 0.25, 0.2, 0.15, 0.15$ has expected length (bits):
checks.expl: Huffman merges 0.15 + 0.15, then 0.2 + 0.25, then 0.25 + 0.3, then the last two, giving lengths 2, 2, 2, 3, 3 and $L = 2.3$. The entropy is 2.29 bits, within one bit as promised.

checks.q: Why are prefix codes preferred among uniquely decodable codes?
opts: they are always shorter
they can be decoded as the bits arrive, and any set of lengths satisfying Kraft can be realized by one
they avoid the Kraft inequality
only prefix codes can reach the entropy
checks.expl: Buy codewords in order of length across the supermarket and they never overlap, so nothing is lost by insisting on the prefix property.

math210.2.4.takeaway: Symbol codes spend at least one bit per symbol, which is hopeless when the next symbol is almost certain, and in English it often is. Arithmetic coding treats the whole file as one interval of $[0, 1)$ of width $P(\text{file})$, subdivided using whatever context-dependent, adaptive probabilities a model supplies. It sends a binary string whose interval fits inside that one, within 2 bits of $\log_2(1/P(\text{file}))$ for the entire file. It cleanly separates modelling from coding.

beats.t: Huffman, and why prefix codes suffice
beats.d: Merging the smallest pairs gives an optimal prefix code: for five symbols of $\tfrac15$ each, or for weights proportional to 1 to 10. A cleverer non-prefix code would gain nothing. Take its lengths as a shopping list, buy the shortest first across the supermarket, and you get a prefix code with the same lengths.
A coin with $P(a) = 0.99$: Huffman assigns 0 and 1, so $L = 1$ bit, against an entropy of 0.08. The code is optimal among symbol codes, twelve times too long, and compresses nothing at all.

The room guessed a newspaper headline letter by letter. The predictions depended on context: after the first letter, every guess was a vowel. They would adapt as the document went on (to Swahili, say). And they were often very confident, with many letters guessed first time. A prediction with 99% on one letter has entropy about 0.11 bits, but any symbol code spends at least 1.

You could rerun Huffman for every context, code blocks of 16 characters ($50^{16}$ possible blocks), or code run lengths. Each needs the probabilities of many strings that never occur. What is wanted is a coder that takes context-dependent, adaptive and highly confident predictions directly.

Write down how many guesses each letter took. An identical twin audience in the next room, making identical predictions, can rebuild the headline from those numbers. All state-of-the-art compressors work this way, with identical deterministic models at both ends.

Compress a bent coin with known bias. Compress an unknown bent coin, starting at 50/50 and learning from the counts as you go. And, in general, compress using an oracle that gives $P(x_t \mid x_1, \ldots, x_{t-1})$ for any context.

A binary string is an interval: 01 is $[0.25, 0.5)$, and each extra bit halves it, so a 1 MB file names one real number to about two million decimal places. Split $[0, 1)$ in proportion to the model's probabilities for the first symbol, split the chosen piece by the probabilities for the second given the first, and so on. The file's interval has width $P(x_1\ldots x_N)$. Send a binary string whose interval lies inside it. In the demo, 92 tosses of a 0.9/0.1 coin became about 48 bits, near the entropy of 0.47 per toss; after a Q, the English model gave U half the interval.

The length is at most $\log_2\frac1{P(\mathbf x)} + 2$ for the WHOLE file, where a symbol code's overhead can reach one bit per symbol. It needs only $N \times I$ conditional probabilities, one set per symbol actually seen. It works for any input alphabet and any output alphabet. And it separates the modelling (the AI problem of predicting well) from the coding. It is used in JBIG, PPM and DjVu, and turned around it becomes Dasher, a writing tool steered by gestures.

math210.2.4.worked: To compress with arithmetic coding: build a model that returns $P(x_t \mid \text{context})$. Narrow an interval by those probabilities, one symbol at a time, and send the shortest binary string whose interval fits inside the final one. The decoder runs the identical model and follows the same subdivisions. The model's quality alone determines the compression.
math210.2.4.watch: Blaming the model when a symbol code compresses badly. With confident predictions, the floor of one bit per symbol is the problem. The model may be excellent, and arithmetic coding with the same probabilities would get within 2 bits of the ideal for the whole file.

checks.q: A coin with $P(a) = 0.99$, $P(b) = 0.01$ is Huffman-coded as 0 and 1. How many times longer than the entropy is its expected length (two decimals)?
checks.expl: $L = 1$ bit, and $H_2(0.01) \approx 0.0808$ bits, so the ratio is about 12.38. Symbol codes cannot go below 1 bit per symbol.

checks.q: A file of 1000 tosses of that coin contains 10 b's. Its information content $\log_2(1/P)$, the size arithmetic coding approaches, is (bits, two decimals):
checks.expl: $10\log_2 100 + 990\log_2\tfrac1{0.99} \approx 66.44 + 14.35 = 80.79$. Arithmetic coding sends at most about 2 bits more; Huffman would send 1000.

checks.q: An adaptive model for an unknown bent coin, with a uniform prior on its bias, has seen 4 a's and 1 b. Its predicted probability that the next symbol is a is (two decimals):
checks.expl: The posterior predictive under a uniform prior is Laplace's rule: $(4 + 1)/(5 + 2) = 5/7 \approx 0.71$.

checks.q: Arithmetic coding's overhead is at most about 2 bits for the entire file because:
opts: it uses a fixed codebook
the file's interval has width exactly $P(\mathbf x)$, and a binary interval of about that size always fits inside, costing $\log_2\frac1{P} + 2$ bits at most
it compresses each symbol separately
it ignores improbable symbols
checks.expl: Multiplying the conditional probabilities gives the joint probability. A snug binary interval costs $\log_2(1/P)$ bits, and the worst misalignment adds 2.

math210.2.5.takeaway: A code whose lengths match the information contents produces output that looks like fair coin flips, so information theory can settle questions without calculation. For noisy channels, inference needs the probability of everything. A channel supplies only $P(y \mid x)$; an input distribution completes the joint. A joint ensemble then gives the entropies $H(X)$, $H(Y)$ and $H(X, Y)$, the conditional entropy $H(X \mid Y) \le H(X)$, and the mutual information $I(X; Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y)$: the overlap that measures how much the output tells you about the input.

beats.t: Pick a bit from the stream
beats.d: Take the code $a{:}\,0$, $b{:}\,10$, $c{:}\,110$, $d{:}\,111$ for probabilities $\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac18$. Is a bit plucked at random from the encoded stream a 1 with probability less than, equal to, or more than half? Averaging each codeword's fraction of ones gives $\tfrac13$, which is wrong: long codewords put more bits in the bucket. Correctly, it is $\sum p_i n_i / \sum p_i l_i = \tfrac78 / \tfrac74 = \tfrac12$.

The code lengths equal the information contents, so $L = H$ and the stream cannot be compressed further. If its bits were not 50/50 and uncorrelated, they could be compressed. So $P(1) = \tfrac12$, with no calculation needed.

Huffman is within 1 bit per character, and arithmetic coding within 2 bits per file. PPM (prediction by partial match) is a practical oracle. It looks up the last five characters wherever they occurred earlier in the file, counts what followed, backs off to shorter contexts to allow for surprises, and works on the fly, like the identical twins.

Stick a uniform pin into $[0, 1)$ and read off the string whose interval contains it: that draws a string from the model. Simulating a coin with $p = 0.01$ this way costs $H_2(0.01) \approx 0.08$ random bits per toss, where the usual method spends 32. Random bits are not free: MacKay once received a CD of them, paid for by US government grants.

One card is white on both sides, one brown on both, one white/brown. A random card shows white. Is the other side white? The room split between $\tfrac12$ and $\tfrac23$. Write down the probability of everything, then condition on the data: of the three equally likely white faces, two have white on the back, so $\tfrac23$. Or: two-thirds of the time the back matches the front. The three doors (Monty Hall) problem is the same puzzle, and memorizing its answer taught the room nothing.

A channel defines only the conditional distributions $P(y \mid x)$; for inference you need a joint distribution. MacKay's example is a 4×4 table with marginals $P(x) = (\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac18)$ and $P(y)$ uniform. Then $H(X) = \tfrac74$, $H(Y) = 2$ and $H(X, Y) = \tfrac{27}8$ bits. $H(X) + H(Y) \ge H(X, Y)$, with equality exactly when the variables are independent.

$H(X \mid Y = y)$ for the four values of $y$ is $\tfrac74$, $\tfrac74$, 2 and 0. Learning a particular $y$ can raise your uncertainty about $x$, leave it unchanged, or lower it. But on average $H(X \mid Y) = \tfrac{11}8 \le H(X)$: data never increases expected uncertainty. The chain rule: $H(X, Y) = H(Y) + H(X \mid Y) = H(X) + H(Y \mid X)$.

$I(X; Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X)$, the overlap of the two entropy bars, here $\tfrac38$ bit. Next lecture: give a channel an input distribution, compute $I(X; Y)$, and find the capacity.

math210.2.5.worked: To analyse any inference or channel problem: write down the joint distribution of every variable, fix what you observe, and renormalize. Information measures come from the same table: marginals from sums, $H(X \mid Y) = H(X, Y) - H(Y)$, and $I(X; Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X, Y)$.
math210.2.5.watch: Answering 50/50 because two possibilities remain. The three cards (and the three doors) show that the remaining cases need not be equally likely: they inherit weight from the ways each could have produced what you saw.

checks.q: Three cards: white/white, brown/brown, white/brown. A random card is placed with a random side up, and the side shown is white. The probability that the other side is white is (two decimals):
checks.expl: There are three equally likely white faces up, and two of them belong to the white/white card: $\tfrac23$.

checks.q: The code $0, 10, 110, 111$ is used for probabilities $\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac18$. The fraction of ones in a long encoded stream is:
checks.expl: The average number of ones per codeword is $\tfrac78$ and the average length is $\tfrac74$, so the fraction is $\tfrac12$, as it must be for a perfectly compressed stream.

checks.q: In MacKay's joint ensemble, $H(X, Y) = \tfrac{27}8$ and $H(Y) = 2$ bits. The conditional entropy $H(X \mid Y)$ is (bits):
checks.expl: By the chain rule, $\tfrac{27}8 - 2 = \tfrac{11}8 = 1.375$, less than $H(X) = 1.75$.

checks.q: For the same ensemble, the mutual information $I(X; Y)$ is (bits):
checks.expl: $H(X) - H(X \mid Y) = \tfrac74 - \tfrac{11}8 = \tfrac38$. Summing $P(x, y)\log_2\frac{P(x, y)}{P(x)P(y)}$ over the table gives the same.

math210.2.6.takeaway: A channel is a set of conditional distributions $Q_{j|i} = P(y = b_j \mid x = a_i)$. Choose an input distribution and you have a joint ensemble: Bayes' theorem gives the posterior on the input, and $I(X; Y)$ measures what the output conveys. The capacity is the maximum of $I(X; Y)$ over input distributions. For the binary symmetric channel it is $1 - H_2(f)$, reached with a uniform input.

beats.d: Three doors. The prior on the prize is $\tfrac13$ each. You chose door 1, and the host opens door 3; the likelihood of that is $\tfrac12$, 1 or 0 depending on where the prize is. The normalizing constant is $\tfrac12$: how well you could predict his move. The posterior is $\tfrac13, \tfrac23, 0$, so switch. The universal rule: write down the joint probability of everything, then condition on what you know.

The binary symmetric channel flips with probability $f$. The binary erasure channel sometimes outputs '?', so the receiver knows the bit was lost but not what it was. The Z channel always delivers a 0 correctly but sometimes turns a 1 into a 0. The noisy typewriter has 27 keys arranged in a circle, and each key prints itself or one of its two neighbours, each with probability $\tfrac13$.

Take a binary symmetric channel with $f = 0.1$ and $P(x = 1) = 0.1$. If you see $y = 1$: $P(x = 1 \mid y = 1) = \frac{0.9 \times 0.1}{0.9 \times 0.1 + 0.1 \times 0.9} = \tfrac12$, and $P(y = 1) = 0.18$. If you see $y = 0$: $P(x = 1 \mid y = 0) = \frac{0.01}{0.82} = \tfrac1{82}$. A sanity check: $P(y = 0) + P(y = 1) = 1$.

$I(X; Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X) = H_2(0.18) - H_2(0.1) \approx 0.21$ bits. The same number comes from $H(X) - H(X \mid Y) = H_2(0.1) - [0.18\,H_2(\tfrac12) + 0.82\,H_2(\tfrac1{82})]$, but that needs three binary entropies and two Bayes computations. The output-side route is usually less work.

Plot $I$ against $P(x = 1)$. It is zero at both ends, symmetric, and peaks at $\tfrac12$. Define the capacity $C(Q) = \max_{P_X} I(X; Y)$; the maximizing input is the optimal input distribution. For the binary symmetric channel, $I = H_2\big(p_1(1 - f) + (1 - p_1)f\big) - H_2(f)$. Since $H_2 \le 1$, with equality at $\tfrac12$, the capacity is $C = 1 - H_2(f)$, which is 0.53 for $f = 0.1$.
Next lecture proves that the capacity is exactly the rate at which virtually error-free communication is possible: two lousy disk drives can emulate one perfect drive. Easy cases first.
Four inputs map to four distinct outputs. With a uniform input, $H(Y) = 2$ bits and $H(Y \mid X) = 0$, so $C = 2$. Reliable communication is trivial: send two source bits per use.

Input A always gives M, C always gives N, and B gives M or N with equal probability: the three cards again. With a uniform input, seeing M gives the posterior $\tfrac23, \tfrac13, 0$, and $I = \log_2 3 - H_2(\tfrac13) = 1 - \tfrac13 = \tfrac23$ bits. Both routes agree, which is not obvious. The optimal input throws away the useless B: use A and C half the time each, and $C = 1$ bit.

math210.2.6.worked: To find a channel's capacity: pick an input distribution and compute $I(X; Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X)$ (usually the easier way round). Then maximize over the input distribution, using symmetry to guess the optimum. Inputs that only add noise may be dropped entirely.
math210.2.6.watch: Assuming the capacity-achieving input must use every symbol. For the ternary confusion channel the optimum puts zero probability on B. An input that only adds confusion is worth nothing.

checks.q: Binary symmetric channel, $f = 0.1$, with $P(x = 1) = 0.1$. You observe $y = 0$. The posterior $P(x = 1 \mid y = 0)$ is 1 in how many?
For the same channel and input distribution, the mutual information $I(X; Y)$ is (two decimals):
checks.expl: $H(Y) - H(Y \mid X) = H_2(0.18) - H_2(0.1) \approx 0.680 - 0.469 = 0.21$ bits, well below the capacity of 0.53, because the input is not uniform.

checks.q: The capacity of the ternary confusion channel (A→M, C→N, B→M or N at random) is (bits):
checks.expl: Use only A and C, each half the time: the output then identifies the input exactly, giving 1 bit per use. Adding B can only reduce $I$.

checks.q: When computing $I(X; Y)$ for a channel, the route $H(Y) - H(Y \mid X)$ is often easier because:
opts: it is a different quantity
$H(Y \mid X)$ comes straight from the channel's rows, while $H(X \mid Y)$ needs a Bayes computation for every output
it avoids logarithms
it only works for symmetric channels
checks.expl: The two expressions are equal. One needs only the output distribution and the channel; the other needs every posterior.

math210.2.7.takeaway: The capacity is the rate of virtually error-free communication. N uses of any channel look like a noisy typewriter: each input's typical outputs form a blob of about $2^{NH(Y|X)}$ strings inside $2^{NH(Y)}$, so about $2^{NI(X;Y)}$ inputs can be kept apart. For the binary symmetric channel, averaging the error of a syndrome decoder over all random parity-check matrices shows it vanishes whenever $K/N \lt 1 - H_2(f)$. Almost every code is good, though the proof names none.

beats.d: $H(Y \mid X) = \log_2 3$ whatever the input distribution, and $H(Y) \le \log_2 27$, so $C = \log_2 9 \approx 3.17$ bits. A uniform input achieves it. So does putting $\tfrac19$ on every third letter (B, E, H, …), and that also shows how to communicate: use only those nine letters, whose output sets never overlap, and there are no errors at all.

Every point with rate below $C$ is achievable, right down to arbitrarily small error. That is the exciting part, proved today for the binary symmetric channel. That points with rate above $C$ are unachievable is proved in the book.
