sys250.1.10.takeaway: Erik Schultheis builds an educational int8 tensor-core matmul for Turing with only CUDA C++'s WMMA API: fragments, load_matrix_sync, mma_sync and store_matrix_sync. Integer matmul is exact, which makes testing easy. The naive 16 × 16-fragment kernel is orders of magnitude from peak. Then the standard recipe, guided by ncu's memory chart and warp-stall reasons: transpose B to column-major for coalesced loads, then register-tile 3 × 3 fragments per warp.

beats.d: The available captions cover the first 46 of the lecture's 77 minutes, through register tiling. The later steps (shared memory and beyond) are not described here.

On CPUs, int8 times int8 widens to int16, so registers do not line up (AVX-512 VNNI has a 4-way dot product; CUDA has dp4a). Tensor cores do int8 from Turing onwards. Integer maths is exact, so results do not depend on the order of operations and there are no tolerances to choose. The target is a Quadro RTX 4000 (TU104), the GPU behind the course's online submission system.

Random matrices tell you that something is wrong, not where. Better: identity matrices, or block-constant 4 × 4 structures so the first wrong output shows the broken tile boundary. For a cheap reference without a fast library, use Freivalds' trick: check $x(AB)$ against $(xA)B$ with a random vector, $O(n^2)$ rather than $O(n^3)$, or compare with cuBLAS.

Assume dimensions divisible by 16 and view each matrix as 16 × 16 blocks. Then it is the naive algorithm over blocks, with $k/16$ inner steps. WMMA needs only fill_fragment, load_matrix_sync, mma_sync and store_matrix_sync, and the fragment's internal layout is officially unspecified. (Newer Hopper instructions like wgmma have no C++ API, only inline PTX, which CUTLASS wraps.)

One warp per 16 × 16 output fragment. On a large matrix it ran at about 4 TOPS, far below the int8 peak. The rule: 'where's my data?' ncu showed about 630 GB moving between L2 and L1 and 206 GB from DRAM, many times the GPU's memory. The top warp stalls were LG throttle (too many loads in flight) and long scoreboard (waiting on a load).

Loading B's fragments along $k$ from a row-major B is strided. Transpose B once (about 6 ms, $O(n^2)$, against the $O(n^3)$ matmul) and load it column-major. Time went from about 1.5 s to under 1 s, with 60% fewer memory requests. The stall ratios looked worse, because they are normalized by issued instructions, and the instruction count fell 45% as index arithmetic disappeared.

Each warp computes a 3 × 3 block of fragments: preload 3 B fragments, then for each A fragment do 3 mma_syncs. That is 6 fragment loads for 9 outputs instead of 2 per output, three times the reuse (PMPP's thread coarsening, here per warp). Memory requests fell another 60–70%, LG-throttle stalls halved, and register indexing removed more address arithmetic.

More accumulators per warp means more registers per thread, so fewer resident warps and less latency hiding. Going to 4 × 4 risks spilling. Tile shapes need not be square (3 × 4), and benchmarking decides; shared memory is the next level of the hierarchy to use.

sys250.1.10.worked: To count fragment reuse: a warp computing a $p \times q$ block of 16 × 16 output fragments loads $p + q$ input fragments per $k$-step for $pq$ outputs. For 1 × 1 that is 2 loads per output; for 3 × 3 it is $6/9 = 0.67$, three times better, paid for in accumulator registers.
sys250.1.10.watch: Reading a worse warp-stall ratio after an optimization as a regression. The stalls are normalized per issued instruction; if the instruction count fell a lot, the ratio can rise while the kernel gets much faster. Check the duration.

checks.expl: The $O(n^2)$ transpose is cheap next to the $O(n^3)$ matmul.

sys250.1.11.takeaway: Adam Paszke (PyTorch, JAX, Dex) on why Google builds Mosaic GPU and Pallas. Transformers made peak performance on a narrow class of programs the priority, and new GPUs look more and more like TPUs: huge tensor-core instructions, asynchronous copies, pipelining. So he wants a Python DSL that is tracing-based (Python control flow becomes metaprogramming) and exposes every hardware trick while removing only boilerplate. Pallas kernels take shaped, mutable refs, and BlockSpecs declare each program's tiles so copies can be pipelined automatically.

beats.d: The available captions cover the first 38 of the lecture's 86 minutes: the motivation, Pallas's basics, and BlockSpecs. The later Mosaic GPU material (async copies, warpgroup MMA, pipelining details) is not described here.

Early PyTorch prioritized generality and speed of development, accepting a 20–30% performance cost. Now Transformers dominate, are simple (matmuls plus a few ops) and are co-designed with accelerators, and at scale every percent is money. So peak performance comes first, made as pleasant as possible. Prebuilt libraries fall off a cliff when you change something; compilers take generations to catch up with Ampere, Hopper and Blackwell.

C++ templates can encode anything, but the errors are awful. String-pasting code generation (as in FlashInfer and Inductor) has scoping hazards. Triton parses the AST and adds constexpr. Pallas, like JAX, traces: Python if picks one branch and for fully unrolls, which is exactly the metaprogramming kernels need. The aim is 'LLM-proof' kernels: short, dense in the decisions that matter, free of boilerplate.

It is open source in the JAX repository, about 6,000 lines, with early PyTorch bindings. Two DSLs: the original MLIR-builder one, and Pallas's Mosaic GPU backend, which is the recommended one. In Mosaic a 'thread' means a warpgroup (128 threads), which he sees as the right granularity for dense linear algebra. Pallas also targets Triton and Mosaic TPU.

Kernel arguments are refs: shaped and mutable. x_ref[...] loads a value (think registers) and z_ref[...] = x + y stores. The body is ordinary jax.numpy. pl.pallas_call(kernel, out_shape=…) turns it into a function on JAX arrays, with outputs passed in as extra refs. A grid=(n,) plus pl.program_id(0) and pl.ds(pid × bs, bs) slicing splits the work, using structured slices rather than pointer arithmetic.

The classic GPU hides global-memory latency with many resident blocks. TPUs cannot, and must be scheduled carefully at compile time. Modern GPUs using big warpgroup MMAs have so much shared memory and so many registers per block that only one fits per SM, so they too need explicit asynchronous copies and pipelining. Other convergences: larger matmul units (two-CTA instructions on Blackwell), a growing gap between matmul and vector FLOPs, and uniform/scalar registers.

A matmul kernel body is just o_ref[...] = x_ref[...] @ y_ref[...]. The parallelism comes from grid=(m/bm, n/bn) and a BlockSpec per operand: a block shape ((bm, K) for $x$, (K, bn) for $y$, (bm, bn) for the output) and an index map from grid indices to block indices (lambda i, j: (i, 0), (0, j), (i, j)).

Because the index maps say, independently of the body, which tile each program reads and writes, Pallas knows the next tiles in advance. It can issue the asynchronous copies itself and overlap memory transfer with compute. The restriction (no data-dependent access in the specs) is what makes the automatic pipelining possible.

sys250.1.11.worked: To tile a matmul in Pallas: choose bm and bn and set grid = (m // bm, n // bn). Give $x$ BlockSpec((bm, K), lambda i, j: (i, 0)), $y$ BlockSpec((K, bn), lambda i, j: (0, j)), and the output BlockSpec((bm, bn), lambda i, j: (i, j)). The body is one dot. For $m = n = 1024$ with 128 × 128 tiles, the grid is 8 × 8 = 64 programs.
sys250.1.11.watch: Writing Python loops or ifs in a Pallas kernel expecting them to run on the device. Tracing unrolls the for and specializes the if at trace time; use the control-flow combinators when a runtime branch is really needed.

checks.q: A Pallas matmul with $m = n = 1024$ and 128 × 128 output blocks. How many programs does the grid launch?
In Pallas, x_ref[...] inside a kernel:
opts: returns the pointer
loads the current value from the mutable ref as an array
copies to the host
is a no-op
checks.expl: Refs are mutable; the slice reads them at that moment.

checks.q: Why can Pallas pipeline copies automatically with BlockSpecs?
opts: it inspects the kernel body at runtime
each program's tiles are declared by index maps independent of the data, so the next tiles are known in advance
GPUs prefetch everything
tensor cores require it
checks.expl: Declared access patterns allow the async copies to be issued early.

checks.q: In a tracing-based DSL like Pallas, a Python for loop in a kernel:
opts: becomes a device loop
is unrolled at trace time
raises an error
runs on the CPU at runtime
checks.expl: Unrolling is the metaprogramming Paszke wants.

ai200.1.0.takeaway: Backpropagation is the chain rule applied node by node over an expression graph: each operation knows only its local derivative, gradients flow from the output back through a topological order, and they ADD wherever a value is used more than once — about a hundred lines of Python, and the same numbers PyTorch gives.

beats.d: Bump an input by a tiny h and see how much the output moves: $(f(x+h)-f(x))/h$. For $f(x) = 3x^2 - 4x + 5$ the slope is about 0 at $x = 2/3$. For $d = a b + c$, nudging $c$ by $h$ moves $d$ by exactly $h$ — the slope with respect to $c$ is 1.

beats.t: Value: a number that remembers where it came from
beats.d: A Value wraps a scalar and records its children and the operation that produced it, so a calculation builds an expression graph as it runs. Each node also carries grad — the derivative of the final output with respect to it — starting at 0.

Set the output's grad to 1 and walk backwards. A + node passes its gradient to both inputs unchanged; a * node gives each input the other input's value times the gradient. That is the chain rule, applied locally. Nudging every leaf a little in the direction of its gradient raises L from -8 to about -7.29, as predicted.

beats.t: A neuron, and tanh's local derivative
beats.d: A neuron computes $\tanh(w \cdot x + b)$. Its local derivative is $1 - o^2$, so at $o = 0.7071$ it is 0.5. Each operation gets a _backward closure that applies exactly its own local rule.

Build a topological ordering of the graph, set the root's grad to 1, and call each node's _backward in reverse order — so a node passes gradient to its inputs only once every node that uses it has passed gradient into it.

If a value is used twice — b = a + a — both paths contribute, and a.grad must be 2, not 1. So every _backward uses +=, never =. The notebook flags the one place the video got this wrong (the exp backward) and fixes it.

beats.t: How finely to break operations is a choice
beats.d: Rewriting tanh as $(e^{2n}-1)/(e^{2n}+1)$ with exp, power, subtraction and division gives the same forward value and the same gradients. Supporting constants takes a few small methods (__radd__, __rmul__, __neg__, __sub__, __truediv__ via a power of -1).

The same neuron in PyTorch, with requires_grad on scalar tensors, gives o = 0.7071 and the same gradients for x1, w1, x2, w2. PyTorch works on tensors; micrograd on single numbers — which is why micrograd chops each neuron into individual adds and multiplies.

beats.t: A tiny neural net library, and training it
beats.d: Neuron, Layer and MLP, each with parameters(). MLP(3, [4, 4, 1]) is trained on four examples: forward pass, loss = sum of squared errors, reset every grad to 0, loss.backward(), then step each parameter by -0.1 times its gradient. The loss falls and the predictions approach the targets.

About 100 lines of engine and 50 of nn, with ReLU neurons. Its demo trains MLP(2, [16, 16, 1]) — 337 parameters — on the two-moons data with a max-margin loss plus L2 regularization and SGD with a decaying learning rate, reaching 100% training accuracy; its tests check forward values and gradients against PyTorch.

ai200.1.0.worked: To trust a gradient, check it two ways. Compute it with backward(), then nudge that one input by a small h and measure $(L(x+h) - L(x))/h$ — the notebook's lol() does exactly this and gets -3.99999 for dL/db where backprop says -4. Then, for a whole model, compare against PyTorch on the same inputs, as the repository's tests do.
ai200.1.0.watch: Forgetting that gradients accumulate. Because _backward adds into grad, a training loop that does not reset every parameter's grad to 0 before loss.backward() steps on the sum of all past gradients — and writing = instead of += in a _backward silently drops every path but the last.

checks.q: The lecture starts from $f(x) = 3x^2 - 4x + 5$ and estimates slopes by nudging x by a tiny h. What is the slope of f at $x = 3$?
checks.expl: The nudge estimates the derivative $f'(x) = 6x - 4$, so at $x = 3$ the slope is 14: raise x by h and f rises by about 14h. At $x = 2/3$ the same estimate gives about 0 — the bottom of the parabola.

checks.q: During backprop, a + node receives gradient g from above. What does it pass to each of its two inputs?
opts: g to each input, unchanged, since a sum's local derivative is 1
g/2 to each input, so that the total gradient is preserved
g times the other input's value, as for a multiplication
Nothing at all: a sum has no parameters, so it stops the gradient
checks.expl: Nudging c in d = a*b + c moves d by exactly h, so the local derivative is 1, and the chain rule multiplies g by 1 for both inputs — a + node routes the gradient through to everything that feeds it. Multiplying by the other input's value is the rule for *.

checks.q: With a = 2, b = -3, c = 10, f = -2 and L = (a*b + c)*f, what is dL/db?
checks.expl: Chain rule: dL/dd = f = -2, dd/de = 1, and de/db = a = 2, so dL/db = -2 x 1 x 2 = -4. The notebook's lol() checks it numerically by nudging b and gets -3.99999.

checks.q: Why does backward() first build a topological ordering of the graph and then call each node's _backward in reverse?
opts: So that the leaf nodes are visited first and their gradients are set to 1
So that each node's gradient is complete before it is passed further back
So that the graph can be drawn left to right by draw_dot afterwards
So that each node is visited twice, once per input it happens to have
checks.expl: A node's _backward pushes its own grad into its inputs. If it ran before every node that uses it had contributed, it would push an incomplete gradient. Reversing a topological order guarantees all of a node's consumers run first. Only the root is set to 1.

checks.q: b = a + a, then b.backward(). a.grad should be 2. Why must every _backward use += rather than =?
opts: Because = would make a.grad negative when a appears twice
Because Python does not allow = on attributes inside closures
Because a value used twice gets gradient from both uses, so they add
Because += is faster when the graph grows to many thousands of nodes
checks.expl: Here both inputs of the + node are the same object, so with = the second assignment overwrites the first and a.grad ends at 1. By the multivariable chain rule the contributions add. The notebook notes the video used = in the exp backward and fixes it.

checks.q: The second notebook rebuilds the neuron with tanh written as $(e^{2n}-1)/(e^{2n}+1)$, using exp, subtraction and division. What does that show?
opts: That exp must be avoided, since it changes the gradients of the inputs
That tanh needs its own backward method, as the composite version is wrong
That division cannot be backpropagated until it is rewritten as a sum
That any breakdown of the operations gives the same values and gradients
checks.expl: The forward value and every gradient come out the same as with the single tanh node. How finely you break a function into operations is up to you; all that matters is that each operation knows its own local derivative — exp's is its output, a power's is $n x^{n-1}$, and division is multiplication by a power of -1.

checks.q: MLP(3, [4, 4, 1]) as built in the lecture: each neuron has one weight per input plus a bias. How many parameters does it have?
checks.expl: Layer sizes 3 to 4 to 4 to 1. First layer: 4 neurons x (3 + 1) = 16; second: 4 x (4 + 1) = 20; output: 1 x (4 + 1) = 5. Total 41. The repository's demo, MLP(2, [16, 16, 1]), has 48 + 272 + 17 = 337.

checks.q: In the training loop, what goes wrong if you delete the line that sets every p.grad to 0 before loss.backward()?
opts: Each step uses the sum of all past gradients, since backward adds into grad
Nothing changes, because backward() always overwrites the old gradients
The loss can no longer be computed, because grad is read in the forward pass
The update flips sign, so gradient descent turns into gradient ascent
checks.expl: Because every _backward does +=, gradients pile up across iterations unless reset — the repository wraps this as zero_grad(). The update itself is p.data += -0.1 * p.grad: minus, to step against the gradient and lower the loss, where the first notebook stepped WITH the gradient to make L go up.

ai200.1.1.takeaway: A bigram language model can be built two ways — count which character follows which and normalise, or train a one-layer net with a softmax on the negative log likelihood — and the two arrive at the same model, which is the point: the neural framing is the one that scales.

beats.t: One file of names, many examples
beats.d: 32,033 names, 2 to 15 letters long. Each name is several examples at once: every character is evidence about which character follows it, and where names start and end.

Wrap each name in start and end markers and count every adjacent pair. The final version uses one token, '.', at index 0 for both start and end, giving a 27 x 27 table N whose row i counts what follows character i.

Normalise each row into probabilities, start from '.', and draw the next character with torch.multinomial until '.' comes back. The names ('mor.', 'axx.', 'minaymoryles.') are bad — a bigram sees one character of context — but they are drawn from the data's statistics.

Normalise with P.sum(1, keepdims=True): a 27 x 1 column of row sums divides each ROW. P.sum(1) gives shape 27, which broadcasts as a 1 x 27 row and divides each COLUMN instead — no error, just a wrong model.

beats.t: Scoring a model: negative log likelihood
beats.d: Maximising the likelihood of the data — the product of the probabilities assigned to every actual next character — is the same as minimising the average negative log likelihood. The smoothed count model scores 2.4765. Adding 1 to every count keeps any pair from having probability 0, which would make the loss infinite.

beats.t: The same model as a neural net
beats.d: One-hot encode the input character and multiply by a 27 x 27 weight matrix W: that selects W's row for the character — 27 logits, read as log-counts. Exponentiate and normalise (together, a softmax) to get probabilities. The loss is the mean NLL of the correct next characters.

On all 228,146 bigrams: forward, set W.grad to None, loss.backward(), W += -50 * W.grad. A regulariser, 0.01 * (W**2).mean(), pulls W toward zero, where all logits are equal and predictions are uniform — the gradient-based twin of adding counts.

The trained net reaches a loss of about 2.48, the counts' level, and with the same random seed it samples almost exactly the same names. The difference is what comes next: the table cannot grow to longer contexts, and the net can.

ai200.1.1.worked: Index the probabilities of the right answers in one step — probs[torch.arange(n), ys] — take the log, average and negate: that is the loss, for the count table and the network alike. Then compare it against the counts model's 2.48 as the target a one-character-context model can reach.
ai200.1.1.watch: Dropping keepdims=True when normalising. P.sum(1) has shape 27 and broadcasts as a row, so each column is divided by a row's total. Nothing errors and the samples still look plausible; only the numbers are wrong.

checks.q: The first count table marks names with separate start and end tokens; the final one uses a single '.' at index 0 for both. Why is one token enough?
opts: Names never contain a dot, so the model cannot mistake it for a letter
A start only ever opens a bigram and an end only closes one, so they never clash
PyTorch needs the count table to be square, so the two markers had to be merged
One shared token means every sampled name starts and ends with one letter
checks.expl: A start token only ever appears as the first character of a bigram and an end token only as the second, so one symbol can play both roles without ambiguity. With two tokens the table had a row for the end token and a column for the start token that could only ever hold zeros.

checks.q: How many training bigrams does the name 'isabella' contribute, once it is wrapped in the start/end token?
checks.expl: '.isabella.' has 10 symbols, so 9 adjacent pairs: one for the first letter, seven between letters, and one for the end. In general a name of n letters gives n + 1 examples — 'emma' gives the 5 shown in the notebook.

checks.q: P is 27 x 27. Why must each row be divided by P.sum(1, keepdims=True) rather than by P.sum(1)?
opts: keepdims makes the sum run over columns instead of rows, as is needed
Without keepdims PyTorch raises an error, because the shapes cannot broadcast
The two are the same; keepdims only changes how the result is printed
Without keepdims the sums broadcast as a row, and columns get divided
checks.expl: P.sum(1, keepdims=True) is 27 x 1, which stretches across the columns, so row i is divided by row i's total. P.sum(1) is shape 27; broadcasting aligns it from the right as 1 x 27, so column j is divided by row j's total — silently wrong.

checks.q: Why does the count model normalise N + 1 rather than N itself?
opts: To shift every index up by one, since '.' takes index 0 in the count table
To make every row sum to exactly one before the division happens
So no bigram has probability zero, which would make the loss infinite
To speed up sampling by removing zeros from the multinomial draw
checks.expl: A pair never seen in training would get probability 0, its log would be minus infinity, and the average NLL of any name containing it would be infinite. Adding a fake count everywhere smooths the model; more added counts make it more uniform.

checks.q: A model that gives every one of the 27 characters probability 1/27 — what average negative log likelihood does it score? Two decimal places.
checks.expl: Each example costs $-\ln(1/27) = \ln 27 \approx 3.30$. The count model gets down to 2.48; the randomly initialised network starts on 'emma' at 3.77 — worse than uniform, because random weights are confidently wrong.

checks.q: In the network, what does xenc @ W compute when xenc is a one-hot vector?
opts: It picks out W's row for the input character: 27 logits, read as log-counts
It adds up W's column for that character into one single combined score
It sorts the 27 characters by their weights before the softmax runs
It scales each weight by the character's index, so later letters count more
checks.expl: Multiplying a one-hot row by a matrix selects one row of the matrix. So W plays the role of the log of the count table: exponentiating gives 'counts' and normalising gives probabilities — the softmax.

checks.q: The final loss adds 0.01 * (W**2).mean(). What does that term pull the model toward?
opts: Larger weights, so that common bigrams are predicted more confidently
W near zero, where all logits are equal and predictions are uniform
A faster effective learning rate, as the squared term has a bigger gradient
Fewer parameters, by setting the least useful weights exactly to zero
checks.expl: If W were all zeros, every logit would be 0, every count exp(0) = 1, and every next character equally likely. Penalising W's size pulls toward that uniform model — the same effect as adding fake counts to N, with 0.01 playing the role of the smoothing strength.

checks.q: With the same seed, sampling from the trained network gives almost exactly the count model's names. Why?
opts: The sampling loop still reads the old count table P, not the network
The seed fixes the names, whatever probabilities the model happens to give
The net has learned nearly the same next-character odds as the count table
Both models memorised the training names and replay them in the same order
checks.expl: The network and the table are two parametrisations of the same bigram model, and training on the NLL drives the network to the table's probabilities (loss about 2.48). The sampling loop uses the network's softmax output — the notebook shows the old P line commented out.

ai200.1.2.takeaway: To see more than one character back, stop counting and learn: embed each character as a small vector, concatenate the last three, and feed them through a hidden layer — Bengio et al.'s MLP — trained on minibatches and judged on data it never trained on.

beats.d: block_size = 3: each example is the previous three characters (padded with '.' at the start of a name) and the next character as the label. A name of n letters gives n + 1 examples.
Shuffle the words and split 80 / 10 / 10 — 182,441, 22,902 and 22,803 examples. Train on the first, tune choices on the second, and keep the third for the end.
C maps each of the 27 characters to a learned vector — 2 numbers at first, so the embedding can be plotted, then 10. C[X] looks up every character of every context at once.

emb.view(-1, 30) lays each context's three 10-dimensional embeddings side by side as one 30-long vector; a 200-unit tanh layer and a 27-way output layer follow. 11,897 parameters in all, and F.cross_entropy computes the loss from the logits.
Each step uses 32 random training examples, not all 182,441: the gradient is noisier but far cheaper, so the model can take hundreds of thousands of steps.
Sweep candidate rates evenly in the exponent — 10 to the power of linspace(-3, 0) — and watch the loss to find a good one. The final run uses 0.1 for 100,000 steps, then decays to 0.01.

beats.t: Judge it on the dev set
beats.d: Training loss 2.126, dev loss 2.170: close, so the model is not simply memorising, and it beats the bigram model's 2.48. Samples ('kaleigh.', 'quinton.', 'jace.') now look much more like names.

ai200.1.2.worked: Write every tensor's shape next to the line that makes it: X is (N, 3), C[X] is (N, 3, 10), the view is (N, 30), the hidden layer (N, 200), the logits (N, 27). Most bugs in this model are a shape that is not what you thought, and the comments in the notebook do exactly this.
ai200.1.2.watch: Reporting the training loss as the model's quality. Only the dev split says how it does on names it has not seen; and the test split is spent once, at the end, or it stops being an honest measure.

checks.q: C is 27 x 10, W1 is 30 x 200 with a bias of 200, W2 is 200 x 27 with a bias of 27. How many parameters does the MLP have? (digits only, no commas)
checks.expl: Embedding 27 x 10 = 270; hidden layer 30 x 200 + 200 = 6,200; output layer 200 x 27 + 27 = 5,427. Total 11,897 — the notebook prints the same. Note the embedding table counts: it is learned like any other weight.

checks.q: With block_size = 3, how many (context, next character) examples does the name 'emma' produce?
checks.expl: Every character of 'emma.' is a target — e, m, m, a and the final '.' — each predicted from the three before it, padded with '.': '...' predicts e, '..e' predicts m, and so on. n letters give n + 1 examples.

checks.q: Why does the forward pass reshape the embeddings with emb.view(-1, 30)?
opts: To average the three characters' embeddings into a single vector
To lay the three 10-number embeddings side by side as one input
To drop the batch dimension so the matrix multiply can broadcast
To sort the context characters by index before the hidden layer
checks.expl: C[X] has shape (batch, 3, 10). The hidden layer wants one vector per example, so the three embeddings are concatenated into 30 numbers — keeping which character was where, which averaging would lose. The -1 lets PyTorch infer the batch size.

checks.q: Each training step indexes 32 random rows of the training set. What does that buy?
opts: An exact gradient, because 32 examples cover all 27 characters
Lower loss at the end, because small batches overfit much less
A noisier but far cheaper gradient, so many more steps can be taken
A larger learning rate, since 32 is the maximum the GPU can hold
checks.expl: A forward and backward pass over all 182,441 examples per step would be slow. A minibatch's gradient only approximates the full one, but it is good enough to move in a useful direction, and the run takes 200,000 such steps.

checks.q: Why does the learning-rate sweep try 10 to the power of linspace(-3, 0) rather than evenly spaced rates?
opts: To try the rates evenly on a log scale, from 0.001 up to 1
To make sure the very last rate tried is always exactly zero
Because PyTorch only accepts learning rates that are powers of 10
To spend most of the 1,000 tries on rates that are close to 1
checks.expl: What matters about a learning rate is its order of magnitude. Spacing the exponent evenly from -3 to 0 spreads the 1,000 candidates evenly across 0.001, 0.01, 0.1 and 1, so the loss-versus-exponent plot shows where training works. The run then settles on 0.1, decayed to 0.01.

checks.q: After training, the loss is 2.126 on the training split and 2.170 on the dev split. What does that comparison tell you?
opts: The model is badly overfitting and the dev split should be discarded
The dev split is easier, so its loss must be higher than the training one
Little overfitting: it does nearly as well on names it never trained on
The model has converged, so a bigger network could not do any better
checks.expl: Overfitting shows as a training loss far below the dev loss. Here they are close, so the model generalises — and both beat the bigram model's 2.48. A small gap is also a hint that the model has room to grow before it starts memorising.

ai200.1.3.takeaway: A deep net trains well only if its activations and gradients stay well scaled from the first step: start with an output that is unconfident, hidden units that are not saturated, weights scaled by fan-in — and batch normalisation to hold every layer's pre-activations near unit Gaussian — then watch the statistics instead of guessing.

beats.d: The notebook keeps a running log as each fix lands: original (train 2.125, val 2.168); softmax confidently wrong fixed (2.07 / 2.13); tanh too saturated fixed (2.036 / 2.103); a principled Kaiming init (2.038 / 2.107); batch norm added (2.067 / 2.105).

W2 is scaled by 0.01 and b2 set to 0, so the first logits are near zero and the first predictions near uniform. The first loss is 3.32 — about $\ln 27$, what a model that knows nothing should score — instead of a large loss spent in the first steps just un-learning random confidence.

If the hidden pre-activations are large, tanh outputs pile up at ±1, where its local gradient $1 - t^2$ is about zero and the unit passes almost nothing backward. Scaling W1 down keeps them in tanh's active range.

beats.t: Kaiming init instead of a magic number
beats.d: Scale W1 by gain / $\sqrt{\text{fan\_in}}$, with gain 5/3 for tanh: randn * (5/3) / sqrt(30). The Linear class later uses / fan_in**0.5 by default.

Standardise each hidden unit's pre-activation over the batch — subtract the batch mean, divide by the batch std — then multiply by a learned gain and add a learned bias, so the layer can still choose its own scale and offset. A bias before batch norm is cancelled by the mean subtraction, so b1 and the Linear layers' biases are dropped.

One example has no meaningful batch statistics, so batch norm keeps running estimates — bnmean_running and bnstd_running, nudged with momentum 0.001 every step (or calibrated over the whole training set afterwards) — and uses them when evaluating or sampling.

Linear, BatchNorm1d (with training mode, eps, momentum and running_mean / running_var buffers) and Tanh, stacked six layers deep — 47,024 parameters — with the last layer's gamma scaled by 0.1 to make the output less confident.

Per tanh layer: mean, std and the share saturated (|t| > 0.97) of activations — about 0.64 std and 2% saturated here; the same for their gradients; each weight's gradient std relative to its data; and, over training, log10 of (lr × gradient std) / (data std), which should sit near -3.

ai200.1.3.worked: Before a long run, check the first step. The initial loss should be about $\ln(\text{vocab})$; the hidden activations should have a std near the same value in every layer with few saturated; and the update-to-data ratios should sit around $10^{-3}$. Each of these is one print statement, and each catches a problem that otherwise costs a full training run.
ai200.1.3.watch: Evaluating a batch-norm network one example at a time with its training-mode statistics. A single example's mean is itself and its std is undefined, so the output is meaningless — switch the layers out of training mode so they use their running mean and variance.

checks.q: Why does the notebook scale W2 by 0.01 and set b2 to 0 at initialisation?
opts: To make the output layer train faster than the hidden layers
To stop the embeddings in C from drifting during the first steps
To keep the weights small enough that no regularisation is needed
So the first predictions are near uniform, not confidently wrong
checks.expl: With near-zero logits every character gets probability about 1/27, so the first loss is about $\ln 27 \approx 3.30$ — the notebook's first step prints 3.32. Random large logits would be confidently wrong, the loss would start far higher, and the first steps would be spent just squashing them. The loss log calls this fix 'softmax confidently wrong'.

checks.q: W1 is initialised as randn * (5/3) / sqrt(fan_in), with fan_in = n_embd × block_size = 10 × 3. What standard deviation is that? Three decimals.
checks.expl: fan_in = 30, $\sqrt{30} \approx 5.477$, and $(5/3)/5.477 \approx 0.304$. Dividing by $\sqrt{\text{fan\_in}}$ keeps the pre-activations' std near 1 however many inputs a unit sums; 5/3 is the gain that compensates for tanh squashing.

checks.q: The diagnostics print the share of tanh outputs with |t| above 0.97 as 'saturated'. Why does the lecture want that share small?
opts: Saturated units output exactly zero, so the forward pass loses them
There tanh's local gradient, 1 − t², is near zero, so little flows back
Saturated units make the loss negative, which breaks cross-entropy
Saturation only matters for the output layer, never for the hidden layers
checks.expl: Backprop through tanh multiplies the incoming gradient by $1 - t^2$. At |t| = 0.97 that factor is about 0.06; at ±1 it is 0. A unit that is saturated for every example never learns — a dead neuron. The loss log's 'tanh layer too saturated at init' fix scales W1 down for exactly this.

checks.q: After batch norm standardises the pre-activations, why does it multiply by bngain and add bnbias?
opts: So the network can learn whatever scale and offset suits each unit
So the pre-activations end up with exactly zero mean and unit std
So the running mean and std can be updated without any gradient
So the output layer receives probabilities rather than logits
checks.expl: Forcing every unit to be exactly unit Gaussian for ever would limit what the network can represent. bngain starts at 1 and bnbias at 0 — so at initialisation the layer is pure standardisation — and both are trained by backprop, letting each unit move away from it where that helps.

checks.q: In the batch-norm network, b1 is commented out and every Linear before a BatchNorm1d has bias=False. Why?
opts: Because biases make the running statistics drift out of date
Because PyTorch cannot backpropagate through two biases in a row
Because a bias adds parameters without helping a deep network
Because batch norm subtracts the batch mean, cancelling any bias
checks.expl: Adding b to every example and then subtracting the batch mean removes b exactly: $(h + b) - \text{mean}(h + b) = h - \text{mean}(h)$. Its gradient is therefore zero and it is wasted. Batch norm's own bnbias (beta) does the job of a bias, after the normalisation.

checks.q: Why does batch norm keep bnmean_running and bnstd_running, updated a little each step?
opts: To normalise the gradients during the backward pass in training
So one example can be evaluated without batch stats of its own
To replace bngain and bnbias once training has fully converged
To detect overfitting by comparing them with the dev split's loss
checks.expl: In training each example is normalised with its batch's mean and std. At evaluation or sampling there may be one example, so the layer uses running estimates of the training statistics instead — nudged with momentum (0.999 / 0.001) during training, or calibrated over the whole training set once it ends.

checks.q: The first batch-norm network has C (27 × 10), W1 (30 × 200, no bias), W2 (200 × 27) with b2 (27), and bngain and bnbias (200 each). How many parameters does it train? (digits only, no commas)
checks.expl: 270 + 6,000 + 5,400 + 27 + 200 + 200 = 12,097, as the notebook prints. The running mean and std are buffers, not parameters — they are updated by the momentum rule, not by gradient descent — and dropping b1 saved 200.

checks.q: The notebook plots log10 of (lr × gradient std) / (parameter std) for each weight, with a line at -3. What does a weight far BELOW the line suggest?
opts: Its gradient is exploding, so the learning rate should be cut at once
It has converged, so it can be frozen for the rest of the training run
Its updates are tiny next to its values, so it is learning too slowly
Its initialisation was too small, so it should be scaled up by 10
checks.expl: The ratio measures how big each step is relative to the parameter itself; the notebook marks about $10^{-3}$ as healthy. Far below means the parameter barely moves per step — the learning rate is too low for it; far above means steps so large the values thrash.

ai200.1.4.takeaway: Backprop is not magic to be trusted but arithmetic to be done: chunk the forward pass into small steps, push the gradient back through each by hand at the level of whole tensors, check every one against PyTorch — then collapse cross-entropy and batch norm into a single analytic backward each.

beats.d: The 2-layer MLP with batch norm from the last lecture, its forward pass split into small named steps — embedding, linear, batch-norm mean, difference, variance with Bessel's correction (n − 1), inverse root, gain and bias, tanh, linear, then cross-entropy unrolled into max-subtraction, exp, sum, reciprocal, log. Each step can be backpropagated alone.

b1, b2, bngain and bnbias get small random values rather than zeros or ones, because a zero can make a wrong backward formula produce the right number by accident. A cmp() helper reports, for every tensor, whether the manual gradient matches PyTorch's exactly or approximately.

beats.t: Exercise 1: every variable, one by one
beats.d: The loss is minus the mean of the log-probabilities at the labels, so dlogprobs is −1/n at each label and 0 elsewhere. Then: a value broadcast in the forward pass has its gradient SUMMED over the broadcast dimension in the backward; a value used twice gets the sum of both paths; a matrix multiply's gradients are matrix multiplies too, fixed by the shapes.
For logits = h @ W2 + b2: dh = dlogits @ W2.T, dW2 = h.T @ dlogits, db2 = dlogits.sum(0). Only one arrangement of the operands produces the right shape, which is how to derive it without memorising.
emb = C[Xb] copies rows of C; going backward, each row of demb is added into dC at the index of the character it came from — and characters that appear several times in the batch accumulate.

dlogits = softmax(logits), minus 1 at the correct class, divided by n. Each row sums to zero: the correct logit is pulled down by 1 − p and every other logit pushed up by its probability. It matches PyTorch to about 5e-9.

beats.t: Exercise 3: batch norm in one line
beats.d: Working through the batch-norm expression analytically gives dhprebn = bngain · bnvar_inv / n · (n · dhpreact − Σ dhpreact − n/(n−1) · bnraw · Σ (dhpreact · bnraw)) — one formula instead of nine steps, matching to about 1e-9.

beats.t: Exercise 4: train with your own backward
beats.d: The full training loop runs under torch.no_grad() with the hand-written gradients feeding the update — no loss.backward() at all — and reaches train 2.0705 / val 2.1099, the same quality as before.

ai200.1.4.worked: Derive one step at a time and check it immediately with cmp(): write the local derivative, multiply by the incoming gradient, then fix the shape. If the forward pass broadcast something, sum over that dimension; if a value was used twice, add the contributions; for a matrix multiply, place the transposes so the shapes come out right.
ai200.1.4.watch: Forgetting that a broadcast in the forward pass is a sum in the backward. counts_sum_inv is (32, 1) but multiplies a (32, 27) tensor, so its gradient must be summed over the 27 columns. Leave out the .sum(1, keepdim=True) and the gradient has the wrong shape — and later broadcasts can carry it along without an error.

checks.q: Why does the notebook initialise b1, b2, bngain and bnbias with small random values instead of the usual zeros and ones?
opts: Because a zero can make a wrong backward formula give the right answer
Because zeros would make the forward pass divide by zero in batch norm
Because random values make the network train faster to a lower loss
Because PyTorch refuses to compute gradients for tensors that are zero
checks.expl: The notebook says so: initialising with e.g. all zeros could mask an incorrect implementation of the backward pass. If a term in your derivative is multiplied by a parameter that happens to be 0, a mistake in that term vanishes and cmp() reports a match.

checks.q: loss = −logprobs[range(n), Yb].mean() with a batch of n = 32. What is dloss/dlogprobs at a label position?
checks.expl: The loss is minus the average of 32 of the entries of logprobs, so each of those entries gets $-1/32 = -0.03125$, and every other entry — which the loss never reads — gets 0. That is exactly how dlogprobs is built: zeros, then −1.0/n at the labels.

checks.q: counts_sum_inv has shape (32, 1) and is multiplied by counts, of shape (32, 27). How is its gradient formed?
opts: By taking the gradient at the label column only, ignoring the rest
By averaging over the 32 rows, since the batch shares one denominator
By copying the gradient of the first column into the (32, 1) shape
By summing (counts × dprobs) over the 27 columns it was broadcast to
checks.expl: Broadcasting reused each row's single value 27 times, so by the multivariable chain rule its gradient is the sum of the 27 contributions: dcounts_sum_inv = (counts * dprobs).sum(1, keepdim=True). A broadcast forward is a sum backward.

checks.q: logit_maxes is subtracted from the logits 'for numerical stability'. What should its gradient be?
opts: Large, since the maximum logit dominates the softmax output
About zero, since shifting a row's logits leaves its probs unchanged
Exactly −1 at the max position and 0 everywhere else in the row
Undefined, because max is not a differentiable operation at all
checks.expl: Subtracting the same number from every logit in a row multiplies numerator and denominator of the softmax by the same factor, so the probabilities — and the loss — do not depend on it. Its gradient is therefore (numerically) zero; it is there only to keep exp() from overflowing.

checks.q: For one example the softmax gives the correct class probability 0.0165. What is that class's entry in dlogits × n? Four decimals.
checks.expl: The cross-entropy gradient with respect to the logits is the softmax output with 1 subtracted at the correct class: $0.0165 - 1 = -0.9835$ (then divided by n). The notebook shows exactly this row: every other entry equals its probability.

checks.q: Why does each row of dlogits sum to zero (the notebook prints about 1e-9)?
opts: Because the softmax is shifted by the row max before it is taken
Because dividing by n spreads the gradient evenly over the batch
Because the softmax row sums to 1 and 1 is taken off at the label
Because the labels are one-hot, so only one entry can be non-zero
checks.expl: dlogits is softmax(logits) − one_hot(label), over n. The probabilities sum to 1 and the one-hot sums to 1, so the row sums to 0: the push down on the correct logit (1 − p) exactly balances the pushes up on the wrong ones (their p's).

checks.q: For logits = h @ W2 + b2, with h of shape (32, 64) and W2 of shape (64, 27), which expression is dW2?
opts: dlogits @ W2.T, which has the shape that W2 has
dlogits.sum(0), as for the bias b2 in the same layer
W2.T @ h, which does not even involve the logit gradient
h.T @ dlogits, the only product giving shape (64, 27)
checks.expl: dW2 must have W2's shape, (64, 27). h.T is (64, 32) and dlogits is (32, 27), so h.T @ dlogits is the one arrangement that fits — and it sums each weight's gradient over the batch. dlogits @ W2.T is (32, 64): that is dh. dlogits.sum(0) is db2.

checks.q: emb = C[Xb] picks rows of the 27 x 10 table C. How is dC built from demb?
opts: Each row of demb is added into dC at its character's index, repeats adding up
dC is demb averaged over the batch and then reshaped to the 27 x 10 table
dC is set to the last demb row seen for each character, overwriting earlier ones
dC is demb @ C.T, the transpose rule used for any matrix multiplication
checks.expl: Indexing copies a row of C into each position of emb. Backward, each position's gradient flows back to the row it came from, and a character that appears several times in the batch receives the sum — the notebook's double loop does dC[ix] += demb[k, j].

ai200.1.5.takeaway: Seeing more context helps, but squashing eight characters into one layer is crude: fuse them a pair at a time — a tree, as in WaveNet — with PyTorch-style modules, and mind the shapes, because one wrong reduction dimension in batch norm silently costs performance.

beats.d: block_size goes from 3 to 8, so every example is the previous eight characters ('..yuheng' predicts '.'). On its own this improves the dev loss from 2.105 to 2.027.

Linear (Kaiming-scaled), BatchNorm1d, Tanh, plus new Embedding, FlattenConsecutive and Sequential classes — a model becomes a list of layers, and model(Xb) gives the logits. Layers are switched to eval mode before evaluating, which batch norm needs.

beats.t: Flatten a pair at a time
beats.d: FlattenConsecutive(n) reshapes (B, T, C) into (B, T/n, C·n) — joining n neighbouring positions — and squeezes away a dimension of size 1. Three FlattenConsecutive(2) blocks fuse 8 characters into 4 pairs, then 2 groups of four, then one: a tree, like WaveNet, instead of one layer seeing all eight at once.

Inside the tree the activations are (B, T, C). The batch statistics must be taken over dims (0, 1) — every example and every position — so each of the C channels gets one mean and variance. Over dim 0 alone, each position gets its own, from fewer numbers; fixing that is the 'fix bug in batchnorm' line in the log.

Context 3 to 8: val 2.105 to 2.027. Flat to hierarchical at the same 22K parameters: 2.029, no gain by itself. The batch-norm fix: 2.022. Scaling to n_embd 24 and n_hidden 128 (76,579 parameters): train 1.769, val 1.993.
The names now read well ('hendrix.', 'jaylene.', 'aubreana.'). But train 1.769 against val 1.993 is a wider gap than before: the bigger model is starting to overfit.

Forwarding the eight examples of 'diondre' one at a time repeats work: a convolution is 'a for loop' that applies the same Linear layers across every position in one efficient pass, reusing the shared intermediate results.

ai200.1.5.worked: Push one batch through the model layer by layer and print each layer's output shape: (32, 8) indices, (32, 8, 24) embeddings, (32, 4, 48) after the first flatten, (32, 4, 128) after its linear layer, and so on down to (32, 27). Any reduction — a mean, a variance — should be checked against those shapes, which is how the batch-norm bug shows itself.
ai200.1.5.watch: Copying a 2-D layer into a 3-D setting unchanged. BatchNorm1d written for (B, C) still runs on (B, T, C), but averaging over dim 0 alone gives every position its own statistics — no error, just a quietly worse model.

checks.q: The hierarchical model: Embedding(27, 24); then three blocks of FlattenConsecutive(2) and Linear without bias (48→128, 256→128, 256→128), each with BatchNorm1d(128); then Linear(128, 27) with bias. How many parameters? (digits only, no commas)
checks.expl: 648 (embedding) + 6,144 + 256 + 32,768 + 256 + 32,768 + 256 (three linear + batch-norm pairs; each batch norm has gamma and beta) + 3,456 + 27 (output) = 76,579, as the notebook prints. The 256-wide inputs are two fused 128-wide positions.

checks.q: Why does the hierarchical model apply FlattenConsecutive(2) three times instead of flattening all 8 characters into the first layer?
opts: Because a Linear layer cannot take more than 48 inputs at a time
Because flattening all 8 at once would make batch norm impossible
Because the embedding only works on pairs of characters at a time
To fuse the context gradually, pairs then pairs of pairs, as a tree
checks.expl: Flattening all eight into one layer crushes the whole context in a single step. Joining two neighbours at a time and then joining those results builds a tree — the WaveNet idea — so information is combined gradually across depth. The commented 'original network' is the flat version.

checks.q: Inside the tree, batch norm sees inputs of shape (32, 4, 128). Why must its mean and variance be over dims (0, 1) rather than 0?
opts: Over dim 0 the result has the wrong number of dimensions and errors
Over (0, 1) is faster to compute, though both give the same answer
So each of the 128 channels gets one estimate, from all 4 positions
So the running mean can be skipped while the model is training
checks.expl: Averaging over dim 0 only gives a (1, 4, 128) mean: separate statistics per position, each from 32 numbers, and running buffers of that shape. It runs without error, which is why it is a bug. Over (0, 1) every channel gets one mean and variance from 128 numbers — the 'fix bug in batchnorm' entry in the log.

checks.q: By the notebook's performance log, which change by itself did NOT improve the validation loss?
opts: Going from flat to hierarchical at the same 22K parameters
Raising the context length from 3 characters to 8 characters
Fixing batch norm to reduce over both the batch and position dims
Scaling up to n_embd 24 and n_hidden 128, with 76K parameters
checks.expl: Val went 2.105 → 2.027 with the longer context, then 2.027 → 2.029 for the hierarchical layout at the same parameter count — no gain on its own — then 2.022 after the batch-norm fix and 1.993 after scaling up. A better architecture still needs the right size and correct code to pay off.

checks.q: The lecture ends by calling a convolution 'a for loop'. What is the point?
opts: A convolution is slower than a for loop but uses less GPU memory
A convolution forwards each position separately, one at a time
Convolutions replace the Linear layers with ones that have no weights
It applies the same layers at every position in one efficient pass
checks.expl: The eight examples from 'diondre' share most of their context, yet forwarding them one by one recomputes the shared parts eight times. A convolution slides the same Linear layers over all positions inside the kernel, reusing intermediate results — the for loop, made efficient.

checks.q: The scaled-up model ends at train 1.769, val 1.993. What does the widening gap between them suggest?
opts: The validation split is broken and should be rebuilt from scratch
The bigger model is starting to overfit the training names
Batch norm is still computing its statistics over the wrong dims
The learning-rate decay at step 150,000 came much too early
checks.expl: In the earlier, smaller models train and val were within about 0.05–0.1; here val is 0.22 higher. More capacity let the model fit the training names better than it generalises — the usual next step is more data or regularisation, or tuning before scaling further.

ai200.1.6.takeaway: A GPT is a bigram model that learned to look back: tokens gather information from earlier positions through masked, scaled self-attention, compute on it with a feed-forward net, and stack those blocks with residual connections and layer norms — each addition visibly lowering the validation loss on Tiny Shakespeare.

beats.t: Characters as tokens, chunks as batches
beats.d: Tiny Shakespeare is encoded one character per integer, split 90 / 10 into train and val. get_batch draws random chunks: x is block_size tokens and y the same chunk shifted by one, so one chunk holds block_size examples, with contexts of length 1 up to block_size.

Each token reads the logits for the next token straight out of an embedding table; generate() samples one token at a time from the last position's softmax and appends it. Trained with AdamW, it produces Shakespeare-shaped gibberish.
Tokens get n_embd-dimensional embeddings and a linear lm_head to the vocabulary; a position embedding table adds where each token sits, since attention by itself has no notion of order.

Each position emits a query and a key; their dot products, scaled by $1/\sqrt{\text{head size}}$, are the affinities (the gpt.py published with the video scaled by the embedding size C instead; a fix after the video changed it). A lower-triangular mask sets the future to −inf, softmax turns each row into weights, and the output is a weighted sum of the values. Val loss: 2.5.

Four heads of size 8, concatenated back to 32: several independent communication channels (val 2.28). A per-position feed-forward net — linear, ReLU — then lets each token compute on what it gathered (2.24). Attention is communication; the feed-forward net is computation.

beats.t: Residuals and layer norm make it deep
beats.d: Blocks are stacked with x = x + f(x), a projection back into the residual stream, and a 4x wider feed-forward layer; layer norm is applied to x before each sub-layer and once more before lm_head. Val loss 2.06.

batch 64, block_size 256, n_embd 384, 6 heads, 6 layers, learning rate 3e-4 and dropout 0.2 on the attention weights, the projections and the feed-forward output — and the samples in more.txt read like a play.
generate() crops the running sequence to its last block_size tokens before every forward pass: the position table has only block_size rows, and the mask is that wide.

ai200.1.6.worked: Track the shapes through one head: x is (B, T, C); q and k are (B, T, hs); q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) is (B, T, T) — one row of affinities per position; after the mask and softmax, @ v gives (B, T, hs). Then multi-head concatenates n_head of those back to C, which is why head_size = n_embd // n_head.
ai200.1.6.watch: Forgetting the mask, or masking after the softmax. Without the −inf entries in the upper triangle, every position can attend to the tokens it is supposed to predict, the training loss collapses, and generation — which has no future to look at — falls apart.

checks.q: get_batch takes x = data[i : i+block_size] and y = data[i+1 : i+block_size+1]. With block_size = 8, how many (context, target) training examples does one such chunk pack?
checks.expl: Position t of x, with everything before it, predicts y[t]: contexts of length 1, 2, … up to 8, each with its own target. Training on every length is also what lets the model generate from a context as short as one token.

checks.q: In a self-attention head, why is wei filled with −inf wherever the lower-triangular tril matrix is 0, before the softmax?
opts: To stop the attention weights from growing too large during training
To make the attention weights symmetric between any two positions
So each position gathers only from itself and earlier positions, never later
So that the softmax output will sum to the head size, rather than to exactly one
checks.src: gpt.py, class Head (commit 10024b1, 'add a single self-attention head')
checks.expl: exp(−inf) = 0, so after the softmax every future position gets exactly zero weight and each row still sums to 1 over the allowed ones. A token predicting the next character must not see it — this is a decoder; an encoder would simply leave the mask out.

checks.q: The lecture scales the attention scores by 1/√(head size), so that they keep roughly unit variance before the softmax. With n_embd = 384 and n_head = 6, by what factor are the scores q · k multiplied? Three decimals.
checks.src: gpt.py at the video's commit 381c613, class Block (head_size) and class Head
checks.expl: head_size = n_embd // n_head = 384 / 6 = 64, and $64^{-1/2} = 0.125$. Scaling by the head size keeps the scores' variance near 1, so the softmax stays diffuse at initialisation instead of turning nearly one-hot. The gpt.py published with the video multiplied by C**-0.5, where C is the embedding size — $384^{-1/2} \approx 0.051$; a community fix merged on 27 January 2023, ten days after the video, changed it to the head size.

checks.q: Replacing one 32-dimensional head with four heads of size 8, concatenated back to 32, lowered val loss from 2.5 to 2.28. What do several heads give?
opts: A larger model, since four heads have four times the parameters
Several independent channels, each with its own queries, keys, values
A longer context, since each head looks at a different block of tokens
Exact repetition: all four heads learn the same weights, then average
checks.expl: Each head has its own key, query and value projections, so tokens can look for several different things at once — the outputs are concatenated, not averaged. Four heads of 8 have the same total width as one of 32, so the gain comes from structure, not size.

checks.q: The Block's docstring says 'communication followed by computation'. Which is which?
opts: Communication is the feed-forward net; computation is self-attention
Both are attention: one head communicates, one head computes the result
Communication is the layer norm; computation is the final lm_head
Attention moves information between positions; the MLP works per token
checks.src: gpt.py, class Block (commit 97dd3f9, 'add a computation block')
checks.expl: Self-attention is the only place tokens exchange information. The feed-forward net applies the same linear–ReLU–linear to every position independently, letting each token process what it gathered. Adding it after attention took val loss from 2.28 to 2.24.

checks.q: Each sub-layer is applied as x = x + self.sa(self.ln1(x)). Why does the 'x +' help a deep stack train?
opts: Addition passes the gradient through unchanged, straight to the earlier blocks
Addition doubles the signal, so that the activations do not shrink with the depth
Addition removes the need for the layer norms that sit inside the block
Addition lets all of the blocks share a single set of attention weights
checks.src: gpt.py, class Block (commit 5c3a2d2, 'introduce the residual block')
checks.expl: As in micrograd, a + node hands its incoming gradient to both inputs unchanged, so a residual stream carries gradient from the loss directly to every block. Each block's attention and MLP branch off it and add their result back through a projection.

checks.q: Why does generate() crop the running sequence to idx[:, -block_size:] before each forward pass?
opts: To save memory, since older tokens no longer affect the prediction
To make generation deterministic once the context is long enough
The position table and the mask only cover block_size positions
Because the tokenizer can only decode block_size tokens at a time
checks.src: gpt.py, BigramLanguageModel.generate (commit 10024b1; renamed GPTLanguageModel after the video)
checks.expl: position_embedding_table has block_size rows, so position block_size has no embedding, and tril is block_size x block_size. Older tokens would matter if the model could see them; it cannot, so the window slides.

checks.q: estimate_loss() switches to model.eval(), averages the loss over eval_iters = 200 batches per split, then calls model.train(). Why both?
opts: eval() freezes the weights, so averaging cannot change the model
Single-batch losses are noisy, and eval mode turns off dropout
200 batches cover the whole validation set exactly once each
train() resets the optimizer, which eval() had suspended for it
checks.expl: One batch's loss jumps around, so the printed train and val numbers average 200. And dropout randomly zeroes activations only in training mode; measuring with it on would report a worse, noisier model than the one you have. model.train() turns it back on.

ai200.1.7.takeaway: A tokenizer is a separate model with its own training set and algorithm: byte-level BPE starts from the 256 bytes and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair, encode() replays those merges in the order they were learned, and many of an LLM's weird behaviours trace back to the chunks this produces.

beats.d: The tokenizer translates between strings and tokens (chunks of text) and is a completely separate stage of an LLM: it has its own training set and its own training algorithm, Byte Pair Encoding, and once trained it implements just encode() and decode(). A lot of an LLM's weird behaviours trace back to it.

Byte Pair Encoding was popularised for LLMs by the GPT-2 paper and code release (Sennrich et al. 2015 is the original reference for BPE in NLP), and GPT, Llama and Mistral all train their tokenizers with it. minbpe implements the three functions — train, encode, decode — in a BasicTokenizer and a RegexTokenizer, plus a GPT4Tokenizer that reproduces tiktoken's GPT-4 encoding.
Encode the text as UTF-8 and start from the 256 possible byte values as the first tokens, so any string in any language — emoji included — can be represented, with no unknown token.

beats.t: Training: merge the most frequent pair
beats.d: Count every adjacent pair (get_stats), mint a new id for the most common (256, 257, …), replace every occurrence (merge), repeat vocab_size − 256 times. On 'aaabdaaabac' minbpe's three merges are aa → 256, then (256, a) → 257 ('aaa'), then (257, b) → 258 ('aaab'): after the first merge two pairs tie at two each, and max() keeps the one counted first. The string becomes [258, 100, 258, 97, 99]. The README's walk-through (aa, then ab, then aa+ab) is Wikipedia's tie-break, not the code's; the ids come out the same.

decode() concatenates each id's bytes and decodes as UTF-8 with errors='replace', because a token sequence can be invalid UTF-8. encode() starts from bytes and repeatedly applies the available pair with the LOWEST merge index — the order the merges were learned — until none applies.

beats.t: Regex splitting, as GPT-2 and GPT-4 do
beats.d: RegexTokenizer first splits the text with a pattern into letters, numbers (GPT-4: at most three digits), punctuation and whitespace, and runs BPE inside each chunk, so no token crosses a category boundary. Trained on enough data at 100K vocab, it should reproduce GPT-4's tokenizer.

Tokens such as end-of-text (id 100257 in GPT-4) are registered after the merges and inserted by splitting on exact matches. encode() refuses them by default — allowed_special must be set — because tokenizing attacker-controlled text as control tokens is a footgun.

GPT4Tokenizer loads tiktoken's cl100k_base ranks, recovers the merges from them, and undoes a historical permutation of the 256 byte tokens; its tests check identical ids to tiktoken. sentencepiece, used by Llama and Mistral, runs BPE on Unicode code points rather than bytes.

ai200.1.7.worked: To see what a model sees, run the text through its tokenizer and print the pieces with their ids. Look for leading spaces, numbers split at odd places, and words in other languages broken into many byte-level pieces: whatever looks arbitrary there is what the network has to learn around.
ai200.1.7.watch: Tokenizing untrusted text with special tokens enabled. If a user's message contains the literal end-of-text string and it becomes the real control token, the user can end documents or impersonate structure — which is why encode() refuses unless allowed_special is set deliberately.

checks.q: BasicTokenizer is trained on 'aaabdaaabac' with vocab_size = 256 + 3, then encodes the same string. How many tokens does it produce?
checks.src: minbpe/basic.py, train(); README.md, quick start; tests/test_tokenizer.py, test_wikipedia_example
checks.expl: train() takes max(stats, key=stats.get), and on a tie max() keeps the pair counted first. Merge 1: aa → 256 (four occurrences). Now (256, a) and (a, b) both occur twice, and (256, a) was counted first, so merge 2: aaa → 257. Merge 3: (257, b), i.e. aaab → 258. The string becomes 258, d, 258, a, c — [258, 100, 258, 97, 99], five tokens for eleven bytes. The README and the test's docstring explain it with Wikipedia's merges (aa, ab, then aa+ab, 'XdXac'); the code reaches the same ids by a different second merge.

checks.q: A RegexTokenizer is trained with vocab_size = 32768. How many merges does it learn? (digits only, no commas)
checks.src: minbpe/basic.py and regex.py, train(); README.md, special tokens
checks.expl: The first 256 ids are the raw bytes, which need no training, so num_merges = vocab_size − 256 = 32,512. The last merge gets id 32,767, and the README notes a first special token should therefore take id 32,768.

checks.q: Why does a byte-level BPE tokenizer never meet a character it cannot encode?
opts: Every string is UTF-8 bytes, and all 256 bytes are already tokens
Its training text is large enough to contain every possible character
It maps every unknown character to one shared special unknown token
It falls back to splitting the text into individual Unicode code points
checks.expl: The vocabulary always starts with bytes 0–255, and any text — Korean, emoji, anything — is a sequence of UTF-8 bytes. Merges only shorten the sequence; the bytes are always there to fall back on. Splitting into code points is what sentencepiece does instead.

checks.q: When encode() runs on new text, which mergeable pair does it merge first?
opts: The pair that occurs the most often in the text being encoded now
The leftmost pair in the text that appears in the merges
The pair whose merged token is longest, to minimise length
The pair with the lowest merge index — the one learned first
checks.expl: Encoding must replay training, in which earlier merges built the pieces later ones combine. So encode repeatedly takes min over the pairs by their merge index and stops when no pair in the text has a merge. Frequency in the new text plays no part.

checks.q: Why does RegexTokenizer split the text with a pattern into letters, numbers, punctuation and whitespace before running BPE?
opts: To make training faster, since smaller chunks need fewer merges
So no merge — and so no token — can cross a category boundary
So that every word becomes exactly one token in the vocabulary
To strip whitespace, which tokenizers are not able to encode
checks.expl: BPE runs inside each chunk and the results are concatenated, so a frequent pair like a letter followed by punctuation can never be merged. The GPT-2 paper introduced this; GPT-4's pattern also limits numbers to at most 3 digits per chunk. Words can still be several tokens, and whitespace is encoded like anything else.

checks.q: RegexTokenizer's default GPT-4 split pattern matches numbers in runs of one to three digits (\p{N}{1,3}). Into how many chunks does it split the number 1234567 before any merging?
checks.expl: The pattern matches greedily from the left: '123', '456', '7'. BPE then runs inside each chunk, so no token can span more than three digits, and a long number is cut at places that have nothing to do with its value — part of why LLMs find arithmetic awkward. GPT-2's pattern, \p{N}+, kept a whole run of digits together.

checks.q: encode() raises an error if the text contains a registered special token such as end-of-text, unless allowed_special is set. Why?
opts: Special tokens cannot be decoded, so they would corrupt the output
Special tokens have ids above the vocab size, so the lookups would fail
So user-controlled text can't silently be turned into control tokens
Because special tokens must be encoded by tiktoken, not by minbpe
checks.expl: Like tiktoken, minbpe makes you declare intent. Otherwise attacker-controlled data — a user prompt containing the literal string — could be tokenized as the real control token. With allowed_special='all' the text is split on exact matches and those parts become the special ids.

checks.q: Why does decode() turn bytes into text with errors='replace' rather than strict UTF-8 decoding?
opts: Because the vocabulary stores all its tokens as Python strings, not bytes
Because replacement characters are what the training data contains
Because strict decoding would remove the spaces in front of tokens
Because a token sequence can be invalid UTF-8, which strict mode rejects
checks.src: minbpe/basic.py and regex.py, decode(); minbpe/base.py, save()
checks.expl: Tokens are byte strings, and many are partial UTF-8 sequences — part of a multi-byte character. A model can emit them in an order that does not form valid UTF-8, and a strict decode would throw. errors='replace' substitutes the replacement character instead; the .vocab file is lossy for the same reason.

ai200.1.8.takeaway: Reproducing GPT-2 (124M) is the GPT from before plus everything that makes it real: the exact architecture so OpenAI's weights load, GPT-2's initialisation, a long list of speed-ups, GPT-3's optimisation recipe — AdamW, clipping, warmup and cosine decay, a 0.5M-token batch via gradient accumulation — and honest evaluation on held-out loss and HellaSwag.

beats.t: Match GPT-2 exactly, then load it
beats.d: 12 layers, 12 heads, n_embd 768, context 1,024, vocabulary 50,257 (50,000 merges + 256 bytes + end-of-text). Module names follow Hugging Face's, so from_pretrained copies OpenAI's weights in — transposing the Conv1D ones — and the model samples sensible text before any training.

A buffer of B·T + 1 tokens becomes x (all but the last) and y (all but the first), viewed as (B, T). The loss is cross-entropy over every position. A tiny batch can be overfitted to check the pipeline before training for real.

The token embedding wte and the output lm_head share one matrix — GPT-2's checkpoint already does. Weights start at std 0.02, and the projections that write into the residual stream are scaled by $1/\sqrt{2 \cdot n_{\text{layer}}}$, because each block adds two contributions and the stream's std would otherwise grow with depth.

TF32 matmuls, bfloat16 autocast, torch.compile, flash attention through F.scaled_dot_product_attention, and the vocabulary padded from 50,257 to the 'nice' 50,304 — each its own commit, each measured in tokens per second.

AdamW with betas (0.9, 0.95) and eps 1e-8, gradient norm clipped at 1.0, a learning rate that warms up linearly for 715 steps to 6e-4 and then decays on a cosine to 6e-5, and weight decay 0.1 on 2-D parameters only.

total_batch_size is 524,288 tokens; with micro-batches of B·T tokens the gradient is accumulated over several forward/backward passes before one optimizer step, and the loss is divided by the number of micro-steps so the accumulated gradient is a mean, not a sum. DDP splits the micro-steps across GPUs and averages.

The 10B-token sample, tokenized with GPT-2's tokenizer, end-of-text between documents, stored as uint16 in 100 shards of 100M tokens, the first shard kept for validation. 19,073 steps of 0.5M tokens is about one epoch.

Validation loss every 250 steps, and HellaSwag in completion style: each of the four endings is appended to the context and the one with the lowest average per-token loss is chosen. The 124M run is compared with OpenAI's GPT-2 checkpoint (val 3.2924; HellaSwag 0.2945) and GPT-3 124M (0.337).

ai200.1.8.worked: When changing the batch size, keep the objective the same: fix total_batch_size in tokens, derive grad_accum_steps = total / (B · T · world_size), and divide each micro-step's loss by grad_accum_steps. Then the gradient matches the big batch's mean whatever micro-batch fits in memory — the play notebook checks exactly this on a tiny MLP.
ai200.1.8.watch: Accumulating gradients without rescaling the loss. backward() adds gradients, so k micro-steps produce the gradient of a SUM of k mean losses — k times too large — which silently multiplies the effective learning rate by k.

checks.q: GPT-2 (124M) ties its token embedding to its output layer: vocab 50,257, n_embd 768. How many parameters does sharing that one matrix save? (digits only, no commas)
checks.src: build-nanogpt train_gpt2.py, GPT.__init__ (commit ec39245, 'weight tie the embedding and unembedding matrix'); play.ipynb, cells 12-14
checks.expl: Each of the two matrices is 50,257 x 768 = 38,597,376 parameters — about 30% of the 124M model. The notebook shows OpenAI's checkpoint stores lm_head and wte with the same values at the same memory address; in the code it is one line, wte.weight = lm_head.weight.

checks.q: _init_weights multiplies the std of every c_proj layer by (2 · n_layer)^−0.5. Why?
opts: To make those projection layers learn faster than the rest of the network
Each block adds two outputs to the residual stream; this stops its std growing
To compensate for the GELU nonlinearity, which halves the variance of its input
Because the projection layers have no bias, so they need less noise
checks.expl: Every block adds attention's and the MLP's projections into the stream, 2 · n_layer additions in all, and adding n random contributions grows the std like $\sqrt{n}$. The notebook adds 100 random vectors scaled by $100^{-1/2}$ and the std stays about 1. Hence the c_proj layers, the ones writing into the stream, are scaled down.

checks.q: total_batch_size = 524,288 tokens, micro-batch B = 64 sequences of T = 1,024 tokens, on one GPU. How many gradient-accumulation micro-steps make one optimizer step?
checks.expl: One micro-step processes 64 x 1,024 = 65,536 tokens; 524,288 / 65,536 = 8. With DDP on 8 GPUs the divisor gains a factor of 8 and it becomes 1 micro-step per GPU. The total is 2^19, about 0.5M tokens — GPT-3's batch size for this model size.

checks.q: In the accumulation loop each micro-step's loss is divided by grad_accum_steps before backward(). Why?
opts: To keep bfloat16 from overflowing when several losses get summed up
To make the learning-rate warmup reach its peak at the right step
Because backward() adds gradients, which turns the mean into a sum
Because DistributedDataParallel already multiplies each loss by 8
checks.src: build-nanogpt train_gpt2.py, training loop; play.ipynb, cells 16-17
checks.expl: cross_entropy averages over a micro-batch, but accumulating gradients sums them across micro-steps, so the 1/N normaliser of the big batch is lost. Dividing each loss by the number of micro-steps puts it back, and the notebook's tiny MLP gives identical gradients both ways.

checks.q: configure_optimizers applies weight decay to some parameters and not others. Which get it?
opts: The 2-D tensors — matmul weights and embeddings — but no biases or norms
Every parameter equally, since AdamW decays all weights in the same way
Only the biases and layer norms, since the big matrices are already tied
Only the embedding tables, which are the largest tensors in the model
checks.src: build-nanogpt train_gpt2.py, configure_optimizers (commit 3a148e4, 'add weight decay, only for 2D params')
checks.expl: The rule in the code is p.dim() >= 2: all weight tensors in matmuls plus the embeddings are decayed (0.1); biases and LayerNorm gains and biases are not. The optimizer is AdamW, and its fused CUDA version is used when available.

checks.q: get_lr warms up for 715 steps to max_lr = 6e-4, then decays on a cosine to min_lr = 6e-5 at step 19,073. What is the learning rate exactly halfway through the decay?
checks.src: build-nanogpt train_gpt2.py, get_lr (commit 90e5d15, 'add learning rate scheduler')
checks.expl: At the midpoint decay_ratio = 0.5, so coeff = 0.5 · (1 + cos(π/2)) = 0.5, and lr = 6e-5 + 0.5 · (6e-4 − 6e-5) = 3.3e-4. The cosine spends longer near the top and the bottom than a straight line would, and min_lr is 10% of max_lr.

checks.q: The speed-up hour swaps the hand-written attention (q @ kᵀ, mask, softmax, @ v) for F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True). It computes the same attention. Where does the speed-up come from?
opts: It never writes the T × T attention matrix out to GPU memory
It approximates the softmax with a cheaper polynomial function
It drops the causal mask, so half of the scores are skipped
It quietly lowers the precision of the scores to 8-bit floats
checks.src: build-nanogpt train_gpt2.py, CausalSelfAttention.forward (commit 7ee630c, 'switch to flash attention')
checks.expl: The code it replaced carried the comment 'materializes the large (T,T) matrix for all the queries and keys': a T × T tensor per head, written to GPU memory and read back for the mask, the softmax and the product with v. Flash attention does all of it in one fused kernel, so that matrix never makes the round trip — no fewer FLOPs (the backward pass even recomputes some), far less memory traffic. is_causal=True keeps the mask. It sits with the hour's other speed-ups: TF32 matmuls, bf16 autocast, torch.compile and the vocabulary padded to 50,304.

checks.q: How does the script score a HellaSwag example?
opts: It asks the model to output the letter A to D of the right ending
It picks the ending with the highest probability for its first token
It counts which ending shares the most words with the given context
It appends each ending and picks the lowest average loss over it
checks.expl: Completion style: the four candidates are rendered as context + ending, a mask marks the ending's tokens, and the per-token cross-entropy is averaged over those tokens only; the lowest is the prediction. A small model cannot handle letter-choice multiple choice, but it can still prefer the likely continuation.

ai210.0.0.takeaway: Deep learning is taught here top-down: train a working image classifier in minutes first, then name what happened — Samuel's loop of weights, an automatic measure of performance and an automatic way to improve it — and learn the discipline that keeps it honest: a validation set, and a test set hidden even from yourself.

beats.d: In 2015 recognising a bird in a photo was an XKCD punchline. The lesson's notebook searches DuckDuckGo for bird and forest photos, downloads about 200 of each per search, removes broken files, fine-tunes a pretrained resnet18 for three epochs, and then asks it whether the test photo is a bird, and with what probability.

beats.t: A DataBlock says what the data is
beats.d: blocks=(ImageBlock, CategoryBlock): images in, categories out. get_items finds the files; RandomSplitter(valid_pct=0.2, seed=42) holds out 20% for validation; get_y=parent_label takes each label from the folder an image sits in; Resize(192, method='squish') makes every image the same size.

beats.t: You don't need what you think you need
beats.d: High-school maths, sometimes fewer than 50 labelled items, and free GPUs are enough. The book teaches the whole game first — Perkins's baseball, Lockhart's lament about how maths is taught — and theory once you have the context and the motivation.
