McCulloch and Pitts's artificial neuron (1943); Rosenblatt's Mark I Perceptron; Minsky and Papert showing one layer cannot learn XOR — and that more layers fix it, which was ignored; the 1986 PDP volumes; and only recently more layers, better hardware and more data.

Don't write the steps; show examples. A model has weights; an automatic test measures how well a weight assignment performs; an automatic mechanism changes the weights to do better. Today: architecture, parameters, predictions, labels, loss — and a trained model is just a program.

No data, no model; no labels, no training; a model only predicts, it does not recommend actions; and a model in the world can create a feedback loop, as predictive policing does when its predicted arrests become its next training data.

beats.t: The cat recogniser, line by line
beats.d: is_cat reads the label from the file name; valid_pct=0.2 and seed=42 fix the validation set; resnet34 is the architecture and error_rate the metric — for people, unlike the loss, which is for SGD. A pretrained model gets a new head, and fine_tune fits the head, then the whole model.

Early layers learn edges and gradients, later ones wheels, text and petals (Zeiler and Fergus). Sound as spectrograms, time series as images, mouse movements, malware bytes — if a person can see the categories, an image model can learn them. The same few lines also do segmentation, sentiment, tabular data and recommendations.

Choosing hyperparameters by looking at validation results overfits the validation set, so keep a test set hidden even from yourself. And pick validation data like the future: the latest dates for time series, unseen drivers or boats when production will see new ones.

ai210.0.0.worked: Before training anything, write down how the data will be split. Ask what new data will look like in use — later dates, new people, new places — and make the validation set look like that, not like a random sample of what you already have. Then keep a test set that you look at once, at the end, with a metric you chose for what actually matters.
ai210.0.0.watch: Judging a model by its accuracy on the data it was trained on, or tuning hyperparameters against the validation set until it stops being unseen. A big enough model memorises its training set; only data it never influenced says how it will do.

checks.q: In the bird notebook's DataBlock, where does each image get its label?
opts: From the name of the folder it was saved in, via get_y=parent_label
From a pretrained model that tags each download as bird or forest first
From the search result's caption, saved with each image
From the file name, whose first letter is upper case for each bird photo
checks.src: 00-is-it-a-bird-creating-a-model-from-your-own-data.ipynb (as of the course release), cells 16 and 21-22
checks.expl: The downloads were saved into bird_or_not/bird and bird_or_not/forest, so the parent folder's name is the label. Reading a label off the first letter of the file name is the chapter 1 pets trick (is_cat), where the dataset's creators encoded cats that way.

checks.q: In Arthur Samuel's 1962 description, what has to be automatic for a program to 'learn' from its experience?
opts: Writing out each step of the task, which the computer then repeats faster
Testing how well the current weights perform, and changing them to do better
Storing every example it has seen, so that it can look the answer up later
Choosing the architecture, after which the weights can be set by hand
checks.expl: Samuel's idea: a weight assignment, an automatic means of testing its actual performance, and a mechanism for altering it to maximise that performance. When adjusting the weights is automatic too, the machine 'learns'. Spelling out every step is exactly what machine learning avoids.

checks.q: Training minimises a loss, yet fastai reports error_rate after every epoch. Why have both?
opts: error_rate is measured on the training set, and the loss on the validation set
They are the same number, which fastai simply prints under two names
The loss has to suit SGD to update weights; the metric is for people to read
The loss is only used with pretrained models; the metric is used for the rest
checks.src: fastbook 01_intro.ipynb, How Our Image Recognizer Works
checks.expl: The loss is the measure of performance the training system uses to change the weights, so it must be easy for SGD to work with. A metric is defined for human consumption — easy to understand and close to what you care about — and fastai reports it on the validation set.

checks.q: What does learn.fine_tune(1) do with a pretrained resnet?
opts: It trains the whole network from random weights for a single epoch
It fits only the new head for one epoch and then it stops right there
It trains every layer for one epoch at one learning rate, the same for all
It fits the new head, then trains it all, the later layers updated faster
checks.src: fastbook 01_intro.ipynb, How Our Image Recognizer Works
checks.expl: vision_learner replaces the pretrained model's last layer with a new randomly initialised head. fine_tune first spends one epoch fitting just what the new head needs, then trains the whole model for the requested epochs, updating later layers faster than early ones, which need little change.

checks.q: A predictive-policing model is trained on past arrests and used to decide where to patrol. What does chapter 1 warn will happen?
opts: More patrols mean more arrests there, which feed retraining, and bias grows
The model drifts toward predicting crime evenly across every district
The model stops working, since it has no labels for crimes not yet committed
Nothing harmful, since the model only predicts and leaves decisions to people
checks.src: fastbook 01_intro.ipynb, Limitations Inherent To Machine Learning
checks.expl: It predicts arrests, not crime, so it partly reflects existing policing bias; officers then patrol where it points, making more arrests there, and those arrests become the next model's training data — a positive feedback loop in which more use means more bias.

checks.q: You are forecasting next month's sales from five years of daily data. How should the validation set be chosen?
opts: A random 20% of the days, with a fixed seed so the split stays the same
The most recent stretch of days, with training on all the days before it
Every fifth day, so validation covers each season evenly across years
The days with the highest sales, since those matter most to the business
checks.src: fastbook 01_intro.ipynb, Use Judgment in Defining Test Sets
checks.expl: Validation data must look like the data the model will face in use — here, the future. A random sample is too easy (the model sees days on both sides of each gap) and unrepresentative; the latest continuous period is what back-testing and Kaggle's grocery competition use.

ai210.0.1.takeaway: A model is only useful once someone can use it: design a project around data you can actually get, train a quick model and let it show you what is wrong with the data, then export it — architecture, weights and data pipeline in one file — and serve it from a plain CPU behind a small web app.

beats.d: The most important thing when choosing a project is data availability. Don't hunt for the perfect dataset; get started, and iterate end to end — a rough version of every step, all the way to the deployed thing — so you learn early where the hard parts are and how much data you really need.

The lesson's notebook labels the pets images with is_cat (cat file names start with a capital letter), builds DataLoaders with ImageDataLoaders.from_name_func and Resize(192), fine-tunes a resnet18 for 3 epochs, and calls learn.export('model.pkl') — the file the app will load.

Chapter 2 downloads search results for grizzly, black and teddy bears into one folder per type, deletes the files that fail to open with verify_images, and describes them with a DataBlock: images in, categories out, labels from the parent folder, a seeded 20% validation split.

beats.t: Crop, squish, pad — or a random crop
beats.d: Resize crops to a square by default and can lose details; squishing distorts shapes; padding wastes computation on black space. RandomResizedCrop takes a different random part of each image on each epoch, so the model sees objects framed many ways.

beats.t: Augment the batch, on the GPU
beats.d: Data augmentation makes random variations that don't change the meaning: rotation, flipping, perspective warping, brightness and contrast. With every image already one size, aug_transforms runs as batch_tfms on whole batches on the GPU.

beats.t: Let the model clean the data
beats.d: A confusion matrix shows which bears are mistaken for which; plot_top_losses shows the images the model is most confidently wrong about — one 'black' bear is plainly a grizzly. Train a quick model first, then fix the labels it exposes with ImageClassifierCleaner, and retrain.

export saves the architecture, the trained parameters and the DataLoaders recipe, so production uses the same transforms; load_learner reads it back, and predict returns the category, its index into dls.vocab, and every category's probability.

beats.t: A web app, served by a CPU
beats.d: The lesson deploys to a Hugging Face Space with Gradio and shows a JavaScript interface in the browser too; the chapter builds the same idea with ipywidgets and Voilà. Serving one user's image at a time leaves a GPU idle, so a CPU server is usually cheaper and far simpler.

ai210.0.1.worked: To ship an image classifier: label folders by class, verify the downloads, build a DataBlock with RandomResizedCrop(224, min_scale=0.5) and aug_transforms(), fine-tune for a few epochs, look at the confusion matrix and the top losses, clean the labels the model exposes, retrain, then learn.export() — and in the app, load_learner the file and call predict on each upload.
ai210.0.1.watch: Cleaning a dataset by hand before ever training on it, when a quick model would point straight at the mislabelled images. And deploying a model trained on clean, artistic web photos to cameras that will see something else entirely — night shots, low resolution, bears from behind.

checks.q: Chapter 2 rejects cropping, squishing or padding every image once to a fixed size. What does RandomResizedCrop do instead?
opts: Crops the centre of every image once, so that each keeps its true shape
Pads each image with black borders, so nothing in the picture is lost
Picks a different random part of each image on every epoch of training
Squishes each image once and then crops the result to the size asked for
checks.expl: Squishing gives unrealistic shapes, cropping can cut out the features needed for recognition, and padding wastes computation on empty space. RandomResizedCrop selects part of each image at random, a different part each epoch, so the model learns objects framed in different ways; min_scale sets the smallest share kept.

checks.q: Why does the chapter pass aug_transforms as batch_tfms rather than as item_tfms?
opts: Augmentations can only be applied to images that already have labels
item_tfms run once before training, so they cannot vary between epochs
batch_tfms also augment the validation set, which item_tfms never do
Once items share one size, a whole batch can be augmented on the GPU
checks.expl: item_tfms run on each item separately — here Resize, which makes every image the same size. Then the images stack into one batch, and aug_transforms (rotation, flipping, warping, brightness, contrast) runs on the whole batch at once on the GPU, which saves a lot of time.

checks.q: The bear model's highest-loss image is predicted grizzly with high confidence but labelled black — and it looks like a grizzly. What does chapter 2 draw from this?
opts: Train a quick model first, then use its errors to find the data to clean
Always clean the whole dataset by hand before any training run begins
Remove every image the model gets wrong, so validation accuracy goes up
Lower the learning rate, since confident wrong answers mean overfitting
checks.src: fastbook 02_production.ipynb, Training Your Model, and Using It to Clean Your Data
checks.expl: The intuitive approach cleans data before training, but a model finds data issues faster. Sorting by loss surfaces mislabelled or non-bear images; ImageClassifierCleaner shows the highest-loss images per category and returns which to delete or relabel — you choose — and then you retrain.

checks.q: What does learn.export save, according to the lesson notebook and chapter 2?
opts: Only the trained weights, so the app must rebuild the architecture
Architecture, trained parameters and how the DataLoaders are built
The training images, so the app can retrain itself on the server
The validation predictions, which the app looks up, not computes
checks.src: 02-saving-a-basic-fastai-model.ipynb, cells 14-15; fastbook 02_production.ipynb, Using the Model for Inference
checks.expl: A model is its architecture plus its trained parameters; export saves both, so they always match, plus the definition of how to create the DataLoaders, so the transforms need not be redefined in production. The notebook writes model.pkl for the app; load_learner reads it back.

checks.q: Calling predict on the grizzly photo returns ('grizzly', tensor(1), tensor([9.0767e-06, 9.9999e-01, 1.5748e-07])). What is the tensor(1)?
opts: The number of images that predict was handed in this one call
A flag, set because the top probability cleared a threshold
The predicted category's index in the vocab: black, grizzly, teddy
How many of the three categories cleared the model's confidence cut-off
checks.src: fastbook 02_production.ipynb, Using the Model for Inference
checks.expl: predict returns the predicted category in the form the labels were given (here a string), the index of that category, and the probability of every category. The index and the probabilities follow the order of dls.vocab, ['black','grizzly','teddy'], so index 1 is grizzly, at probability about 0.99999.

checks.q: Why does chapter 2 say a deployed image classifier almost certainly needs no GPU?
opts: An exported model can only be loaded on a CPU, whatever trained it
Predictions are cached at export, so serving does no real computing
GPUs and CPUs give different answers, so serving must match how it trained
It sees one user's image at a time: too little parallel work for a GPU
checks.expl: GPUs pay off on lots of identical work in parallel; one image is not enough to keep one busy, so a CPU is often more cost-effective. Batching users' images makes them wait, GPU serving needs careful memory management and queueing, and CPU servers are cheaper because there is more competition.

ai210.0.2.takeaway: A neural network is a function that multiplies inputs by parameters, adds them up and replaces negatives with zero, layer after layer — and training is just gradient descent: measure a loss, ask for its gradient, step every parameter a little the other way, repeat. Enough rectified lines added together can fit anything; the rest is making it fast.

beats.d: A notebook built on Ross Wightman's timm benchmarks plots ImageNet accuracy against seconds per image. levit is fast and accurate, ConvNeXt leads the middle, beit the slow end (on a bigger dataset). And parameter count, often used as a proxy for speed, turns out not to be a useful one.

The notebook makes noisy points from 3x² + 2x + 1 and asks you to fit a, b and c with sliders. Going round the sliders twice does better than once, and a number helps: mean absolute error, the distance from each point to the curve.

Put a, b, c in one tensor, call requires_grad_(), compute the loss, call backward(), and read .grad. Subtract the gradient times a small number — the learning rate — inside torch.no_grad(), and loop. Near the answer the steps overshoot, so the learning rate is lowered as training goes: a schedule.

max(m·x + b, 0) is a line with a hook; add two and you get a bend; add enough and you can approximate any function of one input — and the same works in more dimensions. Drawing squiggly lines through points is all deep learning does; GPUs, convolutions and transfer learning make it affordable.

beats.t: A neural net in a spreadsheet
beats.d: The Titanic sheet scales Age by its maximum, takes log10(Fare + 1), turns class, port and sex into 0/1 columns, adds a column of ones for the constant, and predicts with SUMPRODUCT. The nnet sheet adds a second set of parameters, ReLUs each with IF(x<0,0,x), sums them and averages the squared error.

Chapter 4 names them: initialise the weights, predict, compute the loss, compute the gradient, step, repeat, stop. Accuracy can't be the loss — a tiny weight change rarely flips a prediction, so its gradient is zero almost everywhere — which is why the loss must be smooth, and the metric is for people.

Two linear layers in a row are just one linear layer with different parameters. Put a ReLU between them and each can do its own work; with big enough matrices that can approximate any function. Deeper nets reach the same accuracy with smaller matrices, so they train faster and use less memory.

ai210.0.2.worked: Fitting $ax^2+bx+c$ to noisy points: start from abc = [1.1, 1.1, 1.1] with requires_grad_(); compute the mean absolute error; call backward(); then, inside torch.no_grad(), subtract abc.grad × 0.01 and zero abc.grad after each step (abc.grad.zero_()), because backward() adds into .grad rather than replacing it — the notebook's own loop leaves this out. Each pass lowers the loss, until the steps start to overshoot — at which point a smaller learning rate takes over.
ai210.0.2.watch: Stacking linear layers and expecting a more powerful model — without a nonlinearity between them they collapse into one. And reading the loss as if it were the metric: the loss is shaped for the optimiser, the metric for you.

checks.q: The 'which image models are best' notebook plots speed against parameter count for timm's models. What does it conclude?
opts: Parameter count is a poor proxy for speed: speeds vary widely at any one count
Parameter count predicts speed closely, so papers are right to quote it that way
Models with more parameters are always more accurate, whatever their family is
Parameter count matters only on a CPU; on a GPU all of these models run alike
checks.expl: Papers often use parameter count as a proxy for speed, but the plot shows a wide variation in speed at each level of parameter count, so it is not a useful proxy — and as a guide to how much memory a model needs it is not always a great one either.

checks.q: In the quadratic-fitting notebook, if the gradient-descent loop runs long enough the loss starts to rise for a while. Why, and what is the fix?
opts: The gradients overflow; the fix is to clip them into a smaller fixed range
Steps near the answer jump over it; lower the learning rate as you train
The noise in the data takes over; the fix is to add more noisy data points
The quadratic has two minima; the fix is to restart from fresh parameters
checks.expl: Once the parameters are close to the right answer, a fixed-size update jumps right over it. The fix is to decrease the learning rate as training goes on — a learning rate schedule, which fastai and PyTorch can automate. In the notebook's own loop (cell 47) there is a second cause: abc.grad is never zeroed, so each backward() adds to the last, the gradients accumulate and the steps grow; zeroing the gradient after each step removes that one.

checks.q: The notebook's double_relu adds two rectified linear functions, max(m1·x + b1, 0) + max(m2·x + b2, 0). With its starting sliders m1 = -1.5, b1 = -1.5, m2 = 1.5, b2 = 1.5, what is its value at x = -3?
checks.expl: First term: -1.5 × (-3) - 1.5 = 3, which is positive, so it stays. Second term: 1.5 × (-3) + 1.5 = -3, which max(·, 0) replaces with 0. The sum is 3. Each rectified linear is flat at zero on one side of its hook and a line on the other; adding more of them bends the curve further.

checks.q: Chapter 4 decides against using accuracy as the loss for the 3s-and-7s model. Why?
opts: Accuracy can't be computed on a GPU, so training on it would be far too slow
Accuracy is measured on the validation set, and the loss must use training data
A tiny weight change rarely flips a prediction, so its gradient is nearly always 0
Accuracy rewards confident predictions, which makes the model overfit too fast
checks.expl: Accuracy only changes when a prediction flips between 3 and 7, and a small change in one weight almost never does that — so rise over run is zero almost everywhere and the model has nothing to learn from. A loss must respond smoothly to small changes in confidence; the metric is for people.

checks.q: Why does a neural net need a nonlinearity such as ReLU between its linear layers?
opts: Without one, PyTorch cannot compute the gradients of the earlier layers
ReLU halves the parameter count, and that is what makes deep nets fast
Only image models need one; tabular models just stack linear layers
Linear layers in a row collapse into one linear layer, whatever their size
checks.expl: Multiplying and adding several times over can be replaced by multiplying different things and adding once: a composition of linear functions is linear. With max(x, 0) between them each layer does its own useful work — enough, with big enough matrices, to approximate any function. The Titanic sheet's net uses ReLUs too.

checks.q: In titanic.xlsx's nnet sheet a passenger's prediction is ReLU(Lin1) + ReLU(Lin2) and the row's loss is the squared difference from Survived. For a passenger who did not survive, with Lin1 = -1.5 and Lin2 = 0.05, what is the loss?
checks.src: titanic.xlsx (course22 xl/), sheet nnet, columns AC-AH
checks.expl: ReLU(-1.5) = 0 and ReLU(0.05) = 0.05, so the prediction is 0.05. Survived is 0, so the loss is (0 - 0.05)² = 0.0025. The sheet's total loss is the average of this column over every passenger, and training means changing the two rows of parameters to make it smaller.

ai210.0.3.takeaway: A pretrained transformer from the Hugging Face hub can be fine-tuned to almost any text problem once the problem is phrased as text in, label out: build the input string, tokenize and numericalize it, hold out a validation set (and a test set you rarely look at), pick the metric you will be judged on, and train with the largest learning rate that does not break.

beats.d: Sentiment, authorship, legal discovery, sorting documents, triaging email — classification is the most widely useful NLP application. Kaggle's U.S. Patent Phrase to Phrase Matching asks how similar two phrases are (1 identical, 0 unrelated) within a patent class, and that too can be phrased as classifying a piece of text.

Kaggle gives datasets, feedback, a leaderboard and winners' write-ups; its API downloads the data to your own machine. The training CSV has 36,473 rows — 733 unique anchors, 106 contexts, nearly 30,000 targets — and pandas builds one input column: 'TEXT1: ' + context + '; TEXT2: ' + target + '; ANC1: ' + anchor.

A model takes numbers, so text is tokenized (split into words or sub-word pieces) and numericalized (each token replaced by its index in the vocab). AutoTokenizer gives the tokenizer that matches the chosen model, microsoft/deberta-v3-small; ▁ marks where a word starts, and rare words come out in pieces.

Fitting noisy points from a quadratic: a line under-fits, a degree-10 polynomial over-fits, a degree-2 fit is close to the truth. A validation set is held out to tell which is which, and is never used to train. train_test_split builds it — and calls it 'test', so be careful.

Try enough ideas against the validation set and some will improve it by pure coincidence. The test set is checked only once all that is done. Kaggle's public leaderboard works like a test set you can peek at; the private leaderboard, used once at the end, is the real one.

Kaggle names the metric: correlation between predicted and actual scores, from -1 to +1. On California housing, income against value gives 0.68; rooms against income looks as close but scores far lower, because r is very sensitive to outliers. Rachel Thomas's warning applies: optimising a metric is not the same as doing well.

Batch size 128, 4 epochs and a learning rate of 8e-5 found by trial and error — there is no learning rate finder. TrainingArguments adds warmup, a cosine schedule, fp16 and weight decay; AutoModelForSequenceClassification and a Trainer (Transformers' Learner) do the rest, with the metric returned as a dict.

A language model learns by predicting the next word — self-supervised, no labels needed. ULMFiT's three stages: pretrain on Wikipedia, fine-tune the language model on the target corpus (unlabelled reviews included), then fine-tune a classifier on top of its encoder.

beats.t: Chapter 10: tokenizing by word or subword
beats.d: Word tokenizers split on spaces and punctuation with language rules; subword tokenizers learn the commonest letter groups from a corpus and work for any language. fastai adds special tokens such as xxbos, xxmaj and xxunk, and words seen fewer than 3 times become xxunk.

ai210.0.3.worked: The notebook's whole pipeline: df['input'] from three columns; Dataset.from_pandas; tokz = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_nm); ds.map(tok_func, batched=True); rename score to labels; train_test_split(0.25, seed=42); a corr_d metric returning {'pearson': r}; TrainingArguments with lr, bs and epochs; Trainer(model, args, ...).train().
ai210.0.3.watch: Tuning against the validation set — or the public leaderboard — until the gains are coincidence. And trusting a correlation coefficient without plotting the data: a handful of outliers can drag r down (or up) on their own.

checks.q: How does the notebook present each patent phrase pair to the model?
opts: As one string: 'TEXT1: ' + context + '; TEXT2: ' + target + '; ANC1: ' + anchor
As two separate inputs, anchor and target, each one read by its own copy of the model
As the anchor alone, with target and context added later as numeric features
As a pair of embeddings that are averaged together before the network's first layer
checks.expl: The notebook builds one input column by concatenation — context, then target, then anchor — so a single text model reads all three. It frames the task like a classification prompt: for 'TEXT1: abatement; TEXT2: eliminating process', choose a category of similarity: Different, Similar or Identical.

checks.q: deberta-v3-small's tokenizer splits 'ornithorhynchus' into '▁or', 'ni', 'tho', 'rhynch', 'us'. What does that show?
opts: The tokenizer failed: words it doesn't know are dropped and marked unknown
Uncommon words split into sub-word pieces; ▁ marks where a new word begins
Every word is split into its syllables, so the model can learn to say it
Latin words go to a separate tokenizer, which splits them letter by letter
checks.expl: Tokens are like words but can be sub-word pieces. Common words ('▁platypus', '▁is') stay whole; an uncommon one is broken into pieces the vocab does contain, and ▁ marks the start of a new word. Numericalization then maps each token to its integer in the tokenizer's vocab.

checks.q: Why does the notebook rename the 'score' column before training?
opts: Scores must be integers, and the rename turns every score into a class
Otherwise the tokenizer would turn the score into tokens with the text
Transformers always assumes the labels are in a column called 'labels'
Kaggle's submission file needs that name, so it is changed up front
checks.expl: Transformers expects the dependent variable under the column name labels. In this dataset it is score (0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 or 1), so the notebook calls rename_columns({'score':'labels'}) on the tokenized dataset.

checks.q: Why does the notebook say to hold back a test set even when you already have a validation set?
opts: The validation set is too small to estimate the final metric reliably
The test set picks the learning rate; the validation set picks the model
Kaggle requires the test set to be trained on before a final submission
Trying many ideas against the validation set can overfit it by chance
checks.expl: As you try different models, training methods and data processing, some changes improve the validation metrics purely by coincidence — so you end up over-fitting the validation set. The test set is checked only after all of that. Kaggle's public leaderboard is like a test set; the private one is used once, at the end.

checks.q: In the California housing data, MedInc against AveRooms looks about as close a relationship as income against house value, yet r is much lower. Why?
opts: r is very sensitive to outliers, like the districts with very many rooms
AveRooms is a count, and Pearson's r only works between continuous values
House values were capped at 500,000 dollars, which lowers r for every pair
r measures the slope, and rooms rise far more slowly with income than value
checks.expl: Pearson's r is very sensitive to outliers: a few districts with a very high number of rooms, which are not especially valuable, dominate it. Keep only AveRooms below 15 and the correlation comes out close to the income-against-value one. Look at the scatter plot, not only the number.

checks.q: Transformers has no learning rate finder. How does the notebook pick lr = 8e-5?
opts: It copies the rate DeBERTa's authors used to pretrain the model
By trial and error: the largest value that doesn't make training fail
It halves the rate after each epoch until Pearson's r stops improving
It takes the smallest value that still shows some gain in one epoch
checks.expl: fastai offers a learning rate finder; Transformers does not, so the notebook uses trial and error. The idea is the largest learning rate you can find that doesn't make training fail — with batch size and epochs, the only settings it expects you to change for a different model.

checks.q: In chapter 10's ULMFiT approach, which stage sits between the Wikipedia language model and the IMDb classifier?
opts: Training a second language model on Wikipedia, reading the text backwards
Labelling the 50,000 unlabelled reviews by hand, to give the classifier more
Fine-tuning the language model on IMDb reviews, unlabelled ones included
Freezing the language model and training a classifier head on Wikipedia
checks.expl: A language model that predicts the next word, pretrained on Wikipedia, is first fine-tuned to predict the next word of movie reviews — all 100,000, including the 50,000 with no labels, since the next word is the label. Only then is its encoder given a new head and trained to classify sentiment.

checks.q: What does chapter 10 say you trade off when you pick a larger subword vocab?
opts: Better handling of Chinese and Japanese, against worse handling of English
Fewer unknown-word tokens, against the need for language-specific rules
Faster tokenizing, against retraining the tokenizer for every new corpus
Fewer tokens per sentence, against bigger embedding matrices needing more data
checks.expl: A larger vocab means fewer tokens per sentence — faster training, less memory, less state for the model to remember — but larger embedding matrices, which require more data to learn. A small subword vocab approaches character tokenization, a large one word tokenization, with no language-specific rules either way.

ai210.0.4.takeaway: Everything a deep learning library does can be written in a page of PyTorch: clean and scale the table, multiply by coefficients, measure a loss, call backward, step and zero the gradients — then swap the sum for matrix products, add a ReLU and a hidden layer, and you have a neural net. Doing it once by hand is what makes the framework's defaults make sense.

beats.d: On Kaggle's Titanic data: count missing values with isna().sum(), fill them with each column's mode, and take log(Fare + 1) so a few huge fares don't dominate once multiplied by a coefficient — the +1 because some fares are 0.

get_dummies turns Sex, Pclass and Embarked into 0/1 columns — Pclass too, because 1, 2 and 3 are classes, not amounts. Cabin, Name and Ticket have too many values for that. Four continuous columns plus eight dummies make the twelve independent variables.

Random coefficients in (-0.5, 0.5); each column divided by its max (broadcasting divides every row by the vector) so Age stops dominating; predictions are row sums; loss is mean absolute error. No constant is needed: the dummy columns already cover every row.

requires_grad_(), compute the loss, backward(), then inside torch.no_grad() subtract grad × lr with sub_ and clear it with zero_() — because backward adds to whatever gradient is already there. RandomSplitter holds out a validation set, and accuracy (prediction above 0.5) is the metric Kaggle scores.

Some predicted probabilities were above 1 or below 0; torch.sigmoid squashes them into (0, 1), and loss and accuracy both improve. Multiplying and summing each row is a matrix-vector product, so indeps@coeffs does the same job, much faster.

beats.t: A neural net, then a deep one
beats.d: Layer one maps 12 inputs to n_hidden outputs through ReLU; layer two maps them to one output plus a constant, then sigmoid. For depth, loop over a list of layers. The initial ranges are finicky — tiny changes stop training — which long held deep learning back. On data this small, the net does no better than the linear model.

fastai's TabularPandas does the cleaning in one call — Categorify, FillMissing (median), Normalize — so the notebook adds engineered features freely (Deck, Family, Title, TicketFreq). tabular_learner(layers=[10,10]) handles initialisation, lr_find suggests a learning rate, and test_dl reapplies the same processing to the test set.

Train five models from different random starting points and average their predictions: the simplest ensemble, and better than any one of them. The framework hides detail — which is why it is worth having built the thing once yourself — but it saves you from boiler-plate when the goal is the problem.

ai210.0.4.worked: The training loop in four lines: loss = calc_loss(coeffs, trn_indep, trn_dep); loss.backward(); then with torch.no_grad(): coeffs.sub_(coeffs.grad * lr); coeffs.grad.zero_(). Wrap that in one_epoch, call it for 30 epochs from a seeded random start, and check acc() on the validation rows after.
ai210.0.4.watch: Forgetting to zero the gradients, so each step uses the sum of every gradient so far. And feeding raw columns of very different scales — a fare in the hundreds next to 0/1 dummies — so one column swamps the rest.

checks.q: Pclass is already numeric (1, 2 or 3). Why does the notebook still turn it into dummy variables?
opts: The numbers name first, second and third class; they aren't amounts to multiply
get_dummies fails on string columns unless one numeric column is included too
Dummy columns train faster, because each of them holds only zeros and ones
Kaggle's data dictionary requires every categorical column to be one-hot
checks.expl: A coefficient multiplies its column, which only makes sense for counts or measures. Pclass's 1, 2 and 3 correspond to first, second and third class cabins, so each class gets its own 0/1 column, as Sex and Embarked do. Cabin, Name and Ticket have too many unique values for dummies.

checks.q: The linear model has no constant (bias) term and no column of ones. Why does the notebook say it doesn't need one?
opts: The coefficients start in (-0.5, 0.5), which already centres every prediction
The dummy columns cover every row: each passenger is either male or female
Sigmoid adds a constant of its own, so a bias would be counted in twice
Dividing every column by its maximum removes the need for an intercept
checks.expl: Everyone in the dataset is in exactly one of the Sex columns (and one Pclass and one Embarked column), so together the dummies act like a column of ones and their coefficients can supply the constant. The later neural net does add a constant to its second layer.

checks.q: Calling loss.backward() twice without a step makes coeffs.grad double. What does the notebook do about it?
opts: Divides each gradient by the number of backward calls before updating
Recreates coeffs with requires_grad_() before every epoch
Sets the gradients back to zero with grad.zero_() after each step
Wraps backward() in torch.no_grad() so it can't add to old gradients
checks.expl: backward adds the new gradients to whatever is already in .grad. So update_coeffs subtracts grad × lr in place with sub_ and then calls grad.zero_() — both in-place, as the trailing underscore says — inside torch.no_grad(), so the update itself isn't tracked.

checks.q: Why does the notebook pass the linear model's output through sigmoid?
opts: Sigmoid makes the model nonlinear, which turns it into a real neural net
Accuracy needs values that are already rounded to 0 or 1
Sigmoid removes the need for a learning rate, as its output is bounded
Some predicted survival probabilities were above 1, some below 0
checks.expl: A probability of survival belongs between 0 and 1, and the raw row sums were not. torch.sigmoid squashes any number into that range; with it the loss improved a lot, and accuracy improved too — trained, notably, with a learning rate of 100.

checks.q: The notebook's one-hidden-layer net calls init_coeffs(n_hidden=20) for its 12 input columns: a 12 × 20 layer1, a 20 × 1 layer2 and one constant. How many trainable numbers is that?
checks.expl: layer1 holds 12 × 20 = 240 coefficients, layer2 holds 20 × 1 = 20, and the constant is 1: 240 + 20 + 1 = 261. layer1 is divided by n_hidden at initialisation so that the hidden sums come out at a magnitude similar to the inputs.

checks.q: The notebook adds LogFare = np.log(Fare + 1). What is LogFare for a passenger whose fare was 7.25? Two decimals.
checks.expl: np.log is the natural logarithm: ln(7.25 + 1) = ln 8.25 ≈ 2.110. The +1 is there because some fares are 0 and log 0 is infinite; the log squashes the few very large fares that would otherwise dominate. (Lesson 3's spreadsheet used log base 10, which gives 0.916.)

checks.q: The deep version's init_coeffs is full of fiddly constants. What does the notebook say about them?
opts: Tiny changes can stop training altogether, which long held deep learning back
fastai's learning rate finder tunes them, so their exact values do not matter
They are only there to make the notebook reproducible, as the seed is
They stand in for the biases, which the deep model no longer has to learn
checks.expl: The random ranges have to be just right: the tiniest changes can make the model fail to train at all. The notebook names this as a key reason deep learning made little progress in its early days; modern initialisation and normalisation deal with it, and fastai's tabular_learner handles it for you.

checks.q: In the 'why you should use a framework' notebook, how is the ensemble built?
opts: Five architectures are trained, and only the most accurate one is kept
Five models from different random starts, with predictions averaged
One model trained five times as long, with snapshots
Five models each see a fifth of the data, then vote on each passenger
checks.expl: ensemble() creates and trains a tabular_learner and returns its test-set predictions; it is run five times, each from a different random starting point, and torch.stack(...).mean(0) averages them — the simplest form of ensembling, which the notebook reports lands well within the top 25% of entries.

ai210.0.5.takeaway: A random forest is nothing but binary splits, stacked into trees, averaged over many trees grown on random subsets — simple enough to build from scratch in a notebook, hard to break, and unusually easy to interpret. Benchmark a one-split model before anything fancier, and remember what a forest cannot do: predict outside the range it was trained on.

beats.d: For trees, Sex and Embarked become pandas categorical codes instead of dummy columns, and Pclass is treated as a number: 1st, 2nd and 3rd class are ordered, and a tree only cares about order. Even taking the log of Fare is unnecessary, since log doesn't change the order.

A binary split puts every row on one side of a threshold. 'All females survive, no males do' already has a mean absolute error of about 0.215. A score — each side's standard deviation of Survived, weighted by its rows — lets the computer try every column and cut point; the best is Sex. That is the OneR classifier: a strong baseline.

Split each side again: for males the best next split is Age ≤ 6, for females Pclass ≤ 2. Keep going and you have a decision tree, which sklearn's DecisionTreeClassifier builds and draws. Its nodes show samples, values and gini, another impurity measure; with min_samples_leaf=50 the validation error drops to 0.184.

Leaves can't shrink much further without too few rows to predict from. Breiman's answer: grow many bigger trees on random subsets of the rows and average them — their errors are uncorrelated, so they cancel. A random forest also picks a random subset of columns at each split.

Feature importances say Sex matters most, Pclass a distant second. On Titanic the forest is no better than one tree, and both are close to OneR: more complex is not always better, so benchmark simple models. Forests are also hard to mess up — insensitive to normalisation, interactions and non-linear transforms.

Out-of-bag error scores each row with only the trees that never saw it. The spread of the trees' predictions measures confidence; feature importance and dropping redundant columns simplify the model; partial dependence shows one variable's effect with the others held fixed; a tree interpreter explains a single prediction.

Trees predict leaf averages, so a forest can't extrapolate beyond its training targets — fatal for trends like inflation. A forest trained to tell training rows from validation rows finds out-of-domain columns. Suspiciously good accuracy or nonsensical important features suggest leakage. Boosting fits residuals with many small trees, and can overfit.

On Kaggle's Paddy Doctor competition, focus on an effective validation set and rapid iteration. Images are squished to 480 px, then augmented down to 128; a resnet26d from timm is fine-tuned 3 epochs at 0.01, higher than lr_find's conservative suggestion; test_dl, get_preds and the vocab produce a first submission in minutes.

ai210.0.5.worked: Finding the best split by hand: for each column, list its unique values; for each, compute score(col, y, value) — both sides' standard deviation of the target, each times its row count, over the total — and keep the value with the lowest score. The column whose best score is lowest is the split. Repeat inside each side and you have built a decision tree.
ai210.0.5.watch: Skipping the one-split baseline and never learning that the complex model barely beats it. And trusting a forest to forecast beyond the range of its training data: it will flatten out at the edge, systematically too low (or high).

checks.q: The random forest notebook stops treating Pclass as categorical and lists it with the continuous columns. Why?
opts: Pclass has only three values, too few to be worth a dummy variable each
The tree library can't read categorical columns, so they must be numbers
Its values are ordered, and decision trees care only about order, not size
Treating it as continuous adds an intercept, which the dummies had removed
checks.expl: 1st, 2nd and 3rd class have an order, and a binary split only asks whether a value is above or below a threshold, so the order is all a tree uses. For the same reason the log of Fare is unnecessary for a forest — log doesn't change the order — and the notebook kept it only to make its plots readable.

checks.q: Embarked is stored as category codes C = 0, Q = 1, S = 2. How many binary splits does a tree need to put Q in a group of its own?
checks.expl: A split asks 'code ≤ threshold'. One split separates C (≤ 0) from Q and S; a second separates Q (≤ 1) from S. C or S alone takes one split; Q, in the middle, takes two. That is why Jeremy says that in practice he often uses dummy variables for categoricals with fewer than 4 levels and numeric codes for 4 or more — though this notebook itself codes both Embarked and Sex as categories.

checks.q: What does the notebook's score() measure for a candidate binary split?
opts: The validation accuracy of predicting each side's majority class
How many rows land on each side, favouring the balanced splits
The mean absolute error of the split, measured on the training set
How mixed each side is: the target's std on that side, times its rows
checks.expl: _side_score takes the standard deviation of the dependent variable within one side — higher means its rows are less alike — and multiplies it by that side's row count, since a bigger group matters more. score adds both sides and divides by the total. Lower is better: Sex scores 0.408, LogFare at 2.7 scores 0.472.

checks.q: The single best split, on Sex, re-invents the OneR classifier. What does the notebook conclude after building a tree and a forest as well?
opts: Simple models can be nearly as good, so always benchmark them first
OneR works only on Titanic, where sex decided who got into lifeboats
The forest is clearly best, so the simpler models can be dropped now
Single splits overfit, which is why trees need many levels to generalise
checks.expl: OneR's error was about 0.215, and neither the decision tree nor the random forest clearly beat it. The takeaway: more complex models aren't always better, so benchmark simple ones and see whether they are good enough — though simple models will often struggle on harder tasks such as NLP or vision.

checks.q: Why does averaging many trees, each trained on a random subset of the rows, predict better than a single tree?
opts: Each tree sees fewer rows, so it trains faster and overfits much less
Their errors are uncorrelated, and the average of such errors tends to 0
The subsets cover every row, so every single passenger gets a tree of its own
Averaging removes the need for a validation set to choose tree depth
checks.expl: Breiman's bagging insight: a tree trained on a random subset makes more errors than one trained on everything, but different trees make different errors, and the average of many uncorrelated errors is close to zero. A random forest goes further and also picks a random subset of columns at each split.

checks.q: Chapter 9's partial dependence plot for YearMade is not the average sale price for each YearMade. How is it made?
opts: A separate forest is trained per year, and the forests' accuracies compared
YearMade is dropped from the data and the loss in accuracy is measured
Every row's YearMade is set to each year in turn and predictions averaged
Auctions are sorted by YearMade and their prices smoothed with a line
checks.expl: Averages per year would also capture everything else that changed with the year — the products sold, air conditioning, inflation. Instead every row's YearMade is replaced with 1950 and the predictions averaged, then 1951, and so on, so only YearMade varies. Dropping a column and comparing scores is how the chapter tests for redundant features instead.

checks.q: A random forest trained on the first 30 of 40 points with a rising trend predicts the last 10 too low. Why?
opts: The forest needs normalised inputs, and the later x values were not scaled
Thirty points are too few rows to grow trees of any useful depth
min_samples_leaf hides the trend inside the last leaf of every tree
A tree predicts a leaf's average, so it can't exceed its training targets
checks.expl: Each tree predicts the mean of the training rows in a leaf, and a forest averages trees, so neither can predict outside the range of the training targets. That matters for any trend over time, such as inflation — and it is why the validation set must not contain out-of-domain data.

checks.q: The notebook defines gini(cond) as 1 - p² - (1 - p)², where p is the share of the group that survived. What is gini for a group in which 3 of every 4 passengers survived?
checks.expl: p = 0.75: 1 - 0.5625 - 0.0625 = 0.375, the same as 2p(1 - p). Gini is 0 for a group that is all one outcome and peaks at 0.5 for an even mix: it is the chance that two rows drawn from the group differ, so lower means purer, as with score(). (The notebook's prose states it the other way round.)

ai210.0.6.takeaway: Bigger models fit in a fixed GPU by accumulating gradients over smaller batches, and an average of several strong models beats any one. Then the lesson turns to recommendations: give every user and every item a few learned numbers — latent factors — predict a rating as their dot product plus biases, and keep the weights small with weight decay. Softmax and cross-entropy, worked in a spreadsheet, are the loss behind classification.

beats.d: The goal in part 3 of Road to the Top is an ensemble of large models on large images, and the limit is GPU memory: 16,280 MiB on Kaggle. To find out quickly what fits, train for one short epoch on the smallest class, bacterial_panicle_blight — the memory use is the same, the run far faster.

Divide the batch size by accum and add the GradientAccumulation callback: gradients from several small batches add up before one weight update. Training is nearly identical to the full batch, using the memory of a batch accum times smaller. accum=2 made convnext_large, vit_large, swinv2 and swin all fit.

Each architecture is trained twice with different preprocessing, on a different random validation split each time, and its test-time-augmentation predictions are kept. Averaging them — with vit's runs counted twice, since vit had done a bit better — took the submission to the top of the leaderboard in a few lines of code.

Softmax is exp of each output divided by the sum of the exps, so the probabilities add to 1. Cross-entropy is minus the sum of actual × log(probability); with one-hot actuals that is minus the log of the probability given to the right class. The binary form picks log(p) or log(1 - p).

beats.t: Latent factors and the dot product
beats.d: Collaborative filtering recommends from who liked what. Score each movie and user on hidden factors — sci-fi, action, age — and multiply and add: a modern sci-fi fan matches The Last Skywalker at 2.142 and Casablanca at -1.611. We don't know the factors, so we learn them: random start, dot-product predictions, a loss, gradient descent.

collab_filter.xlsx does it on a 15 × 15 crosstab: 5 random factors per user and per movie, MMULT for each prediction, RMSE over the rated cells, Solver for the descent. Chapter 8 does it on MovieLens 100k with a DotProduct module of two Embeddings, and squeezes outputs into (0, 5.5) with sigmoid_range.

Some users rate everything high and some movies are just better, which a dot product can't say, so each gets one learned bias. That model overfits, and with no data augmentation available, weight decay steps in: add wd × the sum of squared weights to the loss, which keeps weights small and the function smooth.

The other approach concatenates the user and item embeddings — which may now have different sizes, from get_emb_sz — and passes them through linear layers and a ReLU. It does a little worse than the dot product here, but can take in any other information about users, items or dates.

ai210.0.6.worked: A rating prediction with biases: users = user_factors(x[:,0]); movies = movie_factors(x[:,1]); res = (users * movies).sum(dim=1, keepdim=True) + user_bias(x[:,0]) + movie_bias(x[:,1]); return sigmoid_range(res, 0, 5.5). Train it with MSELossFlat and fit_one_cycle(5, 5e-3, wd=0.1).
ai210.0.6.watch: Shrinking the batch size to fit a big model and getting a different, noisier training run — gradient accumulation keeps the effective batch the same. And adding parameters such as biases without regularisation, then reading the overfit as 'biases don't help'.

checks.q: What does gradient accumulation do in Road to the Top, part 3?
opts: Adds up the gradients of several small batches, then updates the weights once
Averages the weights of several models, each trained on a different subset
Keeps the activations on the CPU, so that larger models fit on the GPU
Trains in half precision, which halves the memory that every batch needs
checks.expl: Instead of stepping after every batch, train() divides the batch size by accum and adds the GradientAccumulation callback, so the gradients of several smaller batches add up before one update. The loop is nearly mathematically identical to the full batch size, using the memory of a batch accum times smaller.

checks.q: The notebook's train() is called with accum=4. What batch size does it give ImageDataLoaders?
checks.expl: bs=64//accum, and 64 // 4 = 16. GradientAccumulation(64) then steps once 64 images' gradients have been added up, so the effective batch size is still 64 while only 16 images are on the GPU at a time.

checks.q: The ensemble's dict lists convnext, vit, swinv2 and swin, two runs each, in that order; then tta_prs += tta_prs[2:4]. What fraction of the averaged predictions come from vit runs?
checks.expl: Positions 2 and 3 are vit's two runs, so adding them again makes 10 predictions, 4 of them vit: 4/10 = 0.4, up from 2/8 = 0.25. Repeating entries in a plain average is a weighted average; vit had done a bit better than the rest in the small-model experiments.

checks.q: In the entropy sheet, cross-entropy is -SUM(actual × LOG(softmax)) over the five classes. With one-hot actuals, what does that come to?
opts: The sum of the logs of every probability the model assigned
Minus the log of the probability given to the correct class
One minus the probability the model gave the correct class
The squared gap between softmax and actuals, summed up
checks.src: entropy_example.xlsx (course22 xl/), sheets softmax and entropy
checks.expl: Every actual but the right one is 0, so every term but one vanishes: the loss is -log(p) of the true class — here dog, -log10(0.873) ≈ 0.059. A confident right answer costs almost nothing; a confident wrong one costs a lot, since log(p) heads to minus infinity as p goes to 0.

checks.q: The sheet's binary version is -IF(isCat=1, LOG(PredCat), LOG(1 - PredCat)), and Excel's LOG is base 10. What is it for an image that is not a cat, with PredCat = 0.9?
checks.expl: isCat is 0, so the loss is -log10(1 - 0.9) = -log10(0.1) = 1 — the worst row in the sheet, because it confidently predicted the wrong answer. The same prediction for a real cat costs -log10(0.9) ≈ 0.046.

checks.q: Chapter 8 adds a bias per user and per movie to the dot-product model. What can a bias express that the latent factors cannot?
opts: How many ratings each user and movie has, so rare ones count for less
The genre of each movie, which the latent factors never get to learn
That some users rate everything high, and some movies are just better
The date of each rating, so that older opinions can be weighted down
checks.expl: A dot product can say a movie is very sci-fi, very action-oriented and very not old, but not whether most people like it, nor that a user is generous with stars. One learned number added per user and per movie covers both — at first it overfits, which weight decay then fixes.

checks.q: What does weight decay (wd) do, and why does it help with overfitting?
opts: It lowers the learning rate every epoch, so that late steps can't overfit
It drops a random share of the weights at each step of training
It stops training as soon as the validation loss starts to rise
It adds wd × the sum of squared weights to the loss, so they stay small
checks.expl: Large coefficients make sharp canyons in the loss, letting the model fit every training point with an over-complex function. Penalising the sum of squares keeps the weights small; in practice it is applied as parameters.grad += wd × 2 × parameters. With wd=0.1 the overfitting DotProductBias trains much better.

checks.q: In collab_filter.xlsx's dotprod sheet, how is each predicted rating calculated?
opts: The dot product of the user's 5 latent factors with the movie's 5
The average of all of that user's ratings and of that movie's ratings
The rating the most similar other user gave to the same movie
A user bias plus a movie bias, both learned by gradient descent
checks.expl: Each cell is MMULT of the user's row of 5 factors with the movie's column of 5, or 0 where there is no rating; the loss is the RMSE over the rated cells. The factors start random and are optimised with Solver by gradient descent. The separate bias sheet adds a bias per user and per movie on top.

ai210.0.7.takeaway: An embedding is just an array lookup that behaves, for gradients, like multiplying by a one-hot matrix — and what it learns can be read: biases, directions, distances. A convolution is just a small kernel slid across an image, multiplying and adding; stack stride-2 convolutions with ReLUs, pool, drop out, and finish with a dense layer, and you have a CNN.

beats.d: Multiplying a factor matrix by a one-hot vector for index 3 returns row 3. Storing and multiplying one-hot vectors wastes memory and time, so an Embedding layer indexes directly but takes gradients as if it had multiplied. The spreadsheet's movielens_emb and word_emb sheets do the same lookup with MATCH and OFFSET.

A tensor stored on a Module is not a parameter until wrapped in nn.Parameter, which marks it for parameters() and turns on gradients. With create_params — zeros filled from a normal distribution with std 0.01 — DotProductBias can be written without Embedding, indexing the factor matrices directly.

The lowest movie biases belong to films people dislike even when the film matches their tastes; the highest, such as L.A. Confidential, to films people like anyway. PCA on the movie factors pulls out directions such as classic versus pop culture, and cosine similarity between embeddings finds Dial M for Murder as the nearest film to Silence of the Lambs.

A brand-new user has no history. Use common sense: an average-taste user, or better, a tabular model that predicts an embedding from sign-up answers. And watch for a few enthusiastic users steering recommendations for everyone — a representation bias that feedback loops amplify.

A convolution multiplies a small kernel by each 3×3 block of an image and adds the results. The top-edge kernel, rows -1, 0, 1, returns 762 at a top edge of a handwritten 3 and about 0 on flat areas. Without padding an h × w image gives (h - 2) × (w - 2) results.

F.conv2d runs many kernels on a whole batch at once. Padding of ks//2 keeps the size; stride 2 roughly halves it — in general (n + 2·pad - ks)//stride + 1. A colour image has 3 channels, so each kernel is ch_in × ks × ks, and a layer's weights are ch_out × ch_in × ks × ks plus one bias per output channel.

Five stride-2 convolutions take 28×28 down to 1×1, doubling the channels as the grid halves so the computation per layer holds steady; Flatten removes the 1×1 axes. A convolution is a matrix multiply whose weight matrix has fixed zeros and shared weights — far fewer parameters than a fully connected layer.

conv-example.xlsx runs an MNIST digit through two convolution layers, each cell MAX(0, SUM(window × kernel)) — a convolution and a ReLU — then a 2×2 max-pool, then a dense layer of SUMPRODUCTs. Its dropout sheet draws a random number per cell and zeroes the activations whose number falls under the chosen rate.

ai210.0.7.worked: Output size of a convolution, per side: (n + 2·pad - ks)//stride + 1. For simple_cnn's stride-2, 3×3, padding-1 layers on 28×28 input that gives 14, 7, 4, 2, 1. Parameters of a layer: ch_out × ch_in × ks × ks weights plus ch_out biases — for Conv2d(1, 4, 3), 36 + 4 = 40.
ai210.0.7.watch: Ranking items by average rating and calling it quality, when the learned bias separates how good an item is from who happened to rate it. And building a CNN that keeps the channel count fixed while stride-2 layers shrink the grid, so each layer does less and less work.

checks.q: What is an embedding, as chapter 8 defines it?
opts: A matrix that one-hot encodes every user ID before training starts
Multiplying by a one-hot matrix, computed as a direct index lookup
A pretrained vector for each word, downloaded and kept frozen
The PCA projection of a factor matrix onto its two main axes
checks.expl: Row i of a factor matrix is what you get by multiplying it by a one-hot vector for i, but there is no reason to store one-hot vectors or search them. An embedding layer indexes directly, with gradients computed as if it had done the matrix product. collab_filter.xlsx's movielens_emb sheet does the lookup with MATCH and OFFSET.

checks.q: Why is sorting movies by their learned bias more informative than sorting them by average rating?
opts: Bias corrects for movies with few ratings, which an average ignores
Bias is measured on the validation set, and averages on training data
Bias says people dislike a movie even when it matches their tastes
Bias removes the effect of the year each movie happened to come out
checks.expl: An average mixes how good a movie is with who happened to watch it. The bias is what is left after the latent factors have matched the movie to each user's tastes: a low one means people tend not to like it even if it is their kind of film; a high one — L.A. Confidential — that you may enjoy it even if you don't usually like detective movies.

checks.q: What does chapter 8 suggest as the best way to give a brand-new user an initial embedding?
opts: Use the mean of every existing user's embedding vector
Start from random numbers and wait for their first ratings
Copy the embedding of the platform's most active user
Predict it with a tabular model from their sign-up answers
checks.src: fastbook 08_collab.ipynb, Bootstrapping a Collaborative Filtering Model
checks.expl: There is no magic solution. The mean of all users' embeddings can be an uncommon mix of tastes; picking one user to stand for average taste is better; better still is a tabular model whose inputs are the answers to a few sign-up questions and whose output is an embedding — which is why services ask which genres you like when you join.

checks.q: simple_cnn's third convolution takes a 7×7 activation map with kernel size 3, stride 2 and padding 1. How many cells per side does its output have?
checks.src: fastbook 13_convolutions.ipynb, Strides and Padding; Creating the CNN
checks.expl: The chapter's formula is (n + 2·pad - ks)//stride + 1 = (7 + 2 - 3)//2 + 1 = 3 + 1 = 4, matching the #4x4 comment. Each stride-2 layer roughly halves the grid, so 28×28 goes to 14, 7, 4, 2 and finally 1.

checks.q: How many parameters does nn.Conv2d(4, 8, kernel_size=3) have, biases included?
checks.expl: Each of the 8 output channels has a 4 × 3 × 3 kernel — one 3×3 slice per input channel — so 8 × 36 = 288 weights, plus one bias per output channel: 296, the figure learn.summary() reports for simple_cnn's second layer.

checks.q: The top_edge kernel has rows -1 -1 -1, 0 0 0 and 1 1 1. Where does it give a large positive value on an MNIST digit?
opts: Where all nine pixels under it are equally dark
Where the top row is low and the bottom row high
Where the left column is darker than the right
Where the centre pixel is brighter than the rest
checks.expl: The kernel computes -a1 - a2 - a3 + a7 + a8 + a9: zero where the top and bottom rows match, large where the bottom row is much higher. In MNIST 0 is white and 255 black, so that is light above, ink below — a top edge, scoring 762 on the digit 3. Swap the rows, or use columns, to find other edges.

checks.q: Chapter 13 shows a convolution as a special kind of matrix multiplication. What is special about its weight matrix?
opts: It is square, so the output has exactly as many values as the input
Its weights are fixed edge detectors that are never updated by SGD
Some entries are fixed at zero, and others are tied to share a value
It gets a separate bias for every pixel of each input colour channel
checks.expl: Written as a matrix multiply, a convolution's weight matrix has zeros where the filter can't reach — untrainable, they stay zero — and repeated entries that must stay equal: shared weights. The bias is shared across the image too. These constraints mean far fewer parameters than a fully connected layer.

checks.q: In conv-example.xlsx's dropout sheet, what happens to Conv2's activations?
opts: Every activation is halved, so the next layer receives smaller values
The smallest activations are zeroed, leaving only the strongest ones
Each 2×2 block of activations is replaced with its largest value
Each is zeroed where its random number falls under the dropout rate
checks.expl: Every cell gets RAND(); the dropout 'filter' keeps the number only where it exceeds the chosen rate (plus 0.001) and is 0 elsewhere, and the activation is zeroed wherever the filter is 0. The sheet counts the zeros to show the actual dropout. Replacing each 2×2 block with its maximum is the maxpool that follows.

ai310.0.0.takeaway: CS336 teaches language models by building them, because the frontier has become an industry whose details are unpublished and whose behaviour changes with scale. What transfers from small models is mechanics and mindset — above all efficiency, since accuracy is efficiency times resources. The first piece built is the tokenizer, and byte-pair encoding wins because it learns its vocabulary from the corpus.

beats.d: Eight years ago researchers trained their own models, six years ago they fine-tuned BERT, today they prompt a proprietary model. Those abstractions are leaky, and fundamental research still means tearing up the stack — so the course teaches understanding via building.

beats.t: Industrialised, closed, and different at scale
beats.d: GPT-4 reportedly has 1.8T parameters and cost 100M dollars to train, and its technical report gives no details. Small models may not be representative: the share of FLOPs in attention versus the MLP changes with scale, and some behaviours emerge only at scale.

Mechanics (what a Transformer is, how parallelism uses GPUs) and mindset (squeezing the hardware, taking scale seriously) transfer; intuitions about data and modelling only partly. The bitter lesson, read right: algorithms that scale matter, because accuracy = efficiency × resources — so maximise efficiency.

Shannon's entropy of English and n-gram models; then neural LMs, seq2seq, Adam, attention, the Transformer, mixture of experts and model parallelism; ELMo, BERT and T5; GPT-2, scaling laws, GPT-3, PaLM, Chinchilla; then open models — The Pile, OPT, BLOOM, Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, OLMo — at three levels of openness: closed, open-weight, open-source.

Basics (tokenizer, Transformer variants, training); systems (kernels, parallelism, inference with its prefill and decode phases); scaling laws (D* = 20 N*, ignoring inference cost); data (evaluation, curation, filtering, deduplication); alignment (SFT, then learning from preferences or verifiers with PPO, DPO or GRPO). Five assignments, no scaffolding.

Today we are compute-constrained: filter out bad data, tokenize rather than use raw bytes, choose architectures that save memory or FLOPs, train for a single epoch, tune hyperparameters on small models, and align smaller base models. Tomorrow we will be data-constrained.

A tokenizer maps strings to integer sequences and back. Characters: about 150K code points, many rare. Bytes: a tidy 256-symbol vocabulary but a compression ratio of 1, so sequences grow long while attention is quadratic. Words: an unbounded vocabulary, rare words learned poorly, and unseen ones mapped to UNK.

Train the tokenizer on raw text: start with every byte as a token and repeatedly merge the most common adjacent pair, so common sequences become one token and rare ones many. GPT-2 runs BPE within regex pre-tokenized segments; the GPT-2 tokenizer packs 'Hello, 🌍! 你好!' at about 1.67 bytes per token.

ai310.0.0.worked: Training BPE on 'the cat in the hat' with 3 merges: count adjacent byte pairs, merge the most common (t, h) into token 256; recount, merge (256, e) into 257; recount, merge (257, space) into 258. Encoding new text replays the merges in order — 'the quick brown fox' becomes 258 followed by the 15 remaining bytes.
ai310.0.0.watch: Reading the bitter lesson as 'only scale matters'. At large scale waste is unaffordable, so efficient algorithms matter more, not less — the course's question is always the best model for a given compute and data budget.

checks.q: Lecture 1 sorts what a small-scale course can teach into mechanics, mindset and intuitions. Which does it say transfer to frontier models?
opts: All three, since a Transformer works the very same way at every single scale
Only intuitions, as the mechanics change with each new architecture
None, since small models simply aren't representative of large ones
Mechanics and mindset do; intuitions only partly, as they shift with scale
checks.expl: Mechanics (what a Transformer is, how model parallelism uses GPUs) and mindset (squeezing the most out of the hardware, taking scale seriously) transfer. Intuitions about which data and modelling decisions give good accuracy only partly do: more is different — the share of FLOPs in attention, and emergent behaviour, change with scale.

checks.q: What does the lecture call the right reading of 'the bitter lesson'?
opts: Algorithms that scale are what matters: accuracy = efficiency × resources
Scale is all that matters, so algorithmic improvements can be ignored
Hand-built knowledge beats learned features once there is enough compute
Smaller models win, because they are cheaper to run at inference time
checks.expl: The wrong reading is that only scale matters and algorithms don't. The right one: algorithms that scale. Since accuracy = efficiency × resources, efficiency matters even more at large scale, where waste is unaffordable — hence the framing, the best model for a given compute and data budget.

checks.q: The lecture splits inference into prefill and decode. How do the two phases differ?
opts: Prefill trains the KV cache's weights; decode freezes them to sample
Prefill handles the prompt all at once; decode emits one token at a time
Prefill runs on a small draft model; decode always uses the full model
Prefill happens only during training; decode is the one phase used in serving
checks.expl: Prefill is like training: the prompt's tokens are all given, so they are processed together and the work is compute-bound. Decode must generate one token at a time, which is memory-bound. Speed-ups: cheaper models (pruning, quantization, distillation), speculative decoding — exact, using a draft model — and KV caching and batching.

checks.q: By the lecture's TL;DR, the compute-optimal token count is D* = 20 N*. Training compute is proportional to N × D. If your FLOPs budget grows 4-fold, by what factor should the compute-optimal model size N* grow?
checks.expl: With D* = 20 N*, compute is proportional to N* × 20 N* = 20 N*², so N* grows with the square root of the budget: √4 = 2, and the tokens double too — the extra compute is split between a bigger model and more data, as in the lecture's example of a 1.4B model on 28B tokens. The lecture adds a caveat: the rule ignores inference costs.

checks.q: What is the character tokenizer's compression ratio — UTF-8 bytes per token — on 'Hello, 🌍! 你好!'? Two decimals.
checks.expl: One token per character: H, e, l, l, o, comma, space, 🌍, !, space, 你, 好, ! — 13 tokens. In UTF-8 the 10 ASCII characters take a byte each, 🌍 takes four and each Chinese character three: 20 bytes, and 20 / 13 ≈ 1.54. The byte tokenizer scores exactly 1; the GPT-2 tokenizer, 20 / 12 ≈ 1.67.

checks.q: train_bpe on 'the cat in the hat' with 3 merges learns t + h, then th + e, then 'the' + space. How many tokens does encoding 'the quick brown fox' (19 bytes) give?
checks.expl: Only the leading 'the ' can merge: t + h → 256, 256 + e → 257, 257 + space → 258, so 4 bytes become 1 token. The other 15 bytes stay single tokens: 1 + 15 = 16, as the recorded trace shows ([258, 113, 117, ...]).

ai310.0.1.takeaway: Training is resource accounting: every tensor costs bytes set by its count and data type, every matmul costs 2 × m × n × p FLOPs, and a training step costs about 6 × tokens × parameters. With those two ledgers — memory and compute — you can answer how long a run takes and how big a model fits before writing a line of model code.

beats.d: Training a 70B model on 15T tokens is 6 × 70e9 × 15e12 = 6.3e24 FLOPs; 1024 H100s at half their 989.5 TFLOP/s dense peak deliver about 4.4e22 FLOPs a day, so roughly 144 days. AdamW in float32 needs 16 bytes per parameter, so 8 H100s hold about 40B parameters — before activations.

float32 is 4 bytes and the default. float16 halves that but underflows: 1e-8 becomes 0. bfloat16 keeps 2 bytes with float32's dynamic range and coarser resolution, which deep learning tolerates. FP8 (E4M3, E5M2) was standardised in 2022. Lower precision saves memory and compute but risks instability.

A tensor is a pointer into memory plus strides: in a 4 × 4 matrix the next row is 4 elements on, the next column 1. Slicing, view and transpose make views — free, and sharing memory, so mutating one changes the other. A transposed tensor is non-contiguous, so it must be copied with contiguous() before another view.

x @ y.transpose(-2, -1) hides what -2 and -1 mean. jaxtyping annotations document shapes; einsum names every axis and sums those missing from the output; reduce collapses one; rearrange splits or merges, such as (heads hidden) into heads and hidden.

FLOPs measure work, FLOP/s measure hardware speed. A matmul of B × D by D × K is 2BDK FLOPs, and nothing else in deep learning is as expensive at scale, so the forward pass is about 2 × tokens × parameters. MFU — actual over promised FLOP/s — of 0.5 or more is good; bfloat16 runs much faster than float32.
For each weight matrix the backward pass needs one matmul for the weight's gradient and one for its input's: 4 × points × parameters. Forward plus backward: 6 × points × parameters per step.

Parameters are nn.Parameter tensors. Unit-variance weights make outputs grow like sqrt(input_dim), so scale by 1/sqrt(input_dim) (Xavier, up to a constant) and truncate outliers. Seed torch, NumPy and Python's random; memmap token arrays instead of loading terabytes; pin memory to copy batches to the GPU asynchronously.

Momentum averages gradients, AdaGrad divides by accumulated squared gradients, RMSProp averages those exponentially, Adam is RMSProp plus momentum — and the state costs memory. Save model and optimizer state regularly, since long runs crash. Mixed precision: bfloat16 or fp8 for the forward pass, float32 for parameters and gradients.

ai310.0.1.worked: Memory for training a model of P parameters with AdamW in float32: 4P for parameters + 4P for gradients + 8P for the two optimizer moments = 16P bytes, plus activations, which grow with batch size and sequence length. Compute per step: 6 × (tokens in the batch) × P FLOPs; divide by the hardware's FLOP/s times MFU for wall-clock time.
ai310.0.1.watch: Quoting an H100's 1979 TFLOP/s: that figure assumes sparsity, and dense matmuls get half. And forgetting that FLOP/s depend on data type — the same GPU is many times slower in float32 than in bfloat16.

checks.q: Why does the lecture prefer bfloat16 to float16 for deep learning?
opts: It uses half of float16's memory while keeping the same precision
It has a finer resolution than float32, so small gradients stay exact
Same memory as float16 with float32's range; only resolution suffers
H100s multiply only in bfloat16, so float16 runs at a quarter speed
checks.expl: float16 halves memory but has poor dynamic range: 1e-8 underflows to 0, which can make training unstable. bfloat16, from Google Brain in 2018, keeps 2 bytes but has float32's dynamic range, so 1e-8 survives; its worse resolution matters less for deep learning.

checks.q: The lecture totals training at 6 × (data points) × (parameters) FLOPs. Where does the 6 come from?
opts: Two for the forward pass, and four for the optimizer's state update
Six bytes of state per parameter: weights, gradients, Adam moments
Each parameter takes part in six matrix multiplications per layer
Forward is 2 per point per parameter; backward is twice that, 4
checks.expl: A matmul does one multiply and one add per (i, j, k): 2 × points × parameters forward. Backward needs, for each weight matrix, one matmul for the weight's gradient and one for its input's gradient — 4 × points × parameters — so 6 in all.

checks.q: Why does the lecture divide randomly initialised weights by sqrt(input_dim)?
opts: Otherwise each output grows like sqrt(input_dim), destabilising training
It makes every weight positive, so that ReLU never outputs exactly zero
It turns the normal distribution into a uniform one from -1 to 1
It cancels out the learning rate, so one rate suits every layer
checks.expl: With unit-variance weights each output of x @ w sums input_dim terms and scales as sqrt(input_dim); large values can blow up gradients. Rescaling by 1/sqrt(input_dim) makes outputs invariant to the width — Xavier initialisation, up to a constant — and truncating the normal at ±3 rules out outliers.

checks.q: What concrete mixed-precision plan does the lecture give?
opts: bfloat16 for parameters and gradients, float32 only for the loss
bfloat16 or fp8 for the forward pass's activations, float32 for the rest
fp8 everywhere, keeping float32 only for the final saved checkpoint
float16 for the even-numbered layers and float32 for the odd-numbered ones
checks.expl: Higher precision is more accurate and stable but costs memory and compute; lower precision the reverse. The plan: float32 by default, with bfloat16 or fp8 for the forward pass (activations) and float32 for parameters and gradients. PyTorch's AMP library automates this.

checks.q: The lecture's napkin math: 70B parameters, 15T tokens, 6 FLOPs per token per parameter, on 1024 H100s at 989.5 TFLOP/s each with MFU 0.5. About how many days?
checks.expl: Total: 6 × 70e9 × 15e12 = 6.3e24 FLOPs. Per day: 989.5e12 × 0.5 × 1024 × 86,400 ≈ 4.38e22. 6.3e24 / 4.38e22 ≈ 144 days — the 989.5 being half the 1979 TFLOP/s headline, which assumes sparsity.

checks.q: How large a model, in billions of parameters, fits naively on 8 H100s of 80 GB each with AdamW in float32: 4 bytes for parameters, 4 for gradients and 8 for optimizer state, activations ignored?
checks.expl: 16 bytes per parameter; 8 × 80e9 = 640e9 bytes; 640e9 / 16 = 40e9 parameters. The lecture's caveat: activations, which depend on batch size and sequence length, are not counted.

ai310.0.2.takeaway: Modern LLMs differ less than their papers suggest: nearly all use pre-norm, most use RMSNorm, gated activations, rotary position embeddings, no bias terms, d_ff ≈ 4 d_model (8/3 for gated units), heads × head dim = d_model, and weight decay rather than dropout. Where they differ, stability and inference cost — not raw FLOPs — usually decide.

beats.t: From the original Transformer to today's
beats.d: The 2017 Transformer used sine position embeddings, ReLU feed-forward layers and post-norm LayerNorm. The course's variant puts the norm in front of each block, uses RoPE and SwiGLU, and drops the bias terms. Since then dozens of dense models have shipped, with low consensus except one thing — and a trend towards LLaMA-like designs.

Keep the norm off the residual path: almost everyone does, for stability and larger learning rates (Grok and Gemma 2 add a second norm outside the stream).
