RMSNorm drops LayerNorm's mean and bias; it barely changes FLOPs, but FLOPs are not runtime — normalisation is data movement, so fewer parameters to move saves wall-clock time. Bias terms are dropped for the same reasons.

ReLU, GeLU, then gated units: multiply the activated xW1 entrywise by a second projection xV. SwiGLU and GeGLU give fairly consistent gains (Shazeer 2020) and are standard after 2023, though GPT-3 shows they aren't necessary. Some models also run attention and MLP in parallel to fuse matrix multiplies.

We want attention scores to depend only on relative position. Sine embeddings leave cross-terms, absolute ones are absolute, and relative biases are not inner products. RoPE pairs coordinates and rotates them by position-dependent angles — multiplicative, no cross-terms — applied to queries and keys in every layer.

d_ff = 4 d_model almost always (about 8/3 for gated units; T5's 64× worked but its successor went back to 2.5). Heads × head dim = d_model in most models. Aspect ratio d_model/n_layer sits around 100-200, and depth costs parallelism and latency. Vocabularies: 30-50K monolingual, 100-250K multilingual.

Pretraining sees trillions of tokens once, so overfitting is unlikely; newer models drop dropout and keep weight decay — not to control overfitting, but because it interacts with the learning rate schedule.

Softmaxes are where training blows up. The z-loss keeps the output softmax's normaliser near 1 (PaLM, OLMo 2); QK-norm normalises queries and keys before the attention softmax; logit soft-capping squashes logits with tanh.

Decoding one token at a time re-reads the KV cache each step, so arithmetic intensity is poor. MQA shares one key/value head across all queries; GQA uses a few, with little or no perplexity cost. Sliding-window attention bounds the context per layer, and recent models interleave full-attention layers (e.g. every fourth) with windowed ones.

ai310.0.2.worked: Sizing a gated FFN: a ReLU FFN with d_ff = 4 d_model holds 2 × 4 d_model² = 8 d_model² weights. A gated FFN has three d_model × d_ff matrices, so 3 d_ff d_model = 8 d_model² gives d_ff = 8/3 d_model ≈ 2.67 d_model — for d_model = 4096, about 10,900, which implementations round to a convenient multiple.
ai310.0.2.watch: Judging an architecture change by FLOPs alone. RMSNorm and dropped biases save almost no arithmetic yet speed training up, because memory movement, not multiplication, is what those operations cost.

checks.q: What is the one architecture choice the lecture says nearly every modern LM agrees on?
opts: Rotary position embeddings, used by every model since GPT-3
SwiGLU feed-forward layers, which replaced ReLU in every model
Pre-norm: keep the LayerNorm off the main residual signal path
Post-norm, as in the original Transformer, for stable gradients
checks.expl: Almost all modern LMs put the norm in front of each block so it doesn't sit on the residual stream (BERT was post-norm; OPT-350M is an odd exception). The original claimed advantage was removing warmup; today it is stability and larger learning rates. Some recent models add a second norm outside the stream.

checks.q: RMSNorm saves only a sliver of FLOPs. Why does the lecture say it still speeds models up?
opts: It removes warmup, so the same run needs fewer training steps
It lets the model drop attention biases, which halves memory
It cuts the FLOPs of every matrix multiply that follows it
FLOPs are not runtime: moving fewer values saves wall-clock time
checks.expl: Matrix multiplies are the vast majority of FLOPs, so dropping the mean and the bias saves almost no arithmetic. But normalisation is dominated by data movement — a low FLOP-to-memory ratio — so fewer operations and parameters to move do cut wall-clock time, and RMSNorm works as well as LayerNorm.

checks.q: What property is RoPE designed to give the attention score between two tokens?
opts: A learned vector is added for each absolute position of a token
It depends only on their relative position, by rotating q and k
It is zero beyond a fixed window, so its cost grows only linearly
It mixes absolute and relative terms, as sine embeddings do
checks.expl: RoPE wants the inner product of f(x, i) and f(y, j) to depend on x, y and i - j only. Inner products are invariant to rotation, so it pairs up coordinates and rotates each pair by a position-dependent angle — multiplying by sines and cosines rather than adding them, so there are no cross-terms — at every attention layer.

checks.q: Why do MQA and GQA reduce the number of key/value heads?
opts: Decoding re-reads the KV cache every step; fewer KV heads, less to move
Fewer heads improve attention quality by removing redundant heads
It allows a larger training batch, since queries need no gradients
It removes the softmax, which is the least stable part of the attention layer
checks.expl: In training, attention has high arithmetic intensity. In incremental decoding tokens come one at a time and the KV cache is read at every step, so arithmetic intensity is poor. MQA shares one key/value head across all query heads; GQA keeps a few — a knob between expressiveness and inference cost, with little perplexity cost.

checks.q: A ReLU FFN with d_ff = 4 × d_model holds two d_model × d_ff matrices; a gated FFN such as SwiGLU holds three. What d_ff / d_model keeps the parameter count unchanged?
checks.expl: Two matrices of d_model × 4 d_model hold 8 d_model² weights; three of d_model × r d_model hold 3r d_model². 3r = 8 gives r = 8/3 ≈ 2.67 — the 2/3 scale-down the lecture describes, seen in LLaMA 70B (2.68) and Qwen 14B (2.67).

checks.q: T5 (11B) has 128 attention heads of dimension 128 and d_model = 1024. What is (number of heads × head dim) / d_model?
checks.expl: 128 × 128 = 16,384, and 16,384 / 1024 = 16. Most models keep this ratio at 1 — GPT-3 has 96 × 128 = 12,288 = d_model — and T5 is a notable Google exception, as is its d_ff of 64 × d_model.

ai310.0.3.takeaway: A mixture of experts swaps each feed-forward layer for many expert FFNs and a router that sends every token to only a few, so parameters grow while FLOPs per token stay put. The hard parts are the discrete routing decision, which can't be differentiated and is trained with heuristic balancing losses, and the instability and systems complexity that come with it.

beats.d: Replace the big feed-forward layer with many FFNs and a selector layer. Each token uses only a few, so the number of experts can rise without changing FLOPs. At the same FLOPs, more parameters does better; MoEs train faster, compete with dense models, and parallelise across devices — most of the best open models are MoEs.
The infrastructure is complex and pays off mainly across many nodes, and the training objectives are heuristic and sometimes unstable. Most MoEs replace the MLP; MoE attention exists but is rare.

Tokens can choose experts, experts can choose tokens, or routing can be solved globally — but almost everyone uses token-choice top-k: Switch k = 1, Mixtral and Grok 2, Qwen and DBRX 4, DeepSeek 7 or 8. Some routers softmax before choosing top-k; Mixtral, DBRX and DeepSeek v3 softmax after it. Hashing is a common baseline.

DeepSeek and Qwen use many smaller experts plus a few shared experts that every token uses. DeepSeek's ablations favour both; OLMoE's find gains from fine-grained experts only. DeepSeek v3: 256 routed experts, 8 active, 1 shared.

Sparse gating is not differentiable. Reinforcement learning works but its variance and complexity keep it rare; stochastic perturbations were tried and dropped; in practice, heuristic balancing losses spread tokens evenly — the Switch loss downweights frequently used experts — and DeepSeek v3 adds per-expert biases learned online.

Each expert can sit on its own device; libraries such as MegaBlocks use smarter sparse matmuls. Token dropping happens per batch, so other people's queries can drop your token. Keep the router in float32 with a z-loss. Sparse MoEs overfit small fine-tuning sets: fine-tune only the non-MoE MLPs, or use lots of data.

A pretrained dense model can initialise an MoE (MiniCPM, Qwen MoE). DeepSeek's line: v1 with shared and fine-grained experts and balancing losses; v2 adding communication balancing and top-M device routing; v3 with auxiliary-loss-free balancing, multi-head latent attention to shrink the KV cache, and multi-token prediction.

ai310.0.3.worked: Routing one token with top-2 and softmax after top-k: router scores for four experts 2, 1, 0, -1; keep the two largest, 2 and 1; softmax over them gives e/(e + 1) ≈ 0.73 and 0.27. The token's output is 0.73 × expert 1's FFN output + 0.27 × expert 2's; the other experts are never run for it.
ai310.0.3.watch: Counting an MoE's total parameters as its cost. Compute per token follows the active experts, not the total — while memory, communication and load balance follow everything.

checks.q: What does the lecture say an MoE layer replaces, and what does that buy?
opts: Attention heads with experts, which removes attention's quadratic cost
The embedding table with experts, one for each language in the corpus
The FFN, with many FFNs and a router: more parameters at the same FLOPs
The whole model, with several small models whose outputs are averaged
checks.expl: Typically each MLP becomes many expert MLPs plus a selector; each token goes to only a few, so the number of experts — and parameters — grows without changing FLOPs per token. Same FLOPs, more parameters does better, and MoEs also train faster and parallelise across devices. MoE attention exists but is less common.

checks.q: Sparse gating decisions aren't differentiable. Which fix does the lecture say people use in practice?
opts: Learning the routing policy by reinforcement, as REINFORCE does
Adding Gaussian noise to the router so that gating becomes differentiable
Solving a linear assignment problem for every batch of tokens
Heuristic balancing losses that push tokens to spread across experts
checks.expl: RL is arguably the right solution, but its gradient variance and complexity keep it rare; stochastic perturbations (Shazeer 2017, Switch's jitter) were tried and later dropped. In practice: heuristic balancing losses — the Switch Transformer's penalises frequently used experts more strongly — or DeepSeek v3's per-expert biases.

checks.q: Why might an MoE give a different answer to the same query at different times?
opts: Experts are resampled at random each time the model is loaded
The router adds Gaussian noise to each routing decision it makes
Tokens are dropped per batch, so others' queries can drop yours
Each expert was trained on a different random subset of the data
checks.expl: Experts have limited capacity, and when too many tokens route to one, some are dropped — decided across the whole batch. Whether your token is processed then depends on what else is in the batch: other people's queries can drop your token, one speculation about GPT-4's non-determinism.

checks.q: What stability fix does the lecture give for the MoE router?
opts: Dropping the router's softmax in favour of a hard argmax
Freezing the router after warmup so its decisions stop changing
Training the router at ten times the rest of the model's rate
Computing the router in float32, sometimes with a z-loss
checks.expl: Routers rely on softmaxes over exponentials, which are fragile in low precision. Zoph et al. 2022 compute just the expert router in float32 and add an auxiliary z-loss on its logits; the lecture shows what happens to training without the z-loss.

checks.q: With softmax applied after top-k (as in Mixtral), a token's router scores for four experts are 2, 1, 0 and -1, and k = 2. What gate weight does the top expert get? Three decimals.
checks.expl: Top-2 keeps the scores 2 and 1; a softmax over just those gives e² / (e² + e¹) = e / (e + 1) ≈ 0.731, and 0.269 to the second. The other two experts get no weight and are not computed for this token.

checks.q: DeepSeek v1's fine-grained experts are a quarter the size of a standard FFN, and each token uses 6 routed plus 2 shared experts. How many standard-FFN equivalents of expert compute does a token use?
checks.expl: (6 + 2) × 1/4 = 2. Fine-grained experts split each FFN into smaller ones so a token can combine more specialists at the same cost, and shared experts are always on. DeepSeek's ablations favour both; OLMoE's find gains only from fine-grained experts.

ai310.0.4.takeaway: GPUs win by running a huge number of identical threads, and matrix multiplies on tensor cores are far faster than anything else — but compute has outgrown memory, so speed comes from moving less data: lower precision, fused kernels, recomputation, coalesced reads and tiling through shared memory. FlashAttention is all of these applied to attention.

beats.d: Language models improve predictably with compute, and since Dennard scaling ran out, the gains come from parallel hardware — GPU throughput has grown over 1000× in ten years. A CPU optimises for latency with a few fast threads; a GPU optimises for throughput with many tiny ALUs and little branching support.

A GPU has many streaming multiprocessors (SMs), each running blocks of threads on its streaming processors. Threads run in warps of 32 executing the same instruction on different data (SIMT). Registers and shared memory live inside the SM; L2 is on the die; global DRAM is off-chip and far slower, and anything shared across blocks goes through it.

beats.t: Matmuls are special, memory is the wall
beats.d: Tensor cores make matrix multiplies over 10× faster than other floating-point work, and FLOPs have scaled faster than memory bandwidth — it is hard to keep compute fed. The roofline model asks the key question: is a workload memory-bound or compute-bound?

Fewer bits mean fewer bits to move, raising arithmetic intensity. Fusing operations keeps intermediates on-chip — sin²x + cos²x is five kernels naively, one fused, and torch.compile does such fusions. Recomputing cheap activations in the backward pass can beat storing them: three stacked sigmoids need 5/8 of the memory accesses.

DRAM is read in bursts, so a warp's reads should fall in one burst. Tiling loads blocks of the input matrices into shared memory and reuses them, cutting global reads by the tile size — but tile sizes that don't divide the matrix, or misaligned rows, waste work.

Matmul speed rises and dips with size because of alignment and wave quantization: with 256 × 128 tiles, a 1792 output needs 98 tiles but 1793 needs 120, more than an A100's 108 SMs, so a second mostly idle wave runs.

Attention is three matmuls with a softmax between. FlashAttention tiles the matmuls, fuses the exponential, and computes the softmax tile by tile with an online max and a telescoping sum, so the full score matrix never goes to global memory; the backward pass recomputes it tile by tile.

ai310.0.4.worked: Arithmetic intensity of elementwise ReLU on n values: per value, one read and one write and one FLOP. In float32 that is 8 bytes per FLOP; in float16, 4. With intensity this low the operation is memory-bound — the fix is not a faster ALU but fewer bytes moved, by lower precision or by fusing the ReLU into the kernel that produced its input.
ai310.0.4.watch: Counting FLOPs to predict speed. Most non-matmul operations are memory-bound, so their cost is the bytes they move — and a matrix whose size just exceeds a tile multiple can run slower than a larger one.

checks.q: How does the lecture contrast GPUs with CPUs?
opts: GPUs run very many threads for throughput; CPUs a few fast ones for latency
GPUs have more cache per core and far stronger branch prediction than CPUs
GPUs finish each single thread sooner; CPUs process more data in total
GPUs run different instructions on each thread; CPUs run the same one
checks.expl: A CPU optimises for latency — a few fast threads with plenty of control logic and cache. A GPU optimises for throughput: many tiny ALUs, much less support for branching, and within a warp all 32 threads execute the same instruction on different data (SIMT).

checks.q: What does operator fusion save?
opts: FLOPs, by merging several matrix multiplies into a larger one
Trips to memory: intermediates stay on-chip, not written back
Precision, by keeping every intermediate result in float32
Compile time, by caching each kernel after its first launch
checks.expl: Picture the GPU as a factory and memory as a distant warehouse: shipping every intermediate back and forth is wasteful. sin²x + cos²x launches 5 kernels naively but can be one fused kernel, and compilers such as torch.compile do easy fusions like this automatically.

checks.q: Why can recomputing activations in the backward pass beat storing them?
opts: Re-reading stored activations costs memory traffic; recomputing is cheaper
Stored activations lose precision, so recomputed ones are more accurate
The backward pass needs different activations from the forward pass
Recomputation lets the GPU skip the forward pass of the next batch
checks.expl: For low-arithmetic-intensity operations such as stacked sigmoids, writing activations out and reading them back dominates — 8 memory reads and writes for three sigmoids. Discarding them and recomputing from the input needs 5/8 of the accesses: trading compute, which is plentiful, for memory traffic, which is not.

checks.q: How does FlashAttention compute exact attention without writing the full score matrix to memory?
opts: It approximates softmax with a low-rank sketch of the score matrix
Tiles of QKᵀ with an online softmax: a running max, telescoping sum
It drops attention to distant tokens, keeping a sliding window only
It stores the score matrix in float8, small enough to fit in SRAM
checks.expl: It tiles the Q, K, V matrix multiplies through shared memory, fuses the exponential, and computes the softmax tile by tile with the online trick — keep a running maximum and rescale a telescoping sum — so the n × n scores never reach global memory. The backward pass recomputes them tile by tile.

checks.q: With 256 × 128 tiles, a 1793 × 1793 output needs 8 × 15 = 120 tiles, more than an A100's 108 SMs. How many tiles does a 1600 × 1600 output need?
checks.expl: ceil(1600 / 256) = 7 (6.25 rounded up) and ceil(1600 / 128) = 13 (12.5 rounded up): 7 × 13 = 91 tiles, one wave on 108 SMs. At 1793 the count jumps to 120 and a second, mostly idle wave is needed — wave quantization.

checks.q: Elementwise ReLU in float16 reads each value once and writes it once, for one FLOP. How many bytes move per FLOP?
checks.expl: A float16 value is 2 bytes: 2 read + 2 written = 4 bytes per FLOP, against 8 in float32. Fewer bits mean fewer bits to move, so low precision raises arithmetic intensity — which is what limits memory-bound operations like this one.

ai310.0.5.takeaway: Measure before optimising: benchmark for end-to-end time (with warmup and synchronisation), profile to see which kernels actually run. Then the principle is the same at every level — PyTorch, CUDA, Triton or torch.compile — organise the computation to minimise reads and writes, which for elementwise and row-wise operations means fusing them into one kernel.

beats.d: An A100 has 108 SMs, 80GB of DRAM, a 40MB L2 and fast per-SM memory. Threads run f(i); thread blocks are scheduled on one SM and share its memory; a grid is all the blocks. Blocks run in waves, so the last wave can leave SMs idle — aim for at least 4× as many blocks as SMs. Matmuls are compute-bound; nearly everything else is memory-bound.

Spec sheets and papers don't know your library, hardware and workload. benchmark() warms up, calls torch.cuda.synchronize() because CUDA launches are asynchronous, and averages several trials. The PyTorch profiler then shows which CUDA kernels ran — different ones for different sizes, named after their library and tile size — and flame graphs show where an MLP's time goes.

Each operation reads from DRAM, computes and writes back — the warehouse and the factory. manual_gelu, the tanh formula in PyTorch ops, launches a kernel per operation; torch's gelu is one fused kernel, and significantly faster.

A CUDA kernel is the code one thread runs, using blockIdx, blockDim and threadIdx to find its element, with a bounds check for the last block. load_inline compiles it from Python. The hand-written GeLU beats manual_gelu but not PyTorch.

Triton, from OpenAI in 2021, is Python and thinks in blocks, not threads: it handles coalescing, shared memory and scheduling within an SM, while scheduling across SMs stays manual. The Triton GeLU loads a block with a mask, computes, and stores; its PTX shows one thread handling 8 elements (thread coarsening).
torch.compile turns manual_gelu into a generated Triton kernel without hand-written CUDA or Triton. Compilers will keep getting better; hand-written kernels pay off for what they can't fuse.

The naive softmax makes five passes — max, subtract, exp, sum, divide — for 5MN + M reads and 3MN + 2M writes, where MN of each would do. The Triton version gives each row its own block, loads it once (padding with minus infinity), computes in registers and writes once.

ai310.0.5.worked: Choosing a Triton grid: for n elements and BLOCK_SIZE = 1024, launch triton.cdiv(n, 1024) programs. Program pid handles offsets pid × 1024 + arange(1024), with mask = offsets < n so the last block doesn't read or write out of bounds. For a 16384 × 16384 tensor that is 262,144 programs — far more than 4× the 108 SMs.
ai310.0.5.watch: Timing GPU code without torch.cuda.synchronize(): the clock measures how fast Python queued the kernel, not how long it ran. And trusting the first run, which includes compilation and cold caches.

checks.q: Why does the lecture's benchmark() call torch.cuda.synchronize() before stopping the clock?
opts: To flush the L2 cache, so that every trial starts with a cold cache
To force float32, since bfloat16 timings are not reproducible
CUDA launches are asynchronous; without it you'd time the launch
To copy the result back to the CPU so the timing includes it
checks.expl: The CPU queues GPU kernels and moves on, so a timer stopped right after run() measures little more than the launch. benchmark() also does warmup runs first — first calls can be slower from compilation and uncached state — and averages several trials to capture variance.

checks.q: manual_gelu writes the tanh form of GeLU in PyTorch operations; the lecture finds torch's own gelu significantly faster. Why?
opts: The built-in uses the exact formula, which needs fewer arithmetic steps
manual_gelu runs on the CPU, since plain Python arithmetic can't use a GPU
The built-in replaces tanh with a lookup table held in on-chip memory
Each manual op is its own kernel and DRAM round trip; the built-in is one
checks.expl: Every elementwise operation in manual_gelu launches a kernel that reads its input from global memory and writes its result back. torch's gelu (called with the same tanh approximation) does it all in one kernel — the warehouse-and-factory point. The lecture's own CUDA version also beats manual_gelu but not PyTorch's.

checks.q: According to the lecture's table, what does Triton manage automatically that CUDA leaves to you?
opts: Everything, including scheduling thread blocks across the SMs
Only memory coalescing; shared memory is still managed by hand
Coalescing, shared-memory management and scheduling within an SM
Only scheduling across SMs; everything inside an SM stays manual
checks.expl: Triton is written in Python and thinks in thread blocks rather than threads; its compiler handles coalesced DRAM transfers, shared memory and scheduling within each SM, while scheduling across SMs stays manual. Working on blocks enables tricks such as thread coarsening — one thread processing 8 elements.

checks.q: What general rule about arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte) does the lecture give?
opts: Everything on a GPU is compute-bound once the batch is large enough
Elementwise ops are compute-bound, and matrix multiplies memory-bound
Intensity depends only on precision, not on which operation runs
Matrix multiplication is compute-bound; nearly all else is memory-bound
checks.expl: High intensity means compute-bound (good), low means memory-bound (bad). Matmuls reuse each loaded value many times; elementwise and reduction operations touch each value once or twice — which is why fusing them, so data is read and written once, pays off.

checks.q: triton_gelu splits its input into blocks of BLOCK_SIZE = 1024 elements. How many blocks does it launch for a 16384 × 16384 tensor? (digits only, no commas)
checks.expl: 16384 × 16384 = 268,435,456 elements, divided by 1024 = 262,144 blocks (triton.cdiv rounds up, but here it divides exactly). Each program masks with offsets < num_elements so a ragged last block stays in bounds.

checks.q: manual_softmax's comments count reads per step for an M × N input: max MN, subtract MN + M, exp MN, sum MN, normalise MN. How many reads for the lecture's 2 × 3 example?
checks.expl: 5MN + M = 5 × 6 + 2 = 32 reads, alongside 3MN + 2M = 22 writes. A fused kernel reads and writes each value once — MN of each — which is why the comment expects about a 4× speedup.

ai310.0.6.takeaway: No single GPU holds a large model or trains it fast enough, so training is split three ways: data parallelism (with ZeRO sharding its memory away), pipeline parallelism across layers, and tensor plus sequence parallelism within layers. Each spends a different scarce resource — memory, bandwidth or batch size — so real runs combine them by rule of thumb.

beats.d: Single-GPU compute and memory both run out: most large models don't fit on one device. Work is split across GPUs within a node (fast interconnects) and across nodes (slower). The building blocks are collectives — all-reduce, broadcast, reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter — and an all-reduce can be done as a reduce-scatter plus an all-gather, optimal when bandwidth-limited.

beats.t: Data parallelism and its memory problem
beats.d: Split the batch across M machines and all-reduce the gradients: compute scales, communication is 2 × #params per batch, memory doesn't scale at all. Mixed-precision Adam needs about 16 bytes per parameter — bf16 weights and gradients, float32 master weights, two Adam moments — copied on every GPU.

Stage 1 shards the optimizer state: reduce-scatter gradients, each worker updates its slice, all-gather parameters — the same traffic as DDP, so it's free. Stage 2 also shards gradients, sending each layer's gradients as soon as they're computed. Stage 3 (FSDP) shards parameters too, fetching them on demand and overlapping communication with compute, for 1.5× the traffic.

Cutting the model by layers leaves each of n GPUs busy 1/n of the time. Micro-batches fill the pipeline, leaving a bubble of (stages - 1)/(micro-batches), so pipelines need big batches. They save memory and send only activations, point to point, so they suit slower inter-node links; zero-bubble schedules split the backward pass to fill the gaps.

Split matrix multiplies by columns and rows across GPUs, with all-reduces in the forward and backward passes: no bubble and no batch-size requirement, but heavy communication, so keep it within a node. Activations still grow, so sequence parallelism splits the pointwise LayerNorm and dropout work along the sequence. Context and expert parallelism split long sequences and experts.

Until the model fits, use tensor parallelism up to the GPUs in a machine and pipeline parallelism across machines (or ZeRO-3); then scale with data parallelism, accumulating gradients if the batch is small. Tensor parallel 8 is often optimal; activation recomputation can pay for itself by allowing larger batches.

OLMo's 7B used FSDP; DeepSeek uses ZeRO stage 1 with tensor, sequence and pipeline parallelism (v3: pipeline 16, expert 64-way); Yi uses ZeRO-1 with tensor and pipeline; Gemma 2 uses ZeRO-3 with model and data parallelism; Llama 3 405B notes how often GPUs fail at that scale.

ai310.0.6.worked: Will it fit? With bf16 everything except float32 master weights, training costs 12 bytes per parameter. On 8 × 80 GB: unsharded, 80 / 12 ≈ 6.7B parameters. ZeRO-1 keeps 2 + 2 bytes and an eighth of the 8 optimizer bytes: 5 bytes, 16B. ZeRO-2 keeps 2 bytes and an eighth of 10: 3.25 bytes, 24.6B. ZeRO-3 keeps an eighth of all 12: 1.5 bytes, 53.3B.
ai310.0.6.watch: Running tensor parallelism across nodes: its all-reduces in every layer need a fast interconnect, and on slow links it stalls the whole model. And counting only parameter memory — activations grow with batch and sequence length and need their own split.

checks.q: Why does the lecture call ZeRO stage 1 'free'?
opts: Its reduce-scatter plus all-gather costs DDP's all-reduce: 2 × params
It needs no communication, as each GPU updates every parameter itself
It shards the activations, which are training's biggest memory cost
It cuts the batch size each GPU needs, which shortens every single step
checks.expl: An all-reduce can be done as a reduce-scatter then an all-gather — the best you can do when bandwidth-limited. Stage 1 splits the optimizer state: reduce-scatter the gradients, each worker updates its slice, all-gather the parameters. Same 2 × #params traffic as DDP, with memory falling from (4 + K) to (4 + K/N) bytes per parameter.

checks.q: What rule of thumb does the lecture give for combining the three kinds of parallelism?
opts: Pipeline within a machine, tensor parallel across machines, then data
Tensor parallel within a machine, pipeline across machines, then data
Data parallel first until the batch runs out, then tensor, then pipeline
Use just one kind, since combining them multiplies communication costs
checks.expl: Until the model fits: tensor parallel up to the GPUs in one machine — it needs the fast intra-node interconnect, and 8 is often optimal — and pipeline parallel across machines, since only activations cross the slower links point to point (or ZeRO-3, depending on bandwidth). Then data parallel the rest of the way, accumulating gradients if the batch is small.

checks.q: What does sequence parallelism split, and why?
opts: LayerNorm and dropout along the sequence, so those activations scale
The attention heads across GPUs, so that each GPU computes a few heads
The vocabulary across GPUs, so the output softmax fits on each device
The optimizer state across nodes, so long sequences need less memory
checks.expl: Tensor parallelism splits the attention and MLP matmuls, but about 10sbh of activations per layer — LayerNorm, dropout and the block inputs — stay whole on every GPU and keep growing. Those operations are pointwise over the sequence, so splitting them along it (all-gather in, reduce-scatter out) makes activation memory scale linearly too.

checks.q: Model parallelism and ZeRO stage 3 both split the parameters across GPUs. What does each communicate?
opts: Both send gradients only, never activations or the weights
Model parallelism sends activations; ZeRO-3 sends parameters
Model parallelism sends parameters; ZeRO-3 only activations
Both send the full model to every GPU before each step
checks.expl: ZeRO-3 (FSDP) requests each block's parameters when needed and frees them afterwards, overlapping the all-gathers with compute — about 3 × #params of traffic per step. Pipeline and tensor parallelism keep their slice of the parameters in place and pass activations (and their gradients) instead.

checks.q: With bf16 everything except float32 master weights — 12 bytes per parameter: 2 weights, 2 gradients, 8 master weights and Adam state — how many billion parameters fit on 8 × 80 GB GPUs under ZeRO stage 2? One decimal.
checks.expl: Each GPU keeps all the bf16 weights (2 bytes) and an eighth of the gradients and optimizer state: (2 + 8) / 8 = 1.25 bytes. 2 + 1.25 = 3.25 bytes per parameter, and 80e9 / 3.25 ≈ 24.6e9. Unsharded: 80/12 ≈ 6.7B; stage 1 (5 bytes) 16B; stage 3 (12/8) 53.3B.

checks.q: A pipeline has 4 stages and processes 12 micro-batches per batch. What is the lecture's ratio of bubble time to useful compute, (stages - 1)/(micro-batches)?
checks.expl: (4 - 1) / 12 = 0.25: a quarter as much idle time as useful work. More micro-batches shrink the bubble, which is why pipelines need big batches; plain layer-wise parallelism leaves each of n GPUs busy only 1/n of the time.

ai310.0.7.takeaway: Multi-GPU training rests on a handful of collective operations — broadcast, scatter, gather, reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter, all-reduce — that NCCL turns into packets over NVLink and NVSwitch. With them, data, tensor and pipeline parallelism each fit in a few dozen lines of PyTorch; what separates them is which tensors cross the wire and how often.

beats.t: The same theme, one level up
beats.d: Inside a GPU, fusion and tiling cut memory accesses; across GPUs, replication and sharding cut communication. The hierarchy runs from shared memory and HBM (3.9 TB/s on an H100) to NVLink within a node (900 GB/s, 18 links) to NVSwitch across nodes — far faster than the PCIe and Ethernet of a home machine.

World size is the number of devices; each is a rank. Broadcast and scatter send out, gather collects, reduce combines with an associative op, 'all' means every rank gets the result, and all-reduce = reduce-scatter + all-gather. The recorded demo shows it: ranks holding [0, 1, 2, 3] + r all end with [6, 10, 14, 18].

NCCL detects the topology, picks the paths and launches CUDA kernels to move data; torch.distributed wraps it (nccl for GPUs, gloo for CPUs) behind calls such as all_gather_into_tensor. Benchmarked on one node, a 400 MB all-reduce took about 2 ms — roughly 275 GB/s effective.

Each rank takes batch/world_size examples, runs forward and backward, and all-reduces every gradient with AVG — the only difference from ordinary training. Losses differ across ranks, gradients and parameters don't.

Each rank holds a num_dim × num_dim/world_size slice of every layer, computes its share of the outputs, then all-gathers and concatenates the activations to full width before the next layer — a collective in every layer.

Each rank holds a subset of the layers. Rank 0 splits the batch into micro-batches; each rank receives activations from the previous rank, applies its layers and sends the result on, point to point. Overlapping communication with computation to remove the bubble is left out.

Attention and other layers, overlap of communication and compute, and the bookkeeping that real systems need — or, in JAX on TPUs, declaring a sharding and letting the compiler do it. The summary: parallelise over batch, width, depth or length, and choose between recomputing, storing, or fetching from another GPU.

ai310.0.7.worked: Reduce-scatter then all-gather on 4 ranks holding [0, 1, 2, 3] + r: summing element-wise gives [6, 10, 14, 18]; reduce-scatter leaves rank i with element i (6, 10, 14, 18); all-gather sends each rank everyone's element, so every rank ends with [6, 10, 14, 18] — exactly what one all-reduce produces.
ai310.0.7.watch: Forgetting that every collective is a synchronisation point: one slow rank, or a rank that never calls the collective, stalls all the others. The demos call dist.barrier() before printing and torch.cuda.synchronize() before stopping a timer for this reason.

checks.q: In the lecture's bare-bones data parallelism, what is the one step added to ordinary training?
opts: Each rank keeps its own parameters, never synchronised with the others
Rank 0 computes the whole batch's loss and broadcasts it to the rest
After backward, every gradient is all-reduced (averaged) across ranks
Activations are all-gathered after each layer so all ranks see them
checks.expl: Each rank takes its slice of the batch (128 / 4 = 32 examples), runs forward and backward, then all-reduces each parameter's gradient with AVG. Losses differ across ranks — they come from different data — but gradients, and so the parameters after the AdamW step, stay identical.

checks.q: In the tensor-parallel demo, what happens after each layer's slice of the matmul?
opts: Gradients are reduce-scattered, so each rank updates only its slice
Activations go point to point to the rank holding the next layer
Each rank discards the others' outputs and keeps its own columns
Activations are all-gathered and concatenated back to full width
checks.expl: Each rank holds a num_dim × num_dim/world_size slice of every layer (1024 × 256 on 4 ranks), so x @ params[i] yields only its share of the output columns. An all-gather collects every rank's batch × 256 block and torch.cat rebuilds batch × 1024 — a collective in every layer, which is why tensor parallelism wants fast links.

checks.q: How does the pipeline-parallel demo move data between ranks?
opts: All ranks all-reduce the activations once each micro-batch is done
Rank 0 broadcasts the batch, and every rank computes all the layers
Rank 0 splits the batch into micro-batches; ranks send and recv them
Each rank all-gathers the other ranks' parameters before every layer
checks.expl: Each rank holds a subset of the layers (4 layers over 2 ranks). Rank 0 chunks the batch into micro-batches; each later rank recv()s a micro-batch's activations from the rank before, applies its layers and send()s the result on — point to point. Communication and compute are not overlapped, so the bubble remains.

checks.q: What unifying theme does the lecture draw between last week's kernels and this week's multi-GPU training?
opts: Compute is cheap only in float32, so precision decides every design
Distributed training needs no code beyond the standard PyTorch calls
Every speed-up comes from adding more GPUs rather than from changing code
Arrange the computation to avoid data-transfer bottlenecks, at every level
checks.expl: In both cases compute sits far from the data. Inside a GPU the answer was fusion and tiling to reduce memory accesses; across GPUs it is replication and sharding to reduce communication — up a hierarchy from shared memory to HBM to NVLink (900 GB/s per H100, against 3.9 TB/s of HBM) to NVSwitch across nodes.

checks.q: In the collective demo, rank r of 4 starts with the tensor [0, 1, 2, 3] + r. After a SUM reduce-scatter, what single value does rank 2 hold?
checks.expl: Reduce-scatter sums element-wise across ranks — [6, 10, 14, 18] — and gives rank i element i, so rank 2 gets 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 14. An all-gather of the four values then reproduces the all-reduce result on every rank: all-reduce = reduce-scatter + all-gather.

checks.q: The all-reduce benchmark sends 100 × 1024² float32 elements on 4 ranks and counts sent bytes as size × 2 × (world_size - 1). How many GiB is that? Two decimals.
checks.expl: Size: 104,857,600 × 4 bytes = 400 MiB = 0.390625 GiB; × 2 (send input, receive output) × 3 = 2.34 GiB. Divided by world_size × duration, the recorded run measured about 275 GB/s.

ai310.0.8.takeaway: Loss falls as a power law — a straight line on a log-log plot — in data, parameters and compute, which turns design into prediction: fit small models, extrapolate to the large one. That lets you choose architectures, optimizers and the split between model size and data before spending the big budget — while remembering that compute-optimal training is not deployment-optimal.

beats.d: Given ten thousand H100s for a month, which model do you train? Tuning hyperparameters on big models is unaffordable, and cargo-culting existing LMs doesn't say how they were chosen. Scaling laws offer simple, predictive rules: tune on small models and extrapolate.

Theory gave sample-complexity bounds; 1990s and 2000s work found log-linear data scaling; Hestness et al. (2017) showed predictable power laws across translation, language modelling and speech — even anticipating emergence and compute scaling. Kaplan et al. (2020) found such laws for many factors in language models.

Estimation error decays polynomially. Estimating a mean from n samples gives expected squared error σ²/n: log error falls with slope -1. Flexible nonparametric learning in d dimensions gives n^(-1/d) — much shallower — and one argument ties neural slopes to the data's intrinsic dimension.
Changing data composition shifts the offset, not the slope. Repeated data is worth less than fresh data, so effective data saturates with repetition, and data selection should adapt to scale.

Instead of training an LSTM GPT-3, compare the scaling curves of LSTMs and Transformers, or Adam and SGD. Depth matters little past a couple of layers, embedding parameters behave differently, critical batch size grows as the loss target falls, and optimal learning rates shift with scale unless parametrised (muP). Downstream tasks scale less predictably.

Joint laws such as error = n^(-α) + m^(-β) + C fit well and let you trade data against model size. Chinchilla found Kaplan's fits off — mainly from not accounting for learning-rate schedules — and gave three methods: minimum over training curves, IsoFLOP profiles, and a joint fit, the last later found flawed.

Chinchilla's roughly 20 tokens per parameter minimises training compute, but most deployed compute is inference, so models are over-trained: GPT-3 used 2 tokens per parameter, Llama 2 70B 29, Mistral 7B 110, Llama 3 70B 215.

ai310.0.8.worked: An IsoFLOP analysis: choose several compute budgets C; for each, train models of several sizes N with D = C/(6N) tokens; plot final loss against N — each curve is U-shaped — and take its minimum. Fit a power law through the minima, N*(C), and extrapolate it to the budget you can actually afford.
ai310.0.8.watch: Extrapolating a scaling law fitted with a fixed learning-rate schedule, or reading downstream benchmark scores as if they were as predictable as loss. Both errors have produced confident, wrong forecasts.

checks.q: What does Chinchilla's IsoFLOP method (method 2) do?
opts: Fixes several compute budgets, varies model size in each, fits the minima
Trains one huge model and reads the optimum off its learning-rate schedule
Fits one least-squares formula to every run on a model-size and data grid
Takes the lowest point over the union of all the training curves it has
checks.expl: For each FLOP budget, vary the parameter count (and so the tokens) and find the bottom of the U-shaped loss curve; the minima across budgets form a power law for the compute-optimal size. Method 1 takes the minimum over all training curves; method 3 fits a joint law by least squares — and was likely flawed, as a later re-fit of the recovered data found.

checks.q: According to the lecture, how does changing the composition of the training data change a data scaling law?
opts: It changes the slope, so better data makes loss fall faster with size
It shifts the offset, while the slope stays roughly as it was
It turns the power law into an exponential decay in dataset size
It has no effect at all, since only the number of tokens matters
checks.expl: Data composition affects the offset, not the slope: a better or more relevant mix moves the whole log-log line down without changing how fast it falls. Distribution-shift scaling laws built on this show the value of diverse data; repetition, separately, makes extra tokens worth less.

checks.q: Chinchilla's rule is about 20 tokens per parameter, yet Llama 3 70B used 215. Why does the lecture say that can make sense?
opts: Deployment compute is mostly inference, so a small model trained longer pays
Chinchilla's fits were wrong, and 200 tokens per parameter is optimal
Larger vocabularies need more tokens for each parameter to be learned
More tokens per parameter cut the training FLOPs needed for a given loss
checks.expl: Chinchilla answers which model is best for a fixed training budget. Serving cost grows with model size and usage, so the more a model will be used, the more it's worth paying upfront to train a smaller one far past compute-optimal — GPT-3 used 2 tokens per parameter, Mistral 7B 110, Llama 3 70B 215.

checks.q: What design procedure do scaling laws make possible, in the lecture's words?
opts: Tune every hyperparameter on the full-size model, then shrink it
Train a few small models, fit a scaling law, pick by its prediction
Copy all the hyperparameters of the latest large open model as is
Grow one model gradually, re-tuning at each doubling of its size
checks.expl: Rather than the old, unpleasant way — tuning on big models — or cargo-culting existing LMs: train a few smaller models, establish a scaling law (Adam against SGD, Transformers against LSTMs, depth), and choose by its prediction. Caution: downstream task performance often scales much less predictably than loss.

checks.q: Estimating a mean from n samples of N(μ, σ²) has expected squared error σ²/n — the lecture's toy scaling law. With σ² = 4, how many samples bring the expected squared error to 0.01?
checks.expl: σ²/n = 0.01 gives n = 4 / 0.01 = 400. In logs, log error = -log n + 2 log σ: a slope of -1. Neural scaling laws have much shallower slopes, which the lecture relates to nonparametric rates such as n^(-1/d).

checks.q: Slide 50 lists Mistral 7B at 110 tokens per parameter, against Chinchilla's 20. Training compute is proportional to N × D. With the same compute as Mistral 7B's run, how many billion parameters would a Chinchilla-optimal model (20 tokens per parameter) have? One decimal.
checks.expl: Mistral 7B: N × D = 7B × 770B. A model at 20 tokens per parameter with the same product has 20 N² = 7 × 770 (in units of 10^18), so N = √269.5 ≈ 16.4B, trained on about 328B tokens. Mistral chose a model under half that size and trained it far longer — over-training, which the slide justifies: most of a deployed model's compute is inference, so a smaller model is worth the extra upfront cost.

ai310.0.9.takeaway: Inference is a different workload from training: prefill is compute-bound, but generation produces one token at a time and is memory-bound, dominated by reading the weights and the KV cache. So the levers are reading less — smaller KV caches, quantized weights, pruned or new architectures — checking cheaply instead of generating (speculative decoding), and managing memory for ragged, dynamic traffic (continuous batching, PagedAttention).

beats.d: It runs in actual use, evaluation, test-time compute and RL rollouts, and unlike training it is paid every time. Metrics: time to first token, latency per token, throughput. Training sees all tokens at once; generation is sequential, so compute is hard to use fully.

An X (B × D) @ W (D × F) matmul has intensity about B FLOPs per byte when B is small; an H100's ratio of FLOP/s to bandwidth is about 295, so the matmul is compute-limited only if B > 295. With a KV cache, the MLP's intensity is B × T, but attention's is S·T/(S + T): S/2 in prefill, below 1 in generation, and batching can't help because each sequence has its own cache.

Each generation step reads all parameters plus every sequence's KV cache. For Llama 2 13B on an H100: batch 1 gives about 8 ms per token and 125 tokens/s; batch 64, 24 ms and about 2,700 tokens/s; batch 256 doesn't fit and gains less. Copies of the model raise throughput at the same latency; small batches help time to first token.

GQA keeps N query heads but K key/value heads, shrinking the cache N/K-fold (MQA: K = 1). MLA projects keys and values down to a small latent (DeepSeek v2: 16,384 to 512, plus 64 for RoPE). Cross-layer attention shares KVs across layers; local attention keeps the cache independent of length, interleaved with some global layers.

beats.t: Beyond the Transformer, and lossy shortcuts
beats.d: State-space models and linear attention replace the growing KV cache with a fixed state (Mamba, Jamba, BASED, MiniMax-01); diffusion models generate tokens in parallel. Quantization: bf16 by default, fp8, int8 (LLM.int8() keeps outliers in fp16), int4, with AWQ keeping the most activation-sensitive weights precise. Pruning removes unimportant layers or heads, then distils.

A cheap draft model proposes a few tokens; the target scores them in parallel and accepts or rejects them by modified rejection sampling, so the output is an exact sample from the target. Better drafts (Medusa, EAGLE) mean more acceptances.

Requests arrive at different times with different lengths. Continuous batching schedules each decoding iteration, adding new requests as they come, and batches non-attention work across concatenated sequences. PagedAttention stores the KV cache in non-contiguous blocks, ending fragmentation and sharing prefixes with copy-on-write.

ai310.0.9.worked: KV cache per sequence: tokens × (KV heads × head dim) × layers × 2 (key, value) × 2 bytes (bf16). Llama 2 13B at 1024 tokens: 1024 × 40 × 128 × 40 × 4 ≈ 0.84 GB. With 26 GB of weights, a batch of 64 needs about 80 GB; GQA with 8 KV heads cuts the cache 5×, which is what lets the batch grow to 256 and still fit.
ai310.0.9.watch: Optimising generation's FLOPs. A decode step does little arithmetic per byte it reads, so the wins come from moving fewer bytes — the KV cache and the weights — not from faster multiplication.

checks.q: Why does batching more requests not raise the arithmetic intensity of attention during generation, as it does for the MLP?
opts: Attention runs in float32, which halves the FLOPs per byte it reads
Attention runs on the CPU, while the MLP layers run on the GPU
Each sequence has its own KV cache, so no read is shared across it
Attention has no matrix multiplies, only softmax and elementwise ops
checks.expl: MLP weights are the same for every sequence, so B concurrent requests reuse each weight read: intensity about B. In attention Q, K and V all depend on the sequence, so each request reads its own KV cache: intensity S·T/(S + T) — about S/2 in prefill but below 1 when generating one token (T = 1), whatever B is.

checks.q: What guarantees that speculative decoding produces the same distribution as the target model?
opts: The draft is distilled until its outputs match the target's exactly
Only tokens where draft and target agree on the argmax are kept
The target model regenerates every token the draft model proposed
Proposals are accepted or rejected by modified rejection sampling
checks.expl: The draft p proposes a few tokens; the target q scores them in parallel — checking is cheaper than generating — and accepts each with probability min(1, q/p), resampling from the residual max(q - p, 0) on rejection. The result is an exact sample from q; a better draft just means more acceptances.

checks.q: What problem does PagedAttention solve?
opts: Attention's quadratic cost, by skipping blocks of distant tokens
Slow kernel launches, by fusing every layer into a single kernel
KV-cache fragmentation, by storing it in non-contiguous blocks
Precision loss in the KV cache, by keeping its pages in float32
checks.expl: Reserving a contiguous KV region up to the maximum length wastes memory inside it (internal fragmentation) and between regions (external). vLLM's PagedAttention splits each sequence's cache into blocks, as an OS pages memory, and lets sequences share prefix blocks — a system prompt, several samples — with copy-on-write.

checks.q: What trade-off does the lecture draw between batch size, latency and throughput in generation?
opts: Larger batches improve latency and throughput until memory runs out
Smaller batches improve both, since each request gets the whole GPU
Batch size changes neither, because generation is compute-bound
Larger batches raise throughput but worsen latency; smaller, the reverse
checks.expl: Generation is memory-bound: each step reads all the parameters plus every sequence's KV cache. Batching shares the parameter reads, so tokens per second rise — about 125 at batch 1 and 2,700 at 64 for Llama 2 13B on an H100 — but each step reads more cache, so latency grows from about 8 ms to 24 ms.

checks.q: An H100 does 989 TFLOP/s against 3.35 TB/s of memory bandwidth. A bf16 X (B × D) @ W (D × F) matmul with B much smaller than D and F has intensity about B. Above roughly what B does it become compute-limited?
checks.expl: Accelerator intensity = 989e12 / 3.35e12 ≈ 295 FLOPs per byte. The matmul does 2BDF FLOPs over about 2DF bytes of weights, so its intensity is about B: compute-limited only when B > 295. Generation with one token per request is the B = 1 case — a matrix-vector product.

checks.q: Llama 2 13B has 40 layers and 40 key/value heads of dimension 128. In bf16, how many GB (1e9 bytes) does the KV cache take for one 1024-token sequence? Two decimals.
checks.expl: S × (K × H) × L × 2 (key and value) × 2 bytes = 1024 × 5120 × 40 × 4 = 838,860,800 bytes ≈ 0.84 GB. At batch 64 that is about 54 GB on top of 26 GB of weights; GQA with 8 KV heads cuts the cache 5×.

ai310.0.10.takeaway: Published scaling recipes since Chinchilla share three moves: make hyperparameters transfer across scale (muP, or fitted laws for batch size and learning rate), make the Chinchilla sweep affordable (warmup-stable-decay schedules), and size the model by IsoFLOP or joint fits. muP mostly works — but not with everything a modern LM does.

beats.d: Does Chinchilla's approach work in practice? Can fitting scaling laws cost less compute? Should architectures be parametrised so they scale nicely? Three recent models published detailed recipes: Cerebras-GPT, MiniCPM and DeepSeek.

Cerebras-GPT (0.1-13B, Chinchilla recipe) found scaling more predictable with muP. MiniCPM (1-2.5B, matching many 7B models) uses muP for initialisation, fixes the aspect ratio, and fits optimal batch size (growing polynomially as loss falls), learning rate and tokens per parameter directly — about 192, far beyond 20.

A Chinchilla analysis needs runs trained to completion at each data size, so its cost grows from n to n². Warmup-stable-decay holds the learning rate flat and decays only at the end (about 10%), so any stable-phase checkpoint can be decayed into a finished run. It matches cosine in final quality.

DeepSeek (7B and 67B) assumes most hyperparameters are scale-invariant, fits how optimal batch size and learning rate scale from near-optimal small runs, uses a WSD-style schedule with two 10% decay steps, and sizes the model with an IsoFLOP analysis — whose fits predict final losses well.

Llama 3 used IsoFLOPs (a 39:1 ratio) and scaled compute to downstream performance; Hunyuan-1 did IsoFLOPs for MoE (96 tokens per active parameter); MiniMax-01 used architecture scaling laws and Chinchilla method 1.

Two conditions as width grows: activations stay order 1 at initialisation, and change by order 1 after a gradient step. Working through a deep linear network gives width-dependent initialisation and per-layer learning rates — for Adam, scaled as 1/fan-in — where standard parametrisation keeps the rate fixed.

In a width-scaling replication, the optimal learning rate held across SwiGLU and squared ReLU, batch sizes and new initialisations (zero queries). It broke with learnable RMSNorm gains, sign-based optimizers like Lion, and strong weight decay. Overall muP looks easier to tune than standard parametrisation.

ai310.0.10.worked: Fitting a data-model trade-off cheaply with WSD: warm up, then hold the learning rate constant. To evaluate a data size D, take the stable-phase checkpoint at D tokens and run a short decay (about 10% of the run) — a finished model at D for a fraction of a fresh run's cost. Repeat for several D and model sizes, then fit the lower envelope (method 1) or a joint law (method 3).
ai310.0.10.watch: Early-stopping one long cosine run and treating its intermediate losses as finished runs at smaller data sizes: they were never annealed, so the fit — and the predicted optimum — comes out wrong.

checks.q: Why do MiniCPM and DeepSeek use a warmup-stable-decay (WSD) learning-rate schedule for their Chinchilla-style analyses?
opts: Stable-phase checkpoints can be decayed, so no data size needs a fresh run
WSD reaches a lower final loss than cosine for every model size tried
It removes warmup, which is what made the Kaplan fits come out wrong
The rate stays constant throughout, so no scaling analysis is needed
checks.expl: Chinchilla showed a scaling law needs runs trained to completion at each data size — early-stopping a cosine run is not the same — so the cost grows from n to n². WSD holds the rate flat after warmup, so a stable-phase checkpoint can be decayed (about the last 10%) into a finished run at many data sizes for little extra compute.

checks.q: From what two conditions is muP derived, as width grows?
opts: The loss stays Θ(1), and the learning rate is fixed at its small-model value
Activations stay Θ(1) at initialisation and change by Θ(1) after one step
Every weight stays Θ(1), and gradients shrink as one over the width
Each layer's parameter count stays Θ(1), whatever the width is
checks.expl: A1: activations at initialisation stay order 1 per coordinate; A2: after one gradient step their change is also order 1. Working these through a deep linear network gives width-dependent initialisation scales and per-layer learning rates — for Adam, scaling as 1/fan-in — so the best rate found on a narrow model transfers to a wide one.

checks.q: How does the DeepSeek recipe differ from Cerebras-GPT's and MiniCPM's?
opts: It skips muP and fits the optimal batch size and LR directly
It uses muP but trains one model size, extrapolating by hand
It skips scaling laws and copies Chinchilla's 20 per parameter
It tunes each hyperparameter on the full-size final model
checks.expl: Cerebras-GPT and MiniCPM use muP to make hyperparameters scale-invariant. DeepSeek assumes most Transformer hyperparameters already are, collects near-optimal small runs (within 0.25% of the best loss) to fit how batch size and learning rate should scale, sizes the model by IsoFLOP analysis, and uses a WSD-style schedule to keep that cheap.

checks.q: Which deviation from its assumptions does the lecture find breaks muP's learning-rate transfer?
opts: SwiGLU or squared-ReLU activations in place of plain ReLU
Learnable RMSNorm gains (and, notably, strong weight decay)
Training with larger or smaller batch sizes than it derives
Initialising the query matrix at zero, for uniform attention
checks.expl: In the replication muP held across SwiGLU and squared ReLU, different batch sizes, and new initialisations such as zero queries. It broke with learnable RMSNorm gains (removable at little cost), with sign-based optimizers like Lion, and with strong (0.1) weight decay — perhaps the only significant failure. Still, muP looks easier to tune than standard parametrisation.

checks.q: Under muP with Adam, a hidden layer's learning rate scales as 1/fan-in. A rate of 0.01 is tuned at fan-in 1024. What rate does that give at fan-in 4096?
checks.expl: 0.01 × 1024 / 4096 = 0.0025. Standard parametrisation would keep 0.01 and drift away from the optimum as width grows; muP's rescaling is what lets the optimum found on a narrow proxy carry over.

checks.q: To find a model's best data size you train it on 1, 2, …, 8 billion tokens. With a cosine schedule each size is a separate run from scratch, 36B tokens in all. With WSD you keep one stable-learning-rate run and branch a decay for each size, the decay being the last 10% of that size's tokens. How many billion tokens of training does WSD need in total? One decimal.
checks.expl: The stable run only has to reach 90% of the largest size, 7.2B tokens, passing the branch points 0.9, 1.8, …, 7.2B on the way. The decays add 10% of each size: 0.1 × (1 + 2 + … + 8) = 3.6B. That is 10.8B against 36B — the lecture's point that retraining from scratch for every data size turns the cost of a scaling-law fit from n to n², and that restarting from the end of the stable phase avoids it.

ai310.0.11.takeaway: There is no one true evaluation: what you measure depends on the question — a purchase decision, raw capability, harms, or feedback for developers. Every benchmark answers four questions (inputs, how the model is called, how outputs are scored, how results are read), and each answer can quietly change what a number means.

beats.t: What you see, and what it means
beats.d: Model releases quote similar but not identical benchmarks; leaderboards add cost, usage (OpenRouter) and human preference (Chatbot Arena); and there are vibes. Evaluation looks mechanical — prompts in, average out — but it decides where language models go next.

Inputs: which use cases, how many hard tail cases, adapted to the model? Calling: which prompt, chain-of-thought, tools or RAG, model or whole agent? Outputs: are references error-free, which metric (pass@k), what cost, which errors are worse? Interpretation: is 91% deployable, was the test seen in training, are we judging a model or a method?

(1/p(D))^(1/|D|) measures how much probability a model gives a dataset. Since GPT-2 and GPT-3 the field moved to downstream accuracy, but perplexity is smoother for scaling laws and universal. A leaderboard must trust a model's probabilities to sum to one. The maximalist view: drive perplexity to the true entropy and every task is solved — perhaps inefficiently.

MMLU: 57 subjects, multiple choice, really testing knowledge. MMLU-Pro: cleaned, 10 choices, chain of thought, 16-33% lower scores. GPQA: PhD experts 65%, Googling non-experts 34%. Humanity's Last Exam: 2,500 filtered questions. For open-ended answers: Chatbot Arena's pairwise human votes, IFEval's checkable constraints, AlpacaEval and WildBench with model judges.

SWE-Bench (2,294 GitHub issues judged by unit tests), CyBench (40 capture-the-flag tasks), MLE-Bench (75 Kaggle competitions); ARC-AGI to isolate reasoning from knowledge. Safety: HarmBench, AIR-Bench's 314 risk categories, jailbreaks such as GCG that transfer to closed models, and pre-deployment testing by safety institutes.

Most benchmarks are quizzing — the asker knows the answer — while real use is asking. Clio analyses real usage; MedHELM uses clinicians' tasks. Validity needs train-test overlap checked (by exchangeability tests, or by reporting norms) and benchmarks fixed (SWE-Bench Verified, Platinum versions).

Before foundation models we evaluated methods on fixed splits; today we evaluate whole models and systems where anything goes. Exceptions such as the nanoGPT speedrun and DataComp-LM fix the rules to reward algorithmic innovation. Either way, state the rules of the game; HELM's leaderboards let you inspect the individual predictions behind each score.

ai310.0.11.worked: Perplexity by hand: a model gives three held-out tokens probabilities 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125. p(D) = 1/64, |D| = 3, so perplexity = 64^(1/3) = 4 — as uncertain as a uniform choice among 4 tokens. In bits, the average loss is (1 + 2 + 3)/3 = 2 bits per token, and 2² = 4.
ai310.0.11.watch: Comparing two models' scores on 'the same' benchmark when the prompts, shots, chain-of-thought or scoring differ — and treating a score as evidence of capability without checking whether the test set was in the training data.

checks.q: Why does the lecture warn leaderboard runners about evaluating with perplexity?
opts: Perplexity can't be computed for any model whose vocabulary passes 50K
Perplexity rewards long answers, so verbose models end up ranked too high
The evaluator has to trust the model's own probabilities to sum to one
Perplexity needs human raters, which makes it slow and very expensive
checks.expl: Task accuracy can be computed from a black-box model's outputs alone. Perplexity needs the model to report probabilities, and the evaluator must trust that they are honest and sum to 1 — worse in the days of UNK tokens. Perplexity stays useful: smoother than task accuracy for fitting scaling laws, and universal.

checks.q: How does Chatbot Arena evaluate models?
opts: Experts grade every model's answers to one fixed set of 805 instructions
GPT-4 judges each response against a checklist written for its prompt
Unit tests check whether each model's patch resolves a GitHub issue
Users prompt two anonymous models, pick the better; Elo ranks them
checks.expl: A random person types a prompt, sees responses from two anonymised models and says which is better; Elo-style scores come from the pairwise comparisons. The inputs are live, not static, and new models can join. AlpacaEval (805 instructions, GPT-4 judge) and WildBench (checklists) automate this; WildBench correlates 0.95 with the Arena.

checks.q: Why does the lecture call 'asking' prompts more realistic than 'quizzing' prompts?
opts: Asking prompts are shorter, matching the length of real-world traffic
Quizzing prompts are always multiple choice, unlike what people type
When asking, the user doesn't know the answer and gets value from it
Asking prompts come from experts, so their reference answers are right
checks.expl: Quizzing is what standardised exams do: the user knows the answer and tests the system. Asking is how systems are actually used — the user doesn't know and wants the answer — so it produces value. Most benchmarks, MMLU included, are far from real use; Clio and MedHELM try to close the gap, though realism and privacy can conflict.

checks.q: For an open-weight model, which matters more for safety in the lecture's view, capability or propensity — and why?
opts: Propensity, since refusal training holds whatever users do afterwards
Neither, since safety benchmarks only ever measure refusal rates
Propensity, since anyone can read the weights and audit them freely
Capability, since anyone with the weights can fine-tune safety away
checks.expl: A system can be capable of something yet refuse to do it. For an API model that propensity is what counts; with open weights, refusals can be fine-tuned away, so what the model can do is what matters. Hence the dual-use question about evaluations like CyBench: safety, or capability?

checks.q: The lecture defines perplexity as (1/p(D))^(1/|D|). A model gives three test tokens probabilities 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125. What is its perplexity?
checks.expl: p(D) = 0.5 × 0.25 × 0.125 = 1/64, so the perplexity is 64^(1/3) = 4 — as uncertain as choosing uniformly among 4 tokens at each step. Equivalently the average loss is 2 bits per token, and 2² = 4.

checks.q: The lecture defines perplexity as (1/p(D))^(1/|D|), and pre-training minimises the average per-token cross-entropy. A model's average test loss is 2.0 nats per token. What is its perplexity? Two decimals.
checks.expl: (1/p(D))^(1/|D|) = exp(−(1/|D|) · ln p(D)) = exp(average loss) = e² ≈ 7.39 — as uncertain as choosing uniformly among about 7.4 tokens at each step. Minimising the training loss is minimising training perplexity, which is why the lecture says pre-training minimises perplexity on the training set.

ai310.0.12.takeaway: Data is arguably the most important thing to get right, and the part developers disclose least. Pretraining corpora are built, not found: crawl or collect, convert HTML to text, filter for language and quality (by rules or by classifiers), deduplicate — every step a heuristic with consequences — and all of it under copyright law, licences and terms of service.

beats.d: Open-weight releases such as Llama 3 describe architecture and training in detail but say almost nothing about data — for competitive reasons and because of copyright liability. Data work is a long tail that scales with human effort. Training moves from lots of lower-quality data (pretraining) to less, better data (mid-training, then post-training).

BERT: BooksCorpus (7K free self-published books, since taken down) and Wikipedia — documents, not sentences. GPT-2's WebText: 8M pages linked from Reddit posts with at least 3 karma, 40 GB; OpenWebText replicated it. Even Wikipedia can be poisoned with edits timed just before a dump.

A monthly crawl since 2008, as raw WARC or lossy WET text; how HTML becomes text measurably changes downstream accuracy. CCNet deduplicates, identifies language and keeps Wikipedia-like text by a 5-gram model. C4 applies manual rules — punctuation-ended lines of five-plus words, no bad words, no code braces — to reach 806 GB.

GPT-3 used a classifier to find WebText-, Wikipedia- and book-like Common Crawl pages, plus fuzzy deduplication. The Pile's volunteers curated 22 domains (825 GB): Pile-CC, PubMed Central, arXiv, Enron emails, Project Gutenberg, Books3 (from a shadow library, taken down), StackExchange and GitHub. The Stack later cloned 137M repositories for 3.1 TB of permissively licensed code.

Gopher's MassiveWeb used manual rules and SafeSearch; LLaMA mixed CCNet, C4, GitHub, Wikipedia, books, arXiv and StackExchange (1.2T tokens). RefinedWeb argued web data is all you need; FineWeb reached 15T tokens; Dolma 3T. DCLM trained a fastText quality classifier and beat other filters; Nemotron-CC argued such filters drop 90% of the data and added rephrasing and ensembles.

Copyright protects original expression fixed in any medium, needs no registration, and covers most of the internet. Using a work needs a licence ('a promise not to sue') or fair use, weighed on purpose, nature, amount and market effect. Training is arguably transformative, but copying is the first step, and models can still hurt creators' markets. Terms of service can add restrictions on top.

Long context is added late (LongLoRA took Llama 2 7B from 4K to 100K tokens on books and math). Task data turns existing NLP datasets into prompts (Super-Natural Instructions, Flan). Chat data is increasingly synthetic — Alpaca, Vicuna, Baize, WizardLM, OpenHermes — though Llama 2 found 27,540 vendor-annotated examples beat millions of open ones.

ai310.0.12.worked: Building a quality filter the DCLM way: collect positives that look like what you want the model to produce (instruction-style answers such as OpenHermes and ELI5) and negatives from ordinary web text (RefinedWeb), 200K each; train a fast linear classifier (fastText); score the whole pool and keep the top fraction. Then check what was thrown away — Nemotron-CC's critique is that such filters discard most of the data.
ai310.0.12.watch: Treating 'data quality' as an objective property. Every filter encodes a choice — Wikipedia-likeness, Reddit karma, a classifier's idea of good text — and each choice decides what the model will and won't learn.

checks.q: Why, according to the lecture, do open-weight model developers say so little about their training data?
opts: Competitive dynamics, and the risk of copyright liability
Data volumes are too large to describe in a technical report
Licences on their datasets forbid naming the sources used
The data is generated on the fly and never stored anywhere
checks.expl: Llama 3's report, for instance, is transparent about architecture and even training procedure but says almost nothing about data. The lecture's hot take is that data is the most important thing to get right — a long-tail problem that scales with human effort — which is exactly why it is guarded.

checks.q: Which of these is one of C4's manual filtering heuristics?
opts: Keep only the pages a Wikipedia-trained 5-gram model scores as fluent
Keep lines that end in punctuation and contain at least five words
Keep pages linked from Reddit posts with at least three karma
Keep documents a fastText classifier rates as educational
checks.expl: C4 started from one April 2019 Common Crawl snapshot (1.4T tokens) and kept lines ending in punctuation with at least 5 words, dropped pages with fewer than 3 sentences, any 'bad word', a '{', 'lorem ipsum' and so on, and kept English (langdetect at 0.99): 806 GB. The others are CCNet's filter, WebText's Reddit rule and classifier filtering.

checks.q: How did DataComp-LM build its quality classifier?
opts: fastText on 200K OpenHermes and ELI5 positives against 200K RefinedWeb
Human annotators rated a sample of Common Crawl pages from 1 to 5
GPT-4 labelled every document in the 240T-token pool as keep or drop
Pages linked from Wikipedia were positives and random pages negatives
checks.expl: Positives: mostly GPT-4-generated instruction data (OpenHermes-2.5) and r/explainlikeimfive answers; negatives: RefinedWeb. A fastText classifier trained on them was run over all of DCLM-pool to give DCLM-baseline (3.8T tokens), beating other filtering methods. Nemotron-CC later argued such filters remove too much — 90% of the data.

checks.q: Why can a model developer be barred from using a Creative Commons YouTube video, licence or not?
opts: Creative Commons licences never cover the training of models
Terms of service can add restrictions, such as no downloading
Videos are not 'fixed' works, so copyright does not apply
Fair use covers only text, so video needs explicit permission
checks.expl: Licences and fair use decide whether copying a copyrighted work is allowed; a platform's terms of service can still restrict how you obtain it — YouTube's prohibit downloading videos, even Creative Commons ones. Most of the internet is copyrighted, and the threshold for copyright is extremely low.

checks.q: C4 came to 806 GB of text and 156 billion tokens. About how many bytes of text per token is that?
checks.expl: 806e9 / 156e9 ≈ 5.17 bytes per token — roughly a short English word with its leading space. It is a useful ratio for converting between the gigabytes datasets are reported in and the tokens models are trained on.

checks.q: C4 filters a page line by line. Of these five lines, how many survive its line rule? 'Home | About | Contact' — 'Click here to subscribe.' — 'The river floods every spring after the snow melts.' — 'Rooms start at 80 euros per night!' — 'Read the full story'
checks.expl: C4 keeps lines that end in punctuation and have at least 5 words. The navigation bar and 'Read the full story' have no final punctuation; 'Click here to subscribe.' has only 4 words; the river sentence (9 words) and the room-price sentence (7 words, ending in '!') pass. A rule this blunt also drops legitimate short lines — every filter encodes a choice about what counts as text.

ai310.0.13.takeaway: Filtering and deduplication are the mechanics under every dataset from the last lecture. Filtering is one framework — given a little target data T and a lot of raw data R, score R and keep what resembles T — with three instantiations (n-gram model, classifier, importance resampling) used for language, quality and toxicity alike. Deduplication at scale is hashing: exact hashes, Bloom filters, and MinHash with locality-sensitive hashing for near duplicates.

beats.d: KenLM: a Kneser-Ney n-gram model, just counting and normalising; CCNet sorts paragraphs by perplexity and keeps the top third. fastText: a bag of word embeddings with H·(V + K) parameters instead of V·K, with the hashing trick for bigrams; for good-versus-bad it is just a linear classifier. DSIR: fit hashed n-gram models to target and raw data and resample by their ratio.

Estimate a model from R and T, derive a score, keep examples by it. KenLM scores p_T(x), fastText p(T | x) — both keep above a threshold, stochastically — and DSIR scores p_T(x) / p_R(x) and resamples in proportion. Importance resampling is the principled version: sample from q, weight each sample by p/q, resample to get draws from p.

fastText's off-the-shelf identifier covers 176 languages; Dolma keeps pages with p(English) ≥ 0.5. It struggles with short text, low-resource languages, dialects, close pairs such as Malay and Indonesian, and code-switching. OpenMathText combined rules, a KenLM perplexity cut and a fastText classifier to curate 14.7B tokens of mathematical text.

GPT-3 trained a linear classifier with Wikipedia, WebText2 and books as positives and Common Crawl as negatives, and kept pages stochastically by score; LLaMA used pages referenced by Wikipedia. phi-1 had GPT-4 label 100K Python files for educational value and trained a random forest on them. Dolma trained fastText toxicity classifiers on the Jigsaw comments.

Duplicates are exact (mirrors, forks) or near (licences, templates, formatting); removing them trains faster and memorises less. Exact dedup hashes each item and keeps one per hash — C4 does it on 3-sentence spans. A Bloom filter tests membership in little memory: a 'no' is certain, a 'yes' is probably right, and more hash functions drive false positives down exponentially.

Near duplicates are pairs with Jaccard similarity above a threshold. MinHash is a hash whose collision probability equals the Jaccard similarity. LSH sharpens that into a threshold: split n = b·r hash functions into b bands of r, and call A and B a match if every hash in some band agrees, giving 1 − (1 − s^r)^b. More rows move the threshold up; more bands move it down.

ai310.0.13.worked: LSH at s = 0.8 with b = 5 bands of r = 10. One band matches only if all ten MinHashes agree: 0.8^10 ≈ 0.107. A band fails with probability 0.893, and all five fail with probability 0.893^5 ≈ 0.567, so the pair is flagged with probability ≈ 0.433. With the paper's setting n = 9000, b = 20, r = 450 the phase transition sits at (1/20)^(1/450) ≈ 0.993.
ai310.0.13.watch: Reading a Bloom filter's 'yes' as proof. It can be wrong — only a 'no' is certain — so a deduplication pass built on one will occasionally drop an item that was never seen before, at a rate fixed by the memory and the number of hash functions.

checks.q: In the lecture's general filtering framework, how does importance resampling (DSIR) use its score?
opts: It keeps x when p_T(x) clears a threshold, stochastically
It keeps x when a classifier's p(T | x) clears a threshold
It resamples x in proportion to the ratio p_T(x) / p_R(x)
It keeps x when its Jaccard similarity to T clears a cut
checks.expl: The three instantiations differ in the score: a generative model of T (KenLM) uses p_T(x), a discriminative classifier (fastText) uses p(T | x), and DSIR uses the importance weight p_T(x) / p_R(x), resampling rather than thresholding. Jaccard similarity belongs to deduplication, not filtering.

checks.q: phi-1 trained a 1.3B model on a classifier-filtered subset of The Stack's Python. How did it compare with training on the unfiltered Python subset?
opts: Lower HumanEval, though it trained in a third of the steps
Equal HumanEval, from a model a tenth the size
Equal HumanEval, with far less memorised code
Higher HumanEval, and after fewer training steps
checks.expl: 12.19% on HumanEval after 96K steps on the raw Python subset, against 17.68% after 36K steps on the filtered one. The positives came from GPT-4 judging 100K files for 'educational value'; a random forest on codegen embeddings then selected the rest.

checks.q: A Bloom filter answers 'no' when asked whether an item is in the set. What does that tell you?
opts: The item is probably absent, with a small false-negative rate
The item was inserted but has since been deleted from the set
The item is definitely not in the set
Nothing until the remaining hash functions have been checked
checks.expl: Every inserted item sets all of its k bits, so an item that was inserted can never find one of its bits empty: 'no' is certain. 'Yes' can be a false positive when other items happened to set all k bits. Bloom filters also cannot delete — clearing a bit could erase other items.

checks.q: C4 deduplicates by exact match on 3-sentence spans, keeping one copy of each. What drawback does the lecture warn about?
opts: Hashing every span needs memory quadratic in the size of the corpus
Exact span matching cannot catch any duplicated whole documents
Documents shorter than three sentences are all silently discarded
Cutting a span from mid-document can leave the remainder incoherent
checks.expl: Removing all but one copy of a repeated span deletes it from the middle of other documents, which may then not read coherently. Exact matching is simple, precise and parallelises as MapReduce, but it misses near duplicates — the job of MinHash and LSH.
