checks.q: With LSH, two documents with Jaccard similarity 0.8 are hashed with b = 5 bands of r = 10 MinHash functions each. What is the probability that they collide? Three decimals.
checks.expl: A band matches only if all r hashes agree: 0.8^10 ≈ 0.1074. They collide if some band matches: 1 − (1 − 0.1074)^5 ≈ 1 − 0.5667 = 0.433. Raising r makes matching harder; raising b makes it easier.

checks.q: fastText's bag of word embeddings uses vocabulary V = 8192, hidden size H = 16 and K = 64 classes. Counting the embedding and the output head weights (no biases), how many parameters is that? (digits only, no commas)
checks.expl: An 8192 × 16 embedding (131,072) plus a 16 × 64 head (1,024) is H·(V + K) = 132,096 — a quarter of the 8192 × 64 = 524,288 that a direct bag-of-words classifier would need.

ai310.0.14.takeaway: Pretraining gets you GPT-3; post-training gets you InstructGPT. The standard recipe is imitation, then optimisation: supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations extracts behaviours the base model already has, and RLHF then maximises a reward learned from pairwise preferences — first with PPO, now mostly with DPO. Both stages are only as good as their data, and both have side effects worth watching.

beats.d: FLAN recasts existing NLP tasks as prompts (subject lines, topic labels, highlights); Alpaca is short model-written answers; OpenAssistant is long human-written answers, some with references. They differ in length, bullet points and knowledge — and length and style strongly sway preference evaluations, human and GPT-based alike, while mattering little on other benchmarks.

beats.t: What SFT can and cannot teach
beats.d: Folklore, backed by Schulman and Gekhman: fine-tuning on facts the model does not know teaches it to hallucinate. A citation in a demonstration may teach the habit of citing more than the source. SFT works best when it extracts pretraining behaviours rather than adding new ones; even factually correct data can hurt.

A little instruction tuning changes safety a lot: about 500 safety examples mixed into Alpaca-style data make models follow safety guidelines. The hard part is balancing that against over-refusal. To scale instruction tuning, 'midtraining' mixes instruction data into the end of pretraining, then runs a short tuning round — without catastrophic forgetting.

Imitation fits p̂(y | x) to a reference distribution and needs samples from it; optimisation finds the policy that maximises a reward we can measure — the LM is a policy, not a model of a distribution. Scalar or pairwise feedback is far cheaper than demonstrations, and people do not always write the output they would prefer (the generator–validator gap).

Pairwise comparisons from crowdworkers (InstructGPT used about 40, via Scale and Upwork) are hard to make high-quality and verified; annotators may lean on GPT-4; their demographics and style preferences shift the result. GPT-4 judgments agree with humans about as well as humans agree with each other, so AI feedback (UltraFeedback, Constitutional AI) is common.

PPO: policy gradients with variance controls — linearise (TRPO), then clip the ratio — and finicky in practice. DPO assumes a nonparametric policy, solves for the implied reward, and fits it with the pairwise loss: a positive gradient on the chosen answer, a negative one on the rejected, weighted by the implied reward's error. Watch for longer outputs, reward overoptimisation and lost calibration.

ai310.0.14.worked: Checking one SFT example by hand. An Alpaca response defines avg_list(nums) — sum the list, divide by its length — and claims print(avg_list([4, 3, 6, 10, 8])) outputs 6.4. The sum is 31, the length 5, so the function returns 6.2. Fine-tuning on that pair teaches the model to state a wrong result with confidence; this is why crowdsourced and generated data need someone to check correctness.
ai310.0.14.watch: Reading a rising reward as rising quality. Past a point, optimising a learned reward overfits it — the lecture's curves show it for human and noisy-LM preferences — and the gains can be length and style rather than substance.

checks.q: How does the optimisation view of post-training (RLHF) differ from imitation (SFT), as the lecture frames it?
opts: It fits the model's p(y | x) to a reference distribution using expert samples
It maximises a reward that it can measure, and treats the LM as a policy
It trains on far more data, scraped from the web rather than written
It updates only the final layers, while SFT updates every parameter
checks.expl: Imitation is pure generative modelling: fit p̂(y | x) ≈ p*(y | x) from samples of a reference policy. Optimisation finds p̂ maximising E[R(y, x)] for a measurable reward — so the LM is a policy, not a model of some distribution. The first option describes SFT.

checks.q: What does the folklore the lecture cites say happens when you fine-tune a model on facts it does not already know?
opts: It learns to hallucinate, answering without basis
It memorises the facts but cannot use them elsewhere
It forgets as many facts from pretraining
It learns them reliably if each appears once
checks.expl: Schulman (2023) and Gekhman et al. (2023): training on unknown facts teaches the model to produce confident answers it has no basis for. Hence the takeaways — you may not want to fine-tune on tail knowledge even when that is the use case, and correctness feedback from RL could help.

checks.q: Safety-tuning with even a little data changes a model's safety profile a lot. What does the lecture call the real challenge?
opts: Collecting enough harmful prompts to cover every category
Balancing safety against over-refusals of benign requests
Keeping the safety data out of the pretraining corpus
Stopping safety gains from vanishing after a few epochs
checks.expl: About 500 safety examples added to Alpaca-style data significantly improve safety. The hard part is that the same tuning makes models refuse things they should answer, so the two have to be balanced.

checks.q: Which describes DPO's update, as the lecture summarises it?
opts: Up-weight the chosen answer, down-weight the rejected, scaled by error
Fresh on-policy rollouts scored by a separately trained reward model
Supervised training on the chosen answers only, discarding the rejected
Sampling 1024 outputs per prompt and fine-tuning on the best of them
checks.expl: DPO drops the reward model and the on-policy machinery. It solves the KL-regularised RLHF objective for the 'implied reward' under a nonparametric assumption, then fits that reward with the pairwise loss — 'pos gradient on good, neg gradient on bad', scaled by the implied reward model's prediction error. The other options are the PPO setup and the simpler alternatives people tried first.

checks.q: The overoptimisation results compare RLHF on human, noisy-LM and noiseless-LM preferences. Where did optimising the reward NOT overfit past a point?
opts: Human preferences
Noisy LM preferences
Noiseless LM preferences
None — every setting overfit
checks.expl: Across many RLHF-style optimisers, true quality first rises and then falls as the learned reward keeps climbing — for human and noisy simulated preferences. With noiseless LM preferences there is nothing for the policy to exploit, which points at label noise as the driver.

checks.q: One Alpaca example on the slides defines avg_list(nums), which sums a list and divides by its length, and claims print(avg_list([4, 3, 6, 10, 8])) outputs 6.4. What does it actually print?
checks.expl: 4 + 3 + 6 + 10 + 8 = 31 and 31 / 5 = 6.2. The example's stated output is wrong — a reminder of the lecture's point that getting annotators (or models) to really check correctness is hard, and that SFT on a wrong answer teaches it.

ai310.0.15.takeaway: RLHF cannot be scaled cleanly because a learned reward gets overoptimised. Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards sidesteps that by working where the reward is exactly what we want — is the maths answer right, do the tests pass. GRPO made it simple: PPO without the value model, with the advantage taken as a z-score within a group of rollouts. DeepSeek R1, Kimi K1.5 and Qwen 3 show the recipes, and their flaws.

beats.d: Policy gradients have too much variance; TRPO linearises around the current policy; PPO clips the probability ratio (AlpacaFarm uses a clip range of 0.2). For language models the reward is shaped: a per-token KL penalty against the reference model plus the full reward on the last token, with advantages from generalised advantage estimation. It works, but it is complicated and the value model is memory-hungry.

beats.t: Why not PPO, why not DPO
beats.d: PPO needs a value model and a complicated implementation. DPO needs pairwise, Bradley-Terry-style data, and it is offline — while a verifier gives each rollout its own score. GRPO starts from PPO, removes the value function, and sets each rollout's advantage to its reward's z-score within the group sampled for the same prompt.

Subtracting any state-dependent baseline keeps the policy gradient unbiased; dividing by the group's standard deviation does not, and it upweights questions that are too easy or too hard. Normalising by response length biases it further. Dr. GRPO (Liu et al. 2025) removes both, which brings it close to REINFORCE with a leave-one-out baseline.

R1-Zero: GRPO on DeepSeek-V3 with only accuracy and format rewards — no process reward models, no MCTS, both listed among the unsuccessful attempts. Its chains of thought grew and an 'aha' moment appeared, though follow-ups argue the length comes from the biased objective and the base model already says 'aha'. R1 adds a long-CoT SFT start, a language-consistency reward and a final SFT/RLHF stage, then distils 800K traces into Qwen 2.5.

Data curation drops multiple-choice and true/false questions (guesses earn false positives) and keeps only problems the model fails at best-of-8. Its RL loss comes from a DPO-style derivation with a squared-loss surrogate. A length reward pushes correct answers to be short; a curriculum samples problems in proportion to 1 − success rate. RL infrastructure matters: rollouts are slow inference, often in another framework, with uneven batch lengths.

The same playbook — filter by best-of-n difficulty, drop what the model gets right without a chain of thought, drop near-duplicates of validation data, check CoT quality by hand — then GRPO on only 3,995 examples. Thinking-mode fusion mixes thinking and non-thinking data under tags. General-purpose RLHF afterwards costs a little maths and STEM ability.

ai310.0.15.worked: GRPO's advantage for one prompt. Sample four rollouts; the verifier scores them 1, 0, 0, 0. The group mean is 0.25 and the standard deviation (dividing by n) is √(0.25 × 0.75) ≈ 0.433. The correct rollout's advantage is (1 − 0.25) / 0.433 ≈ 1.73; each wrong one gets (0 − 0.25) / 0.433 ≈ −0.58. Had all four been right, every advantage would be 0 — and the division by a near-zero standard deviation is why a small stability term (1e-4) is added.
ai310.0.15.watch: Treating GRPO's standard-deviation division as harmless normalisation. It is not a valid baseline: it biases the gradient and re-weights questions by how easy or hard they are, and length normalisation adds its own bias — part of why R1-Zero's responses grew.

checks.q: Why does the lecture say DPO is a poor fit for RL with verifiable rewards?
opts: It needs a separate value model, which is memory-hungry to train
It cannot use a KL penalty against a reference model at all
It only works for models smaller than about seven billion parameters
The data is not inherently pairwise, and DPO itself is offline
checks.expl: A verifier scores each rollout on its own, not as a Bradley-Terry comparison between two, and DPO trains on a fixed dataset rather than the policy's own samples (it can be made online only by iterating). The value model is the objection to PPO, not DPO.

checks.q: What is the problem with GRPO dividing each group's rewards by their standard deviation?
opts: It makes the advantage depend on response length, so longer answers win
It is not a valid baseline, so the policy gradient is biased
It requires a learned value model to estimate the deviation
It discards every rollout whose reward equals the group mean
checks.expl: Any state-dependent term can be subtracted from the reward without biasing the policy gradient; a division cannot. The standard-deviation term upweights questions that are too easy or too hard. The length bias is a separate term — the normaliser — which Dr. GRPO also removes.

checks.q: Which rewards did DeepSeek R1-Zero's reinforcement learning use?
opts: Step-by-step scores from a learned process reward model
Human pairwise preferences between complete responses
Answer accuracy, plus a format reward for thinking tags
Value estimates from Monte Carlo tree search over steps
checks.expl: R1-Zero applied GRPO to DeepSeek-V3 with accuracy rewards (is it correct?) and format rewards (use thinking tags). It did not use process supervision; PRMs and MCTS appear in the paper's unsuccessful-attempts section, which ended speculation that they were necessary.

checks.q: Why did Kimi K1.5 exclude multiple-choice and true/false questions from its RL data?
opts: A lucky guess can be scored as correct, giving a false positive
Their answers are much too short to train long chains of thought
Their verifiers could not parse letter-coded answers reliably
The base model had already memorised most of those benchmarks
checks.expl: With a verifiable reward, a lucky guess on a 4-way or 2-way question earns full reward, reinforcing reasoning that did not produce it. Kimi also kept only problems the model fails at best-of-8, so the RL signal comes from questions it cannot already solve.

checks.q: A GRPO group of four rollouts scores 1, 0, 0, 0. Taking the advantage as the z-score within the group (standard deviation dividing by n, ignoring the small stability term), what is the correct rollout's advantage? Three decimals.
checks.expl: Mean 0.25; variance 0.25 × 0.75 = 0.1875, so σ ≈ 0.433. Advantage (1 − 0.25) / 0.433 = √3 ≈ 1.732. (With the n − 1 standard deviation it would be 1.5 — the convention matters, which is one reason implementations differ.)

checks.q: Kimi K1.5's curriculum samples problems in proportion to (1 − success rate). How many times as often is a problem the model solves 40% of the time sampled as one it solves 90% of the time?
checks.expl: (1 − 0.4) / (1 − 0.9) = 0.6 / 0.1 = 6. The aim is to stop spending rollouts on problems that are already solved; together with easy-to-hard difficulty labels it forms the curriculum.

ai310.0.16.takeaway: Policy gradient, worked through in code. For a language model the state is the prompt plus the response so far, the action is the next token, and the reward comes once at the end. The gradient of expected reward is just SFT weighted by reward — unbiased but noisy — and a baseline cuts the noise without changing the answer. GRPO takes its baseline from the group of responses to the same prompt; a toy sorting task shows how much each choice matters.

beats.d: State s: prompt plus response so far; action: the next token; transitions are deterministic (s' = s + a), so planning and test-time compute are possible. Rewards are outcome rewards on the whole response, and verifiable — computed deterministically — so discounting and bootstrapping matter less. The policy is just the (fine-tuned) language model; the objective is expected reward.

∇E[R] = E[∇ log π(a | s) R(s, a)]: sample a response, then update as in SFT but weighted by its reward. With rewards in {0, 1} it updates only on correct responses — SFT on a dataset that changes as the policy does. Sparse rewards make it very noisy; RLHF's learned reward models are more continuous.

Maximise E[R − b(s)] instead: it differs from E[R] by a constant that does not depend on the policy, so the gradient stays unbiased while its variance can fall. The optimal b(s) is hard to compute; the usual heuristic is the mean reward E[R | s] = V(s), which makes R − b(s) the advantage A(s, a) = Q(s, a) − V(s).

Generate several responses per prompt, score them, and turn rewards into deltas: raw, centred on the group mean, normalised by the group standard deviation, or max-only. The loss is −log-prob × delta (naive), or a probability ratio against the old policy, optionally clipped (ε = 0.01 here). p_old must be frozen; an optional KL penalty uses the estimator E_p[q/p − log(q/p) − 1].

On sorting three numbers, raw rewards learn little. Centring helps — below-average responses get pushed down, and a prompt whose responses all score the same gives no update — but training still sticks in local optima. Normalising by the standard deviation adds little here, and Dr. GRPO drops it to avoid length bias. RL systems are harder than pretraining: inference workloads and several models to manage.

ai310.0.16.worked: The two-state baseline example. In s1 the actions earn 11 and 9; in s2 they earn 0 and 2. Raw, the update would favour s1's worse action (9) over s2's better one (2). Subtract b(s1) = 10 and b(s2) = 1 and the rewards become +1, −1, −1, +1: each state's better action is pushed up and its worse one down, and the sample standard deviation of the update weights falls from about 5.32 to about 1.15.
ai310.0.16.watch: Forgetting to freeze p_old. If the old policy's probability is computed with gradients on, the ratio p / p_old is identically 1 and its gradient is exactly zero — the code runs, the loss is finite, and nothing learns. Compute p_old under no_grad and treat it as a constant.

checks.q: Unlike RL for robotics, transitions for a language model are deterministic: the next state is the old state plus the generated token. What does the lecture say that makes possible?
opts: Dropping the reward and training on the transitions alone
Discounting future rewards using a separately learned value function
Treating the problem as supervised learning from the start
Planning and test-time compute over possible continuations
checks.expl: T(s' | s, a) is deterministic, s' = s + a, so you can plan and spend test-time compute in a way you cannot with a physical robot; the states are also 'made up', which gives a lot of flexibility. Discounting and bootstrapping are less applicable here, because rewards are outcome rewards on the whole response.

checks.q: With rewards in {0, 1} (correct or not), what does the naive policy gradient update amount to?
opts: SFT on correct responses, on data that shifts with the policy
SFT on every response, with incorrect ones weighted negatively
A pairwise loss pushing correct responses above incorrect ones
A value-function regression on each prompt's success rate
checks.expl: The update is ∇ log π(a | s) R(s, a): with R = 0 the term vanishes, so only correct responses are reinforced — like SFT, but on the policy's own samples, which change as it learns. Pushing incorrect responses down needs a baseline (centred rewards).

checks.q: In the sorting experiments, what does centring each prompt's rewards on the group mean change, compared with raw rewards?
opts: Every response gets a positive update, scaled by its own reward
Below-average ones go down; an all-equal group gives no update
The update becomes independent of how long each response is
Training reaches the global optimum on all three prompts
checks.expl: Subtracting the mean makes deltas negative for responses below the group average, and zero for all of them when every response scored the same. It helps, but the lecture notes training still gets stuck in local optima — RL is not trivial.

checks.q: Why must p_old be frozen (computed without gradients) in the GRPO ratio p(a | s) / p_old(a | s)?
opts: Otherwise the clipping range collapses to zero width and nothing is clipped
Otherwise the KL penalty becomes negative and diverges
Otherwise both models share an optimiser state and drift
Otherwise the ratio is identically 1 and its gradient is zero
checks.expl: If p_old is the same function of the same weights with gradients on, p / p_old is the constant 1 and the gradient is 0 — the trace shows grad = 0.0. Under torch.no_grad() p_old is a constant and the gradient of sigmoid(w) / sigmoid(2) at w = 2 is 1 − sigmoid(2) ≈ 0.119.

checks.q: Two states: in s1 the actions earn 11 and 9, in s2 they earn 0 and 2. With baselines b(s1) = 10 and b(s2) = 1, what is the sample standard deviation (dividing by n − 1) of the four baselined rewards? Three decimals.
checks.expl: The baselined rewards are +1, −1, −1, +1: mean 0, sum of squares 4, so √(4/3) ≈ 1.155. The raw rewards 11, 9, 0, 2 have standard deviation √(85/3) ≈ 5.323 — the baseline cuts the spread by more than four times without changing which action is better in each state.

checks.q: The lecture's partial-credit reward gives one point for each prompt number that appears in the response and one for each adjacent pair in the response that is in order (x ≤ y). What does it give the response [0, 3, 1, 2] to the prompt [3, 1, 0, 2]?
checks.expl: All four prompt numbers appear (4 points); of the adjacent pairs (0, 3), (3, 1) and (1, 2), two are in order (2 points): 6. The exact-position reward gives the same response only 1 (just the leading 0 is in place) — the partial-credit reward is the denser signal.

ai310.1.0.takeaway: One call to pipeline() hides three steps — preprocess, run the model, post-process — and choosing a model is mostly choosing which half of the Transformer the task needs: an encoder to understand the whole input, a decoder to generate, or both to turn one sequence into another.

beats.t: NLP is the field, LLMs are the current tool
beats.d: NLP covers classifying sentences, labelling each word, extracting answers and generating text. LLMs are a subset defined by scale, by doing many tasks without task-specific training, and by learning from examples in the prompt. Their limits come with them: hallucination, bias, finite context windows and heavy compute.

beats.t: pipeline() is three steps in one call
beats.d: The text is preprocessed into something the model can read, the model runs, and its raw predictions are post-processed into a label and a score. The default model for a task is downloaded once and cached; running it again reuses the cached weights, not a cached answer.

beats.t: The task decides what the output can be
beats.d: Zero-shot classification takes the candidate labels at call time, so no fine-tuning on your labels is needed. Question answering EXTRACTS a span from the context you pass; it does not generate an answer. Named-entity recognition regroups sub-word pieces such as S, ##yl, ##va, ##in back into one entity.

Language models are pretrained self-supervised — the objective is computed from the text itself, causal (next word) or masked (fill the blank). Fine-tuning then trains on labelled data for one task, needing far less data, time and money than training from scratch, which is why sharing weights matters.

beats.t: Encoder, decoder, and the mask that keeps training honest
beats.d: The encoder's attention sees the whole sentence; the decoder generates and may only attend to words already produced. In training the decoder is fed the whole target, so an attention mask hides positions at and after the word being predicted. Architecture is the skeleton; a checkpoint is the weights loaded into it.

beats.t: Every task is a body plus a head
beats.d: BERT for classification adds a linear head on the final [CLS] state; for token classification, a head per token; for question answering, start and end logits for a span. GPT-2 predicts the next token with labels shifted by one. ViT cuts an image into 16x16 patches and treats them as tokens, with a [CLS] token just like BERT.

beats.t: Pick the architecture by asking three questions
beats.d: Bidirectional or one-way understanding? Generating new text or analysing existing text? Transforming one sequence into another? Classification, NER and extractive QA point to an encoder; open generation and chat to a decoder; translation and summarisation to an encoder-decoder. Full attention is quadratic in length, which is what Longformer's local windows and Reformer's LSH attention work around.

beats.t: Inference has two phases with different costs
beats.d: Prefill tokenizes and processes the whole prompt at once, which is computationally intensive; it sets the time to first token. Decode then produces one token at a time, each step attending to everything before it, which is memory-intensive. Temperature, top-k, top-p, repetition penalties and stop sequences shape what decode picks; the KV cache trades memory for not recomputing the past.

bert-base-uncased, trained on Wikipedia and BookCorpus rather than the open web, still fills 'This woman works as a [MASK]' with gendered jobs. Fine-tuning on your own data does not remove what pretraining put there.

ai310.1.0.worked: Before reaching for a model, name the task's output. A label for the whole text is a classification head on an encoder; a label per token is token classification; a span copied out of a document is extractive QA; new text is a decoder, or an encoder-decoder when the new text is a transformation of an input. Then find a checkpoint already fine-tuned for that task on the Hub and run it through pipeline() before writing any training code.
ai310.1.0.watch: Treating the question-answering pipeline as if it could answer from knowledge. It extracts a span from the context it is given, so a context that does not contain the answer still yields a confident-looking span — just a wrong one.

checks.q: You call a sentiment-analysis pipeline on a raw sentence and get back a label and a score. What happened in between?
opts: The text was preprocessed into model inputs, the model ran, and its predictions were post-processed into a label and score
The model read the raw string directly; pipeline() only chose which pretrained checkpoint to download for the task
A pretrained model was briefly fine-tuned on your sentence, and the fine-tuned copy produced the label and score
The sentence was looked up in a cache of earlier answers, and a stored prediction was returned when one matched
checks.src: 1.3 Transformers, what can they do? — Working with pipelines
checks.expl: pipeline() connects a model with its preprocessing and postprocessing. The model never sees a raw string, and nothing is trained at call time. What gets cached is the downloaded model, so a second run skips the download — not the computation.

checks.q: The question-answering pipeline is given a question and a context paragraph. What can its answer be?
opts: Any sentence the model composes from its training data, guided by the context
A summary of the context rewritten so that it addresses the question
Only a span copied out of the context, located by start and end positions
A yes or no, with the context used only to compute the confidence score
checks.expl: The pipeline extracts information from the provided context; it does not generate. Under the hood a span-classification head predicts start and end logits over the context's tokens, so the answer is always a piece of the text you passed in.

checks.q: During training a translation decoder is fed the entire target sentence at once. Why can it not simply copy the word it is asked to predict?
opts: Because the target sentence is shuffled before it reaches the decoder
Because an attention mask hides that position and every later one
Because the decoder reads only the encoder's output, never the target
Because training uses a different language for the target each time
checks.expl: Feeding the whole target speeds training, so the decoder is masked: predicting the fourth word, its attention can use positions 1 to 3 only. The second attention layer still sees the encoder's output for the WHOLE source sentence, because word order differs between languages.

checks.q: ViT splits a 224 x 224 image into non-overlapping 16 x 16 patches. How many patch embeddings does the encoder receive, before the [CLS] token is added?
checks.expl: Each side holds 224 / 16 = 14 patches, so there are 14 x 14 = 196. Each patch becomes one embedding — the image is 'tokenized' into patches — and a learnable [CLS] embedding is prepended, so the sequence is 197 long.

checks.q: You need to tag every word of a sentence as person, organisation, location or none. Which architecture does the chapter point you to, and why?
opts: Decoder-only, because modern LLMs are decoders and handle every task best
Encoder-decoder, because the output is itself a sequence of labels to generate
Encoder-only, because each word's label depends on context on both sides of it
Decoder-only, because labelling one word at a time is a left-to-right process
checks.expl: Named-entity recognition is understanding, not generation: a word's label can depend on the words after it as well as before. Encoders attend in both directions, and a token-classification head on top gives one label per token.

checks.q: Users say the first word of a chatbot's reply takes a long time to appear, but the rest then streams quickly. Which phase is the bottleneck?
opts: Decode, because each new token must attend to all previous ones
Prefill, because the whole prompt is processed at once first
Sampling, because top-p must sort the vocabulary every step
Tokenization of the output, which runs after generation ends
checks.src: 1.8 The two-phase inference process; Key performance metrics
checks.expl: Time to first token is primarily set by prefill, which tokenizes and runs the entire input through the model before anything is generated. Decode then governs time per output token; it is the memory-intensive phase, and the KV cache is what speeds it up.

ai310.1.1.takeaway: Supervised fine-tuning is next-token cross-entropy on your own examples — so the decisions that matter are which tokens carry the loss, what format the data is in, and whether the end-of-sequence token matches the chat template.

beats.t: The whole method in one call
beats.d: SFTTrainer takes a model name and a training dataset and trains. Everything else on the page is a choice about the data, the loss mask or the cost of the run.

Language modelling (a text field) or prompt-completion, each either standard (plain strings) or conversational (role and content messages). A conversational dataset has the chat template applied automatically. Anything else is mapped into one of these first — the medical-reasoning example folds Question, chain of thought and Response into a prompt and a completion.

beats.t: The loss is the pretraining loss, on chosen tokens
beats.d: Token-level cross-entropy: minimise $-\sum_t \log p_\theta(y_t \mid y_{\lt t})$. Prompt and completion are concatenated and tokenized together; the labels are the inputs shifted by one; padding positions get the ignore index (-100) so they add nothing to the loss.

loss is averaged over NON-masked tokens; mean_token_accuracy is the share of non-masked tokens whose top-1 prediction is right; entropy is the spread of the predicted distribution; grad_norm is measured before clipping; num_tokens counts what has been processed.

With a prompt-completion dataset the loss covers the completion only, by default (completion_only_loss=False turns that off). With a conversational dataset, assistant_only_loss=True restricts it to the assistant's replies — which needs generation and endgeneration markers in the chat template; TRL patches them in for known families such as Qwen3.

packing=True fills each sequence with several examples. model_init_kwargs passes loading options such as bfloat16 through SFTConfig. A LoraConfig as peft_config trains adapters instead of the whole model, usually at a higher learning rate (about 1e-4) because only the new parameters are learned.

Needs a chat template — role markers, special tokens, turn boundaries — and a conversational dataset; chat_template_path can borrow one from another model. A base model that already ships a template still needs its EOS token aligned with it (eos_token in SFTConfig), or replies do not terminate correctly.

Tool-calling data carries tool calls, tool-role responses and a tools column of JSON schemas. Vision-language data adds image or images columns; set max_length=None there, because truncation can cut image tokens and break training.

ai310.1.1.worked: Before the first run, write down which tokens of one example should carry loss, then check the setting that does it: completion-only for prompt-completion data, assistant_only_loss for conversations, nothing extra for plain text. Then train for a few steps and read mean_token_accuracy and loss — both are over non-masked tokens, so they tell you whether the mask is what you meant.
ai310.1.1.watch: Fine-tuning a base model into a chat model and leaving the EOS token as it was. The model learns the template's turns but never the token that ends them, so it keeps generating past its answer; the fix is eos_token in SFTConfig, matched to the template.

checks.q: What does SFTTrainer minimise for each training example?
opts: A reward that a separate preference model assigns to the whole completion
The squared distance between output and reference embeddings
The number of positions where the output differs from the reference
The negative log-likelihood of each target token given those before it
checks.src: Looking deeper into the SFT method — Computing the loss
checks.expl: SFT is token-level cross-entropy, the same objective as pretraining: $-\sum_t \log p_\theta(y_t \mid y_{\lt t})$. The labels are the input shifted by one position, and masked positions (padding, or tokens excluded by the loss settings) contribute nothing. No reward model is involved; that is the next stage of alignment.

checks.q: You pass a prompt-completion dataset to SFTTrainer and change no settings. Which tokens does the loss see?
opts: Only the completion tokens; the prompt tokens are masked out
Every token, prompt and completion alike, just as in pretraining
Only the prompt tokens, so the model learns to read inputs
Only the last token of each completion, just before EOS
checks.expl: For prompt-completion data the trainer computes the loss on the completion only by default; completion_only_loss=False puts the prompt back in. The prompt is still in the input — the model conditions on it — it just is not something the model is graded on reproducing.

checks.q: Default completion-only loss. A logging interval holds one example: 4 prompt tokens, all predicted correctly at top-1, and 6 completion tokens, of which 3 are predicted correctly. What mean_token_accuracy is logged?
checks.src: Logged metrics; Train on completion only
checks.expl: mean_token_accuracy is the proportion of NON-masked tokens whose top-1 prediction matches. The prompt is masked, so it is in neither the numerator nor the denominator: 3 / 6 = 0.5. Counting it would give 7 / 10 = 0.7 and flatter the model with tokens it was never trained to produce.

checks.q: assistant_only_loss=True needs the chat template to contain generation and endgeneration markers. What job are those markers doing?
opts: Telling the tokenizer where each turn ends so that turns can be packed
Switching the model into generation mode, which training turns off
Placing the EOS token after every user message in the conversation
Marking which rendered tokens are the reply, the only ones given loss
checks.src: Customization — Train on assistant messages only
checks.expl: Once a conversation is rendered through the template it is one token sequence; the markers are how the trainer knows which stretch of it is the assistant's response, so that the user and system messages can be left out of the loss. For known families such as Qwen3, TRL patches the markers in itself.

checks.q: When SFTTrainer trains LoRA adapters rather than the whole model, the page suggests a higher learning rate, about 1e-4. Why?
opts: Because the frozen base weights need a stronger push to move
Because only the new adapter parameters are being learned
Because adapters are trained in lower precision than the model
Because packing is turned on whenever PEFT is in use
checks.expl: With an adapter the pretrained weights stay frozen and only the small set of new parameters is trained from scratch, which tolerates — and needs — larger steps than nudging an already-trained network. The frozen weights do not move at any learning rate.

checks.q: You instruction-tune a Qwen base model whose tokenizer already has a chat template, and the result never stops generating. What does the page say must be aligned?
opts: The learning rate, which must be lower for chat-tuned models
The packing flag, which merges turns and hides their ends
The EOS token, which must match the template's end-of-turn token
The max_length, which must be None so that no turn is ever truncated
checks.expl: A base model with a predefined template does not need clone_chat_template, but its EOS token must be aligned with the template — eos_token in SFTConfig, for example the template's end-of-turn token — so that the model learns to emit the token that ends a reply.

ai310.1.2.takeaway: Quantization buys memory with precision: the weights are stored in fewer bits and accuracy is preserved as far as the method can manage — and which method fits is decided by your hardware and by what you need to do next (load, fine-tune, compile, save), which is what the compatibility table lays out.

beats.d: Weights are normally stored in full precision (fp32); half precision (fp16, bf16) is increasingly the norm for large models; some methods go on to integers such as int8 or int4. Fewer bits per weight means less memory to load and run the model, at some cost in accuracy that each method tries to minimise.
Some methods need a calibration step to reach greater accuracy and extreme compression (1-2 bits). Others quantize on the fly: point them at a full-precision checkpoint and they work out of the box.

beats.t: Bits are a property of the method
beats.d: The bits column differs row by row: AQLM 1–2, AWQ 4, bitsandbytes 4 or 8, GPT-QModel 2, 3, 4 or 8, FBGEMM_FP8 only 8. And low bit widths are not reserved for calibrated methods — HIGGS, HQQ, optimum-quanto and Metal all quantize on the fly at 2 bits.

beats.t: The table's columns are the tradeoffs
beats.d: For each method: on-the-fly or not; CPU, CUDA, ROCm, Metal and Intel GPU support; torch.compile; the bit widths; PEFT fine-tuning; whether Transformers can serialize the result. A method is a row of answers to those questions.

beats.t: bitsandbytes: load and fine-tune in one step
beats.d: On the fly, 4 or 8 bits, CUDA and CPU and Intel GPU (partial on ROCm and Metal), PEFT fine-tuning supported, serializable. The fit when you want to take a downloaded model straight to a quantized fine-tune.
Not on the fly — the model is quantized beforehand and loaded already quantized. 4 bits, CUDA, ROCm, CPU and Intel GPU, no Metal; PEFT and serialization supported.

1 to 8 bits, runs on CPU, CUDA, Metal and Intel GPU, compiles — but it is not on the fly, does not support PEFT fine-tuning, and is not serializable with Transformers. It is for running a model, not for training it further.

beats.t: Tools for doing it without code
beats.d: Community Spaces convert a repository for you (bitsandbytes, GGUF and MLX), and an AutoQuant notebook runs several methods; DeepLearning.AI's two short courses are the suggested start for newcomers.

ai310.1.2.worked: Fix the constraints in order and let them eliminate rows. Hardware first (a Mac rules out AWQ; Metal favours GGUF), then the next step (fine-tuning with PEFT rules out GGUF; loading straight from a full-precision checkpoint needs an on-the-fly method such as bitsandbytes), then whether the result must be saved with Transformers. Whatever survives is the shortlist; only then compare bit widths.
ai310.1.2.watch: Reading every coloured cell as a yes. Yellow is partial support — bitsandbytes on ROCm and Metal, torchao on Metal — and a '?' (AWQ, EETQ and Quark under torch.compile) means unknown, not supported. Check the exact cell for your hardware and your next step.

checks.q: According to the overview, what does quantization trade, and for what?
opts: Precision of the stored weights, for lower memory, while keeping as much accuracy as it can
Context length, for a smaller model, while keeping the same weights at the same precision
Training speed, for faster inference, by retraining the model in a lower-precision format
Nothing at all: it is a lossless re-encoding of exactly the same weights into a smaller file
checks.expl: Quantization stores the weights in a lower precision — fp32 to fp16 or bf16, or further to int8 or int4 — which lowers the memory needed to load and use the model. It is lossy: each method tries to preserve as much accuracy as possible, which is why some need calibration.

checks.q: A model's weights take 16 GB stored in bf16. Ignoring the small overhead of scales and metadata, how many GB do the same weights take at int4?
checks.expl: bf16 is 16 bits per weight and int4 is 4, so each weight shrinks by a factor of 4: 16 GB / 4 = 4 GB. From fp32 (32 bits) the same model would have been 32 GB, which is why half precision is already the norm for large models.

checks.q: According to the overview, what does a method's calibration step buy you?
opts: Support for PEFT fine-tuning, which on-the-fly methods lack
The ability to run on a CPU rather than only on a GPU
A result that Transformers can serialize and reload
Greater accuracy, and extreme compression to 1–2 bits
checks.expl: The overview: 'Some methods require calibration for greater accuracy and extreme compression (1-2 bits), while other methods work out of the box with on-the-fly quantization.' The table rules out the rest — bitsandbytes is on the fly and supports PEFT, and CPU support and serialization vary method by method. Nor is calibration the only way down to 2 bits: several on-the-fly methods offer it.

checks.q: You want to load a freshly downloaded full-precision model in 4-bit on an NVIDIA GPU and fine-tune it with LoRA, with no separate quantization pass. Of these three, which does the table support?
opts: bitsandbytes, which quantizes on the fly and supports PEFT
AWQ, since it is 4-bit and it supports PEFT fine-tuning too
GGUF, since llama.cpp runs on CUDA as well as on a CPU
None of them; all three need the model quantized first
checks.expl: Two columns decide it. On the fly: bitsandbytes yes, AWQ and GGUF no — they load a model that was quantized beforehand. PEFT fine-tuning: bitsandbytes and AWQ yes, GGUF no. Only bitsandbytes passes both.

checks.q: You want to run a quantized model locally on an Apple Silicon Mac. Of GGUF, AWQ and bitsandbytes, which does the table mark as fully supported on Metal?
opts: AWQ, because 4-bit kernels exist for every GPU backend
GGUF, the llama.cpp format, which is supported on Metal
bitsandbytes, because quantizing on the fly avoids kernels
All three, because int4 arithmetic is the same on any chip
checks.expl: Support is per backend, not per bit width. GGUF is green on Metal; AWQ is red there; bitsandbytes is only partial (yellow). Quantizing on the fly still needs kernels for the hardware it runs on.

checks.q: You want 2-bit weights on an NVIDIA (CUDA) GPU and have no calibration data, so the method must quantize on the fly. Which of these does the table allow?
opts: AQLM, which goes down to 1 or 2 bits
AWQ, the most common 4-bit format
HIGGS, which supports 2 and 4 bits
FBGEMM_FP8, which was built for CUDA
checks.expl: Three columns decide it: on the fly, CUDA GPU, bits. AQLM reaches 2 bits but is not on the fly; AWQ is neither on the fly nor 2-bit; FBGEMM_FP8 is on the fly on CUDA but 8-bit only. HIGGS is green for both on the fly and CUDA, at 2 or 4 bits (HQQ and optimum-quanto would also qualify).

ai310.1.3.takeaway: The harness turns 'how good is this model?' into a reproducible command — but only if you know what the number depends on: the backend and its parallel layout, whether the model exposes logprobs, how answers were extracted, and whose prompt procedure the task follows.

beats.d: Over 60 standard academic benchmarks with hundreds of subtasks, run against models from transformers, vLLM, commercial APIs and more. It is the backend of Hugging Face's Open LLM Leaderboard, and it uses publicly available prompts so that results are reproducible and comparable between papers.

beats.t: Install the core, then a backend
beats.d: The base package no longer pulls in transformers or torch; each backend is an extra — lm_eval[hf], lm_eval[vllm], lm_eval[api]. lm-eval ls tasks lists what can be run.

beats.t: The hf backend passes model_args straight through
beats.d: Anything AutoModel accepts works: a local path, a Hub revision to evaluate a partially trained checkpoint, a dtype, a PEFT adapter (peft=PATH), delta weights, a GPTQ model. batch_size auto finds the largest batch that fits, and auto:N recomputes it N times for tasks whose examples vary a lot in length.

The hf backend can evaluate a GGUF file, but without a separate tokenizer it rebuilds one from the GGUF — which can take hours or hang. The gguf model type instead scores a llama.cpp server, computing loglikelihoods by exact teacher forcing; perplexity (loglikelihood_rolling) is not implemented there.

If the model fits on one GPU, accelerate launch gives every GPU its own full copy: K GPUs, K times faster. If it does not fit, parallelize=True splits the weights across GPUs. Both can be combined. Native tensor parallelism (tp_plan=auto) needs the number of key-value heads divisible by the TP degree. Multi-node is not supported natively.

beats.t: vLLM and SGLang for speed, HF as the reference
beats.d: vLLM runs tensor parallel and data parallel together; each data-parallel replica is a ray actor holding tensor_parallel_size GPUs. Its outputs occasionally differ from Hugging Face's, which the harness treats as the reference — a comparator script checks one against the other.

A model that returns no logits or logprobs — most chat APIs — can run generate_until tasks only. loglikelihood, loglikelihood_rolling and multiple_choice need the probabilities of the prompt's continuations. For generative tasks on closed chat models, read a few outputs first (--limit 10) to confirm answer extraction and scoring work.

--output_path saves results and --log_samples saves every response for post-hoc analysis; --use_cache resumes interrupted runs (per GPU count); --check_integrity verifies task data; --predict_only returns generations without scoring, for tasks that would execute untrusted code; write_out.py shows exactly what the model is fed.

In order: what people who train LLMs agree on, an official implementation, what evaluators agree on, then the harness's own pick among common ones. The point is to reduce the harm when people compare runs across papers — which the project discourages, and which happens anyway.

ai310.1.3.worked: Treat an evaluation as an experiment with a config. Fix the backend, the model_args (revision, dtype, adapters), the parallel layout and the task version; run with --log_samples and --output_path; read some logged samples before reading the score; and when two backends disagree, check against the hf backend with the comparator before believing either.
ai310.1.3.watch: Reading a generative-task score from a chat API without looking at its outputs. If the answer extraction does not match the model's response format, correct answers are scored as wrong, and the number measures the parser rather than the model — which is why the README asks for --limit 10 first.

checks.q: Evaluating a GGUF model through the hf backend seems to hang before the first task starts. What does the README identify as the cause and the fix?
opts: The GGUF file must be converted to safetensors first; convert it, then rerun
The hf backend cannot read GGUF at all; serve the model with llama.cpp instead
No separate tokenizer was passed, so one is being rebuilt from the GGUF file
The batch size is too large for a quantized model; set batch_size to auto
checks.expl: Without a tokenizer path, Hugging Face reconstructs the tokenizer from the GGUF file, which can take hours or hang indefinitely. Passing tokenizer=/path/to/tokenizer in model_args cuts that from hours to seconds. The hf backend does read GGUF — via pretrained= the folder and gguf_file= the file.

checks.q: Your model fits comfortably on one GPU and you have four. Which setup does the README use to make the evaluation about four times faster?
opts: parallelize=True, which splits the model's weights across all four GPUs
tp_plan=auto, which shards the weights with native tensor parallelism
batch_size auto:4, which recomputes the largest batch four times
accelerate launch, so that each GPU loads its own full copy of the model
checks.src: Multi-GPU Evaluation with Hugging Face accelerate
checks.expl: Data parallelism: each GPU holds a separate full copy and takes a share of the examples, so K GPUs are K times faster. parallelize=True and tp_plan split ONE copy across GPUs — the tool for a model too large for one GPU, not a speed-up for one that fits.

checks.q: With the vllm backend you pass tensor_parallel_size=2 and data_parallel_size=4. How many GPUs does the run reserve?
checks.src: Tensor + Data Parallel and Optimized Inference with vLLM
checks.expl: Each of the 4 data-parallel replicas is dispatched as a separate ray actor, and each actor reserves tensor_parallel_size = 2 GPUs because its copy of the model is split across two. 4 x 2 = 8 GPUs: tensor parallelism splits a model, data parallelism multiplies it.

checks.q: You want to score a chat-completions API model on a multiple-choice task that is scored by loglikelihood, and the API returns no logprobs. What does the README say?
opts: It runs, but the harness has to estimate the logprobs by sampling
It cannot: without logprobs, only generate_until tasks can be run
It runs once you pass the API model's own tokenizer to the harness
It cannot, because API models only run perplexity-style tasks
checks.expl: Likelihood tasks rank answer options by the probability the model assigns to each continuation, so they need logits or logprobs. Models that supply none — the ChatCompletions and Anthropic rows say 'no logprobs' — can run generate_until tasks only.

checks.q: Before trusting a generative-task score from a closed chat model, what does the README recommend doing?
opts: Run the whole task twice and average, as chat APIs sample at random
Raise max_retries, because failed calls are scored as wrong answers
Switch to the completions endpoint, the reference for every score
Read a few outputs with --limit 10 to confirm answers are extracted
checks.src: Model APIs and Inference Servers (note on closed chat models)
checks.expl: A generative task is scored by extracting an answer from free text. If the extraction does not fit the model's response format, the score measures the parser, not the model — so look at about ten outputs first, and if needed use a system prompt in model_args to set the format.

checks.q: When implementing a task, the harness prefers the procedure LLM trainers agree on, then an official implementation, before its own choice. What is that order for?
opts: So its numbers agree with other groups' runs, as people compare across papers anyway
So every task scores a little higher, which makes the leaderboard easier to read
So that no prompt is ever made public, which keeps tasks out of training data
So the harness can skip its own validation, since agreed procedures are known correct
checks.expl: The stated aim is to decrease the harm when people inevitably compare runs across different papers, a practice the project discourages. Its prompts are deliberately public — that is what makes results reproducible — and the order is a guideline that can be overruled.

ai310.1.4.takeaway: vLLM's speed comes from treating the KV cache as managed memory — paged into fixed-size blocks, shared between requests by hashing whole prefixes, evicted least-recently-used — and its usefulness from serving all of that behind an OpenAI-compatible API.

beats.d: A library for LLM inference and serving, begun at Berkeley's Sky Computing Lab and now a large open-source project. Three ways in: run models (the Quickstart), build applications (the User Guide), or build vLLM itself (the Developer Guide).

State-of-the-art serving throughput; efficient management of attention key and value memory with PagedAttention; continuous batching, chunked prefill and prefix caching; CUDA graphs; quantization from FP8 to INT4, GPTQ, AWQ and GGUF; optimized attention kernels; speculative decoding; and prefill, decode and encode that can be disaggregated.

Hugging Face models (200+ architectures, from decoder-only to MoE, state-space and multimodal), parallel sampling and beam search, tensor, pipeline, data, expert and context parallelism, streaming, structured outputs, tool calling, multi-LoRA, an OpenAI-compatible server, and a wide range of hardware.

LLM loads the model and engine; SamplingParams sets temperature, top-p and the rest; llm.generate adds the prompts to the engine's waiting queue and runs it for throughput. Unless told otherwise, vLLM applies the model repository's generation_config.json; generation_config='vllm' restores vLLM's own defaults.
llm.generate does not apply the model's chat template. For an Instruct or Chat model, apply the template yourself with the tokenizer, or call llm.chat with OpenAI-style message lists.

vllm serve MODEL starts a server on localhost:8000 implementing the OpenAI API — list models, completions, chat completions — so existing OpenAI clients work by changing the base URL. One model at a time; --api-key makes it check keys (several, for rotation). The attention backend is chosen automatically, or set with --attention-backend.

beats.t: Prefix caching: reuse, do not recompute
beats.d: The KV-cache blocks of processed requests are kept and reused when a new request starts with the same prefix — almost a free lunch, since outputs do not change. Each block's hash combines its parent block's hash, its own tokens, and extras such as LoRA IDs, image hashes or a cache salt; only full blocks are cached.

beats.t: A block pool with an LRU free queue
beats.d: All blocks are allocated up front as a pool, each with a reference count. A request reusing cached blocks 'touches' them out of the free queue; new blocks are popped from its head, evicting whatever cached block was least recently used. A finished request's blocks are freed in reverse order, so its last block — hashing the longest prefix, least likely to be reused — goes first.

A per-request cache_salt is folded into the first block's hash, so only requests with the same salt can share cached blocks. That blocks timing attacks in which one tenant infers another's cached content from latency.

ai310.1.4.worked: To serve a model: vllm serve it, then point the openai client's base_url at http://localhost:8000/v1 and use completions or chat completions unchanged. To get prefix-cache hits, put the shared part of every request — system prompt, long document — at the very start, identical token for token, because reuse is decided block by block from the first token.
ai310.1.4.watch: Expecting prefix caching to reuse any shared text. A block is reusable only if it is full and every token before it matches too, so a shared passage after a differing first line, or a partial final block, is recomputed.

checks.q: The landing page lists PagedAttention first among what makes vLLM fast. What does it manage efficiently?
opts: The model weights, paging each layer in from disk as it is needed
The memory that holds the attention keys and values for requests
The queue of incoming requests, batching them as they arrive
The precision of the attention scores, storing them as FP8
checks.src: Welcome to vLLM — vLLM is fast with
checks.expl: PagedAttention is 'efficient management of attention key and value memory' — the KV cache, held in blocks rather than one contiguous slab per request. Batching requests as they arrive is a separate feature (continuous batching), and so is quantization.

checks.q: You load an Instruct model with LLM and call llm.generate on plain prompt strings, and the answers look wrong. What does the quickstart point out?
opts: generate needs SamplingParams, or else it decodes greedily from the prompt
Instruct models can be used only through the OpenAI-compatible server
generate does not apply the chat template: apply it, or use llm.chat
The prompts must be tokenized first, since generate expects token IDs
checks.expl: An Instruct model was trained on text in its chat template, and llm.generate passes your string through as-is. Apply the template with the tokenizer (apply_chat_template with add_generation_prompt) or call llm.chat with message lists. The server, by contrast, uses the tokenizer's template by default.

checks.q: You create LLM without passing SamplingParams, and the sampling defaults turn out not to be vLLM's own. Why?
opts: vLLM applies the model repository's generation_config.json by default
vLLM reuses the defaults of the last server started on that machine
vLLM picks sampling defaults at random unless a seed is supplied
vLLM reads its defaults from the OpenAI API that it is imitating
checks.src: Quickstart — Offline Batched Inference; Online Serving
checks.expl: If the Hugging Face repository has a generation_config.json, vLLM uses the sampling values the model's creator recommends. To use vLLM's defaults instead, pass generation_config='vllm' to LLM, or --generation-config vllm to vllm serve.

checks.q: Two requests contain an identical 4-token block, but the tokens before that block differ. Can the second request reuse the first one's cached copy of the block?
opts: Yes, because a block's hash is computed from its own four tokens only
Yes, but only if both requests use the same sampling parameters
No, because cached blocks are never shared between two requests
No, because each block's hash folds in its parent's, so its prefix
checks.expl: vLLM hashes each block by its own tokens AND the hash of the block before it, so a block is identified by everything up to its end. That is exactly right for a KV cache: a token's keys and values depend on all the tokens before it, so the same four tokens after a different prefix have different K and V.

checks.q: Block size 16. An earlier request with a 64-token prompt is fully cached. A new 50-token prompt matches it in its first 40 tokens and then differs. How many of the new prompt's tokens are served from the prefix cache?
checks.expl: Only full blocks that match token for token, from the start, are hits. Tokens 1-16 and 17-32 match; the third block (33-48) matches only 8 of its 16 tokens, so it misses — and every block after a miss has a different parent hash. 2 x 16 = 32 tokens hit; 18 are computed.

checks.q: When a request finishes, vLLM adds its freed blocks to the free queue in reverse order, so its last block is evicted first. Why that order?
opts: The last block was the one written most recently, so it is the coldest
Its last block hashes the longest prefix, so it is least likely reused
The last block is usually partly full, so it can never be cached
Reversing the order makes queue moves O(1) instead of O(n)
checks.expl: A later block is identified by a longer prefix, so fewer future requests will match it; the first blocks — a shared system prompt, say — are the likeliest hits. Evicting from the head of the free queue then throws away the least useful blocks first. The O(1) moves come from the doubly linked list, not from the order.

ai310.1.5.takeaway: An LLM can only emit text, so 'tool use' is a protocol: the system prompt describes the tools, the model writes an action in an agreed format and stops, the agent parses and runs it, and the result goes back into the prompt as an observation — Thought, Action, Observation, in a loop until the task is done.

beats.t: An agent is a model with a body
beats.d: A system that uses an AI model to interact with its environment to reach a user's objective. The brain — usually an LLM — reasons, plans and decides which action to take; the body is the set of tools it has been given, and it can do nothing those tools do not allow.

Simple processor (output changes nothing), router (output picks a branch), tool caller (output picks the function and its arguments), multi-step agent (output decides whether the loop continues), multi-agent (one agentic workflow starts another).

beats.t: The brain predicts tokens until EOS
beats.d: LLMs are mostly decoders predicting the next token from the previous ones, autoregressively, until they emit the end-of-sequence token. Each model has its own special tokens to open and close messages and turns.

Before the model sees a conversation, every message is concatenated into one prompt by the model's chat template; the model does not remember, it rereads everything each turn. The system message sets behaviour and, for an agent, lists the tools, the action format and how to lay out thoughts.

beats.t: A tool is a function the LLM is told about
beats.d: It needs a description of what it does, a callable, typed arguments and, optionally, typed outputs. Good tools complement the model — a calculator for arithmetic, a search for anything after its training data. A @tool decorator can build the description from the function's name, docstring and type hints; MCP standardises the interface across frameworks.

The LLM decides the next step, the agent calls a tool with arguments, and the result is appended to the prompt for the model to reflect on — a while loop that runs until the objective is met. Chain-of-Thought reasons step by step without tools; ReAct interleaves reasoning with actions and observations; models such as DeepSeek-R1 are trained to think in delimited reasoning tokens.

beats.t: Actions: JSON, code, or function calls
beats.d: A JSON agent writes the action as a JSON object; a code agent writes an executable code block, more expressive (loops, conditionals, libraries) but a security risk to run; a function-calling agent is a JSON agent fine-tuned to emit a new message per action. All rely on stop and parse: the model stops once the action is complete, and a parser extracts the tool and its arguments.

beats.t: The failure the dummy agent shows
beats.d: Left to generate freely, the model writes its Action and then an Observation of its own — invented weather, with no tool run. The fix is to stop generation at 'Observation:', run the real function, append its output as the Observation, and resume.
smolagents' CodeAgent does the same loop with code actions: tools defined with type hints and docstrings that describe every argument, a final_answer tool, and a cap on steps (max_steps).

ai310.1.5.worked: Build the loop by hand once. Write a system prompt that lists one tool and the exact action format, call the model with stop set to the observation marker, parse the JSON it produced, run the function, append 'Observation:' and the real result to the assistant message, and call the model again. Every agent framework is this, plus error handling.
ai310.1.5.watch: Trusting text after the action. A model that is not stopped will happily write the observation itself — fluent, plausible and fabricated — and then a final answer built on it. Stop at the observation marker, and treat only what the tool returned as the source of truth.

checks.q: An LLM's output chooses which function to run and with what arguments, but your program runs it once and stops. Where does that sit on the unit's spectrum of agency?
opts: Router: the output chooses between two fixed paths in the program
Simple processor: the output has no effect on what the program does
Tool caller: the output decides which function runs, and with what
Multi-step agent: the output controls whether the loop carries on
checks.src: What is an Agent? — The spectrum of agency
checks.expl: Choosing the function and its arguments is the tool-caller level (run_function(llm_chosen_tool, llm_chosen_args)). It becomes a multi-step agent only when the model's output also decides whether to keep iterating — the while loop of Thought, Action, Observation.

checks.q: Three turns into a chat with an agent, how does the LLM 'remember' what the user said in the first turn?
opts: Every message is concatenated into one prompt, which it rereads in full
It stores earlier turns in its weights, updating them after every reply
The system message keeps a summary that the model rewrites every turn
It does not: each turn is answered from the newest user message only
checks.expl: Chat is a UI abstraction. The chat template concatenates all messages, with the model's special tokens marking each turn, into a single prompt; the model reads it in full every time. That is also how tool results get in: they are appended as messages and the whole conversation is sent again.

checks.q: When an agent 'uses' a weather tool, what does the LLM itself actually do?
opts: It calls the weather API itself, over a connection the framework opens
It writes text describing the call; the agent parses it and runs the tool
It recalls the weather from its training data, formatted as a tool result
It hands the conversation to the tool, which then writes the final reply
checks.src: What are Tools? — How do tools work?
checks.expl: LLMs take text in and give text out; they cannot call anything. Providing a tool means describing it in the system prompt so the model can write a text invocation such as call weather_tool('Paris'). The agent executes it, appends the result, and sends the updated conversation back to the model.

checks.q: A question needs today's exchange rate. Why does the unit's comparison point to ReAct rather than Chain-of-Thought for it?
opts: ReAct reasons in more steps, and more steps make the arithmetic reliable
Chain-of-Thought is a training technique, so it needs a fine-tuned model
ReAct interleaves actions and observations; CoT reasons without tools
Chain-of-Thought cannot be used with chat templates or system messages
checks.src: Thought: Internal Reasoning and the ReAct Approach
checks.expl: Both reason step by step, but Chain-of-Thought stays inside the model — good for logic and maths — while ReAct alternates thoughts with tool actions and their observations, which is what info-seeking tasks need. Both are prompting strategies; training a model to think in delimited reasoning tokens is the training-level technique.

checks.q: A code agent writes a Python block as its action instead of a JSON object. What does the unit give as the gain and the cost?
opts: Gain: loops, conditionals and libraries; cost: running generated code is risky
Gain: no parser is needed at all; cost: the model must be fine-tuned for code
Gain: actions run faster than JSON; cost: it can no longer call outside APIs
Gain: no system prompt is needed; cost: stop-and-parse no longer applies
checks.expl: Code can express loops, conditionals, nested functions and library calls that a JSON blob cannot, and is easier to debug. But executing LLM-generated code invites everything from prompt injection to harmful code, so the unit recommends a framework with safeguards. Code agents still stop and parse: the block is delimited and its end is signalled.

checks.q: In the dummy agent, the model writes an Action and then, by itself, an 'Observation' with plausible weather — though no tool ran. What fix does the unit apply?
opts: Lower the temperature, so the model stops inventing its observations
Put the weather in the system prompt, so no tool call is ever needed
Ask the model to mark invented text, and filter that out afterwards
Stop at 'Observation:', then run the tool and insert its real output
checks.expl: The model was hallucinating — generating an observation rather than receiving one. Passing stop=['Observation:'] ends generation right after the action; the agent then runs get_weather, appends 'Observation:' and the real result to the assistant message, and resumes generation from there.

res400.2.2.takeaway: Most of research is the outer loop — choosing which problem is worth solving and ripe for solving — and taste for that can be learned: fertile ground, ambition with a real attack, one core contribution per paper, and no gaming of proxy metrics.

beats.d: A PhD offers freedom, ownership, deep expertise, and keeps future choices open. It also brings deadline grind, discarded months of work and identity crises; if you are unsure, lean slightly negative, and try research before committing — which is exactly why research experience is valued in admissions: the student knows what they are getting into.

Strong letters from people you did research with matter most; a publication helps; grades matter little beyond not being low. Time spent on grades would have been better spent on research, early and under several supervisors.

Understand their incentives — tenure, funding, recognition. Pre-tenure advisers tend to be hands-on and low-level; senior ones work at a higher level of abstraction. Ask their students specific questions, look at where alumni went, and choose the whole lab, because you will see its students every day.

Solving problems is the simple inner loop. Most of the time goes on the outer loop: which problems are worth solving and ripe for solving. Advisers are masters of it — 'taste' is real — and you acquire it by practice and apprenticeship.

Fertile ground that papers can build on; your adviser's interests; ambition, because a 10x more important problem is at most 2-3x harder — aiming at 10x forces first principles and a new strategy; but with an attack, as Hamming put it; and an area you can be 'the person who did X' in. Five years of work is about 10,400 hours, so the skills should be worth having anyway.

Incremental 'cockroach' papers — 2% on a benchmark, hard to reject, rarely cited; the 'next logical step' nobody has bothered with; the easy poster. Your adviser can be wrong, and you may sometimes ignore them. And do not just play the paper game: think from first principles and do what others should but do not.

Learn what bad looks like by reviewing — only good examples is a binary classifier trained on positives. Match the expected gestalt. Identify the single core contribution and organise everything around it; contributions are not additive. Default structure, one point per paragraph, every step justified (no laundry list), and an internal deadline two weeks early.

Release your code — it forces better habits and invites follow-ups — and document it for the future you. A talk's goal is to make the audience care about the problem, teach them something and entertain them, not to recite your paper: pictures over text, no dense results tables, no outline slide, and watch the thin band between bored and confused.

Go, and treat the hallways as the main event: the papers are old news, and much of a field's knowledge is never written down but held by its community. Finally, gaming proxy metrics — self-citation, remixed or resubmitted papers, missing baselines — catches up with you. Do good work and communicate it properly.

res400.2.2.worked: Run a candidate project through the checklist before starting: is it fertile (will it lead to more work)? Is it ambitious, and is there a concrete attack? Can it be described in a sentence — 'the person who did X'? Will the skills be worth having even if it fails? If the honest answer is 'it is the next logical step', look again.
res400.2.2.watch: Mistaking a stream of accepted incremental papers for progress. They get in because a reviewer cannot point to anything to kill them, so the acceptances feel productive — but they are not cited and do not move the field.

checks.q: Karpathy notes that research experience is prized when PhD programs choose students. What reason does he give?
opts: It proves the student can already publish at the top venues
The student is likelier to know what they are getting into
Admissions weigh it above reference letters and grades alike
It shows the student can work without an adviser from day one
checks.expl: After listing the hardships, he advises trying research first, and notes that a main reason research experience is desirable in PhD hiring is not the research itself but that the student is more likely to know what they are signing up for. Reference letters, not experience, are what he calls most important.

checks.q: Karpathy calls a PhD 'an exercise in the outer loop'. What is the outer loop?
opts: Running many experiments in parallel and keeping the ones that work
Writing results up fast so the next paper can begin straight away
Rereading the literature until the open problems become obvious
Deciding which problems are worth solving and which are ripe to solve
checks.src: Research topics — An exercise in the outer loop
checks.expl: Solving a problem is the inner loop. The outer loop is the meta-problem — imagining solving hypothetical problems and asking what it would unlock and whether anyone cares — and it is where most of a PhD's time goes. The 'taste' academics talk about is skill at this loop.

checks.q: Why does Karpathy argue that a problem 10x more important is not 10x harder?
opts: Aiming at 10x forces first-principles thinking and a new strategy
Important problems attract collaborators, who share out the work
Bigger problems get more funding, which buys the compute to solve them
Reviewers are more lenient with papers on more important problems
checks.src: Research topics — Be ambitious: the sublinear scaling of hardness
checks.expl: In his experience a 10x more important problem is at most 2-3x harder, because the ambition itself changes the approach: you confront an approach's real limits and innovate. Aim for 10% and you get it by working hard; aim for 100% and you will likely still get there, but by a different route. Hamming's caveat follows: it still needs a reasonable attack.

checks.q: Using Karpathy's working year — 260 working days of 8 hours — how many years does it take to reach Gladwell's 10,000 hours? Give two decimal places.
checks.expl: A working year is 260 x 8 = 2,080 hours, and 10,000 / 2,080 = 4.81 years. That is why he says five years (10,400 hours) is exactly enough to become an expert — so choose an area whose skills you will value whatever the papers achieve.

checks.q: Karpathy packed a second, minor contribution into his video-classification paper. What lesson does he draw?
opts: Two contributions make a paper about twice as likely to be cited
Minor ideas belong in the appendix, where reviewers expect them
Contributions are not additive: the minor one diluted the paper
A second contribution is fine if the experiments support it too
checks.src: Writing papers — Identify the core contribution
checks.expl: He had reasoned that two contributions are better than one. They are not: the second was minor, distracted from the first, and no one cared. A paper sells a single thing that was not obvious before, and everything in it is organised around that one contribution.

checks.q: If most papers at a conference are old news by the time it meets, why does Karpathy still insist you go?
opts: Attending is how reviewers learn to recognise your name on papers
Much of a field's knowledge is never written down; its people hold it
The talks give results in much more detail than the papers have room for
The posters show the newest results before they ever reach arXiv
checks.expl: Research is a social endeavour, and each field has knowledge that never gets serialised into papers — what to work on next, which methods really work, the inside story of a paper. The hallway is the main event that is not on the schedule: learn from the hivemind first, then influence it.

spch100.0.0.takeaway: Homework for Life: at the end of each day, ask what the most story-like moment was and write a line or two. Done daily it builds a storyteller's lens, fills a bank of small stories, and — the part Dicks did not expect — slows time down.

beats.d: When the doctor says to take food away from a food-throwing toddler, his wife warns it will be hard for him because he grew up hungry — a secret he never told her — and admits she quietly unpacks the oversized lunches he packs every morning.
Moments like that are everywhere. We miss most of them, and when we do see one we have no way of catching it.
His dramatic stories — dying, jail, homelessness — are only okay on stage. The small ones are what audiences love, because everyone has a secret and everyone knows hunger.
Every night: if I had to tell a five-minute story from something that happened today, however benign, what was the most story-like moment? Write a sentence or two. Not the story.
Walking an old dog at 2 a.m., in boxers, in the rain, becomes a moment he will own forever instead of an annoyance. Forgotten childhood memories start surfacing too.
Days stop blurring together. He can touch any moment from years of entries and be back inside it.
Five minutes every day, and patience: the early entries are weak, and the lens can take months to sharpen.

spch100.0.0.worked: Same time, same place, every night, one line per moment however ordinary — 'walked Kaylee at 2 a.m., underwear, birds, rain, beauty'. A few weeks later, reread the list and mark the entries that still pull you straight back into the moment.
spch100.0.0.watch: Waiting for something dramatic before writing anything down. The practice depends on logging the ordinary; skipping the 'boring' days is exactly what keeps the lens from sharpening.

checks.q: What question does Dicks ask himself each night?
opts: What was the most dramatic thing that happened to me today, worth a full story?
What was the most story-like moment of today, if I had to tell a story from it?
What did I learn today that I could teach in a five-minute talk?
Which conversation today would make the funniest story at dinner?
checks.expl: The words 'as benign as it might be' matter: the point is the best moment of an ordinary day.

checks.q: Why doesn't he write the whole story down?
opts: It would be too much work, and he would stop doing it
Writing it out would fix the story before it was ready
He keeps the full stories in a separate notebook instead
Stories should be told aloud, never written
checks.expl: He says outright that writing the story would be too much. A sentence or two keeps the habit alive.

checks.q: Which effect of the practice did he not expect?
opts: Winning more StorySLAMs with smaller, quieter stories
Sleeping better after writing each night
Time slowing down, so days stop disappearing
Finding his dramatic stories went down better
checks.expl: He calls it a magical elixir: the days creep by, and none is lost.

spch100.0.1.takeaway: Half of a first impression is vocal, and most professionals switch into a flat 'professional' voice. Giang's five fixes: respect what the voice does, build a taste for voices, look in the vocal mirror, read children's books aloud, and record yourself regularly.

beats.d: Visual image is only half the first-impression puzzle. The other half forms the moment you open your mouth: how confident, friendly and trustworthy you seem.
Ask a child to act like an adult and they go serious and monotone. We do the same at work, and become less engaging and less influential.
'Wow, that's a great career path' — amazed, sarcastic, defeated, and a disappointed mother. The meaning lives beneath the words.
Watch the most-viewed TED talks, notice whose voice draws you in and whose annoys you, and ask why — the way you develop a sense of style.
