Record yourself, watch it back, and list what you like and what the voice says about you that you do not intend.
Children's books are full of emotive words that force inflection. One recorded video a month gives twelve markers a year, so invisible progress becomes visible.

spch100.0.1.worked: Record sixty seconds of how you normally explain your work. Listen back and write two columns: what you like, and what the voice says about you that you did not mean. Repeat monthly and compare against the first.
spch100.0.1.watch: Assuming good content is enough. Correct words said in the wrong voice are not effective, and listeners decide on confidence and trust within seconds.

checks.q: Besides visual image, what makes up the other half of a first impression?
opts: Your verbal content — the words you choose to say first
Your vocal image — what people conclude when you speak
Your body language — what people read in how you stand
Your credentials — what people know about you beforehand
checks.expl: He splits the first impression roughly fifty-fifty between visual image and vocal image.

checks.q: What does the 'great career path' demonstration show?
opts: The same words can mean opposite things, depending on how they're said
Sarcasm is the hardest tone to read, so avoid it at work
Praise sounds false unless it names something specific about the person
Listeners believe the words over the tone when the two disagree
checks.expl: The same sentence came out amazed, sarcastic, defeated and disappointed.

checks.q: Why make one video a month?
opts: To build an archive of clips you can post on social media
To compare your voice with the speakers you've chosen as models
To make otherwise invisible progress visible, one marker a month
To replace live practice, which is hard to schedule every week
checks.expl: Progress in communication is hard to see; twelve markers a year make it visible and keep you going.

spch100.0.2.takeaway: Abrahams's method for speaking on the spot: be interested rather than interesting, treat anxiety as go-time, take a beat, trade perfection for connection, and reach for a practised structure — Problem-Solution-Benefit, or Answer-Detail-Describe — instead of a list.

beats.d: Start conversations with curiosity: comment on your surroundings ('did I miss the memo on the blue?') and keep them going with 'tell me more'.
It is hard-wired but manageable. Reframing nerves as excitement helps: it is your body saying this matters.
Not preparing; believing there is one right way to say it; and answering instantly. Take a beat — a clarifying question or a paraphrase buys the moment you need.
Our brains are not set up for lists. Problem-Solution-Benefit is the structure of every advertisement and works for any pitch.

beats.t: Small talk is hacky sack, not tennis
beats.d: Keep the ball in the air together. Mix supporting turns (ask more about their topic) with shifting turns (move the topic) — roughly two-thirds to three-quarters supporting.

beats.t: Q&A as opportunity, answered with ADD
beats.d: Answer, give a Detailed example, then Describe why it matters to them. It keeps you from taking the listener on your discovery of the answer.
Judging yourself mid-sentence steals bandwidth, so turn the judging down. Finish each thought out of breath: the inhale becomes a pause and leaves no room for 'um'.

spch100.0.2.worked: Asked 'so what do you do?', answer in ADD: one sentence that answers it, one concrete example, then why it matters to the person asking. Then stop.
spch100.0.2.watch: Thinking out loud — listing points as they occur to you. It says far more than needed and leaves the listener with nothing they can remember.

checks.q: According to Abrahams, what is the wrong place to start small talk?
opts: Asking the other person an open question
Commenting on something in your surroundings
Feeling that you must be interesting
Saying 'tell me more' before they have finished
checks.expl: The pressure to be interesting is the problem; being interested is the fix.

checks.q: What does ADD stand for?
opts: Answer, give a Detailed example, Describe why it matters
Ask a question back, Discuss it, then Decide together
Agree with the point, Deflect, then Defer to the expert
Address the asker, Define your terms, Deliver the answer
checks.expl: He uses it for Q&A — answer, example, relevance — and demonstrates it on a mock interview question.

checks.q: How does he reduce filler words like 'um'?
opts: Speaking a little faster, so there is no gap left to fill
Memorising the opening so the first words come without 'um'
Pausing deliberately before each new point while holding your breath
Finishing each thought out of breath, so the inhale becomes a pause
checks.expl: You cannot say 'um' while breathing in, so the pause replaces the filler.

checks.q: In small talk, roughly what share of turns should support the other person's topic?
opts: About a third, so that you lead the conversation
About half, so neither person dominates
Roughly two-thirds to three-quarters of them
Every turn, so you never change the subject
checks.expl: The rest are shifting turns, which move the topic or the focus.

spch100.1.0.takeaway: The story spine reduces any story to six prompts — Once upon a time, Every day, One day, Because of that, Because of that, Until finally — a wireframe to build detail onto, and it works on a Pixar film, on history, or on a trip to the grocery store.

beats.d: Distil the story to its most basic form — a gesture if you draw, an outline if you write — so that every scene you add later pushes the plot forward.
Once upon a time… Every day… One day… Because of that… Because of that… Until finally…
A couple saves for adventure; one day she dies; because of that he flies off, takes a scout along, compromises; until finally he learns the ultimate adventure is caring for those you love.

beats.t: Dead Poets Society and Martin Luther
beats.d: The same six prompts carry a school drama and a religious revolution — the structure is scale-free.
Once you know where you start and where the story ends, it is far easier to choose details that support the ending. Try it on a trip to the grocery store.

spch100.1.0.worked: Fill all six prompts in one sitting — ending first if that is easier — then read the two 'because of that' lines aloud and check that each is caused by the line before it.
spch100.1.0.watch: Letting 'because of that' quietly become 'and then'. A list of events in order is not a chain of causes, and it is the causes that push a story forward.

checks.q: Which prompt forces cause and effect?
opts: Once upon a time
Every day
Because of that
Until finally
checks.expl: If 'and then' would work just as well, the story has gone slack at that point.

checks.q: What does the spine give you before any details?
opts: A wireframe or outline of the whole story
A cast of characters and what each one wants
The final line, so you know where to stop
A title and a theme to build the scenes on
checks.expl: Details come afterwards, chosen to push toward the ending.

checks.q: What ordinary story does the video suggest practising on?
opts: A film you watched last week
Your CV, told as a career story
A family wedding
Going to the grocery store
checks.expl: Anything in your life can be structured as a story spine; it suggests five to ten minutes on something that small.

spch100.1.1.takeaway: Most conversational humour is prepared: a true answer and a playful answer to the questions you are always asked, saying the opposite as a cheap and reliable move, and priming yourself with ten minutes of a comedian you love. The deep path is an improv class.

beats.d: Conversations open on the same tracks — what do you study, what do you do. Prepare a true answer that shows your values and a playful one, and split-test them, as he did.
On a hot day when everyone is complaining, 'man, it's cold out here' gets a chuckle. Much of humour is simply the unexpected.
Watch ten to fifteen minutes of the comedian whose vibe you want before you go out. You carry their demeanour in, not their lines.
You do not need to be excellent. Saying the opposite will make you the funniest person in most groups.
Improv classes teach scene-building and structure — almost everything about being funny live, if the class is any good.

spch100.1.1.worked: Write your three most-asked questions and, under each, a true answer and a playful one. Use the playful ones in real conversations and keep whichever actually gets a laugh.
spch100.1.1.watch: Trying to be spontaneously quick like a professional comedian with no prepared material. Speed comes from long practice; the prepared answer is available today.

checks.q: What does he suggest preparing for the questions you are asked most?
opts: A true answer that reveals your values, and a playful one
A memorised joke that works for any version of the question
A question to ask back, so the focus moves off you
A short story about the most surprising answer you've had
checks.expl: They are free gimmes, like an uncle's ready-made joke.

checks.q: Why does saying the opposite tend to get a chuckle?
opts: People enjoy anyone who disagrees with the group
Humour is often just the unexpected happening
It shows you're confident enough to be wrong
It changes the subject away from a complaint
checks.expl: It is not the funniest kind of humour, but it is the easiest and most reliable.

checks.q: What does 'priming yourself' mean here?
opts: Rehearsing three jokes out loud before you walk into the room
Reading the news first so you have topical material to riff on
Watching ten minutes of a comedian whose vibe you want, before you go
Borrowing a comedian's best lines and using them in conversation later
checks.expl: It uses recency on yourself: the demeanour carries over even when the lines do not.

spch100.2.0.takeaway: Dicks's case is that a told story is remembered, earns trust and changes the teller — and that telling one well is a matter of deciding what to say before you say it, not of having lived a dramatic life.

beats.d: Friends pushed him to his first Moth StorySLAM. He hoped his name would stay in the hat, his wife made him go up, and with the first words at the microphone he knew he wanted to come back.

beats.t: Stories are kept, data is not
beats.d: Nobody asks to see a slide deck again, but people re-watch films they know by heart. Whatever you put inside a story gets remembered.
After a vulnerable story, strangers hand him their secrets — five women told him about miscarriages they had told no one else. Going first gives other people permission.
He opened the talk with a story so the audience would like him before he asked them for anything. A story earns trust, and trust makes people follow.
He refused a Gatorade on a 100-degree golf course and only understood why when he asked himself: a hungry child learns never to accept food he cannot pay back.

beats.t: Most of us were trained to tell bad stories
beats.d: Our audiences love us and put up with rambling. The fix is simple decision-making — think about what you will say before you say it — which anyone can learn.

spch100.2.0.worked: When one of your own reactions seems out of proportion — refusing help, snapping at a stranger, avoiding a place — ask why you did it, then ask again. The answer that comes from years earlier is usually the story; the reaction is its doorway.
spch100.2.0.watch: Believing you need a dramatic life to have stories. He has been through car crashes and jail and calls those the hardest to tell; what works is the small moment you would normally walk past.

checks.q: According to Dicks, what mainly separates a good storyteller from a bad one?
opts: Having lived a dramatic, eventful life
Deciding what to say before saying it
A trained performer's voice and timing
Memorising the story word for word first
checks.expl: He calls storytelling decision-making: simple strategies anyone can learn. He says he is not gifted, just someone who thinks before he speaks.

checks.q: Why does he open the talk with his own story before giving any advice?
opts: To show the audience he has won enough contests to be worth hearing
To warm the room up with a laugh before the serious advice starts
So the audience likes and trusts him before he asks them to act
To prove that only a hard life gives you stories worth telling
checks.expl: He says it outright: a story earns trust and makes people want to follow you — persuasion, but benevolent.

checks.q: What did refusing a free drink on the golf course reveal when he asked himself why?
opts: A habit from a hungry childhood still ran his behaviour
That he still felt he hadn't earned a place in that group
That he quietly resented his friend's easy generosity
That he was trying too hard to look independent and tough
checks.expl: Children who grow up hungry learn never to accept food they cannot reciprocate. He would not have known without asking.

spch100.2.1.takeaway: A story is about the instant someone changes — usually small and internal — and the dramatic events around it only matter as the road to that instant.

beats.t: The crash that is not the story
beats.d: At seventeen, two days before Christmas, he goes through a windshield after a day spent buying surprise presents for friends; his heart stops in the ambulance.
His parents go to check the car before they come to him. His friends, alerted by a McDonald's phone tree, crowd the emergency-room doors chanting his name. They gave him the gift of family.

beats.t: Why nobody cries at the death
beats.d: Audiences blink when he dies and cry when his friends arrive. Nobody can connect to a windshield; everybody can connect to finding out they are loved.
A story is change over time: either I now see something differently, or I have become someone different. The change itself takes an instant.
Most of his stories are moments an outsider would not notice, because most change happens inside your head. A small change of mind or heart is enough.
His son promised to build him a fountain when he dies. Three months later he realised that playing golf with his son was the one childhood promise to himself he had kept.

spch100.2.1.worked: Write the moment as 'before, I thought X; in that instant, I thought Y'. Then work backwards: what does the audience need to know for Y to land? Anything that does not serve that instant can go — including the drama.
spch100.2.1.watch: Mistaking the biggest event for the story. The crash is spectacular and inert; the instant of feeling loved is small, and it is what the audience actually responds to.

checks.q: In the car-crash story, what is the five-second moment?
opts: Going through the windshield two days before Christmas
His heart stopping in the ambulance, on the way to the hospital
Realising, as his friends crowd the doorway, that he is loved
His parents checking the car before they came in to see him
checks.expl: The crash is the road. The change is from feeling alone to knowing he has a family.

checks.q: Why do audiences not cry when he describes dying?
opts: Nobody can connect to the experience of going through a windshield
He hurries through that part so it doesn't upstage the ending
The details are too graphic, so listeners pull back from them
They know he survived, so his death holds no real suspense for them
checks.expl: People wince at gore but cannot connect to it. The emotional response comes at the moment they recognise from their own lives.

checks.q: What did the golf-bench moment finally mean to him?
opts: That his son wanted more time together than golf could give
That he should give up golf and spend weekends with his son
That he still resented the way his own father had raised him as a boy
That playing golf with his son kept a promise he'd made as a boy
checks.expl: He let the moment roll around for three months; the realisation arrived later, which is why he argues for being curious about yourself.

spch100.2.2.takeaway: Ira Glass reduces a story to two building blocks — the anecdote, which carries momentum, and the moment of reflection, which carries meaning — and says the craft is weaving them together while baiting the listener with questions.

beats.d: We were taught a topic sentence followed by supporting facts. Broadcast stories work on two different blocks: the anecdote and the reflection.

beats.t: The anecdote is a sequence of actions
beats.d: This happened, which led to this, which led to this. Even the dullest sequence — a man wakes, the house is too quiet, he walks downstairs — feels like a train with a destination.
The quiet house raises a question, and the listener assumes it will be answered. Keep raising and answering questions from the first line.
At some point someone has to say why you are listening — the bigger thing the story is driving at.
A thrilling anecdote that means nothing, or a smart idea with no story under it. You need both, and a good piece flips back and forth between them.

spch100.2.2.worked: Draft in alternation: a little action, a line of meaning, more action, more meaning. If the meaning lines could be deleted without anyone noticing, they are not reflections yet; if the action lines are summaries, they are not anecdote.
spch100.2.2.watch: Falling in love with a great anecdote that predictably leads nowhere. Glass calls that the bane of his existence — and says you must be ruthless enough to see that one of the two blocks is missing.

checks.q: What are Ira Glass's two building blocks of a story?
opts: The setup and the punchline that pays it off
The anecdote and the moment of reflection
The character and the problem they must solve
The hook and the question it leaves open
checks.expl: The anecdote is the sequence of actions; the reflection says why it matters.

checks.q: In his example of a man waking in a quiet house, what is the 'bait'?
opts: The unusual quiet, which raises the question why
The man waking up, which tells us who the story is about
The staircase, which promises movement and a destination
The early hour, which suggests something has gone wrong
checks.expl: The quiet plants a question, and any question you raise implies you will answer it.

checks.q: Which failure does he call the bane of his existence?
opts: A beautiful reflection with no anecdote to carry it
A story that answers its questions too early
A thrilling anecdote that means absolutely nothing
Interviewees who explain the point instead of showing it
checks.expl: Without a moment of reflection, even a surprising sequence of events tells the listener nothing new.

spch100.2.3.takeaway: Dicks's essential stake is the elephant: an early, clear signal of what the story is about and what could go wrong, which gives the audience a reason to stay — and which may turn into a different stake as the story develops.

beats.d: They make an audience worry, wonder, root for you or hope for your demise. They are what drives people to the end of a story.

beats.t: Why a speaker needs it more than a film
beats.d: Films have trailers, so we walk in knowing the stakes. When you start to speak, nobody knows what you are about to say.
A boy pulls a spoon out of a leaf pile, Dicks declares it the spoon of power, and now he must have it. Will he get the spoon? That question carries the story.
His tyre disintegrates a hundred miles from home; seven hours later all his money is in a stranger's hand and the tank is empty. How will he get home?
On a widower's porch, lying about a charity, getting home stops mattering. The new stake is how he will face what he has done.
A pitch, a keynote, a product launch all need one. 'I have been waiting two and a half years to tell you this' is an elephant.

spch100.2.3.worked: In the first thirty seconds, state the situation that creates the question, not a summary of the story: where you are, what you want, what is in the way. Every later sentence then reads as a step toward the answer.
spch100.2.3.watch: A cheap hook — a shocking first line unrelated to what the story is really about. The elephant has to be the question the story actually answers, at least for now.

checks.q: Why does a spoken story need an elephant more than a film does?
opts: Films can show the danger, while a speaker can only describe it
Films have trailers, so their audience already knows the stakes
Live audiences are less patient than people sitting in a cinema
A spoken story is shorter, so it has less time to build stakes
checks.expl: A film audience arrives knowing what kind of story it is. A listener has no idea until you tell them.

checks.q: What does it mean that an elephant can change colour?
opts: The narrator can switch from one character's view to another's
The tone can darken as the story goes on, from comic to sad
The ending can reveal that the stake was never real in the first place
The main stake can shift as the story turns, as on the widower's porch
checks.expl: The first stake gets the audience in; a new one can take over once the story turns.

checks.q: Which of these openings is an elephant?
opts: My tyre has just disintegrated, I have no phone and no money, and I am a hundred miles from home.
This is a story about loneliness, and about a stranger who taught me what it means.
I want to tell you about something that happened to me once, years ago, on a very long drive home.
Let me start with some background about my family, my car, and why I was on that road at all.
checks.expl: It gives the listener a question to hold — how will he get home? — without summarising the story.

spch100.2.4.takeaway: Stanton's craft notes from Pixar: know the punchline, make a promise, make the audience care, and let them assemble the meaning themselves — two plus two, never four.

beats.d: Know your ending, and make everything from the first sentence to the last lead toward it.
The greatest story commandment. You stop flicking channels on the one programme that made you care, and that is by design.
A good beginning promises the story will be worth the time — like a pebble pulled back in a slingshot.
Audiences are born problem-solvers and want to work for their meal without noticing. A well-organised absence of information draws them in.
Short-term tension (will Dory forget?) running inside long-term tension (will they find Nemo?), built on honest conflict.
Characters have an inner drive they cannot escape; stories die when things go static; a theme runs underneath; and the rarest ingredient is wonder.
Not plot or fact, but a truth you have felt — Marlin's promise to Nemo came from a boy told he would not live.

spch100.2.4.worked: Take the emotional peak of your story and remove the sentence that names the emotion. Replace it with two concrete details from which the listener can work the emotion out. That is two plus two.
spch100.2.4.watch: Giving the audience four: explaining the feeling, the lesson and the meaning outright. It feels clear to the teller and leaves the listener with nothing to do — and nothing to care about.

checks.q: What does Stanton mean by 'give them two plus two, not four'?
opts: Give the audience two examples for every point you want them to learn
Let the audience assemble the meaning from the clues you provide
Tell the audience the meaning twice, so nobody can possibly miss it
Keep each story to two short scenes, so it ends in under four minutes
checks.expl: The audience wants to work for its meal; the order and choice of elements decides whether they engage.

checks.q: How does he define drama, quoting William Archer?
opts: Conflict between what we want and fear
A beginning, a middle and a turning point
Anticipation mingled with uncertainty
Surprise followed quickly by relief
checks.expl: Have you made the audience want to know what happens next, and how it will all end?

checks.q: What does he call the greatest story commandment?
opts: Make me care
Know your audience
Never use dialogue
End with a twist
checks.expl: Emotionally, intellectually or aesthetically — just make me care.

spch100.2.5.takeaway: Vonnegut draws stories as curves of fortune over time and shows that a handful of shapes — man in a hole, boy gets girl, Cinderella — are what audiences actually respond to.

beats.d: Up the side runs fortune, from sickness and poverty to wealth and boisterous health; along the bottom runs time, from beginning to end. It is the shape of the curve that matters.
Start a little above average, fall into trouble, climb out again. People never get sick of it.
An ordinary day, an ordinary person; they find something wonderful, lose it, and get it back.
She starts at the bottom, rises with each gift from the fairy godmother, drops at midnight — but not to the bottom, because she will remember the dance — and ends off the scale.

spch100.2.5.worked: Before telling a story, sketch its curve on a napkin. If the line never dips, there is no trouble to get out of; if it never rises, you have only bad news. The dip-and-recovery is what holds a listener.
spch100.2.5.watch: Telling a flat line — a pleasant sequence of events with no fall and no recovery — and wondering why nobody leans in.

checks.q: What do Vonnegut's two axes represent?
opts: Tension (low to high) and time (start to finish)
Fortune (ill to good) and time (beginning to end)
Character (weak to strong) and the length of the plot
Fortune (poor to rich) and the number of events
checks.expl: The G-I axis is good fortune to ill fortune; the B-E axis is beginning to end.

checks.q: Why does Cinderella not fall back to the bottom at midnight?
opts: The fairy godmother promises to come back for her
She still has one glass slipper as proof of the night
The prince starts searching for her straight away
She will remember the dance for the rest of her life
checks.expl: The loss is real but she ends above where she began, because the memory stays.

checks.q: Which shape is 'somebody gets into trouble and gets out of it again'?
opts: Man in a hole
Boy gets girl
Cinderella
A flat line
checks.expl: Vonnegut says people never tire of it.

spch100.2.6.takeaway: Watching Dicks build a story live from a homework-for-life entry shows the craft as a chain of decisions: know the change, open on its opposite, start as late as possible, aim every beat at the end.

beats.t: Find it in the last 72 hours
beats.d: He scans three days of entries and picks a film night with his sixteen-year-old daughter. Within 72 hours there is nearly always something worth telling.
Before telling it he names what he is trying to say — how often will moments like this happen again? — and asks what its opposite is. That becomes the beginning.
He opens during the car chase with minutes of the film left, not when they arrive at the cinema.

beats.t: The ending found in the telling
beats.d: Mid-story he remembers watching her walk into the house from the car. Profound moments often happen in benign places — alone at the wheel, in a drive-through queue.

beats.t: End on the wish, not the hug
beats.d: He closes hoping she will agree to a make-up cuddle. An unresolved ending keeps the story alive in the listener.
First what worked, then what did not: a bloated opening, too little suspense, stakes he could raise. A B minus — still better than most stories told at dinner.
His son's tale of smuggled dead crabs was an anecdote until a question found the change: I don't believe people; I have to learn for myself.

spch100.2.6.worked: Ask 'what changed in me?' and write it as 'from X to Y'. The first sentence lives in X as close to the change as possible; the last lives in Y. If you cannot find an X, probe the meaning further or accept it is an anecdote.
spch100.2.6.watch: Starting at the chronological beginning — 'so we got to the cinema'. Every sentence before the stakes appear is a sentence the audience spends waiting for a reason to care.

checks.q: What does 'start with the end' mean in Dicks's method?
opts: Tell the ending first, then flash back to how you got there
Know the change you are trying to convey before you begin
State the moral of the story in your very first sentence
Memorise your last line so you never lose your way to it
checks.expl: You cannot aim at an ending you have not chosen; the change you want to convey decides everything else.

checks.q: If you cannot find an opposite of your final moment to begin with, what is most likely true?
opts: You have an anecdote, or have not yet found what the moment means
The story should be told backwards, starting from the last moment
The story needs more detail before its shape will become clear
The final moment is too small, and a bigger one should replace it
checks.expl: His son's crab story became a story only once a question uncovered what it meant.

checks.q: Why does he prefer ending on the wish for a hug rather than the hug?
opts: The hug itself would sound too sentimental to tell
He wasn't sure the hug ever actually happened
Ending on the hug would make the story run too long
An open ending keeps the story alive in the listener
checks.expl: People wonder what happened next, and the story keeps working in them.

spch100.2.7.takeaway: Tamsen Webster takes Randy Olson's And, But, Therefore — the three acts of a story in three words — and adds a Yet for the moment of truth that makes the resolution persuasive.

beats.d: Two pieces of information that set the scene: stories are powerful, and there is plenty of advice about them.
The problem: we rarely have time to apply that advice to our messages.
The resolution: we need simpler ways to give messages a story's shape.
The moment of truth inside the second act — the extra fact that makes the audience agree with the Therefore. Here: the easier something is, the more likely we are to use it.

spch100.2.7.worked: When you have ten seconds to prepare, say four lines: the situation (And), the problem (But), the fact that changes their mind (Yet), and what should happen (Therefore). It is a story's skeleton without the story.
spch100.2.7.watch: A Yet that is just another restatement of the problem. If deleting it changes nothing, the audience has not been given a reason to accept your Therefore.

checks.q: Which act of a story does the 'But' stand for?
opts: The setup, or background
The conflict, or problem
The resolution, or fix
The moral, or takeaway
checks.expl: And is setup, But is conflict, Therefore is resolution.

checks.q: What does Webster's added 'Yet' supply?
opts: A second problem that raises the stakes just before the resolution
A joke that relaxes the audience before the hard part arrives
The moment of truth that makes the audience accept the resolution
A summary of the setup, so the audience remembers the context
checks.expl: It is the extra piece of information that persuades the audience the Therefore follows.

checks.q: When is this structure most useful?
opts: When the audience already agrees with you and needs no persuading
When you must shape a message quickly, with no time for a full story
When the story runs longer than ten minutes and needs firm signposts
When you are writing a report rather than speaking to an audience
checks.expl: She presents it as the fast way to apply story structure on the fly.

spch100.3.0.takeaway: Dicks revisits Homework for Life: the daily note gets sharper with practice, and the bank pays off when you need a story for a message — you match a small personal moment to it by adjacency instead of borrowing someone else's.

beats.t: The person with the most stories wins
beats.d: The best storytellers have the most stories to choose from. He started Homework for Life because he was running out.
If his family would only be returned for a story about today, which moment would he tell? Two columns: the date, and a line or two.
In 2015 he noticed 1.3 moments a day, mostly things he did. Last year it was 7.8 — including things heard, said or only thought — because the lens got sharper, not his life.
Most people remember perhaps fifty days of a year with any clarity. A daily record turns a year back into 365 days.
A contract manager wanted his team to be more specific. Dicks hates pickles and always tells servers not to put one on the plate — a story about being specific.
The manager wanted to use the pickle story himself. It would land the message but reveal nothing about him, and revealing yourself is what makes people connect.

spch100.3.0.worked: Write the message you need ('be specific', 'ask before you build'). Scan your bank for a small personal moment where you behaved that way about something unrelated. Tell the moment, then bridge: 'that is how I want us to be about X.'
spch100.3.0.watch: Borrowing a good story from someone else. It may land, but it costs you the thing a story is for: the audience learning something true about the person in front of them.

checks.q: How many moments a day was Dicks noticing in 2015, compared with recently?
opts: About 1.3 then, about 7.8 now
About 5 then, about 5 now
About 10 then, about 3 now
One a week then, one a day now
checks.expl: His life did not get more interesting; the lens got sharper, and he now counts things heard, said or thought.

checks.q: What does matching a story 'by adjacency' mean?
opts: Telling your stories in the order they happened, one after another
Choosing a story from the same industry as the message you need
Using a small personal moment that mirrors the message's behaviour
Placing two stories side by side so the audience compares them
checks.expl: The pickle story is about restaurants, not contracts, but it carries exactly the behaviour he wants.

checks.q: Why shouldn't the manager simply use Dicks's pickle story?
opts: It belongs to Dicks, and a borrowed story always sounds second-hand
It is about restaurants, so his team wouldn't see the connection to contracts
It reveals nothing about the manager, which is where a story's power is
It is too long to tell in a team meeting about contracts
checks.expl: The more we reveal about ourselves, the more connected the audience gets.

spch100.3.1.takeaway: No life is too boring for stories; the difference is noticing. The observant teller treats the mind's small flags — frustration, surprise, laughter — as stories arriving.

beats.d: The comforting belief that great speakers simply have more interesting lives. It is an excuse.

beats.t: No boring stories, only boring storytellers
beats.d: A rough truth, and an important one.

beats.t: The friend with the ordinary life
beats.d: Work, a baby, cafés, the daycare, cycling home — and always a story about the coffee queue or the barista, because she was observant.
Deciding that you are one is what changes what you see.
When you are frustrated, surprised or laughing, your mind raises a flag that says pay attention. Most of the time we let those moments fly past.

spch100.3.1.worked: At the end of a day, list the moments your mind raised a flag — irritation, surprise, a laugh — however trivial. Those, not the day's events, are your raw material.
spch100.3.1.watch: Looking for events. The observant friend's days held no events at all; what she had was a habit of noticing.

checks.q: What is 'boring life syndrome'?
opts: A fear that your own life is too dull to interest an audience
The belief that good speakers just have more interesting lives
Telling the same few stories so often that they go stale
Being so bored at work that nothing seems worth noticing
checks.expl: It is seductive because it excuses us from noticing our own material.

checks.q: Which of these is the 'flag' the speaker describes?
opts: A sudden moment of frustration, surprise or laughter
A notification that someone has mentioned you online
A deadline that forces you to look back over your week
A compliment from your boss that you want to remember
checks.expl: Those reactions are the mind saying: pay attention, something happened here.

checks.q: Why did the friend with an ordinary life have so many stories?
opts: She travelled more than most people and met strangers
She worked as a writer and practised every single day
She was observant and saw the world as a storyteller
She exaggerated small events until they sounded big
checks.expl: Her life was not extraordinary; her noticing was.

spch100.3.2.takeaway: A speaker's simplest capture habit: when something strikes you as curious, odd or frustrating, take a photo into a folder called Stories. When a talk needs an illustration, scan the folder.

beats.d: A hotel suggestion box with no paper or pens, a rental car tyre botched with glue and four and a half hours stranded, a cooking class on mole with up to a hundred ingredients.
Each was a moment that sparked curiosity or frustration, and each took two seconds to capture.
When preparing a talk or a video and the point needs an illustration, scan the folder of hundreds of moments.
We all have thousands of stories; we just forget to record them. 'I don't have a story' is not believable.
Presentations, interviews and pitches all tell a story about a product, a person or an idea.

spch100.3.2.worked: Make the capture smaller than the decision: photograph first, decide later. When preparing anything, open the folder before you open a blank page.
spch100.3.2.watch: Trying to remember the moment instead of recording it. The flat tyre feels unforgettable for a week and is gone in a month.

checks.q: What should go into the Stories folder?
opts: Only photos of events important enough to build a talk on
Anything that piques your curiosity, interest or frustration
Photos of audiences, so you remember who laughed and when
Slides from other speakers' talks that you thought worked
checks.expl: The test is that it caught your attention, not that it was important.

checks.q: When is the folder used?
opts: When preparing a talk or video and a point needs a story
At the end of each year, to choose the best story to tell
Every week, to post the best photo straight to social media
Never; capturing the moment is the whole of the exercise
checks.expl: It replaces searching a blank memory under pressure.

checks.q: Why does the speaker not believe clients who say they have no stories?
opts: Everyone has been on holiday, and holidays are full of stories
Clients exaggerate how little has happened to them, out of modesty
We all have thousands of stories and simply fail to record them
A good speaker can invent a story when no true one is available
checks.expl: We are walking story banks that forget to keep a record.

spch100.3.3.takeaway: Two exercises for an empty story bank: Homework for Life to catch new moments as they happen, and First-Last-Best-Worst to dig old ones out of the past.

beats.d: Every day ask which moment you would tell a story about; write the date, the moment, and optionally a lesson. Early entries feel trivial — that is normal.
A pool of stories, more mindfulness as you walk around, and patterns: you start to see what triggers you and how you react.
Across the top: first, last, best, worst. Down the side: prompts such as gift, car, teacher, pet, holiday.

beats.t: One or two words per cell
beats.d: Do not write stories yet; just get the memories down.
Scan the table for the memories that make you think 'that could be a story' — roughly half will be new ideas.

spch100.3.3.worked: Fill the grid fast, without judging, in one sitting. Then star two cells and run each through the five-second-moment test: what changed in me?
spch100.3.3.watch: Writing full stories into the grid. It slows you down, you fill four cells instead of twenty, and the best memories surface late.

checks.q: What are the four column headings of the grid?
opts: Who, what, where, when
First, last, best, worst
Past, present, future, never
Happy, sad, angry, afraid
checks.expl: Each prompt — gift, car, teacher — is asked four ways.

checks.q: How much should you write in each cell?
opts: A full paragraph, so you don't lose the details
Only the date, and fill the rest in later
One or two words to remember the memory
Nothing at all until you can name the lesson
checks.expl: Speed matters; developing the story comes later.

checks.q: How do the two exercises differ?
opts: Homework for Life catches new moments; the grid digs out past ones
Homework for Life is for business stories; the grid is for personal ones
The grid is done once a week; Homework for Life is done every month
The grid catches new moments; Homework for Life digs into the past
checks.expl: One trains your eye forward, the other mines your memory.

spch100.3.4.takeaway: Aaker's family rules for creating signature stories, not just finding them: carve out areas of incompetence, be sneaky and brand ordinary days as special, seek highs and lows, and bank the results — six words is enough.

beats.d: Her father cannot take a photograph; her husband needs a full protocol before he can take the bins out. Cheerful incompetence generates stories — and spares you the job.
Her father took the children on outings he wanted and called them special days. Those are the ones they remember.
Signature stories are not winning after winning. They need an arc — like James Bond or Jurassic Park.
Long queues, a dead phone, an au pair with heatstroke. Written up honestly in the holiday card, it became the best story — and people remember the peak and the end.
Six-word stories ('Married the wrong girl. Fixed it.'). Ask 'what was the story of today?' instead of 'what did you do today?'

spch100.3.4.worked: When a day goes badly, decide while it is happening that it will be a story: notice the details, take the photo of the unhappy moment, and write the six words that night.
spch100.3.4.watch: Only banking wins. A collection of successes has no arc, and nobody asks to hear it twice.

checks.q: Why carve out an area of incompetence?
opts: It keeps you humble, which makes you easier to trust
It generates stories and spares you a task
It hands responsibility to someone who enjoys it
It shows the family that experts are boring
checks.expl: Her father's photography and her husband's bins are both stories and both chores avoided.

checks.q: What did her father do with outings the children did not want?
opts: Cancelled them and promised a better day out later
Paid the children a little to come along anyway, as a bribe
Branded them as special days, which made them memorable
Went alone and told them about it at dinner
checks.expl: Anticipating something as special made it remembered as special.

checks.q: Why was the bad Disneyland day worth recording?
opts: A signature story needs highs and lows, and people remember the peak and the end
The tickets were so expensive that the family felt it had to get its money's worth
Bad days are funnier to retell than good ones, so they are the better stories
It made the children laugh at the time, which is what a signature story needs
checks.expl: Designing for memories rather than experiences is what creates a life of stories.

spch100.3.5.takeaway: Philipp Humm's twelve lessons fall into two groups: how to get more stories (say yes to fear, find magic in the mundane, use 'how are you?' as practice, keep a bank) and how to tell them (start near the challenge, zoom in, quote the dialogue and your inner voice, give the why, show the change).

beats.d: Dan Martell skipped his teenage years of drugs and crime because they made him emotional. Success impresses people; struggle changes them.
A workshop participant spent 93 seconds on job title and background before his story began, and lost the room.
Not the helicopter shot ('I faced a big challenge') but the trench: where am I, what am I doing, thinking, feeling, hearing?
Outer dialogue ('Phillip, what the hell was that?') and inner dialogue ('how am I going to turn this around?') make the story play like a film.
Beginners give events, amateurs give the goal, pros give the reason it mattered. Memorable stories show a moment of change.
Say yes to what scares you; find magic in the mundane with Homework for Life; answer 'how are you?' with a tiny true story; keep a story bank.

spch100.3.5.worked: Before telling a moment, close your eyes and answer the five zoom questions aloud. Use one sensory detail, one quoted line, and one line of inner voice. Cut the background.
spch100.3.5.watch: Staying in the helicopter: 'it was a stressful period at work'. Nothing is visible, so nothing is felt.

checks.q: What does 'zooming in' mean in Humm's war-film image?
opts: Describing the whole battlefield before showing any one soldier
Dropping into one specific scene with its sights, sounds and thoughts
Cutting quickly between scenes so the story moves at the pace of a film
Telling the story from the point of view of someone watching from afar
checks.expl: Ask where am I, what am I doing, thinking, feeling and hearing.

checks.q: According to Humm, what separates a pro storyteller from an amateur?
opts: Starting with background, so the audience knows who you are
Sharing what the goal was clearly, before saying how it went
Sharing why the goal mattered, not just what the goal was
Ending with a lesson stated plainly, so nobody can miss it
checks.expl: The what gives information; the why gives emotion.

checks.q: What does he suggest doing when someone asks 'how are you?'
opts: Tell a tiny, true story from your day
Say 'busy' and ask how they are instead
Ask them first, then match their answer
Change the subject to something funnier
checks.expl: Make your life the arena: every small exchange is practice.

spch100.3.6.takeaway: Ira Glass on the part nobody tells you: finding a decent story takes as long as producing it, a good team kills a third to a half of what it tries, and luck comes from putting enough material through your hands.

beats.d: We imagine the real work is shooting and editing; often finding the decent story takes longer than making it.
His staff do nothing but look for stories and try them, and kill between a third and a half of everything they try.
When the feeling you had is not in the tape, kill it. Killing it makes room for something better.

beats.t: Everything is trying to be crap
beats.d: Like entropy: anything you record drifts toward pointless, digressive and boring unless you prop it up aggressively at every stage.
Do enough interviews every week that once a month you stumble on something so good it pays for the other weeks.

spch100.3.6.worked: Treat your story bank as a pipeline, not a vault: try stories out loud on friends, keep the ones that land, and cut the rest without arguing with yourself.
spch100.3.6.watch: Keeping a story because you loved the moment, even though it falls flat every time you tell it. The feeling you had is not automatically in the telling.

checks.q: Roughly what share of the stories his team tries end up killed?
opts: Almost none, once a story is chosen
Between a third and a half
About nine in every ten tried
Exactly one in every ten
checks.expl: And he describes the team as among the best at the job.

checks.q: What does he mean by 'all production is trying to be crap'?
opts: Equipment fails so often that most recordings can't be used in the end at all
Interviewees perform for the microphone, so most of what they say is fake
Material drifts toward pointless and boring unless you fight it at every stage
Audiences are so hard to please that most finished stories will disappoint
checks.expl: He compares it to entropy.

checks.q: How do you put yourself in a position to get lucky?
opts: Do enough material on a schedule that a great story turns up every month
Wait for a story that excites you, and only then commit time to producing it
Only chase big stories, since small ones rarely become great ones in the end
Study stories that worked before and copy their structure as closely as you can
checks.expl: Volume on a schedule is what produces the rare great one.

spch100.3.7.takeaway: Ira Glass's best-known advice: for years your taste will be better than your work, which is why most people quit — and the only way to close the gap is a large volume of work on a deadline.

beats.d: You want to make things because you love them, so your taste is good from the start.
For the first couple of years what you make is not that good, and your taste is good enough to tell. Many people quit there.
Nearly everyone he knows who does interesting creative work spent years in that phase. It is normal.
Finish one story every week or month, ideally with someone expecting it. Only volume closes the gap.
He plays a clip of himself eight years in: ill-conceived writing, every third word stressed. Talk the way people normally talk.

spch100.3.7.worked: Set a weekly deadline with an external witness — someone who expects the recording on Friday — and keep it even when the piece disappoints you.
spch100.3.7.watch: Waiting until the work matches your taste before you put it out. The work only catches up through the volume you are postponing.

checks.q: What is 'the gap' Glass describes?
opts: The time it takes to go from one finished project to the next
The distance between your good taste and your not-yet-good work
The distance between what your audience wants and what you make
The pause a skilled storyteller leaves before the key line lands
checks.expl: You can see your work disappoints you precisely because your taste is good.

checks.q: What does he say closes the gap?
opts: Better equipment, once you can afford it
Waiting until inspiration finally arrives
Studying the theory of story before writing
A large volume of work on a deadline
checks.expl: Ideally with someone waiting for the work, even if they do not pay you.

checks.q: What delivery fault does he point out in his own year-eight tape?
opts: Stressing every third word instead of talking the way people talk
Speaking so fast that the listener couldn't follow the story at all
Pausing so often that the story lost all of its forward momentum
Reading from notes, so his voice sounded flat and rehearsed throughout
checks.expl: Underlining every third word for emphasis sounds unnatural.

spch100.4.0.takeaway: Julian Treasure's TED talk in three parts: seven habits that make people stop listening, four foundations that spell HAIL, and a toolbox of register, timbre, prosody, pace, pitch and volume — warmed up before anything important.

beats.d: Gossip, judging, negativity, complaining, excuses, exaggeration that turns into lying, and dogmatism.
Honesty, authenticity, integrity, love. Love tempers honesty, and it is hard to judge someone while wishing them well.
Nose, throat or chest: depth carries authority. Timbre — rich, smooth, warm — can be trained with breathing, posture and exercises.
Avoid one note and avoid making every statement sound like a question. Use silence. Get quiet to draw people in.
Arms up and sigh, lip buzz, tongue la-la, rolled R, and the siren from high to low.

spch100.4.0.worked: Before an interview, do the warm-up in the corridor (the siren if you only have time for one), then say your opening line once from the chest, slowly, with silence before the key word.
spch100.4.0.watch: Upspeak: making every sentence end like a question. It takes away a prosody tool you need for real questions and makes statements sound unsure.

checks.q: What does HAIL stand for?
opts: Humour, anecdote, insight, and a lesson
Honesty, authenticity, integrity, love
Hear, acknowledge, inquire, then lead
Honesty, attention, intention, listening
checks.expl: Four foundations to stand on so that what you say is welcomed.

checks.q: Where does Treasure say to speak from when you want weight?
opts: The nose
The throat
The chest
The head voice
checks.expl: He links depth to perceived power and authority.

checks.q: Which warm-up does he say he would keep if he could only do one?
opts: The siren, from high 'we' to low 'aw'
The lip buzz, held on one long breath
The rolled R, to wake up the tongue
The long sigh, from high to low
checks.expl: He says the pros call it the siren.

spch100.4.1.takeaway: Vinh Giang's five foundations — rate, volume, pitch as melody, tonality, and the pause — coached live on a student, then applied to accents, interviews, imitation and nerves. The voice is behaviour, so it can change.

beats.t: You are not trapped in your voice
beats.d: Changing your mouth movements and breath changes how you sound. The way you speak is a set of behaviours.
Vary the rate. Speak at a five, not a three. Use melody, because a song sticks and a page does not. Let your face carry the emotion. Pause.
A student answers 3-2-1 style, then again with more volume, gestures and a lower pitch at the end of sentences, then with long pauses and no opening 'so'.
Record twenty improvised minutes, send it to a speech pathologist for pronunciation and to an ESL teacher for grammar, then fix one thing at a time.
Spend 5–10 per cent of the time on connection: answer 'tell me about yourself' with a prepared story. Copy great speakers the way a chef copies recipes, then add your own lemon.
Burn off adrenaline with a quick walk or push-ups, use breathing, and focus on the audience. When an unused part of your voice feels fake, tell yourself it is only unfamiliar.

spch100.4.1.worked: His interview answer: a prepared story (selling MP3 players at 13, and what it taught him about selling the wrong way and the right way), linked to the job, takes about three minutes and builds rapport before the questions start.
spch100.4.1.watch: Calling an unfamiliar voice 'fake'. It is the same instrument — you have just never used those keys, and calling them fake stops you exploring.

checks.q: Why does Giang compare a song with a page of a book?
opts: Songs are shorter, so the listener can hold the whole thing in their head
Both hold about as many words, but the melody makes the song memorable
A song repeats its chorus, so repetition is what makes it stick
Reading a page aloud is harder than singing, so it sounds flat
checks.expl: So speaking with more melody makes what you say stick.

checks.q: What does he say causes a monotone voice?
opts: Speaking too fast to let the pitch move
Too much volume, which flattens the melody
A monotone body — including a neutral face
Reading from notes instead of talking
checks.expl: Your face controls the emotion under your words.

checks.q: What is his advice for someone worried about their accent?
opts: Have a speech pathologist and an ESL teacher review twenty improvised minutes
Copy one native speaker's accent exactly, sound by sound, until it is yours
Slow right down and fix every sound at once, so the accent fades in weeks
Keep quiet in meetings until a coach says your accent has become neutral
checks.expl: Then work on one thing at a time, so you do not freeze up.

spch100.4.2.takeaway: Roger Love, interviewed on MarieTV: the voice you have is one you imitated, monotone and timid volume are learned, the falling pitch at every full stop makes people sound sad, and nose breathing saves the voice.

beats.d: We copied our parents to connect with them. That outdated voice may now be holding you back, and you can build a new one.
He argues that sounds carry the emotion that gets a message remembered, and that great songwriters are storytellers who move you from emotion to emotion in three minutes.
Most people use one or two notes. Loud on one note sounds angry; loud with melody sounds happy.
Dropping in pitch at every comma and full stop, as children are taught, sounds sad. He recommends lifting instead.
You need different voices for work and home. Close your lips and breathe through your nose at the full stops so the voice lasts.

spch100.4.2.worked: The voicemail test: record a greeting, listen back, and notice what you settle for. That settled-for voice is the one everyone hears. Keep recording until the melody goes up and down.
spch100.4.2.watch: The coaches in this unit disagree. Giang tells a student to end sentences lower for authority; Love says lift the ends for warmth; Treasure warns against making every statement sound like a question. Use all three: lift inside the sentence for warmth, land the key claim low, and never end every line on a question.

checks.q: According to Love, why does loud speech sometimes sound angry?
opts: Volume always sounds angry, so drop it whenever you can
It is loud and stays on one note — with melody it sounds happy
Loud voices push the pitch up, and a high pitch always sounds tense
It is loud and fast — slowing down makes the same volume calm
checks.expl: Volume mixed with melody is heard as energy, not anger.

checks.q: What is the 'descending scale'?
opts: A singing exercise that walks the voice down from the high notes to low
Getting quieter and quieter toward the end of every sentence you say
Dropping pitch at every comma and full stop, which he says sounds sad
Slowing down at the end of a talk so the last point lands heavily
checks.expl: He traces it back to how children are taught to read aloud.

checks.q: What does he say is the main reason speakers lose their voice?
opts: Breathing in through the mouth
Speaking too loudly for too long
Not warming up before speaking
Talking too fast without pausing
checks.expl: The nose moistens the air; breathe through it at commas and full stops.

spch100.4.3.takeaway: Rebecca Martin on the pause: why it works (time to think, time to process, and a sign of status), how to make it natural (tie it to a breath), and the three places it pays off most (before you start, around your main message, and at transitions).

beats.d: You get time to think, the audience gets time to process, and it shows you think your words are worth waiting for. Rushing comes across as junior.
Breathe in, speak at the top of the breath, finish the thought as the breath runs out, then breathe in again. That in-breath is the pause.
Read an article aloud and take a full breath at every full stop.
Three breaths and eye contact with three people. It feels too long; in practice it becomes one and a half breaths, and the room's attention goes up.
Pause around your key line and stay with the audience while you do. Plan pauses between sections, where moving or a sip of water is fine.

spch100.4.3.worked: She delivers a line ('we are only scared of how powerful and beautiful we actually are') and holds the silence, breathing and checking in silently with the audience, before moving on.
spch100.4.3.watch: A pause in the wrong place — in the middle of a sentence, or after a weak point. A pause makes whatever comes just before it sound important.

checks.q: What does Martin say a natural pause must be tied to?
opts: A slide change
A gesture
A breath
A sip of water
checks.expl: When the thought runs out with the breath, the in-breath is the pause.

checks.q: What does she suggest before the first word of an important talk?
opts: Three breaths and eye contact with three people
A short joke to relax the room before you begin
Thanking the organisers and the audience warmly
Reading the agenda aloud so people know the plan
checks.expl: It settles your nerves and signals that something important is about to happen.

checks.q: What does rushing through your content tell the audience, according to her?
opts: That you are well prepared and know the material inside out
That you are of junior status and do not want to take up their time
That the material is easy, so the audience can follow it quickly
That you are excited about the topic and want to share every bit of it
checks.expl: Pausing shows you are secure in your role and in the value you bring.

spch100.4.4.takeaway: Alex Lyon's five habits that come across as confidence even when you are nervous: eye contact (one thought, one look), an occasional smile, a planted ready position, gestures from a home base, and pauses with a nod.

beats.d: About 90 per cent of the time, three to five seconds per person, everyone in the room several times. Glance at notes and come straight back.
A stone face looks like a deer in the headlights. Smiling relaxes you and warms up your eye contact.
Feet shoulder-width apart, weight forward, knees soft, no swaying. Walk with a purpose, then stop and plant again.
Home base: hands loosely together at the waist, or relaxed at your sides. A small gesture about once a sentence.
One second after a sentence, two after a key idea, and a small nod. Audiences tend to nod back.

spch100.4.4.worked: Practise 'one thought, one look' out loud: say half a sentence to one person, move your eyes as the next half starts, and repeat until it is automatic.
spch100.4.4.watch: The advice to look over people's heads. It may calm you, but nobody feels connected, so it does not look confident.

checks.q: How long does Lyon suggest looking at each person?
opts: Under a second each, so nobody feels singled out
About three to five seconds — one thought, one look
As long as they keep looking back at you, then move
About ten seconds each, so they feel fully seen
checks.expl: Long enough to finish a thought and for them to feel a connection.

checks.q: What is the 'ready position'?
opts: Feet together, hands clasped in front, weight resting back on the heels
One foot slightly forward, leaning on the lectern with both hands
Hands in pockets, weight on the heels, shifting gently side to side
Feet shoulder-width apart, weight on the balls of the feet, knees soft
checks.expl: Plant from the waist down; be animated from the waist up.

checks.q: What does he recommend adding to the longer pauses?
opts: A small nod
A sip of water
A glance at the slides
A smile at the floor
checks.expl: It looks confident and audiences tend to nod along.

spch100.4.5.takeaway: A communication coach's three levels — rookie, pretty good, natural — assessed on voice, body and words. You move up by first getting self-awareness, then using your full range, and finally having more than one way to make any point.

beats.d: Flat delivery, vocal fry, filler words in every breath, a body that does nothing, no structure. He calls them habits, not who you are.
Two unscripted minutes on camera, transcribed, so you can see the filler words and the circling.
Range, but kept safe. A small set of gestures used over and over. Repeated, non-functional movement — he uses a speaker who keeps moving as the example.
Structures such as PREP and 3-2-1 filter your thinking so the listener does not have to sort it out.
All five vocal dials, purposeful body language, a face that matches the voice, and other ways to say the same thing: analogy, prop, story.

spch100.4.5.worked: 'Read more books' three ways: the analogy (reading is to the mind what exercise is to the body), the prop (a book holds years of someone's work), and the story (his father, after a half-million-dollar loss: every book you read is a soldier in your army).
spch100.4.5.watch: Moving without a reason. If a movement does not serve the message, it distracts — and small habits like touching your glasses add up.

checks.q: What does the coach say keeps 'pretty good' speakers stuck?
opts: They know no frameworks, so their points come out unstructured
Fear of judgment stops them using the edges of their range
Their accent makes them hold back from using much expression
Too much volume, which flattens the melody of what they say
checks.expl: And he says the fear is mostly false — people are thinking about themselves.

checks.q: How does he define non-functional behaviour?
opts: Any behaviour that distracts from the message
Any gesture made with both hands at once
Standing still when you could be moving
Any movement that you did not plan and rehearse in advance
checks.expl: If it does not serve the message, it should go.

checks.q: Why does the face matter as much as the voice?
opts: Cameras show the face up close, so it gets judged before the voice is heard
Smiling is polite, and people forgive a weak voice if the face is warm
If they see an emotion but don't hear it, or the reverse, they don't feel it
The face controls the voice, so a still face always makes a flat voice
checks.expl: Natural speakers match how they look to how they sound.

spch100.4.6.takeaway: Matt Abrahams of Stanford on nerves: anxiety has symptoms and sources, and you deal with both. Then the tools that reduce the fear of forgetting — a goal (know, feel, do), a structure (what, so what, now what), and a lower bar for speaking on the spot.

beats.d: Fight or flight: faster heart, shallow breath, a thinner voice, sweating, dry mouth. All normal, and all unhelpful when you speak.
Belly breaths with an out-breath twice as long as the in-breath ('the rule of lung'); something cold in your palm if you blush or sweat.
Fear of a bad future outcome. Get present: move, play music, count back in sevens. And remember you are there to serve the audience.
It is hard to get lost with a map. Set a goal of what they should know, feel and do, then choose a structure — problem, solution, benefit, or what, so what, now what.
Reframe, lower your standard to doing what is needed, find out why you were asked, then structure. Feedback, apologies and Q&A all work this way.
Two or three themes, each backed by an example, a figure, and a third-party endorsement. Be concrete, invite people in, and use time-travel language: imagine, picture this, remember when.

spch100.4.6.worked: Feedback after a meeting in what / so what / now what: 'You went fast through the implementation plan' / 'so people may think it is not thought through' / 'next time, slow down and add detail.'
spch100.4.6.watch: Building the clock. When we are unsure, we keep adding to an answer that was already complete. Tell the time.

checks.q: What is Abrahams's 'rule of lung'?
opts: Breathe in for twice as long as you breathe out
Hold your breath before the first line
Breathe out for twice as long as you breathe in
Breathe through the mouth
checks.expl: The relaxation response happens on the out-breath.

checks.q: What does he say is the main source of speaking anxiety?
opts: Fear of not reaching a goal — a feared future outcome
Bright lights and a big room, which trigger fight or flight
Low blood sugar, which is why you should eat before speaking
The size of the audience — the bigger it is, the worse it gets
checks.expl: So the antidote is getting present.

checks.q: What are the three parts of his communication goal?
opts: A hook, a body, and a close that repeats it
What the audience should know, feel and do
Who you are, what you want, and why now
What, so what, and now what for the audience
checks.expl: Information, emotion, action.

spch100.4.7.takeaway: Patrick Winston's MIT lecture: speaking skill is knowledge and practice far more than talent. Start with a promise, cycle and fence your ideas, choose tools by purpose, be remembered through the star, and finish on your contributions and a salute rather than 'thank you'.

beats.d: He was a better skier than an Olympic gymnast because he had the knowledge and the practice. Quality depends on knowledge, practice and, much less, talent.
Not with a joke. With an empowerment promise.
Cycle three times, because a fifth of the room is drifting. Build a fence around your idea. Number the sections so people can get back on. Ask a question and wait — seven seconds is normal.
The board for teaching (its speed matches thinking, and it gives your hands a job); props for memory; slides for exposing ideas — few words, no reading aloud, no laser pointer.
Symbol, slogan, surprise, salient idea, story — what made his arch-learning work memorable by accident.
Collaborators go on the first slide; contributions go on the last. End with a joke, a benediction, or a salute — not 'thank you for listening'.

spch100.4.7.worked: His job-talk shape: within five minutes, a vision (a problem someone cares about plus a new approach) and evidence that you have done something (the steps needed); conclude by listing your contributions to mirror those steps.
spch100.4.7.watch: 'Thank you for listening' as the last words. It implies the audience stayed only out of politeness. Mouth a thank you once the applause starts.

checks.q: Why does Winston advise against opening with a joke?
opts: Jokes are unprofessional in a lecture with something to teach
People are still settling in and adjusting to your voice
A joke uses up the minutes you need for the empowerment promise
If the joke fails, the audience stops trusting the rest of the talk
checks.expl: A joke works at the end, once people are used to you.

checks.q: What are the five points of Winston's star?
opts: Hook, setup, punch, tag, callback
Problem, approach, steps, demo, contributions
Symbol, slogan, surprise, salient idea, story
Pace, pitch, pause, posture, presence
checks.expl: Each starts with S; together they make work recognisable.

checks.q: What should the final slide be labelled?
opts: Contributions
Any questions?
Thank you!
Conclusions
checks.expl: It stays up while people ask questions and leave, so it should say what you did.

spch100.5.0.takeaway: Marianna Pascal, after twenty years training Southeast Asian professionals: how well someone communicates in English has little to do with their level and a lot to do with their attitude. Speak it like a computer game — focused on the target — not like a piano exam where you are marked on mistakes.

beats.d: A factory supervisor with very low English who listened calmly and said exactly what he meant.
Her daughter dreaded piano because success meant few mistakes. Many learners bring the same dread to English.
In a cybercafe, a bad player watched by friends shows no embarrassment — all his attention is on the bad guys.
The fluent sales rep panics and talks in circles; the counter girl asks 'heart okay or not? brain okay or not?' and solves it.
For every native speaker there are five non-native speakers. English is a tool to get a result, not an art to master.
Trying to be correct and effective at the same time costs you your listening, your words, and your apparent confidence.

spch100.5.0.worked: The engineers' barbecue: 'the hot dog contains the cheese' fails three times; a Japanese engineer says 'cheese… integrator!' and everyone understands. That is real English working.
spch100.5.0.watch: Mistaking fluency for effectiveness. The sales rep had more English and got a worse result, because her attention was on herself.

checks.q: What does Pascal say how well people communicate in English mostly depends on?
opts: The size of their vocabulary
Their attitude towards English
How native their accent sounds
How many years they studied it
checks.expl: Faizal had a very low level and communicated beautifully.

checks.q: What is the 'one thing' she recommends?
opts: Avoid speaking up until your grammar is fluent enough to be correct
Learn ten new words a day so you never get stuck mid-sentence
Focus on the other person and the result you want, not on yourself
Watch films without subtitles until your ear can follow natives
checks.expl: Like the gamer focused on the target.

checks.q: Which three things does she say shut down when you try to be correct under pressure?
opts: Listening, speaking, and confidence
Memory, vocabulary, and grammar
Grammar, spelling, accent and pronunciation
Pace, pitch, and volume of voice
checks.expl: And listeners may mistake the third for a lack of ability.

spch100.5.1.takeaway: Tracey Derwing, co-author of a research book on pronunciation teaching: focus on intelligibility (how much is understood) and comprehensibility (how easy it is), not on removing every trace of accent — some very noticeable features hardly matter, and some quiet ones matter a lot.

beats.d: Intelligibility is how much the listener understands; comprehensibility is how much effort it costs them.
Many materials drill every difference from the local accent, but many differences never affect understanding.
Very noticeable, rarely important: listeners adjust to it almost immediately.
Pairs like p and b separate many words, so mixing them up costs much more understanding.
Research shows some speakers with heavy accents are very easy to understand. It depends which features are involved.

spch100.5.1.worked: Ask the listener, not the mirror. A word someone actually misheard is worth fixing; a sound that is merely 'not native' may not be worth your time.
spch100.5.1.watch: Spending months on the most noticeable sound in your accent because people comment on it, while a less noticeable stress or consonant problem keeps causing misunderstandings.

checks.q: What is comprehensibility?
opts: How much of what you say the listener understands
How close your accent is to a native speaker's
How much effort the listener needs to understand you
How native you sound to a listener from that country
checks.expl: Intelligibility is how much they understand; comprehensibility is how hard it is.

checks.q: Why does Derwing say the 'th' sounds deserve less attention than they get?
opts: Listeners adapt to them almost at once, so they rarely block understanding
Adults can't learn them, so time is better spent on other sounds
They are so rare in English that listeners hardly ever hear them
Native speakers often drop them too, so nobody notices the difference at all
checks.expl: They are salient, not important.

checks.q: What does 'high functional load' mean for a pair like p and b?
opts: It is the hardest pair for learners to hear, so it takes the longest to fix
It is the most noticeable accent feature, so listeners judge it first
It only matters in British English, where the pair is clearer
Many words differ only by that pair, so confusing it costs understanding
checks.expl: That is why it matters more than f versus th.

spch100.5.2.takeaway: Marc Green at TEDxHeidelberg argues for going beyond fluency to a native-like level — minimise your accent, learn the expressions locals actually use, and absorb cultural habits. This is the opposite view to the previous two lessons, and worth hearing in full.

beats.d: He copied down the Russian word for 'exit' as the name of his station — the story that started him learning languages.
About a quarter of the cards gets you basics; over half is fluency, when the language becomes subconscious. Mastery is slower and optional.
He calls it the most overlooked part of learning a language. The perfect-sentence technique: rate, hear, repeat, until no accent is heard.
Textbook French says 'le travail'; friends say 'mon boulot'. You learn these one at a time, from people.
Gestures, 'ouch' versus 'aïe', 'uh-huh' versus 'mm-hmm' — picked up through active listening.

spch100.5.2.worked: His tools when you are not living among native speakers: copy characters from TV shows, write down any expression you do not know, and learn song lyrics, because the emotion helps the phrases stick.
spch100.5.2.watch: The tension with Derwing and Pascal is real. Their evidence says intelligibility is enough for being understood; Green's claim is about social belonging, which is a different goal. Decide which one you are working on before you spend the hours.

checks.q: What is Green's 'perfect-sentence technique'?
opts: Writing one perfect sentence a day and asking a native speaker to correct it
Memorising one famous quotation a week, word for word, until it sounds natural
Saying one sentence to a native speaker until they hear no accent in it
Recording a full chapter of a book and comparing it with a native narrator
checks.expl: It can take a long time even for one sentence.

checks.q: Which three areas does he say take you to a native-like level?
opts: Accent, local expressions, cultural traits
Grammar, vocabulary and fluent spelling
Reading, writing, listening and speaking
Accent, grammar, and a much larger vocabulary
checks.expl: All three need contact with native speakers.

checks.q: How does his goal differ from Derwing's?
opts: He wants to be understood quickly; she wants learners to sound native
They have the same goal, but he gets there through accent work first
He is talking about written fluency; she is talking about speech
He aims to be accepted as one of the group, not just understood
checks.expl: Being understood and being treated as a native speaker are different targets.

spch100.5.3.takeaway: Safwat Saleem, an animator who stuttered as a child, stopped using his own voice after comments mocked his Pakistani accent — then realised that 'normal' is just what people have been exposed to, and that the only way to widen it is to keep speaking.

beats.d: 'Have you forgotten your name?' — what classmates said when he stuttered, and what people chant in his recurring dream.
Positive at first, then: 'his voice is annoying', 'can't follow because of the Indian accent'. He couldn't edit part two.
Ancient texts barely mention blue. One theory is that cultures only see a colour once they can make it.
Studies on bias suggest favouritism toward people we relate to. Few children's books show children of colour, so the circle of normal stays small.
He is using his voice in his work again, and says giving up is not an option.

spch100.5.3.worked: The talk is itself a model of story structure: a recurring dream opens it, the comments are the turning point, Homer's colours are the reflection, and it ends back on the voice — with jokes all the way through ('I clearly have a Pakistani accent').
spch100.5.3.watch: Hearing a comment about your accent as a verdict on your competence. Saleem's first reaction was to take it personally; the reframe was that it described the commenter's experience.

checks.q: Why does Saleem tell the story of Homer and the colour blue?
opts: To show that ancient people saw colours differently because their eyes were different
To show people only 'see' what they've been exposed to — and 'normal' works that way
To explain why he turned to animation rather than film to tell his own stories
To show that translation always loses meaning, as with an accent across languages
checks.expl: An accented narrator is not 'normal' only because few are heard.

checks.q: What did the online comments first make him do?
opts: Stop using his own voice in his work
Take accent classes to sound neutral
Hire a narrator for every new video
Delete the video and the comments
checks.expl: Until he understood what the comments were really about.

checks.q: Which comment does he correct on stage?
opts: That the video was too long — it was ten minutes
That he spoke too fast — he says it was nerves
That his voice was annoying — he says it isn't
That he had an Indian accent — it is Pakistani
checks.expl: One of several jokes in the talk.

spch100.5.4.takeaway: A short drill on English rhythm: content words (the information) are stressed and clear, function words are squeezed in between, so 'MICE EAT CHEESE' and 'the MICE might have been EATing the CHEESE' keep the same three beats.

beats.d: Content words — subject, verb, object — carry the information. Function words like the, a, in, will help but are not the main information.
MICE EAT CHEESE → THE MICE EAT THE CHEESE → … → THE MICE MIGHT HAVE BEEN EATING THE CHEESE.
More words, same rhythm: the stressed words stay evenly spaced.
'Might have been' becomes 'mitabin'. The content words are the loudest and clearest part.

spch100.5.4.worked: Clap on MICE, EAT and CHEESE and fit everything else between the claps. If a sentence gets slower as it gets longer, you are giving the function words full stress.
spch100.5.4.watch: Pronouncing every word clearly and equally. It sounds careful but makes the important words harder to pick out.

checks.q: Which of these is a content word?
opts: the
cheese
because
might
checks.expl: Nouns, main verbs and adjectives carry the information.

checks.q: What happens to the beat as function words are added?
opts: It stays about the same, with the function words squeezed in
It slows down a little with every function word that is added in
It gets a new beat for each word, so the sentence takes longer
It moves onto the function words, which become louder and longer
