checks.expl: English is timed by its stressed words.

checks.q: What should be the loudest and clearest part of the sentence?
opts: The function words
The final word
The content words
The opening word
checks.expl: That is what makes the rhythm English.

spch100.5.5.takeaway: Pronunciation with Emma on thought groups: we speak in short meaningful chunks with small breaks between them, link the words inside each chunk, and can change the meaning — or add emphasis — by moving the breaks.

beats.d: One pause separates inviting Grandma from eating her. Thought groups are what the pauses mark.
Breaks depend on meaning, emphasis and speed — but some splits sound natural and others make the listener work.
Keep subject and verb, and set phrases like 'in the middle of the night', together.
Too short means over-divided; out of breath means not divided enough.
Give a word its own chunk to make it stand out: 'I told you — repeatedly — I don't want to discuss it.'
Inside a chunk, words connect ('turn it off'). That is why native speech can be hard to follow, and why chunking yours helps others follow you.

spch100.5.5.worked: 'I told him naturally he'd have to pay.' With the break after 'him', naturally means of course he would pay. With the break after 'naturally', it describes how you told him.
spch100.5.5.watch: Pausing wherever you run out of words rather than where the meaning breaks. The listener then has to put the pieces together.

checks.q: What decides where a thought-group break goes?
opts: Wherever you need to breathe, so the breath sets the length
The meaning — words that belong to one idea stay together
The commas — break wherever the sentence has punctuation
The number of syllables, about five or six in each group
checks.expl: There are no fixed rules, but meaning is the guide.

checks.q: How can you emphasise a single word using thought groups?
opts: Say it faster
Put it at the end of the sentence
Give it its own short chunk
Repeat it twice
checks.expl: Isolating it draws the listener's attention.

checks.q: Where does linking between words happen?
opts: Inside a thought group, not across the breaks
Across the breaks, so the groups join smoothly
Only at the ends of sentences, before a pause
Nowhere in careful speech, only in fast speech
checks.expl: The chunk flows as one unit.

spch100.5.6.takeaway: A teacher's ten-step shadowing method, built on the view that most learners start shadowing too early: choose a short clip, understand it, take dictation, study it, repeat sentence by sentence, record and compare, shadow with and without the transcript, read aloud from memory — and then talk about it yourself.

beats.d: 30–90 seconds, one speaker, someone you would like to sound like, speaking clearly.
Listen for the gist and the emotion, then do a dictation to find what your ear misses.
Note phrases and collocations, and how they are said: stress, tone, rhythm. She calls this the most important stage.
One sentence at a time, for accuracy. Record it, compare it with the original, try again.
With the transcript, just behind the speaker; then blind, while walking or cooking.
Read it aloud from memory in the speaker's style, then speak about the same topic yourself.

spch100.5.6.worked: A clip about friendship becomes: shadow it, then talk for two minutes about what friendship means to you, using the phrases you just practised.
spch100.5.6.watch: Shadowing a whole film scene on day one. Without understanding and analysis you copy the sound roughly and learn little.

checks.q: Why does she recommend an optional dictation step?
opts: It is easier than shadowing, so it warms you up before the hard part
It replaces shadowing for learners who are not yet ready to speak aloud at all
It shows what your ears are not picking up, such as linking and reductions
It gives you a written transcript to read from while you shadow
checks.expl: The gaps in your dictation are your gaps in listening.

checks.q: What is 'blind shadowing'?
opts: Shadowing with your eyes closed to focus on the sound alone
Shadowing without the transcript, just behind the speaker
Shadowing a speaker you can only hear, not see, on the video
Reading the transcript silently while the speaker talks
checks.expl: It builds fluency and processing speed.

checks.q: What is the bonus step after the ten?
opts: Speak about the clip's topic yourself
Find a harder clip and start again
Write a summary of the clip from memory
Translate the clip into your own language
checks.expl: Shadowing should end in your own speech.

spch100.5.7.takeaway: Six habits for thinking directly in the language instead of translating: speak and accept mistakes, learn in chunks, listen a lot (for the big picture), link words to images, think out loud, and keep sentences short and simple.

beats.d: It slows you down so you miss your turn, and your sentences follow your first language's patterns.
Better to say it wrong and be corrected than stay silent translating. Note the correction.
Learn 'my name is…', not 'name'. A word-for-word version from Spanish or French ('I call myself…') sounds wrong.
Listen for the gist, not every word; connect words to images rather than translations.
Talk to yourself as you do chores. Keep it short and simple: the goal is communication, not poetry.

spch100.5.7.worked: Label things at home with sticky notes in English, so the first word you think of when you see the plant is the English one.
spch100.5.7.watch: Building the long, layered sentences you would use in your first language. That is the moment you start translating.

checks.q: What are 'chunks'?
opts: Groups of related words learned together, like food or travel
Whole natural phrases learned as a unit, like 'my name is'
Short pauses that split a sentence into easy-to-say pieces
Words translated in pairs, one from each language, to memorise
checks.expl: They avoid word-for-word translation.

checks.q: What does KISS stand for here?
opts: Keep it short and simple
Know idioms, speak slowly
Keep in step with speakers
Kind, interested, sincere, simple
checks.expl: Communication, not poetry.

checks.q: Why does translating in your head make your English less natural?
opts: Because it makes you use more idioms than natives do
Because it slows you down so much you lose your accent
Because it copies the structures of your first language
Because translated words are always more formal in English
checks.expl: Your English ends up sounding like a translation.

spch100.5.8.takeaway: How good storytellers in English move between tenses: past perfect for background, 'would' for routines, past simple for the main events, and the historical present to zoom in on the key moment. Notice it in what you listen to before forcing it into your own stories.

beats.d: Past simple once, past continuous in progress, used to for habits, present perfect for relevance now. Not wrong — but real storytellers move between tenses freely.
'By the time he recovered, the empire had already collapsed' — so the order of events is clear.
'For thousands of years, people had been…' — adds duration to the background.
'Every morning I would wake at six…' Then the past simple breaks it: 'one day the doorbell rang'.
'Two years later he catches sight of a young boy.' It brings the listener into the scene.

spch100.5.8.worked: The full pattern in one story: past perfect sets the scene, 'would' gives the routine, past simple says what happened, the present zooms into the moment.
spch100.5.8.watch: Switching tenses at random. The historical present works because it marks the moment that matters; used everywhere, it just sounds confused.

checks.q: What does the past perfect do in a story?
opts: Marks the climax, the moment everything in the story changes
Describes habits that happened again and again in the past
Shows something was already true before the story's moment
Shows what is going to happen later, after the story ends
checks.expl: It keeps the order of events clear.

checks.q: What is the historical present used for?
opts: Pulling the listener into a key moment, like zooming in
Setting out the background before the main events begin
Describing habits the narrator had at that time in life
Wrapping the story up, to bring the listener back to now
checks.expl: 'She opens the door. The crowd goes silent.'

checks.q: How does 'would' work in a story?
opts: It always marks a condition, like 'if I had known, I would have gone'
It describes repeated past habits, which the past simple interrupts
It shows the narrator is unsure whether the events really happened
It replaces the past perfect, to show what happened before the story
checks.expl: 'I would read the paper… one day there was a knock at the door.'

spch100.5.9.takeaway: Natalia of Upskill Me, who teaches public speaking to non-native speakers, on seven mistakes in second-language presentations: translating the slides, under-preparing, never timing yourself, saving questions for the end, memorising every word, never writing anything down, and ignoring your inner state.

beats.d: Rebuild the talk for this audience; fewer words on slides, because reading replaces listening.
Charismatic speakers in their first language often go silent in their second. Spontaneity comes after rehearsal.
You may think three minutes have passed when it has been fifteen. Do a full timed run.
Invite questions as you go: a talk is a conversation, and questions show trust.
Learn the first two and last two sentences. Write each bullet as a full sentence you can say — the first line of a paragraph.
Write the one big idea as an answer, not a title. Then work on your state, because confidence comes from having done it many times.

spch100.5.9.worked: Bullet point 'five thousand dollars' versus 'we have added five thousand dollars of value to the product.' The first reminds you of the topic; the second gives you correct English to start the paragraph with.
spch100.5.9.watch: Memorising every word. When one word goes, you are stuck looking for it instead of thinking about the audience.

checks.q: What does she say to memorise word for word?
opts: The whole talk, so nothing can go wrong on stage
Only the opening and closing two sentences
Only the slide titles, in the right order
Only the key numbers and the main message
checks.expl: The body runs on bullet points written as sentences.

checks.q: Why write bullet points as full sentences?
opts: They look more professional on slides than single words or fragments do
They are easier to translate from your first language when preparing
They give you correct English to start each part, not just the topic
They let you read the talk aloud word for word if you lose your place
checks.expl: Non-native speakers usually need help with how to say it, not what to say.

checks.q: Which of these is a 'one big idea' rather than a title?
opts: We have found a strategy to double sales next quarter
How we can increase our sales over the next quarter
Sales strategy review for the coming quarter and beyond
Our sales performance: an overview of the last quarter
checks.expl: A big idea answers a question; a title asks one.

spch100.5.10.takeaway: A coach for non-native leaders in American companies on three shifts: treat a presentation as sharing with specific people, stop over-explaining and give the bottom line first, and practise until you sound human rather than perfect.

beats.d: Presenting is about you; sharing is about the people in the chairs and what they need. It changes your preparation and your energy.
A specialist presenting to other directors has to translate the specialism, not show it off.
Over-explaining comes from a culture that values the journey, or from trying to prove your English. Both are inefficient here.
Not every number on the slide — what the numbers mean and what action follows.
Perfect pronunciation in a monotone puts people to sleep. Master your job's high-frequency words, then work on rhythm. Practise standing up if you will present standing up.

spch100.5.10.worked: A CFO explaining quarterly numbers to non-finance colleagues: instead of reading the table, say whether it means growth, and what to do as a result — invest in training, slow down, change course.
spch100.5.10.watch: Scripting everything. When something goes wrong live, you have never practised carrying on through a mistake.

checks.q: Why does she suggest thinking of a presentation as 'sharing'?
opts: It sounds more modest, so the audience is less likely to judge you
It moves your focus from yourself to the people receiving it
It means you can drop the slides and simply talk to the room
It lowers the stakes, so you prepare less and stay relaxed
checks.expl: Preparation becomes connection rather than memorisation.

checks.q: What are two reasons she gives for over-explaining?
opts: Too many slides, and too little time to get through all of them in order
Nerves, and not knowing the audience's level well enough beforehand
A culture that puts the journey first, or wanting to prove your English
Wanting to sound humble, or fearing that a short answer seems rude
checks.expl: Identifying which one applies makes it faster to fix.

checks.q: Which pronunciation does she say to master first?
opts: The high-frequency words of your job
Every vowel sound, one at a time
Idioms and slang your colleagues use
The 'th' sounds, since they are the hardest
checks.expl: Then let it go and work on rhythm and intonation.

spch100.5.11.takeaway: A Babbel podcast on whether humour travels: puns and cultural references mostly do not, comedians who move between languages have to rebuild their acts, and Eddie Izzard argues that universal material can travel if you add the new language a few minutes at a time and rehearse with a conversation tutor.

beats.d: Spanish puns told in English get blank looks; 'did you get a haircut?' makes no sense in French.
Much humour depends on what people grew up watching. Seinfeld dubbed into German flopped.
Gad Elmaleh's 90-minute French show, full of props and characters, had to be rebuilt for American stand-up.
Universal material, performed in English with a few minutes of French at the end, slowly becoming all French — rehearsed for hours with a conversation tutor in a café.
Stress and timing in a language you are learning are the hard part. Filler words and intonation help you sound natural before you are fully fluent.

spch100.5.11.worked: 'Local jokes get local laughs.' Jokes about shared human situations — a misunderstanding, a family moment — survive the move between languages far better than wordplay.
spch100.5.11.watch: Translating a joke that works in your first language word for word. Even when you explain it, it rarely lands. The closing minutes are Izzard on why he does it: a deliberately political answer about learning languages rather than building walls.

checks.q: Why did the Spanish jokes fall flat in English?
opts: They were too long for an English audience
They relied on rude words that were bleeped
They were puns that only work in Spanish
The hosts didn't understand the Spanish
checks.expl: Wordplay depends on the original words.

checks.q: How does Eddie Izzard build a show in a new language?
opts: He hires a translator for the whole script, then learns the new version by heart
He starts with universal material and adds the new language bit by bit, with a tutor
He drops the verbal jokes and builds the show from physical comedy instead
He memorises local jokes and swaps them in for every reference that doesn't travel there
checks.expl: He rehearses the act he has been improvising with his tutors.

checks.q: What does 'local jokes get local laughs' mean?
opts: References only one place understands only work in that place
You should perform only locally until your act is good enough
Local audiences laugh more, because they know the comedian
Jokes about the place you're in always get the biggest laugh
checks.expl: Material that relies on shared human experience travels further.

spch100.6.0.takeaway: Peter McGraw's benign violation theory, from the Humor Research Lab at Boulder: something is funny when it seems wrong and OK at the same time. That explains what is funny, what is not, and how to adjust a joke that misses.

beats.d: His talk about moral violations got laughs instead of disgust — a church raffling off a Hummer — and he set out to explain why.
A violation, a reason it is benign, and both at once.
Low commitment to the norm, psychological distance, or another reading (play-fighting, tickling).
Purely benign is dull; purely malign is upsetting. Falling down stairs unhurt is funny; badly hurt is not — unless it happens to someone else.
Big violations need distance; small ones get funnier closer up. The Silverman strategy softens; the Seinfeld strategy sharpens.

spch100.6.0.worked: His opening — 'turn to a stranger and start tickling them' — was a violation (wrong to ask), made benign by the audience (open-minded), distance (in the future), and another reading (it is a talk about humour).
spch100.6.0.watch: Fixing a flat joke by adding more edge when the real problem is that nobody feels safe. Ask which side is missing: the wrong, or the OK.

checks.q: According to the benign violation theory, when does humour occur?
opts: Whenever something is surprising enough to break a pattern
When a situation is a violation and benign at the same time
When the audience feels superior to the person in the joke
When a joke has three parts: setup, turn and punchline
checks.expl: Both appraisals have to happen together.

checks.q: Why can't you tickle yourself, in McGraw's terms?
opts: Your skin adapts, so the feeling never builds up
It is a malign violation — it feels like an attack
There is no violation — it is purely benign
You know it is coming, so you laugh too early
checks.expl: Without any threat there is nothing to be funny.

checks.q: Which of these is NOT one of the ways he lists to make a violation benign?
opts: Making it louder
Low commitment to the violated norm
Psychological distance
An alternative interpretation that makes it OK
checks.expl: Volume is not part of the theory.

spch100.6.1.takeaway: Steve Kaplan, who teaches comedy writing: funny is anything that makes you laugh, but comedy is the truth about flawed people trying to cope with a world that is too hard for them — which is why it can hold sadness.

beats.d: The Apartment is sad, with an attempted suicide in it, and still a comedy, because its people are flawed and trying.
Drama helps us dream about who we could be; comedy helps us live with who we are.
If you are not laughing, it is not funny to you — like jangling keys for a baby.
Unusual characters in a typical situation, or typical characters in an unusual one, trying to deal with it.
He does not care for comedy that punches down, or for slapstick with no human story behind it.

spch100.6.1.worked: Turn a story where you looked foolish into comedy by showing what you were sincerely trying to do. The laugh comes from the gap between the effort and the result, not from you calling yourself an idiot.
spch100.6.1.watch: Confusing 'getting a laugh' with comedy. Jangling keys gets a laugh; nobody would spend a year writing it.

checks.q: How does Kaplan distinguish 'funny' from 'comedy'?
opts: Comedy has to have jokes in it; funny is anything that is merely pleasant to watch
Funny is for one-liners on a stage; comedy is for stories in film and on television
Funny is whatever makes you laugh; comedy is the truth about flawed people coping
Comedy is whatever makes a crowd laugh; funny is what makes one person laugh alone
checks.expl: His example is a baby laughing at keys — funny, not comedy.

checks.q: Why does he call The Apartment a comedy even though it is sad?
opts: Its people are flawed and doing their best in a world too hard for them
It has a happy ending, which matters more than anything sad on the way
It has enough slapstick scenes to outweigh the attempted suicide in it
It was marketed as a comedy, and the label decides how audiences see it
checks.expl: Comedy can hold sadness and even tragedy.

checks.q: What does he say comedy helps people do, compared with drama?
opts: Escape reality
Learn facts
Dream of who they could be
Live with who they are
checks.expl: Drama is about who we could be.

spch100.6.2.takeaway: Greg Dean, who has taught stand-up since 1982: a joke turns on one thing with two meanings. Find it to identify the joke, strip everything that does not serve it to fix the joke, and mine its other meanings to write new ones.

beats.d: People bring him whole pages that contain one joke. Find the connector — the one thing with an expected and an unexpected meaning.
A divorce joke shrinks from three sentences to one by cutting 'long and messy', the holiday, and every rationalisation: 'After my divorce I had a sex change — from very seldom to not at all.'
Never restate the expected meaning in the punch.
Setup, expected meaning, the words that cause it, a list of other meanings, a punch for each.
Once you know the mechanism, okay jokes are easy. The hard part is the great ones that reveal something true, and that takes a lot of writing.

spch100.6.2.worked: 'For Father's Day I took my father out' — expected: to dinner. Mine 'took out': kill (with a 45), hit (with a right cross), remove (out of an urn), date (the goodnight kiss was awkward). Each meaning is a new punch.
spch100.6.2.watch: Writing around the joke. If you cannot point to the single word or phrase with two meanings, you do not yet know where your joke is.

checks.q: What is the 'connector' in Dean's joke structure?
opts: The pause before the punch that lets it land
One thing in the joke that has two meanings
The tag that adds a second laugh after the punch
The moment the audience first sees the twist
checks.expl: The setup leads to one meaning, the punch reveals the other.

checks.q: What does he say to strip out when fixing a joke?
opts: Everything that doesn't serve the joke, including rationalisations
Only the swear words, which get cheap laughs instead of real ones
Any mention of yourself, so the joke is about the situation instead
The setup's details, so the punch arrives before anyone can guess it
checks.expl: He quotes Patton Oswalt.

checks.q: In the 'joke mine', what do you list after finding the words that cause the expected meaning?
opts: Other topics the setup could be about
Possible tags to add after the punch
Other comedians' jokes on the same words
Unexpected meanings of those words
checks.expl: Each unexpected meaning leads to a different punch.

spch100.6.3.takeaway: Greg Dean's three kinds of setup: the performed one-liner setup that misdirects, shared knowledge already in the audience's head, and observation, where both setup and punch are already known and the comedian just connects them.

beats.d: The comedian says the setup. Its job is clear misdirection toward a target assumption.
Satire and parody depend on what the audience already knows. Without it, the joke means nothing.
That is why comedians use news, TV and common experiences — and why they must know whether this audience shares them.
Both halves are known: dogs hate air blown in their faces, but stick their heads out of car windows. The comedian notices and presents the pair.

spch100.6.3.worked: At a team offsite, a joke about last quarter's planning tool relies on shared knowledge — it works with your team and dies with a client.
spch100.6.3.watch: Using a shared-knowledge joke with a mixed audience. The people who do not have the reference feel shut out, not amused.

checks.q: What makes a 'shared knowledge' setup different?
opts: The comedian performs it as a song, so the tune carries the setup
It is always a pun on a word the whole audience already knows well
The setup is already in the audience's mind, so only the punch is said
It needs a prop or a slide, so the audience sees the setup first
checks.expl: Satire and parody rely on it.

checks.q: In an observational joke, where are the setup and the punch?
opts: Both are already in the audience's mind; the comedian connects them
The setup is in the news; the punch is in the comedian's own notes
The setup is in the previous joke; the punch is in this one alone
Both are performed by the comedian, but in the opposite order
checks.expl: Carlin's dog joke is his example.

checks.q: What is the purpose of a performed one-liner setup?
opts: To explain the joke so nobody misses the point
To introduce the comedian before the first laugh
To get a small laugh that warms up the big one
To create misdirection toward a target assumption
checks.expl: The punch then shatters that assumption.

spch100.6.4.takeaway: How late-night writers produce a hundred topical jokes a day: pick a story with two subjects, free-associate a list for each, find a surprising link between the lists, and reach it from the setup with a who/what/where/why/when/how question.

beats.d: The volume needs an algorithm.
Surprise (setup and punch) and two unlike things joined by a hidden similarity.
For the Disney robot-Trump story: one list about Trump, one about Disney.
Trump deporting Aladdin — surprising, recognisable, and it fires several laugh triggers for that audience.
'What did robot Trump do at Disney?' gets you from setup to punch.

spch100.6.4.worked: Long lists give each show its own angle on the same story — one used deportation, another sent Jeff Sessions to the Country Bear Jamboree.
spch100.6.4.watch: Stopping at short lists. The first few associations are the ones every other writer has too.

checks.q: What are the two lists in the late-night formula?
opts: Good jokes and bad jokes, to compare what works
Free associations for each of the two subjects in the story
Setups on one list and possible punchlines on the other
Facts about the story and the writers' opinions about it
checks.expl: The joke comes from linking an item from each list.

checks.q: How do writers get from the setup to the link they found?
opts: By asking who/what/where/why/when/how questions about the setup
By adding a pun on one word of the setup and building out from it
By reading the setup aloud faster until the link becomes obvious
By adding a tag to the setup that names the link outright
checks.expl: 'What did robot Trump do at Disney World?'

checks.q: Why do longer lists help?
opts: They make each joke longer and more detailed
They impress the head writer at the morning meeting
They help writers steer clear of swearing
They lead to links other writers did not find
checks.expl: That is how shows find different angles on the same story.

spch100.6.5.takeaway: Scott Dikkers, founding editor of The Onion, on eleven 'funny filters' — irony, character, shock, hyperbole, wordplay, reference, madcap, parody, analogy, misplaced focus and meta — shown with Onion headlines.

beats.d: Take the opposite of your literal meaning, buy into it, and play it straight.
Two traits shown together: a philandering string theorist who 'can explain everything'.
Shock is a cheap laugh; use it sparingly. The best hyperbole defies physics.
Wordplay can be done well. Reference just points out a small shared moment nobody else has noticed — Seinfeld built a career on it.
Silliness as garnish; every Onion story parodies a news article; an analogy with many connection points (Al Gore as Superman's father) is a rich seam.
Obsess over the trivial to highlight what matters; make fun of humour itself.

spch100.6.5.worked: 'Secondhand smoke linked to secondhand coolness' — misplaced focus: the real danger is ignored in favour of something unimportant, which makes you notice the danger.
spch100.6.5.watch: Leaning on shock because it is easy. It works in mixed company, but it is the cheapest filter, and a little goes a long way.

checks.q: How does Dikkers say irony works?
opts: Take the opposite of your literal meaning and play it completely straight
Make a pun on a key word, so the sentence carries two meanings at once
Exaggerate the claim until it becomes physically impossible to believe
Refer to another well-known joke or story, so the audience fills it in
checks.expl: 'I love soup' written as a sincere celebration of soup.

checks.q: What makes the best hyperbole, in his view?
opts: Small exaggerations the audience can still believe
Exaggeration backed by real statistics and numbers
Exaggeration past the point of physical possibility
Swearing for emphasis at the moment of the claim
checks.expl: His example is Rodney Dangerfield's olive.

checks.q: What is 'misplaced focus'?
opts: Looking at the wrong person in the scene, so the audience is misled
Focusing on something trivial so the reader thinks about what matters
A camera trick that blurs the main subject and sharpens the background
Forgetting the punchline on purpose, so the silence becomes the joke
checks.expl: Secondhand smoke linked to secondhand coolness.

spch100.6.6.takeaway: A TED-Ed lesson by comedy writer Cheri Steinkellner: funny comes from specific details, characters with a flaw played up, incongruity found by mind-mapping and 'what if', and small tools like zig-zig-zag and the punch word last.

beats.d: Much comedy is noticing the ordinary things nobody notices.
Who, what, when, where, why, how — and the more specific, the funnier.
Commedia dell'arte types (the know-it-all, the lovable loser): find the flaw, play it up, or flip opposites.
Mind-map from a word ('pickle'), then go from what is to what if. Write the dumb ideas down too.
Rule of three (zig, zig, zag), punch at the end of the line, and the claim that k-sounds are funny.

spch100.6.6.worked: 'A rabbi, a priest and a coconut walk into a bar' breaks the pattern; changing 'bar' to 'disco' moves the funny word to the end.
spch100.6.6.watch: Treating rule-of-thumb claims as laws. 'K-words are funny' is a writer's habit, not a finding; test it on your own lines.

checks.q: What is the Commedia dell'arte rule for a comic character?
opts: Give them a catchphrase to repeat
Make them win every time they try
Find the flaw, then play it up
Make them speak in rhyme and verse
checks.expl: Or play with opposites.

checks.q: What does 'zig, zig, zag' describe?
opts: The rule of three: set up a pattern, then break it
Three jokes in a row, each one bigger than before
Changing topic three times so the audience can't settle
A pattern of three that keeps going in the same direction
checks.expl: A rabbi, a priest and a coconut.

checks.q: Why do specific details help?
opts: They make the story longer, so the punchline lands with more weight
They prove the story really happened, so the audience trusts it
They are easier for the teller to remember under pressure on stage
They give the listener something precise to picture, which is funnier
checks.expl: The more specific the details, the funnier the story.

spch100.6.7.takeaway: Jerry Seinfeld shows The New York Times how he wrote his Pop-Tart bit over two years: funny first line, funny words, links as tight as a jigsaw, syllables counted, and the biggest laugh at the end.

beats.d: 'Pop-Tart' is fun to say; the first line should be funny right away.
'Chimps in the dirt playing with sticks' — four of seven words are funny.

beats.t: Tell them it is a story
beats.d: 'In the midst of that darkness and hopelessness, the Pop-Tart appears' gets a laugh because it signals a story.
Links between jokes have to be smooth; if one is a split second too long he shaves letters and counts syllables, like songwriting.
In a long bit the biggest laugh must come last. His: 'They can't go stale, because they were never fresh.'

spch100.6.7.worked: He writes longhand on yellow legal pads with the same Bic pen he used for every Seinfeld episode, and spends years on something that 'means absolutely nothing'.
spch100.6.7.watch: Letting the biggest laugh sit in the middle of a story. Everything after it feels like a let-down, however good it is.

checks.q: Where does Seinfeld say the biggest laugh in a long bit must go?
opts: At the end
At the start
In the middle
Wherever it fits
checks.expl: That is why the ending is the hardest part.

checks.q: What does he compare tightening the links between jokes to?
opts: Cooking — tasting as you go
Songwriting — counting syllables
Building a house — brick by brick
Painting — layer over layer
checks.expl: He shaves letters off words to get the timing.

checks.q: Why does he say 'chimps in the dirt playing with sticks' works?
opts: It rhymes, so it is easy for the audience to remember
It is true, so the audience believes it straight away
Four of its seven words are funny on their own
It is short, so the laugh comes quickly
checks.expl: Word choice matters.

spch100.6.8.takeaway: Mike Birbiglia on the storytelling advice he uses constantly, from Ira Glass: tell a little story, say how you feel about it, repeat — the jokes are in how you feel — and end by zooming out, then back in for a tag.

beats.d: Comics' strength is how they feel about things; that is where the jokes come from.
To know the story has an ending, and to know that something is changing.
Know where it starts and ends, then see how many jokes the audience lets you get away with. If you lose them, skip to the end.
Hook, pull forward, zoom out to the bigger meaning, then come back for a final tag.
Talk about what you actually think about. Topical material you do not care about is not interesting.

spch100.6.8.worked: His analysis of a friend's Russia story: the hook (in Russia, no Russian), the pull (the Russian mom, drinking, robbing a train), the zoom-out (I'd never thought about whether I would rob a train), and the tag.
spch100.6.8.watch: Stacking jokes with no feeling between them. Without the 'how I felt' beats, a story becomes a list of bits.

checks.q: What structure did Ira Glass give Birbiglia?
opts: Setup, punch, tag, then repeat the pattern until the story is over
Tell a little story, say how you feel about it, then a bit more story
A beginning, a middle and an end, with a joke in each of the three
Three jokes to warm up the room, then the story with the feelings
checks.expl: The feelings are where the comedy lives.

checks.q: What does he suggest if the audience is not with a story?
opts: Skip to the ending
Tell it louder
Start again from the top
Explain the setup
checks.expl: Knowing the ending lets you bail out.

checks.q: What is the 'zoom out' at the end of a story?
opts: A list of thanks to the people who appear in the story
A recap of the events, in order, so nobody is lost
A move to a bigger joke that has nothing to do with the story
A step back to what it means more widely, before a final tag
checks.expl: Then you zoom back in for the tag.

spch100.6.9.takeaway: Jennifer Aaker and Naomi Bagdonas on the Future of Storytelling podcast: why humour works on the brain and at work, the 'humour cliff', and a starter kit — a levity list, then exaggeration, contrast and the rule of three, all built on truth and misdirection.

beats.d: They cite research that people remember more when they laugh — viewers of comic news shows recalled more current events, and students taught with humour scored higher.
They report that a four-year-old laughs about 300 times a day; a 40-year-old takes over two months to laugh that much.
One is the 'born with it' myth. Humour is a skill with a science to it.
For ten days, write down three funny or odd things at the end of each day.
Exaggeration, contrast, and the rule of three — applied to any true observation.
The two foundations: lead the brain one way, then turn it.

spch100.6.9.worked: The remote-work observation (no one wears trousers on video calls) done three ways: exaggerated ('how did we put on trousers?'), contrasted (finding good lighting versus time saved on trousers), and as a list of three (hallway chats, eye contact, trousers).
spch100.6.9.watch: Trying to be funny before noticing anything. The techniques need raw material; the levity list is where it comes from.

checks.q: What is a 'levity list'?
opts: A list of jokes to memorise for meetings
Three funny or odd things written down at the end of each day
A list of comedians to watch for ten days in a row
A ranking of which colleagues have the best sense of humour
checks.expl: They suggest doing it for ten days.

checks.q: In the rule of three, where does the funny item go?
opts: Last, after two normal items
First, to grab attention early
In the middle, as a surprise
All three items, repeated
checks.expl: Two items set the pattern; the third breaks it.

checks.q: What do they call the two foundations of humour?
opts: Timing and volume
Wit and charm
Truth and misdirection
Surprise and repetition
checks.expl: Lead the audience one way, then shift.

spch100.6.10.takeaway: A speaking coach breaks down three techniques from real best-man speeches that anyone can use in a work presentation: misdirection, exaggeration and self-deprecation — with a warning about overdoing the last one.

beats.d: 'A once-in-a-lifetime achievement… I've graduated law school. There's also a wedding.' The audience assumed the wedding.
'He had the wedding website up before he met Michelle.' Built on a true trait: he plans everything.
His brother's friends recall good deeds; his friends recall the goat they stole.
Self-deprecation repeated becomes self-loathing, and the audience starts to feel sorry for you.

spch100.6.10.worked: For a work talk: 'This project took a huge amount of dedication — mostly from the coffee machine.' Misdirection toward the team, a turn at the end.
spch100.6.10.watch: Exaggerating a trait the person is sensitive about. The planner in the example was proud of planning; pick traits people would happily admit to.

checks.q: Why did the law-school line get a laugh?
opts: It was rude about the groom's family
The audience expected the achievement to be the wedding
It was a pun on the word 'achievement'
It was so long that the audience laughed out of sheer relief
checks.expl: Misdirection: lead one way, turn at the end.

checks.q: What is the risk the coach mentions with self-deprecation?
opts: It becomes self-loathing and the audience feels sorry for you
It is too easy, so the audience thinks you didn't prepare
Nobody understands it unless they already know you well
It insults the couple by making the day about yourself
checks.expl: Use it, but not again and again.

checks.q: What makes the wedding-website exaggeration work?
opts: It is completely made up, so nobody is hurt
It is about the speaker, not about the groom
It uses wordplay on the word 'website'
It stretches a real trait everyone recognises
checks.expl: The trait is true; only the scale is exaggerated.

spch100.6.11.takeaway: David Nihill at Talks at Google: after a year posing as a stand-up to beat his fear of speaking, he argues presenters should go for fun before funny — build on your own stories, then use comedians' techniques for structure, timing and memory.

beats.d: He says comedians are judged every 12 seconds, and business talks now compete with entertainment. He counted laughs in top TED talks and found they rival comedy films.
Your own story carries no risk if it does not get a laugh — and nobody knows if you mess it up. Keep a funny-story file.
Open with something the whole room shares before the specific story.
Setup, punch, tag. Move the funny word to the end and stop — Obama's salmon joke ends on 'smoked'.
Two items set a pattern; the third breaks it — on a book blurb, a sign, an email.
A memory palace so you never go blank; speak 10–15 per cent louder to cut filler words; take questions before your conclusion.

spch100.6.11.worked: Pitches too: 'we have a year-on-year growth rate of 80 per cent' puts the impact word last. It feels odd to say and sounds natural to the audience.
spch100.6.11.watch: Ending on Q&A. If nobody asks anything, the talk dies on silence. Take questions, then deliver a planned final slide and line.

checks.q: What does Nihill mean by 'fun before funny'?
opts: Play a game with the audience before the talk to loosen the room
Start from your own stories; one that gets no laugh still works
Tell your best joke first, so the rest of the talk feels like fun
Keep humour out of work talks until you are confident on stage
checks.expl: Stories carry no risk of the silence a failed joke gets.

checks.q: Where should the funny word go in the sentence?
opts: At the start, to grab attention
In the middle, hidden in the setup
At the very end, followed by a pause
Repeated twice for emphasis
checks.expl: Then stop and let them react.

checks.q: Why take questions before your conclusion?
opts: So you control the ending even if nobody asks anything
To save time, since questions at the end always run long
Because audiences prefer to ask while the talk is fresh
To avoid hard questions by leaving too little time for them
checks.expl: Comedians never end on a flat note.

spch100.7.0.takeaway: Chris Duffy, a former elementary teacher and improv teacher, at TED: the difference between people with a great sense of humour and everyone else is often just whether they notice and accept their honest, odd reactions — and you can retrain that.

beats.d: A worksheet on shapes comes back with friends' names; an anonymous question card reads 'What are balls for.' — with a full stop.
His weekend students had to unlearn the idea that there was a right answer.
A tax lawyer started with brown, white and black shoes; with practice he got to shoes covered in gold.
Every comedian he knows keeps a running list of odd things they notice.
He made himself CEO of LinkedIn on LinkedIn; the site emailed everyone to congratulate him — until its trust team shut the account.

spch100.7.0.worked: 'Faith, you are taking a pretty disrespectful tone for someone who works for me.' The joke is just committing to the absurd premise he had already set up.
spch100.7.0.watch: Mistaking a filter for taste. Rejecting every odd thought before you look at it leaves you nothing to choose from.

checks.q: What does Duffy say often separates people with a great sense of humour from others?
opts: How many jokes they can remember and how quickly they can find one to fit
Whether they notice and accept their honest reactions instead of boxing them
How much comedy they watch, since funny people absorb the rhythm of it
Whether they were funny as children, before school taught them to be serious
checks.expl: Kids do it naturally; adults can relearn it.

checks.q: What was the 'seven weird types of shoes' exercise designed to do?
opts: Turn off self-judgement and let unexpected ideas through
Teach the group new vocabulary for describing everyday things
Test how many ideas each person can hold in memory at once
Find the best answer by comparing everyone's lists afterwards
checks.expl: The tax lawyer's list changed once he stopped censoring himself.

checks.q: What habit does he say every comedian he knows shares?
opts: Writing new material late every night
Performing somewhere every single day
Keeping a notebook of odd things they notice
Reading the news each morning for topics
checks.expl: There turns out to be no shortage of material.

spch100.7.1.takeaway: Dave Morris, an improviser, at TEDxVictoria: life is improvised, and the seven skills he teaches on stage — play, let yourself fail, listen, say yes, say 'and', play the game, relax and have fun — are the ones that make conversation and collaboration work.

beats.d: Improvisation is a way of making something — theatre, jazz, hip-hop, MacGyver's gadgets.
Play happens in the moment; fear of failure drags you back into your head. Failing does not make you a failure.
'Listening is the willingness to change.' Collaboration means taking your ego out of it.
The audience says yes to every question and builds a story in seconds; saying no stops it cold. 'And' adds a brick; 'but' contradicts.
Rules — slides, a brief, a job application — free you to improvise within them.

spch100.7.1.worked: His live demo: 'Do you want to tell a story with me?' 'Yes.' 'Is it about a knight?' 'Yes.' … a whole story in thirty seconds. Then the same questions answered 'no': nothing.
spch100.7.1.watch: Being a yes-man. Agreeing without adding anything keeps things pleasant but goes nowhere — the 'and' is the contribution.

checks.q: How does Morris define listening?
opts: Waiting quietly for your turn
Repeating back what was said
The willingness to change
Taking notes as they speak
checks.expl: If you are not willing to change, you are not really listening.

checks.q: What is the difference between 'yes, and' and 'yes, but'?
opts: 'And' builds on the idea; 'but' contradicts it
They mean the same; 'but' is just more honest
'But' is more polite, because it softens a no
'And' is for comedy; 'but' is for real meetings
checks.expl: Each person adds a brick.

checks.q: Why does he say rules help improvisers?
opts: They make the game fair, so nobody can dominate
They prevent mistakes, which keeps scenes smooth
They impress audiences who can see the skill
They channel creativity by giving it constraints
checks.expl: Within the game's rules, you are free.

spch100.7.2.takeaway: Patricia Ryan Madson, who taught improvisation at Stanford for decades, at Google: improvising is a way of living — start anywhere, accept what is in the box, make sense rather than jokes, take a bow for your mistakes, and wake up to the world around you.

beats.d: Improvisers do not wait for inspiration or the perfect beginning; the first step shows you the second.
Everyone opens an imaginary box. Whatever is in it is fine — trying to have a good idea blocks having any idea, and you cannot help being original.
'Don't make jokes, make sense.' Improv looks funny because it makes sense of what is happening.
When you make a mistake, raise your arms and say 'ta-da', which moves your attention to what comes next.
Eyes closed, describe the room — nobody can fully. Ask: where am I, what am I doing, what would improve this moment? Notice who made your day possible.

spch100.7.2.worked: The audience's boxes held a peacock feather, two cans of corn, a live cat, someone's wife's left shoe — fifty people, fifty different things, without anyone trying to be original.
spch100.7.2.watch: Trying to be clever. Madson's whole method rests on the opposite: the obvious, honest response is usually the one that works. NOTE: the first thirteen minutes are a thank-you list to Google. She closes with a parable about a water tank of unknown size: you do not know how much time you have, so do not let it drip away.

checks.q: What does Madson mean by 'don't make jokes, make sense'?
opts: Avoid humour at work, because sense is valued more than laughter there
Scenes work by making sense of what is really happening, not by being clever
Explain each joke afterwards, so the whole audience makes sense of it
Plan the logic of a scene in advance, so the jokes have something to hang on
checks.expl: The humour follows from the sense.

checks.q: What is the 'circus bow' for?
opts: Ending a performance with a flourish so the crowd knows to clap
Greeting the audience before the first scene begins, to warm them up
Responding to a mistake so your attention moves to what comes next
Asking for applause when a scene has gone especially well
checks.expl: Ta-da, instead of curling up in embarrassment.

checks.q: What did the imaginary gift-box exercise show?
opts: That people can't help being original when they accept their first idea
That most people aren't creative until they have been trained to be
That a good gift needs to be planned, so ideas need planning too
That improv needs props to get people's imaginations started
checks.expl: Trying to come up with a good idea gets in the way.

spch100.7.3.takeaway: Andrew Tarvin, an engineer who left Procter and Gamble to teach humour, at TEDxTAMU: humour is a skill you learn by practice. Borrow point of view from stand-up, heightening from improv, and commitment from sketch — and know the difference between a bad joke and an inappropriate one.

beats.d: 'Wow, that's fun' — his grandmother's reading of WTF, and his case for a more playful outlook.
Voted teacher's pet, an engineer — he learned comedy by running an improv group like a project: practice three times a week, review shows like game tape.
Share a perspective to connect or to make a point — humans should come with error messages.
'If this is true, what else is true?' — and use yes-and to turn small talk into conversation.
Confidence makes the performance; staircase wit shortens with practice.
Nobody was ever fired for a bad joke. Keep it positive and inclusive, and a joke that misses is just a nice statement.

spch100.7.3.worked: Small talk: 'How about this weather?' — 'Yes, and if you weren't here, what would you be doing in it?' The yes-and moves the exchange from filler to learning about the person.
spch100.7.3.watch: Waiting to feel funny before trying. Tarvin's argument is that the confidence comes from the practice, not the other way round.

checks.q: What does Tarvin say we learn from improv?
opts: How to memorise lines so well that they sound made up on the spot
How to explore and heighten a point of view: if this is true, what else is?
How to share a point of view about everyday life in a short, tight monologue
How to commit fully to a character, however silly the premise is
checks.expl: Accept and build.

checks.q: What is 'staircase wit', and what does he say about it?
opts: Thinking of the right line too late; a sign of instinct that practice shortens
A pun that climbs step by step, each line building on the one before
A stand-up technique of building laughs in steps toward one big punchline
Thinking of the line too late, which shows you will never be quick on stage
checks.expl: From four hours later, to minutes, to the moment.

checks.q: How does he distinguish a bad joke from an inappropriate one?
opts: A bad joke is long and slow; an inappropriate one is short and too quick
Inappropriate jokes are often funnier, which is exactly why people risk telling them at work
There is no real difference; both get you in trouble with the audience
A bad joke just misses; an inappropriate one has the wrong subject, target or timing
checks.expl: No one gets fired for a bad joke.

spch100.7.4.takeaway: Jennifer Aaker and Naomi Bagdonas, who teach a Stanford course on humour, at Talks at Google: humour at work is less about being funny than about small, intentional moments of levity — and doing it well means understanding status, humour styles, and where the lines are.

beats.d: Bagdonas did improv at night and was so serious at her consulting job that a client guessed she spent Fridays re-ironing blouses.
Madeleine Albright wore a huge bug brooch to meet the Russian minister after the State Department was bugged.
Write down a few true, odd observations each day. A CEO 'accidentally' left his screen shared while searching 'things inspirational CEOs say during hard times'.
Juniors feel they must prove credibility first; seniors who stay serious miss the approachability humour brings. Self-deprecation lowers status for juniors and signals confidence for seniors.
Ask how it will make others feel; never punch down; check your distance from the subject.
Four styles — stand-up, magnet, sniper, sweetheart. When a joke dies, name it; when you cross a line, own it and find the blind spot.

spch100.7.4.worked: Bagdonas kept being goofier with a dry colleague and got nothing — like a tourist shouting louder in English. She switched to the colleague's style: a silent cat-headed bobblehead left on her desk, which became a running joke.
spch100.7.4.watch: Speaking louder in your own humour style. If someone is not responding, they may just have a different style, not no sense of humour.

checks.q: What is their biggest tip for having more humour in your life?
opts: Learn ten good jokes that suit work
Watch more comedy to absorb its rhythm
Don't look for what's funny, look for what's true
Always go for the laugh when you see a chance
checks.expl: Become an observer of your own life.

checks.q: How does self-deprecation work differently by status, according to them?
opts: It can lower juniors' perceived status but signal confidence in seniors
It helps everyone equally, since nobody is threatened by a modest joke
It hurts seniors more, because people expect leaders to look flawless
It only works for comedians, who have the status to make fun of themselves
checks.expl: Some people over-use it, which can cost them status.

checks.q: What do they recommend when a joke gets crickets?
opts: Repeat it louder in case they missed it
Explain it in detail so they get it
Apologise and move on to serious content
Name it lightly — 'well, that didn't work'
checks.expl: Naming it often cuts the tension enough to get a laugh.

spch100.7.5.takeaway: A conversation-skills channel's breakdown of talk-show clips: three kinds of joke that make people like you less — exposing sensitive information after someone shows discomfort, guilt-trip jokes, and teasing people below you — and what to do instead.

beats.d: A host keeps pushing a guest to name an ex while she clearly wants to stop.
Verbal hesitation, and self-soothing body language — self-hugging, touching the face or neck. Time to pivot.
Turn the joke on yourself ('you don't want a drink? great, more for me'), then invite them to talk about what they do want to discuss.
'I guess my invitation got lost' — the guest is visibly uncomfortable, or fires back.
The same 'nerd' tease is mockery from a host to less famous guests and affection from a wife who compliments her husband first.

spch100.7.5.worked: Sofia Vergara calls her husband a nerd — after calling him handsome — and it lands, because they are close, he is not sensitive about it, and the compliment comes first.
spch100.7.5.watch: Ploughing ahead because the room is laughing. Other people's laughter does not mean the person you are teasing is fine.

checks.q: Which two signs of discomfort does the video say to watch for?
opts: Laughing too loudly and clapping too soon after a joke
Verbal hesitation and self-soothing body language
Silence and holding eye contact for too long
Yawning, leaning back and folding the arms
checks.expl: When you see them, pull back and change topic.

checks.q: Why do guilt-trip jokes backfire?
opts: They make the person want to spend less time with you
They are too subtle, so the other person doesn't notice
They take too long to set up for a casual conversation
They only work on television, where the guilt is staged
checks.expl: They are often hurt feelings disguised as humour.

checks.q: When does teasing tend to land well?
opts: With strangers, since they have no history that could make it hurt
With people below you at work, who know it is just your way of joking
When it is about something they care about deeply, to show you know them
Between people who are close, about something they aren't sensitive about
checks.expl: A compliment first helps.

spch100.7.6.takeaway: A conversation-skills channel's breakdown of Norm Macdonald: how he made bad jokes kill — a mischievous smile, explaining jokes the audience already got, deliberately obvious punchlines after a pause, and turning his own fumbled delivery into the joke.

beats.d: It signals that something worth laughing at is coming.
'Like a flower — yeah, cauliflower. No offence, but your face looks like a cauliflower.' The explanation gets the bigger laugh.
A build-up and a pause, then: kickboxing combines the grace of boxing with… kicking.
Telling a joke in the first person while making it clear it never happened to him — the bad performance becomes the joke.
His three-minute moth joke only works on a talk show. In life, use light playfulness where it is unexpected, like the start of an interview.

spch100.7.6.worked: When you flub a story — skip a key detail, botch the punchline — the video suggests treating it as the start of a new joke about how bad you are at telling it.
spch100.7.6.watch: Half-committing. A mildly dull punchline is just boring; the anti-joke only works if it is as flat as possible, delivered with total confidence. The last two minutes of the video are an advert for the channel's course.

checks.q: What should you do, according to the video, when a joke doesn't land?
opts: Apologise briefly and move straight on to the next thing
Move on quickly, as if nothing happened, and don't draw attention
Explain it with a big expectant smile, as if it were brilliant
Repeat it louder and slower in case they missed some of the words
checks.expl: The explanation becomes the joke.

checks.q: Why does a deliberately obvious punchline work?
opts: Audiences expect jokes to be non-obvious, so extreme obviousness surprises
It is so easy to understand that nobody in the room is left out of it
It is shorter than a clever punchline, so the timing is easier to get right
It rhymes with the setup, and rhyme makes any punchline sound finished
checks.expl: But you must commit completely.

checks.q: What does the video say a flubbed delivery can become?
opts: A reason to stop and start the joke again
The beginning of a new joke about your bad delivery
A lesson to note for next time, not a moment to dwell on
A callback for later in the evening
checks.expl: People love a joke about how bad you are at telling jokes.

spch100.7.7.takeaway: A short lesson on callbacks: bring back something that got a laugh earlier, and you create the feeling of an inside joke with the room — as long as the original worked.

beats.d: Tell a joke, let time pass, then refer back to it.
It feels like an inside joke between friends — nobody who missed the first part would get it — plus a little nostalgia.
The original must have landed. Calling back a dud reminds people it died.
A callback brings things full circle, and rescues you when you cannot find a final punchline.

spch100.7.7.worked: In a meeting, an early laugh about the conference-room projector that never works becomes the closing line: 'and if all else fails, we'll present it on the projector.'
spch100.7.7.watch: Calling back too often. One or two callbacks feel clever; five feel like a private club the newcomers are not in.

checks.q: What is the one condition for a callback to work?
opts: It must be short and come quickly
The original joke must have landed
It must come at the very end of a talk
It must be a pun on the earlier line
checks.expl: Otherwise you remind people of the miss.

checks.q: Why do callbacks bond an audience?
opts: They create the feel of an inside joke only those present would get
They are louder and bigger than the jokes that came before them
They explain the topic again, so latecomers can catch up with it
They are surprising every time, however often the room has heard them
checks.expl: Plus a little nostalgia.

checks.q: Where does the lesson suggest a callback works especially well?
opts: As the opening line, to set the tone early
In the middle of a story, to keep it moving
In written slides, where people can reread them
As the closer, to bring things full circle
checks.expl: It makes the ending feel complete.

spch100.7.8.takeaway: An Emmy-winning comedy writer's safest way to open with humour: acknowledge the elephant in the room — anything that could distract the audience or you — in one light line, then get on with the talk.

beats.d: Anything that might distract your audience or distract you.
People will wonder what happened. 'Turns out once you're over 47 you shouldn't skateboard.' Then carry on.
An 8 a.m. Vegas conference: 'My mom always said the best cure for a hangover is a 45-minute lecture on gastroenterology.'
If you will visibly shake, a light admission ('if I pass out, drag me back to my seat and tell me I was great') can relieve both you and them.
About twelve seconds. Most of the time you need not mention nerves at all — only when the elephant is that big.

spch100.7.8.worked: Naming the obvious shows you are present in the same moment as the audience, which is why it lands even when the line itself is mild.
spch100.7.8.watch: Spending five minutes on the elephant. A long apology or story turns a distraction into the topic.

checks.q: What counts as an 'elephant in the room' here?
opts: Anything that could distract the audience or you
A controversial topic everyone in the room is avoiding
An important guest whose presence is felt
A joke about animals to break the ice
checks.expl: A sling, a hungover crowd, or your own visible nerves.

checks.q: How long should acknowledging it take?
opts: Five minutes, so it doesn't feel rushed
As long as it takes for people to relax
A few seconds — about twelve — then carry on
Until the whole room has laughed at least once
checks.expl: It is a throwaway, not a story.

checks.q: What does the writer say about admitting nerves?
opts: Never do it: nerves should stay hidden, or the audience will worry
Always do it, as your first line on stage, so the room is on your side
Do it at the end, once the talk has gone well and nobody can doubt you
Usually unnecessary — only when they are big enough to be noticed
checks.expl: Then a light line can relieve both sides.

spch100.8.0.takeaway: Celeste Headlee, a public-radio interviewer, at TED: the skills that make a good interview make a good conversation. Forget performed attention; learn ten rules — and mastering just one will already help.

beats.d: She cites Pew findings on polarisation and a teacher who calls conversational competence the most overlooked skill we fail to teach.
Eye contact, nodding, repeating back — if you are really paying attention, you don't need to show it.
Don't multitask; don't pontificate (assume you have something to learn); use open questions — 'what was that like?'
Let your own thoughts go by; say when you don't know; don't equate your experience with theirs; don't repeat yourself; stay out of the weeds.
Listen — we talk at about 225 words a minute but can listen at 500, and the mind fills the gap. Be brief.

spch100.8.0.worked: 'Were you terrified?' gets 'yes'. 'What was that like?' makes them stop and think, and you get the real answer.
spch100.8.0.watch: Waiting with a clever question while they are still talking. By the time you ask it, it may already have been answered.

checks.q: Why does Headlee dismiss tips like nodding and repeating back?
opts: They come across as rude when the speaker notices you doing them on purpose
If you are really paying attention, you don't need to perform it
They take so long that the conversation loses its natural rhythm
They only work on radio, where nobody can see what the host is doing
checks.expl: There is no reason to learn to look attentive if you are attentive.

checks.q: Which is an open question in her sense?
opts: Were you very angry with them?
Did you enjoy it as much as you'd hoped?
What was that like?
Is that really how it happened?
checks.expl: Open questions start with who, what, when, where, why or how.

checks.q: What does she say about matching someone's story with your own experience?
opts: Don't — it is never the same, and it is not about you
Always do it, because sharing a similar story is how you show empathy
Do it only with close friends, who know you mean it kindly
Do it at the end, once they have finished telling theirs
checks.expl: Conversations are not a promotional opportunity.

spch100.8.1.takeaway: Celeste Headlee on her book We Need to Talk: conversation is a skill we practise, not information we memorise. The habits that hurt it most — like shifting attention to ourselves — are the ones we can't see, so ask the people around you.

beats.d: You don't go once. And being bad at listening is a human problem — babies arrive knowing how to scream, not listen.
Shift responses move attention to you; support responses keep it on them. Conversational narcissism is always taking the ball.
List the five things that annoy you most; ask people close to you how many you do. Usually it is all five.
When her friend's father died, Headlee shared her own loss. The friend snapped, 'You win.' She needed someone to listen, not a matching story.
Listening to someone you disagree with gives them nothing and gives you a lot. If you can't listen right now, say so and come back.

spch100.8.1.worked: Her advice to a scientist who couldn't start conversations: ask where he's from, then ask what it's like. Questions people know the answer to, about things they care about, take the pressure off both of you.
spch100.8.1.watch: Sharing a similar story to show empathy. It feels generous and is usually a shift response.

checks.q: What is a 'support response'?
opts: Agreeing with everything they say, so they feel backed up
A reply that keeps attention on what the other person is talking about
Offering practical help with the problem the other person has raised
Changing the subject politely when the other person seems uncomfortable
checks.expl: A shift response moves attention to yourself.

checks.q: How does Headlee suggest finding your own bad habits?
opts: Record every conversation for a week and listen back for your worst habits
Take an online test that scores how well you listen, and where you go wrong
List five habits that annoy you in others; ask people close to you which you do
Ask a stranger after a short chat, since they have no reason to spare you
checks.expl: You'll usually find you do many of them.

checks.q: What did her grieving friend need, in hindsight?
opts: Someone to bear witness and listen
Practical advice on what to do next
A similar story, to feel less alone
Distraction from the loss for a while
checks.expl: The matching story did nothing for her.

spch100.8.2.takeaway: Julian Treasure at TED: we are losing our listening in a noisy, recorded, headphone world. Five tools to get it back — silence, the mixer, savouring, listening positions — and RASA for conversation.

beats.d: Making meaning from sound, using pattern recognition, differencing and filters most of us are unaware of.
Recording, noise, headphones creating 'personal sound bubbles', and media that has to shout.
Three minutes of silence a day; the mixer (count the channels in a noisy café); savouring mundane sounds.
The most important tool: consciously choose how you listen to suit what you are hearing.
Receive, appreciate, summarise, ask.

spch100.8.2.worked: In a meeting, RASA sounds like: attention on the speaker, small 'mm' and 'right' sounds, then 'So what you're saying is…', then a question.
spch100.8.2.watch: Skipping 'summarise' because it feels slow. It is the step that proves you heard, and it often corrects a misunderstanding before it costs anything.

checks.q: What does RASA stand for?
opts: Repeat, ask, smile, agree
Receive, appreciate, summarise, ask
Respond, analyse, share, and then act
Relax, attend, speak, answer
checks.expl: It is also the Sanskrit word for juice or essence.

checks.q: Which exercise does Treasure call the most important?
opts: Listening positions — consciously choosing how you listen
Three minutes of silence every day to reset your ears
The mixer — picking out each channel of sound in a room
Savouring the mundane sounds you usually ignore entirely
checks.expl: It turns your filters into levers.

checks.q: What is 'the mixer' exercise?
opts: Mixing several pieces of music together and naming each one in turn
Talking over background noise until your voice carries without strain
Counting how many separate sound channels you can hear in a noisy place
Listening to two people at once and repeating back what each one said
checks.expl: It sharpens the quality of your listening.

spch100.8.3.takeaway: William Ury, co-author of Getting to Yes, at TEDxSanDiego: listening is the missing half of communication and the heart of negotiation. It helps you understand, connect, and get heard — and the hardest part is quieting yourself first.

beats.d: Shouted at for half an hour, Ury just listened until the president asked, 'So, what should I do?' — then proposed a Christmas truce.
Listening helps you understand the other side, builds rapport and trust, and makes them more likely to listen to you.
From inside their frame of reference: what is said and unsaid, the emotions and needs behind the words.
A businessman's list of demands turned out to mean one thing: freedom. The dispute settled in four days.
A moment of quiet before a hard conversation lets you notice and let go of your own reactions.

spch100.8.3.worked: Ury's follow-up when the list came: 'You seem to have everything. What are these things really going to give you? What do you most want in your life?'
spch100.8.3.watch: Defending yourself when someone is shouting. It feels natural and starts an argument you cannot win.

checks.q: Why does Ury call listening 'the cheapest concession'?
opts: It is quick, so it saves time in a long negotiation
It costs nothing and brings large benefits
It avoids paying money to settle the dispute
It ends negotiations sooner than arguing would
checks.expl: It helps you understand, connect, and get heard in return.

checks.q: What did the Brazilian businessman really want, under his list of demands?
opts: The company headquarters
A higher share price
Freedom
An apology
checks.expl: Once that was clear, the negotiation became much easier.

checks.q: What does Ury say helps you listen to others?
opts: Listening to yourself first, in a moment of quiet
Taking notes, so you can't drift off into your own thoughts
Asking many questions, so the other side keeps talking
Mirroring body language to show you are paying attention
checks.expl: Noticing your own reactions lets you set them aside.

spch100.8.4.takeaway: Chris Voss, former FBI hostage negotiator, in a short clip on the mirror: repeating someone's last few words is a reflex tool that invites them to keep talking, without the hint of interrogation in 'what do you mean by that?'

beats.d: 'IQ will get you hired, EQ will get you fired.' People skills keep you in the job.
In any moment, a mirror can bail you out.
'What do you mean by that?' has an edge of interrogation however well meant; a mirror feels like an invitation.
People expand, feel encouraged, and do not feel cornered.

spch100.8.4.worked: Client: 'The last vendor just didn't get our business.' You: 'Didn't get your business?' — and silence. They will usually tell you exactly what was missing.
spch100.8.4.watch: Mirroring in a flat or sarcastic tone, or rapid-fire. Said with curiosity and followed by silence, it invites; said any other way, it mocks.

checks.q: What is a mirror in Voss's sense?
opts: Copying someone's posture to build rapport
Repeating the last few words someone said
Agreeing with them so they keep talking
Summarising their whole point in your words
checks.expl: It invites them to continue.

checks.q: Why does he prefer a mirror to 'what do you mean by that?'
opts: The question can feel like interrogation; a mirror feels like an invitation
The question is too long, and a short mirror keeps the conversation moving faster
A mirror sounds smarter, because it proves you were listening word for word
The question ends the topic, while a mirror keeps the other person on the subject
checks.expl: People feel encouraged rather than cornered.

checks.q: What does 'IQ will get you hired, EQ will get you fired' mean?
opts: Intelligence is all that matters once you're inside a company
Emotional skill is what gets you promoted, not what keeps you employed
You can get the job on credentials and lose it for lack of people skills
Employers now prefer EQ to IQ, so they hire on people skills first of all
checks.expl: His point is that you need both.

spch100.8.5.takeaway: Alison Wood Brooks, who teaches 'How to Talk Gooder' at Harvard Business School, on the science of conversation: four maxims (TALK), a study showing we read others' topic preferences poorly, and a simple fix — prepare topics in advance.

beats.d: Every turn involves choices: stay on this topic or switch, ask or answer, joke or not.
Topics, Asking, Levity, Kindness — the last defined as receptiveness to opposing views, responsive listening, and reflection afterwards.
People guess their partner's topic preferences only a little better than chance, and a simple language algorithm does better.
Underweighted: they raised the topic, they laughed, they called back to it. Overweighted: mirror questions, often just politeness.
Jotting five topics beforehand raised enjoyment, lowered anxiety, and led to more interesting conversations.
In Q&A: power makes people think less about others' preferences, and low-status people laugh more out of deference.

spch100.8.5.worked: Before meeting a client you know a little, five topics on a card: the project they mentioned last time, their move to a new office, a book you both like, what's changing in their industry, their weekend hobby. You may use none; having them is what lowers the anxiety.
spch100.8.5.watch: Assuming they enjoy the topic because you do. Brooks's data shows we heavily project our own preferences.

checks.q: What does TALK stand for?
opts: Tell, ask, listen, keep going
Topics, asking, levity, kindness
Timing, attention, laughter, knowledge
Truth, accuracy, logic, kindness
checks.expl: A play on Grice's conversational maxims.

checks.q: Which cue does Brooks say people overweight as a sign of interest?
opts: Laughter at the other person's jokes about it
Who introduced the topic in the first place
Callbacks to the topic later on, after the conversation has moved
Mirror questions like asking 'how was your weekend?' back
checks.expl: Those are often just politeness.

checks.q: What did preparing five topics in advance do in her studies?
opts: Increased enjoyment and reduced anxiety
Made conversations feel forced and scripted
Made no real difference to how they went
Shortened conversations, since topics ran out
checks.expl: Prepared pairs also landed on more interesting topics.

spch100.8.6.takeaway: Charles Duhigg, in an animated talk: every discussion can hold three kinds of conversation — practical, emotional, social — and we connect when we match. Deep questions are the everyday way to find out which one you are in.

beats.d: He came home wanting sympathy; his wife gave advice. Both valid — but mismatched, so neither heard the other.
Practical (plans and problems), emotional (feelings; we want empathy, not solutions), social (identity and relationships).
Recognise which conversation is happening, then match it or invite the other person to match you.
'What do you love about your job?' instead of 'Where do you work?' They invite values and experiences.
Patients ignored his advice until he began by asking 'What does this diagnosis mean to you?' — listened — and then asked to move on to options.

spch100.8.6.worked: The experiment he recommends: ask someone 'When was the last time you cried in front of another person?' and then share your own answer. He cites research where people dread it beforehand and rate it as one of their best conversations afterwards.
spch100.8.6.watch: Answering an emotional conversation with practical advice. It is the commonest mismatch, and it makes good advice land as an attack.

checks.q: What are Duhigg's three kinds of conversation?
opts: Formal, informal and intimate
Practical, emotional, social
Business, personal, and family
Opening, middle, and closing
checks.expl: All three can happen in one discussion.

checks.q: What is the 'matching principle'?
opts: Recognising which conversation is happening and matching it, or inviting them to match you
Copying the other person's body language and tone so they feel at ease with you
Matching the other person's volume and pace, so neither of you seems to dominate it
Agreeing with whatever the other person says, to keep the peace in a tense moment
checks.expl: Mismatches are why people stop hearing each other.

checks.q: Which is a deep question?
opts: Where did you go to school, and what did you study there?
What time is the meeting, and who else is going?
What was high school like, and how did it change you?
How many people work there, and what do you do?
checks.expl: It asks about experience and meaning, not just facts.

spch100.8.7.takeaway: Vanessa Van Edwards at TEDxLondon: we are contagious, non-verbally, verbally and emotionally. Show your hands, smile for real, swap autopilot small talk for questions that spark, and reframe nerves as excitement.

beats.d: She says we look at hands first; hidden hands unsettle people. Her analysis found the most-viewed TED speakers used many more gestures.
Fear is caught (she cites a sweat study); so is happiness — but only a real smile, reaching the upper cheeks.
In her lab, listeners could hear a happy 'hello' and rated it as more likeable.
In 500 speed-networking conversations, 'What do you do?' and 'How are you?' scored worst. 'Working on anything exciting?' sends the brain looking for good things.
She cites a study where people who said 'I'm excited' before singing scored higher than those who said 'I'm nervous'.

spch100.8.7.worked: 'Been busy lately?' makes people search for stress. 'Anything good happen today?' makes them search for something good — and she argues you become more memorable for asking.
spch100.8.7.watch: Treating the numbers as laws. These are her lab's findings and cited studies; the practical point — questions that invite good news work better than autopilot ones — holds either way.

checks.q: Why does she suggest 'Working on anything exciting?' instead of 'Been busy?'
opts: It is shorter, so it fits easily into a quick passing exchange at work
It sends their mind looking for exciting things instead of stress
It sounds more professional than a casual question about being busy
It avoids talking about work, which most people would rather forget
checks.expl: The brain looks for hits that match the question.

checks.q: What distinguishes a real smile, in her talk?
opts: It shows the teeth, top and bottom
It lasts longer than a polite smile does, by a second or two
It reaches the upper cheek muscles, near the eyes
It is symmetrical on both sides of the mouth
checks.expl: People catch the real one, not the fake.

checks.q: What reframe does she recommend before a nerve-racking task?
opts: Saying 'I'm excited' instead of 'I'm nervous'
Saying 'I'm calm' until you really believe it
Saying nothing about it, so it doesn't grow
Taking three deep breaths before you start
checks.expl: Anxiety and excitement feel similar; the label changes the mindset.

spch100.8.8.takeaway: Kio Stark on talking to strangers: it creates 'fleeting intimacy' and frees us from seeing people as categories. Know the local rules — and try the ways in: smile, triangulate, notice, dogs and babies, disclose.

beats.d: An old man told her to step off the storm drain in case she disappeared — a small, warm exchange that made her feel noticed.
'Stranger' is a shortcut that leads to bias. Most strangers aren't dangerous; we just have no context.
People are often more open with strangers — and with strangers we explain everything instead of expecting mind-reading.
Civil inattention in the US; Danes avoiding 'excuse me'; Egyptian hospitality.
Smile; triangulate on a shared sight; notice (compliment shoes); talk to the dog or baby; disclose something true.

spch100.8.8.worked: Triangulation at a conference: standing by the same overloaded coffee station, 'Do you think they're testing which of us gives up first?' — a third thing you both see, and an easy start.
spch100.8.8.watch: Ignoring signals. Stark's first step is finding someone who is making eye contact; breaking the local rules a little is the point, ignoring someone's clear 'no' is not.

checks.q: What is 'triangulation' in Stark's sense?
opts: Talking to three people at once to spread the attention
Commenting on a third thing you and the stranger can both see
