Introducing two strangers to each other so you're not alone
Asking three questions in a row to keep the exchange going
checks.expl: Public art, someone preaching, odd clothes.

checks.q: What is the 'dogs and babies principle'?
opts: Avoiding people with dogs or babies, since they are busy and don't want to talk
Talking to their dog or baby to see whether the person is open to talking
Complimenting their pet first, because owners always enjoy hearing that
Asking about their children, since parents are always happy to talk about them
checks.expl: The dog or baby is a social conduit.

checks.q: What tends to happen when you disclose something personal to a stranger?
opts: They make an excuse and leave
They change the subject to something safer
They tend to disclose in return
They become suspicious of your reasons
checks.expl: We meet disclosure with disclosure.

spch100.8.9.takeaway: LeeAnn Renninger, from TED's The Way We Work: most feedback is either too soft to register or too direct to hear. Great feedback-givers use four parts — micro-yes, data point, impact, question — and ask for feedback regularly.

beats.d: She cites Gallup: only 26 per cent of employees strongly agree that the feedback they get improves their work.
A short question that signals feedback is coming and gives a choice: 'Can I share some ideas about that meeting?'
What you saw or heard. Convert blur words ('not reliable') into specifics ('you said 11; I still don't have it').
'Because of that, I was blocked.' Then: 'How do you see it?' — turning compliance into commitment.
Ask for feedback regularly rather than waiting for it.

spch100.8.9.worked: Positive feedback needs specifics too: 'I liked how you added those stories, because it helped me grasp the concepts faster' tells the person exactly what to keep doing.
spch100.8.9.watch: Blur words in praise ('great job'). They feel kind and tell the person nothing about what to repeat.

checks.q: What is a 'micro-yes'?
opts: A small compliment given first so the criticism that follows is softer
A short yes/no question that signals feedback is coming and gets buy-in
Agreeing quickly with the other person's view before you disagree
A one-word answer that closes the feedback conversation politely
checks.expl: It paces the conversation and gives autonomy.

checks.q: What is a 'blur word'?
opts: A word that can mean different things to different people, like 'proactive'
A filler word such as 'like' or 'um' that blurs the point you are making
A long word that sounds impressive but leaves the listener unsure
A technical term that the person receiving the feedback might not know
checks.expl: Convert it into an actual data point.

checks.q: Why end feedback with a question?
opts: To be polite, so the feedback ends on a friendly note
To end the conversation quickly, before it becomes a debate
To create commitment and joint problem-solving, not just compliance
To check they were listening before you move on to the next point
checks.expl: It stops being a monologue.

spch100.8.10.takeaway: Julia Dhar, three-time world schools debating champion, on disagreeing productively — find common ground, debate ideas not identities, hold the humility of uncertainty — with Modupe Akinola of Columbia adding the negotiation view: ask probing, open and neutral questions.

beats.d: Her first debate at age ten made every cable-news mistake: attacking the person, then going to extremes.
The best persuaders start with whatever everyone agrees on, however narrow — a shared reality.
Debaters don't pick their sides. At work, collect ideas anonymously on one template; half the best ones in her government project came from people who'd rarely be heard.
Ask: what have you changed your mind about? Pre-commit to what would change yours. Mr Rogers moved a sceptical senator in 1969.
Probing ('what qualities does John bring?'), open ('what would you need to know to use my approach?'), neutral ('how would you assess the project?').

spch100.8.10.worked: Instead of 'Hasn't the project been a great success?' (leading) ask 'How would you assess the project so far?' (neutral) — less confrontational, and you learn what they actually think.
spch100.8.10.watch: Arguing with the person rather than the idea. The moment you say 'that's such a finance view', you've made it about identity, and they will defend themselves, not the idea.

checks.q: Where does Dhar say productive disagreement starts?
opts: With your strongest argument
With common ground, however narrow
With the other side's weakest point
With data
checks.expl: It invites everyone into a shared reality.

checks.q: Which is a neutral question?
opts: Hasn't the project been a great success?
Are we using my approach, yes or no?
How would you assess the project so far?
Why do you want John?
checks.expl: Leading and closed questions provoke defensiveness.

checks.q: Why does Dhar suggest collecting ideas anonymously?
opts: To separate ideas from the identity of the person who proposed them
To save time, because nobody has to present their own ideas aloud
To avoid disputes later about who should get the credit for an idea
To make meetings shorter by sorting the ideas before anyone arrives
checks.expl: Ideas are then judged on their merits.

spch100.9.0.takeaway: Chris Anderson: a speaker's number one task is to transfer an idea into the listener's mind. Not a formula — red rug, childhood story, call to action — but one idea, built carefully out of what the audience already has.

beats.d: Overused devices come across as clichéd or manipulative. What great talks share is an idea, recreated in every listener.
A pattern of information that helps you understand and navigate the world. A worldview is built from millions of them.

beats.t: One idea, a reason to care
beats.d: Cut to one through-line, then stir curiosity by showing a gap in how they see things.
Build from what the listener already knows; a metaphor shows the shape. Test it on friends.
Ask who the idea benefits. One that only serves you will be seen through.

spch100.9.0.worked: Jennifer Kahn explaining CRISPR: 'It's as if, for the first time, you had a word processor to edit DNA.' Cut and paste is a concept everyone already has, so the new idea snaps into place.
spch100.9.0.watch: Jargon you no longer notice. Anderson's warning is that terms you live with every day are completely unfamiliar to the audience — testing on a friend is how you find them.

checks.q: According to Anderson, what do all great TED talks have in common?
opts: A personal childhood story that opens the talk and sets the tone
An inspiring call to action the audience can take home
They build a single idea in the listener's mind
A round red rug and a speaker who never uses notes
checks.expl: The devices are optional; the idea is not.

checks.q: What does he say is the main tool for earning the audience's permission?
opts: Curiosity — revealing a gap in their understanding
Humour, so they relax enough to listen to the idea
Credentials, so they trust you before you begin
Statistics that prove the idea matters to them
checks.expl: A disconnection in their worldview makes them want it bridged.

checks.q: Why does the 'word processor for DNA' line work?
opts: It is technically complete, so experts in the room can't fault it
It builds the new idea from a concept the listener already has
It uses scientific vocabulary, which signals the speaker's authority
It is funny, and a laugh helps an unfamiliar idea go down easily
checks.expl: Metaphor shows the shape of the pattern using something familiar.

spch100.9.1.takeaway: The villain of clear explanation is the curse of knowledge: once you know something, it is hard to remember not knowing it. Made to Stick's answer is to find the core, make it concrete, make people feel it, and tell a story.

beats.d: Sticky ideas are simple, unexpected, concrete, credible, emotional, and told as stories.
Tappers expected to be understood half the time; listeners named 3 songs in 120. The tune was only in the tapper's head.
Rich's brother taught her to ski and forgot to mention getting off the lift. He had forgotten what not knowing feels like.
Prioritise; the model is a proverb. Too many options, even irrelevant ones, paralyse people.
Abstract truths travel in concrete language; people give to one person, not a region; stories are remembered.

spch100.9.1.worked: Jerry Kaplan, 29, with no slide deck, dropped a plain leather folder on the table: 'here is a model of the next step in the computer revolution'. The partners picked it up, imagined it as a laptop and argued about memory chips — the concrete object did the explaining, and he raised 4.5 million.
spch100.9.1.watch: Thinking at the expert's altitude. Experts want to talk chess strategy; the listener needs to know how the bishop moves.

checks.q: In the tapping study, how often did listeners name the song?
opts: About half the time
About one time in four
About 3 times in 120
Never
checks.expl: The tappers predicted 50 per cent.

checks.q: What does SUCCES stand for?
opts: Simple, unexpected, concrete, credible, emotional, stories
Short, useful, clear, correct, easy, and sincere
Structure, urgency, contrast, credibility, energy, story
Simple, unique, catchy, credible, exciting and social
checks.expl: The final S is dropped from 'success'.

checks.q: Why did Kaplan's leather folder work?
opts: It looked expensive, which signalled how serious the project was
It made an abstract idea concrete enough to handle and argue about
It contained detailed specifications that settled every argument
It surprised them with its colour, so they remembered the meeting
checks.expl: Concreteness makes an idea mean the same thing to everyone.

spch100.9.2.takeaway: Melissa Marshall: scientists and engineers have to invite the rest of us in. Say why it matters, cut the jargon without dumbing it down, use examples and analogies, and replace bullet points with one sentence and a picture.

beats.d: Relevance first: the bone research matters because of osteoporosis.
'Space and time', not 'spatial and temporal'. As simple as possible, but no simpler.
The ways in for someone outside the field.
Bulleted slides overload the language part of the brain. One readable sentence plus a visual.
Science minus bullets and jargon, divided by relevance, times passion.

spch100.9.2.worked: Genevieve Brown's slide: one readable sentence — the structure of trabeculae is so strong it inspired the design of the Eiffel Tower — and an image, instead of a bulleted list about bone mesh.
spch100.9.2.watch: Confusing accessible with dumbed down. Marshall's point is that you can be clear without compromising the idea.

checks.q: What question does Marshall say a technical speaker must answer first?
opts: How does it work, step by step, in practice?
So what — why is it relevant to us?
Who funded it, and why should we trust them?
What method did you use to get the results?
checks.expl: Relevance is the way in.

checks.q: What should replace a slide full of bullet points?
opts: A table with the same points laid out in rows
Two slides of shorter bullets instead of one
One readable sentence plus a visual
A short video that explains the same points
checks.expl: The sentence is something to key into if they get lost.

checks.q: In her equation, what do you divide by?
opts: Relevance to the audience
The time you have to speak
Your passion for the subject
The amount of jargon you use
checks.expl: Then multiply by passion.

spch100.9.3.takeaway: A live before-and-after makeover of one business slide. Visualise — make it clear where to look — and verbalise — tell people what to see and what to do about it.

beats.d: Tables are read, graphs are seen. A line graph showed the trend the table at the bottom of the slide buried.
Border, gridlines, the box around the data, diagonal labels, trailing zeros — each removal makes the data stand out.
Solid for what was measured; dashed lines and hollow markers for projections, so nobody mistakes a target for a result.
No ACCTS, MOS or undefined ASP; one name per metric; the title at the top left where the eye starts.
The original read as good news. Asking the client showed the target was out of reach, so the slide became a decision.

spch100.9.3.worked: Before: a red star, '77% achieved in nine months', 'great market and successful launch'. After: the title asks whether to reassess the target or change the salesforce strategy, and two graphs show accounts per manager flattening since the sales-team integration, so the forecast of 25 per manager will not happen.
spch100.9.3.watch: Watch the first 24 minutes. After that the session turns into a book launch (giveaways, a discount code, workshop dates) and audience questions.

checks.q: Why do graphs usually beat tables for making a point?
opts: Graphs look more professional, so executives trust the numbers more readily
Tables use the slower verbal system; graphs use the faster visual one
Graphs hold more numbers in the same space than a table ever could
Executives prefer colour, and a table has to stay black and white
checks.expl: Reading numbers means scanning and holding them in your head.

checks.q: How do they show forecast data beside actual data?
opts: The same solid line, labelled 'forecast' at the end
They leave the forecast out until someone asks for it
A different format, such as dashed lines and unfilled markers
On a separate slide, so the two never get confused at all
checks.expl: The formatting itself carries the uncertainty.

checks.q: What turned the slide from a success story into a call to action?
opts: Pressure-testing the assumptions with the client
A new colour scheme that highlights the shortfall in red
Adding more data so the trend became undeniable
Removing the title so the graph spoke for itself
checks.expl: Make assumptions explicit and talk to people about them.

spch100.9.4.takeaway: Nancy Duarte studied cinema, literature and thousands of presentations and found a shape: what is, what could be, back and forth, then a call to action and the new bliss. The audience is the hero; the presenter is the mentor.

beats.d: We react physically to stories; presentations flatline. She set out to find why.
The presenter is not Luke Skywalker but Yoda, helping the audience cross into the new idea.
Contrast the status quo with what could be, and make the gap as wide as possible.
Move back and forth between the two; resistance is used, the way a sailing boat uses the wind.
End with the call to action and a picture of the world with the idea adopted.

spch100.9.4.worked: King's bad check: 'America has given the Negro people a bad check, a check which has come back marked insufficient funds' (what is), then 'we have come to cash this check' (what could be). The first great roar came at that contrast, carried by a metaphor everyone understood.
spch100.9.4.watch: Making yourself the hero. The idea goes nowhere unless the audience takes it up. A content note: the last two minutes are her own life story and mention childhood abuse.

checks.q: In Duarte's model, what role does the presenter play?
opts: The hero, who has crossed over and returns to tell of it
The villain, who stands for the old way of doing things
The narrator, who stays outside the story and explains it
The mentor who helps the audience cross over
checks.expl: The audience is the hero of the idea.

checks.q: How does a Duarte-shaped talk begin?
opts: With a joke that relaxes the room and earns attention
With what is — the status quo — set against what could be
With the call to action, so the audience knows the ask
With credentials, so the audience trusts the mentor
checks.expl: The contrast is the inciting incident.

checks.q: What is the 'new bliss'?
opts: A picture of the world with your idea adopted, used as the ending
The opening hook, which makes the audience want what could be
The question and answer session, once the formal talk is over
A product demo at the end that shows the idea working live
checks.expl: Jobs ended on Gretzky's puck; King on 'free at last'.

spch100.9.5.takeaway: Simon Lancaster: lift the audience from the first line rather than starting with a ritual thank-you. Choose the feeling you want — pleasure, connection or alertness — and open with a joke, a story or a question.

beats.d: Most openings are 'delighted to be here'; he claims students' brain activity in lectures is lower than in sleep.
His go-to is Einstein's driver, plus spare one-liners for when the tech fails. Self-deprecation lifts the audience.
Telling them what you'll tell them is boring three times. Wrap the point in a story — his is the twins in the neonatal unit.
Emotional, factual, philosophical, or a prolonged dilemma.
Maya Angelou: people never forget how you made them feel.

spch100.9.5.worked: The open dilemma: it's 1935, you are Gandhi, your sandal falls under the departing train — do you board or go back for it? Left open through a whole speech, answered at the end: he threw the other sandal down too, so whoever found them would have a pair.
spch100.9.5.watch: Treat the three 'drugs' — dopamine, oxytocin, cortisol — as a memorable framing, not settled neuroscience; the brain-chemistry claims are simplified. The opening drug jokes and the 'psychopaths' line are bits, not data.

checks.q: Which opening does Lancaster recommend for connection and empathy?
opts: A question to the room
A striking statistic
A personal story
A joke at your expense
checks.expl: Stories let the audience see the world through your eyes.

checks.q: What is his objection to 'tell them what you're going to tell them'?
opts: It takes too long, so the audience has lost interest before the main point arrives
It amounts to announcing you'll be boring, being boring, then saying you were
It is too emotional for a business setting, where people expect plain structure
It confuses the audience by giving away the ending before the story has started
checks.expl: You can't stamp a point into someone's head.

checks.q: How did the Gandhi question work in the speech he describes?
opts: It was asked, left open through the speech, and answered at the end
It was answered immediately, so the audience could relax and listen
It was rhetorical, with no answer, so each listener supplied their own
It was asked only at the end, to leave the audience something to think about
checks.expl: The image stayed wedged in the audience's minds.

spch100.9.6.takeaway: Simon Lancaster: rhetoric used to be taught to everyone; now it is the privilege of a few. Threes, repetition, balance, metaphor, exaggeration and rhyme make arguments compelling — which is why you should know them both to use and to resist.

beats.d: Tricolon: 'veni, vidi, vici'. Short, three-part phrases sound complete and credible.
Repeating the opening clause is the sound of passion — and why market traders use it.
Antithesis makes thinking sound balanced, even when the balance is an illusion.
We use one roughly every 16 words, and they steer decisions on investment, crime and war.
Emotional people overstate; rhymes feel true because they are easy to process.

spch100.9.6.worked: 'Calais jungle' turns migrants into wild animals; 'financial storm' makes a crisis sound like weather that nobody caused, while Pope Francis's harsher image demands a clean-up. Same events, different conclusions, decided by the picture.
spch100.9.6.watch: Using the devices to dress up a weak argument. His own improvised demo shows they can make an absurd case sound plausible. A content note: there is strong language near the end.

checks.q: What is a tricolon?
opts: A rhyme at the end of a line
A metaphor in three parts
Putting points in threes
A question repeated three times
checks.expl: 'Government of the people, by the people, for the people.'

checks.q: Why, according to Lancaster, do balanced sentences persuade?
opts: Balanced sentences are shorter, so the audience can remember them word for word
A balanced sentence suggests balanced thinking, even when that's an illusion
Balanced sentences usually rhyme, and rhyme makes any claim sound more true
Balanced sentences carry metaphors, which do the persuading for the speaker
checks.expl: Our brains like balance.

checks.q: What does the 'financial storm' metaphor imply, in his reading?
opts: That the crisis was natural and nobody was to blame
That the bankers caused it and should pay for the damage
That it will last a long time and get worse before better
That experts predicted it and were ignored by politicians
checks.expl: A storm sweeps in and sweeps away with no need for action.

spch100.9.7.takeaway: Kevin Hale: investors and customers will do the selling in their own heads once they understand you — so your job is clarity. Lead with what you make, give them three nouns to picture, and cut everything that doesn't add excitement.

beats.d: YC reckons that for every company it interviews, another just as good was missed because its application did not express the idea clearly.
Ambiguity, complexity, mystery and the ignorable — buzzwords the listener filters out like banner ads.
Three nouns — product, problem, customer. 'Lumini is building X-ray vision for soldiers and first responders.'
X must be a household success, Y must want it, and Y must be a big market.
Concision tells the listener you have thought deeply and are efficient.

spch100.9.7.worked: 'Our company will make low-cost and low-power-consumption medical devices based on artificial intelligence and IoT suitable for sub-Saharan communities' becomes 'affordable medical devices for sub-Saharan Africa'. The AI and IoT were the how; 'low cost' was the word that earned its place.
spch100.9.7.watch: Padding to look bigger. Hale sees founders defending against imagined objections inside the description itself, and every inflating word moves the listener further away.

checks.q: Which three nouns should a listener be able to picture from your description?
opts: The team, the market, and the revenue so far
What you make, the problem, the customer
The mission, the vision, and the values
The price, the product, and where it's sold
checks.expl: Without them they can't ask the next questions.

checks.q: When does 'X for Y' fail, in Hale's terms?
opts: When X is a household name that the listener already knows
When Y is a big market with lots of competition in it
When X is small or obscure, as in 'Buffer for Snapchat'
When Y clearly wants X, so the comparison adds nothing
checks.expl: Buffer is smaller than Snapchat, so the comparison shrinks you.

checks.q: What does concision signal to an investor?
opts: That you have thought deeply and work efficiently
That the business is small and the idea is simple
That you are nervous and want the meeting to end
That you lack the data to back up a longer pitch
checks.expl: Efficient with words suggests efficient with thoughts and actions.

spch100.9.8.takeaway: Michael Seibel: a pitch is a 30-second version you can give anyone and a 2-minute version for someone you must convince. Anything longer is mostly a chance to say something they don't like.

beats.d: What you do (the mom test), how big the market is, and traction or speed.
Two sentences of 'aha'. If they look as though they already knew it, you didn't nail it.
One sentence on how you make money; then founders, technical mix, how long you've known each other, full-time.
Instrument, cap, amount, minimum check. This is where jargon belongs.
Flip the power: plan to need little money, get warm intros, and book every meeting in the same week.

spch100.9.8.worked: 'We're Airbnb and we allow you to rent out the extra room in your house' rather than 'we're a marketplace for space' — the first needs no prior knowledge, the second needs a follow-up question.
spch100.9.8.watch: Running from the business-model question. Listing advertising, maybe virtual goods, maybe something else tells the listener you don't know; say what your industry usually does and move on.

checks.q: What are the three sentences of Seibel's 30-second pitch?
opts: Who the team is, what the product is, and the ask
What you do, how big the market is, your traction
The problem, the solution, and the long-term vision
The mission, the company history and your goals
checks.expl: From there a conversation can start.

checks.q: What does he advise if your business model is advertising?
opts: Avoid mentioning it until investors ask directly
List several options to look flexible and open
Say it plainly in one sentence and move on
Promise to decide on the model after launch
checks.expl: Facebook and Google are advertising businesses.

checks.q: How should investor meetings be scheduled?
opts: All in the same week, after warm introductions
One a week, so you can learn from each meeting
Cold emails to as many investors as possible
Only after launch, once you have real users
checks.expl: Fundraising is a sprint, not a marathon.

spch100.9.9.takeaway: Kindra Hall, in a customer-success podcast: calling something 'our story' doesn't make it one. Business stories need an arc — normal, explosion, new normal — with a named character, real emotion and a specific moment, and there are four kinds worth having: value, founder, purpose and customer.

beats.d: 'This is our story — we believe in excellence' or a list of gigabytes is just words with a label on.
Normal (the situation and what was at stake), explosion (the inflection point), new normal (what is possible now).
A character with a name, emotion that can be matter-of-fact, and a moment zoomed in so the listener sees it.
Value, founder (including your own founding moment in a role), purpose, and customer — with low production value often more believable.
The true detail you need is there if you think harder; a made-up one is hard to keep straight.

spch100.9.9.worked: The host, Josh, tells his company's founding story unrehearsed and it comes out as a résumé — consulting, then meetings, then customer success managers. Hall's edit: add the matter-of-fact emotion (information slipping away), cut the steps that don't matter, find the moment he realised, and loop back to 'information slipping through your fingers like grains of sand'.
spch100.9.9.watch: Telling it chronologically. 'First we did this, then this' is a natural first draft and reads like a résumé; the story is in the moment, not the sequence.

checks.q: What are the three parts of Hall's story arc?
opts: Problem, solution, and the benefit
Hook, body, and a strong close
Setup, conflict, and resolution
Normal, explosion, new normal
checks.expl: The explosion doesn't need fireworks — just the inflection point.

checks.q: What does Hall say about emotion in a business story?
opts: It must be dramatic, or the story won't be remembered
Matter-of-fact frustration is enough if the audience has felt it
It should be avoided, since business audiences distrust it
Only customer stories need it; founder stories can be factual
checks.expl: 'This isn't right' is an emotion.

checks.q: Which is NOT one of her four business story types?
opts: Value story
Founder story
Competitor story
Customer story
checks.expl: The fourth is the purpose story.

spch100.9.10.takeaway: Kindra Hall, interviewed at length: the stories that sell are small, true moments, and a sales team can systematically build one for every point of its pitch. 'Can I tell you a story?' moves a sceptic into curiosity, and it is working when they tell one back.

beats.d: Her origin story: a family minivan, five people doing five things, united by a storytelling-festival tape.
She used to think her life wasn't dramatic enough to tell. The small, everyday stories are the ones people relate to.
Not product claims but the dress that didn't fit last year and does this year.
Telling people what they should do is the oldest form of selling; a story lets them want it themselves.
A client's team took four differentiators and ten pitch points and went into the company to find a real story for each, then put them in the sales manual.

spch100.9.10.worked: A volunteer firefighter calmed a frightened woman who had been misled to get the door open by asking 'Can I tell you a story?' and telling her about a colleague who went in without backup and didn't come out. She calmed down, asked questions, and let them work.
spch100.9.10.watch: Skipping the first quarter-hour is tempting: it is the host's praise and Hall's own origin story, which is itself a demonstration. The teaching runs from about 15:00 to 42:00.

checks.q: How did the sales team Hall describes build its story catalogue?
opts: They hired actors to perform composite customer stories on video
They found a true story inside the organisation for each key pitch point
They wrote composite customers that combined the best of several real ones
They used competitors' stories and swapped in their own product's name
checks.expl: It meant talking to customer service and breaking down silos.

checks.q: According to Hall and her mentor Donald Davis, how do you know a story is working?
opts: They tell a related story back to you
They take notes on what you're saying
They laugh at the right moments
They ask for a brochure or a demo
checks.expl: Then you are two people sharing stories.

checks.q: What does Hall insist on about business stories?
opts: They must be dramatic
They must be short
They must be true
They must be about the founder
checks.expl: This is not an opportunity to falsify.

spch100.9.11.takeaway: Chris Voss's accusation audit: list every accusation the other side could make against you and say it first. Naming a negative doesn't plant it — it inoculates against it.

beats.d: Start with what you would want to deny — 'I don't want them to think I'm greedy.'
From denial to observation: 'You're probably going to think I'm greedy.'
'Am I wasting my time?' and 'are there better alternatives?' come up in every deal.
It deactivates the negative thinking so people get collaborative faster.

spch100.9.11.worked: Opening an audit call: 'You're probably wondering whether this is another consultant about to tell you to buy more software, and whether this hour is a waste of your time.' Said first, the owner doesn't have to sit on it.
spch100.9.11.watch: Sarcasm. An accusation audit delivered with an edge sounds like a dare; it has to be a plain, calm observation.

checks.q: Where does Voss say to start your accusation list?
opts: With your strengths, so the list feels balanced
With what you would want to deny
With their weaknesses, to level the field
With the price, since that's always the issue
checks.expl: Then shift from denial to observation.

checks.q: What does he say happens when you name a negative that isn't there?
opts: It plants the idea in their head, so only name real ones
It makes you look weak before the negotiation starts
It confuses them about what you're really offering
It inoculates against it rather than planting it
checks.expl: He admits he doesn't know why; he knows it works.

checks.q: When should you do the accusation audit?
opts: Up front, before they raise the objections
Only if they object, so you don't plant ideas
At the close, once the offer is on the table
In writing afterwards, as a follow-up email
checks.expl: Don't wait for them to ask.

spch100.9.12.takeaway: Alex Lyon, from his mentor Allen Weiner's book: most questions are direct — yes/no, multiple choice, fill in the blank — and deserve a direct answer of about one sentence plus one sentence of detail, then silence.

beats.d: True/false, multiple choice, fill in the blank, and essay. The first three are direct.
The headline answer, about a sentence of detail, then a mental full stop.
'No; however, I can have it done by Tuesday.'
A clipped 'turnovers' sounds like a coach brushing off the press.
The talk was your monologue; short answers allow many turns.

spch100.9.12.worked: 'When can you have that project done?' is fill in the blank: 'Wednesday looks best — that leaves a day for testing.' 'Can you have it by Monday?' is yes/no: 'No; however, I can have it by Tuesday.'
spch100.9.12.watch: Burying the answer under background. The line from The Hunt for Red October is the rule: you're liable to be asked some direct questions — give them direct answers.

checks.q: Which kind of question is 'Does Monday or Wednesday work better?'
opts: Essay
Fill in the blank
Multiple choice
True/false
checks.expl: Pick one, add a sentence, stop.

checks.q: What should follow a direct answer?
opts: About one sentence of detail, then stop
A full explanation of the background to it
A question back, to check what they meant
Nothing at all — a one-word answer is best
checks.expl: One-word answers overcorrect.

checks.q: Why do concise answers suit Q&A?
opts: They hide weaknesses, since there's no time to dig into them
They allow back-and-forth dialogue, which audiences find satisfying
They save the speaker effort for the important parts of the talk
They avoid follow-up questions, so the session ends on time
checks.expl: The monologue is over.

spch100.9.13.takeaway: Michael Seibel on Y Combinator interviews: the founders who go furthest answer the question asked, briefly, and say 'I don't know' when they don't. A different answer hijacks the path the interviewer was walking towards yes.

beats.d: In high school he was praised for saying 'I don't know'. Years of interviews showed him why.
Having a few minutes doesn't mean filling them; impact rises as words fall.
The interviewer is walking a path towards yes; dodging the question interrupts it.
Straight, fast, concise, ideally with real numbers.

spch100.9.13.worked: Asked 'how many users came back last week?', the strong answer is the number, or 'I don't know — I can pull it tonight', not a tour of the roadmap.
spch100.9.13.watch: Answering the question you wish you'd been asked. It feels like steering; to the listener it reads as evasion.

checks.q: What did Seibel notice about the founders who do best in interviews?
opts: They talk the longest, using every minute to show how much they know about it
They answer the question asked, and say 'I don't know' when they don't
They bring slides and numbers, so every answer is backed up with evidence
They steer each question back to the strongest part of their story
checks.expl: Straightforward beats impressive.

checks.q: Why is not answering the question costly?
opts: It is rude, and the interviewer takes it personally
It wastes time, but has no other real cost to you
It takes over the interviewer's line of thought towards yes
It shows nerves, which investors read as a lack of conviction
checks.expl: It makes it harder to get to yes.

checks.q: What does he say about the number of words you use?
opts: Their impact goes up the fewer you say
More detail is always safer in an interview
Use every minute you're given to make the case
Words don't matter much — only the numbers do
checks.expl: Concise and on track.

spch100.9.14.takeaway: Chris Voss: deliver bad news by bracing people — 'I've got bad news' — pausing for a count of two, then saying it. Not 'how are you?', which they have learned to dread.

beats.d: He was told of a hostage's death this way at 5am, and made the same call to others all day.
Well-meant, but people learn it means bad news, and in a crisis it sounds clueless.
'I've got bad news', a count of two, then the news.
A longer pause becomes excruciating.

spch100.9.14.worked: Telling a client their campaign lost money: 'I've got bad news.' (one, two) 'The ads you ran in September cost more than the bookings they brought in.' Then stop and let them respond.
spch100.9.14.watch: Cushioning. A paragraph of reassurance before the news is the 'how are you?' habit in another form.

checks.q: What does Voss say to do instead of opening with 'how are you?'
opts: Send an email first, so the news isn't a shock
Say 'I've got bad news', pause briefly, then deliver it
Start with some good news to soften what comes next
Ask how their week was, so they feel cared about
checks.expl: It braces them.

checks.q: How long should the pause be?
opts: About ten seconds, to let it sink in
As long as it takes them to reply
No pause — get it over with quickly
About a count of two
checks.expl: Longer is excruciating.

checks.q: Why is 'how are you?' a poor opening for bad news?
opts: People link it with bad news coming, and it can sound clueless
It is too formal for a call that is going to be emotional
It takes too long, and the other person wants the news now
It is impolite to ask about someone's day before giving news
checks.expl: You often already know how they are.

spch100.9.15.takeaway: Chris Voss: 'Have you given up on this project?' restarts conversations that have gone silent. When they reply, summarise their facts and feelings until you get a 'that's right' — being understood matters more to many people than winning.

beats.d: Nobody likes to give up, and nobody wants to say yes without knowing what it commits them to; replies often come within minutes.
There's a good chance you contributed to the silence.
The facts, and how they feel about the facts — including feelings driving them that they're blind to.
Once people feel understood they may change their minds about decisions already made.

spch100.9.15.worked: A prospect who went quiet after a proposal gets one line: 'Have you given up on fixing the booking problem?' When they reply, the summary might be: 'It sounds like the cost was fine, but you're worried about the time it would take your staff to learn a new system during the busy season.'
spch100.9.15.watch: A summary of facts only. Voss's point is the feelings about the facts; leave those out and they won't feel understood.

checks.q: Why does 'have you given up on this project?' work?
opts: It threatens them with losing the deal entirely
It offers a way out that also includes a discount
Nobody likes to give up, and nobody wants to say yes to it
It is so polite that nobody can bring themselves to ignore it
checks.expl: It restarts stalled negotiations.

checks.q: What should your summary include?
opts: The facts and how they feel about the facts
Only the facts, so emotions don't take over
Your offer, restated clearly one more time
Your own feelings about how things went
checks.expl: That earns the 'that's right'.

checks.q: For whom, does Voss say, is being understood often more important than the deal?
opts: Nobody, once money is involved
The assertive negotiator
Only friends and family
Only the buyer in a deal
checks.expl: Being understood can matter more than getting what they want.

spch100.9.16.takeaway: Matthew Dicks: in 1997 he and his friend Benji launched a wedding-DJ company knowing nothing about weddings or music. Unable to compete on equipment, they competed on story — 37 bookings from 37 couples at their first bridal show, and 100 of the first 100 they ever met.

beats.d: Benji asked if he wanted to be a wedding DJ. He says yes to everything, planning to turn a yes into a no later if he must.
The practice party went terribly; their first wedding was free, and he ended up in the cake-cutting photos.
One table, one plain red flyer, and stories — about that first wedding, and about two friends who bonded over a cartoon theme song at McDonald's.
A couple's worry got a story about an earlier couple with the same problem, and their options.
37 weddings booked before they had done their second, and a company that ran for more than 25 years.

spch100.9.16.worked: A bride says she doesn't much like her father but knows she has to dance with him. Instead of advice, Dicks answers with a story: a year ago Janet had the same problem; here is what Janet did, and here are some of your options.
spch100.9.16.watch: This is the opening of one of his courses, so the last minute is a pitch for his teaching. The method is in the middle: what they did at the bridal show and in client meetings.

checks.q: Why did Dicks and Benji decide to 'fight with story'?
opts: They had studied storytelling and wanted to test it at a show
They couldn't compete on music, equipment or effects
The bridal show required every vendor to tell a story
Their flyer was too long, so they talked to couples instead
checks.expl: Everyone else had lights and smoke machines.

checks.q: How did he answer a bride's worry about the father-daughter dance?
opts: With a story about an earlier bride who had the same problem, and her options
With a discount on the dance package, so the worry about cost went away
By changing the subject to the music she wanted for the rest of the night
With a playlist of songs that suit a father-daughter dance of any length
checks.expl: The story carried the advice.

checks.q: What was their goal at the bridal show?
opts: To have the best-looking booth at the show
To hand out more flyers than any other DJ there
To book the most expensive weddings of the coming season
To become people the couple would want at their wedding
checks.expl: Except that the couple would be paying them to come.

spch100.10.0.takeaway: Telling your life story in five minutes, against a timer, is a selection test. The limit forces choices, and the parts you choose are the ones you feel define you — which is what to share with an audience.

beats.d: Found on a list of dinner questions: tell your partner your life story in five minutes.
She sets the timer and goes: a wealthy town she never fitted into, choosing Buffalo for its community, a career in marketing.
Anxiety as a teenager, therapy, and now social media for an organisation fighting mental-health stigma.
A programme she'd say shaped her life didn't make the five minutes.
Each attempt narrows in on what defines you.

spch100.10.0.worked: Her five minutes become one arc she hadn't planned: not fitting in among wealth as a child, choosing a city for its community, therapy in high school, and now helping change how her community sees mental illness. The timer found the thread.
spch100.10.0.watch: Treating it as a résumé. The point is not to cover everything but to see what you select; if your five minutes are dates and job titles, do it again and say what each choice meant.

checks.q: What does the five-minute limit do?
opts: Forces choices, revealing what you feel defines you
Makes the story funnier, because there's no time for the slow parts
Ensures you cover every stage of life in the right order
Helps you memorise a version you can tell anywhere
checks.expl: Selection is the exercise.

checks.q: What did she notice about her own attempt?
opts: She ran out of time before she'd reached the age of ten
She left out something she'd have called life-shaping
She talked only about her work and never about family
She couldn't think of anything to say for the first minute
checks.expl: What you omit is information too.

checks.q: How should you use the exercise over time?
opts: Do it once, and keep that version as your story
Only with strangers, who don't know your history
Repeat it to keep narrowing in on what defines you
Write it as an essay instead, to get the order right
checks.expl: The more you do it, the clearer the points.

spch100.10.1.takeaway: A story bank only works if you can find the right story later. Michelle Knight files hers in five categories and tags each with emotion, lesson and offer, so a launch, a post or a video can pull exactly the story it needs.

beats.d: Stress about what to share disappears when the stories are already collected.
Idea, written, posted — with a link to where each story was used, so it can be reused.
Career moments, personal growth, relationships, challenges, and daily life behind the scenes.
Emotion, lesson and offer connection: the coloured markers on the folders.
Phone and voice notes, a weekly review. Once you start looking, you see stories everywhere.

spch100.10.1.worked: Her most-used story: signing her first paying client on a live stream after running home from work. It sits under career moments, tagged for excitement and fear, with the photo her husband took attached — and it has been reused on webinars and sales pages.
spch100.10.1.watch: The tool tour. The video is sponsored by a project-management app and spends time on its AI features; the method works in any spreadsheet or notes app.

checks.q: Which is NOT one of Knight's five categories?
opts: Career and business moments
Challenges and obstacles
Competitor analysis
Daily life and behind the scenes
checks.expl: The other two are personal growth and relationships.

checks.q: Why tag a story with its lesson?
opts: So search finds it when you type the lesson into the bank later
So you remember the point months later when you go to use it
So you can cut the story down to the lesson when time is short
So the platform's algorithm can match it to the right audience
checks.expl: Some stories sit untouched for six months.

checks.q: What does the offer-connection tag do?
opts: Lets you find the stories that lead naturally to a product or service
Sets a price for each story, depending on how much it is likely to sell
Tracks how many views each story got, so you know which offer to push
Hides the private stories from anyone who hasn't bought the offer yet
checks.expl: This is where storytelling and selling meet.

spch100.11.0.takeaway: Jenny Hoyos, whose shorts average millions of views, gives her framework in four minutes: a surprising question, constant progression, conflict, uncertainty — and a quick answer. She says it works for asking for a raise as well as for a feed.

beats.d: People stay to find out the answer, so ask something surprising first.
Show how close you are — each ingredient added is a step towards the answer.
Without it nobody is invested. Her mother is the B plot.
Keep the outcome in doubt right up to the end.
Give the answer concisely; she finishes her five-minute slot in four.

spch100.11.0.worked: Can she cook a burger in the car faster than the drive-through queue moves? Each ingredient marks progress, her mother supplies the conflict ('You're doing all this for one subscriber?'), and the answer — faster, if basically raw — comes in the last seconds. Over 45 million views.
spch100.11.0.watch: Over-delivering at the end. Once the question is answered, stop.

checks.q: How does Hoyos recommend starting a short story?
opts: With your name and channel, so viewers know who's talking
With a surprising question the audience wants answered
With the ending, then show how you got there
With background, so viewers understand the stakes
checks.expl: The question holds them to the end.

checks.q: What role did her mother play in the burger video?
opts: The B plot that adds conflict
The director behind the camera
The judge who tastes the result
The narrator who explains each step
checks.expl: Viewers also wanted to see what would happen between them.

checks.q: Why say which ingredients are still to come?
opts: To give viewers the recipe, so they can make it at home afterwards
To fill time while the burger cooks off camera
To make progress visible, so viewers feel how close the answer is
To help the video show up in searches for each ingredient
checks.expl: Constant progression keeps people from stopping.

spch100.11.1.takeaway: Kallaway: a hook has one job — to make the viewer opt in — and needs two things: topic clarity and on-target curiosity. When a hook fails, it is one of four mistakes: delay, confusion, irrelevance or disinterest.

beats.d: Short-form retention decays steeply from the first second; every second without the topic loses viewers.
Fewer, simpler words, active voice, and no second way to read the sentence.
'You' instead of 'I', and a need-to-have pain point instead of a nice-to-have topic.
Open a curiosity loop: each answer raises a new question.
A versus B — stated ('most people use X, I have something faster') or implied.

spch100.11.1.worked: Confusing: 'These guys built a 30 million dollar empire and the online money they made is most difficult to earn if you don't develop a journaling practice like they did.' Clear: 'These guys built a 30 million dollar empire, and their secret for earning money online was their insane journaling practice.' The same idea, reordered.
spch100.11.1.watch: Vague suspense. 'You won't believe this' has zero context; anyone who stays is staying for your face or the caption. The video also plugs his paid hooks course and an AI tool along the way.

checks.q: What two things must a hook deliver, according to Kallaway?
opts: Topic clarity and on-target curiosity
Humour and a sense of urgency
A face on screen and music under it
A question and a promise to answer it
checks.expl: Then the viewer can decide to opt in.

checks.q: Which fix addresses 'irrelevance'?
opts: Cut the first two lines, so the topic arrives in the first second
Use simpler words, so nobody can read it two ways
Frame it with 'you' and a pain point the viewer already has
Add music that matches the mood of the topic
checks.expl: The viewer needs to see it is for them.

checks.q: What is 'implied contrast'?
opts: Stating both A and B explicitly, so the viewer can see the difference at once
Stating your alternative and letting the viewer supply the baseline they know
Contradicting yourself on purpose, so the viewer stays to hear which is true
Using a split screen, so the old way and the new way are shown side by side
checks.expl: Your take against the field of options they already know.

spch100.11.2.takeaway: A creator coach's team catalogued hundreds of shorts with over a million views across more than 40 niches. The strongest pattern: the first three seconds stack several hooks — text, movement, a cut, sound — and the visuals carry most of the weight.

beats.d: Every short over a million views from the Shorts tab and 40-plus niche searches, logged in a spreadsheet.
Movement into frame, loud music, a zoom, and the 'what is happening?' moment.
Story openings, exclamations, questions, relatability and humour.
Only 8 per cent of the viral shorts used any.
Mostly entertainment; inspirational drew the most views, educational the most engagement.

spch100.11.2.worked: A relatable short layering three hooks in three seconds: a person running towards the camera (movement), 'POV: that friend' on screen (relatable text), and a spoken question to the viewer.
spch100.11.2.watch: Survivorship. The sample contains only videos that already went viral, with no flops to compare, so treat the percentages as patterns worth testing, not causes. She also plugs a paid guide midway.

checks.q: What share of the viral shorts used three or more hooks in the first three seconds?
opts: About a quarter
About half
96 per cent
All of them
checks.expl: Only one used a single hook.

checks.q: What did the team find about hashtags?
opts: Only 8 per cent of the viral shorts used any
Every viral short used five or more of them
They roughly doubled views compared with none
They were needed to appear in the Shorts tab
checks.expl: Her advice: stop stressing about them.

checks.q: Why be careful with conclusions from this sample?
opts: It is too small to show any pattern, at only a few dozen videos in all
It only includes videos that already went viral, with no comparison
It covers one niche only, so the patterns may not apply anywhere else
It was sorted by an AI tool, which may have mislabelled the hooks
checks.expl: Patterns among winners are not proof of what made them win.

spch100.11.3.takeaway: Brendan Kane, on a sales podcast: in a three-second world you compete with LeBron James and Netflix, not just your rivals. A hook point wins the first part of the conversation; then a story has to hold the attention, and credibility has to make people believe it.

beats.d: Attention, story, credibility — fail any one and the others are wasted.
'Meditation is the key to focus' has been seen a thousand times; 'meditation is a scam' stops the scroll.
Copywriter Craig Clemens: express the problem better than the customer can, and you earn trust.
Purpose, mission and product mean nothing until they have stopped.
Views to reach for the hook, retention for the story, comments and conversions for credibility.

spch100.11.3.worked: A Mother's Day campaign for a photo-book company was aimed at mothers over 45. Tested broadly, it landed hardest with women aged 18 to 25 — who tagged their mothers, reaching the core audience better than narrow targeting would have.
spch100.11.3.watch: Subversion as a gimmick. Kane uses it sparingly, and the story must deliver; 'cold calling sucks' followed by a vanilla pitch burns the credibility you were after.

checks.q: What are Kane's three pillars, in order?
opts: Hook, story, credibility
Story, hook, offer
Credibility, hook, call to action
Price, product, promotion
checks.expl: If you can't grab attention you never get to the story.

checks.q: Which metric does he use to judge whether the hook works?
opts: Likes, compared with the channel's average for the past month
Comment length, which shows how deeply people engaged with it
Views to reach — how many who saw it watched past three seconds
Follower count, measured the day after posting, against the day before
checks.expl: A view is counted at three seconds.

checks.q: Why make a hook interesting to outsiders?
opts: Outsiders buy more often than insiders, who already have a supplier
It widens reach, and non-buyers can share it with people who do buy
Algorithms penalise niche content, so a broad hook is the only way to grow
It removes all the jargon, which insiders secretly find tiring as well
checks.expl: The daughters shared it with the mothers.

spch100.11.4.takeaway: Jenny Hoyos, in a long interview: a short is a moment, not a squeezed-down long video. Hook with a visual shock, build with 'but' and 'so', make progress visible, and land the answer on the last word — then let the analytics say which part failed.

beats.d: A glucose monitor reacting to pasta is a short; a complete guide to diabetes is a long video.
Cold-open on the finished dish so the curiosity becomes 'how?'.
A timer or ingredient checklist shows how close the end is; 'finally' or 'sit back, this will take a while' make people leave.
Aspirational yet relatable, like Spider-Man and Peter Parker; she does the cool thing and her mother tells her off.
Viewed-versus-swiped tests the hook; a retention graph shows an early exit, a specific drop, or a slow slide from weak progression.

spch100.11.4.worked: Pasta with her mother, told with 'but': we boil the water and add salt — but that's far too much salt, so I'll add more water. We take out the pasta — oh no, it's still raw — so I'll leave it in longer. Every beat is a small conflict, so the progression never runs in a straight line.
spch100.11.4.watch: Over-delivering. If the question is 'what's two plus two?', the last word is 'four'; anything after it is a reason to swipe. Her analytics advice near the end: when the retention graph drops, look a few seconds before the drop, because what came before it is what made people leave.

checks.q: What does Hoyos say to use instead of 'and then'?
opts: 'But' and 'so'
'Next' and 'after'
'Meanwhile'
'Finally' and 'then'
checks.expl: Conflict keeps the progression non-linear.

checks.q: What is a 'mechanism' in her sense?
opts: A camera rig that keeps the shot steady while you move around the room
A visible sign of progress, like an on-screen timer or a checklist
An editing app that cuts out pauses automatically
A sponsor segment placed at the point viewers usually leave
checks.expl: Without one, viewers feel there's no end in sight.

checks.q: Where should the answer to the hook's question come?
opts: In the first five seconds
In the middle
As the very last word
In the description
checks.expl: Once they have the answer, they leave.

spch100.12.0.takeaway: YouTube's head of recommendations, Todd Beaupré, with creator liaison Rene Ritchie: the algorithm doesn't push your video out; it pulls the best videos for each viewer at the moment they open the app. Focus on audiences, compare your videos with each other, and stop reading the first hour.

beats.d: Candidates are found and ranked for each viewer at that moment, using history and context.
Even in the first hour, videos reach people who have never watched the channel; the system learns per audience.
Click-through, absolute and relative watch time, surveys, likes, dislikes and comments — weighted differently by device.
Longer videos rise because people watching on TV want them; the algorithm follows the audience.
Same diners, same restaurant; a different value proposition deserves a different brand — and the system copes either way.

spch100.12.0.worked: Ritchie's own channel: a big phone review could count on hundreds of thousands of views, an accessibility video a few thousand. Not a penalty — a smaller audience for the topic, like an arthouse film next to a blockbuster. Judge each against its own kind.
spch100.12.0.watch: Over-reading the first hours. Someone on a phone clicks a notification at once; someone saving an hour-long video for the TV watches it at night or at the weekend.

checks.q: How does Beaupré describe the way recommendations work?
opts: Each new video is pushed to subscribers first, then to everyone else if it does well
Candidate videos are pulled and ranked for each viewer as they open it
Videos are ranked once, globally, and everyone sees the same top results
The newest videos are shown first, then sorted by how many views they have
checks.expl: Each viewer gets a different ranking.

checks.q: What does he say about which metric matters most?
opts: Click-through rate, above everything else, since it decides reach
Watch time, since that is what pays and what the system ranks on
No single metric; many are combined and weighted by context
Likes, as the most direct sign that viewers were satisfied
checks.expl: No metric on its own is a good indicator of value.

checks.q: Why is the subscriptions-feed traffic source useful to a creator?
opts: Its audience is the same for every video, so differences point at content
It brings in the most views of any traffic source for most channels
It ignores retention, so you can see the clicks without any other noise
It shows how much revenue each video earns from loyal subscribers
checks.expl: A clean way to separate the content from the algorithm.

spch100.12.1.takeaway: Five shapes in a retention graph, and what each one says: flat is good, gradual is normal, spikes are gold, dips are exits — and the typical-retention band shows whether you beat your own average.

beats.d: Viewers locked in for that section.
Normal — unless it's steep, which points at pacing.
Rewinds, rewatches, shares. Find out what caused them.
Tangents, slow explanations, weak transitions.
Your last ten videos of similar length; stay above it.

spch100.12.1.worked: His forward-looking plan: open past videos, screenshot the graphs, note the biggest dips and best spikes, leave the old videos alone, and apply the lessons to the very next upload.
spch100.12.1.watch: Treating one number as the whole story. He calls retention YouTube's 'number one signal'; YouTube's own head of recommendations says no single metric decides. His 50 and 60 per cent benchmarks are his opinion, not YouTube's.

checks.q: What does a spike in the retention graph usually mean?
opts: People rewound, rewatched or shared that moment
People left at that point in large numbers
An ad played and viewers waited until it was over
The video ended and the next one began
checks.expl: Study it and recreate it.

checks.q: What is the grey band in the typical-retention view?
opts: Your subscribers' retention, compared with non-subscribers
YouTube's average for all videos of a similar length
Your typical retention for recent videos of similar length
The ad breaks, shown where viewers might drop off
checks.expl: Your own baseline, not anyone else's.

checks.q: What is his fix for a dip?
opts: Add a longer intro so viewers settle in first
Cut or speed up that kind of section in future videos
Re-upload the video with that section cut out
Add hashtags so the video finds a better audience
checks.expl: If it feels slow at 1.5x, it is slow.

spch100.12.2.takeaway: A conversation between YouTube's Shorts product lead, Todd Sherman, and Jenny Hoyos. Short form serves snackable moments; the system estimates whether people valued their time; and viewed-versus-swiped is the first number to check when a short underperforms.

beats.d: A short competes with a quick game, an article, even one crossword clue — anything that fills a minute.
Hoyos's process: ideas from things every human does, five story cuts, the edit as a jigsaw.
Surveys help estimate whether time was valued, allowing for length; rewatchability helps short shorts.
On her channel, time-based metrics tracked views; likes, comments and shares did not.
Feed viewers never see them; the channel page and sponsors do.

spch100.12.2.worked: When a creator asks Sherman why a short flopped, he pulls up their last ten videos side by side. Almost always, the one in question had a much higher swiped-away share — the hook didn't land.
spch100.12.2.watch: Generalising from one channel. Hoyos's finding about likes and shares is a correlation on her own data; Sherman's point is that the system combines every signal, weighted by how well each predicts enjoyment.

checks.q: What is the first metric Sherman checks when a short underperforms?
opts: Likes per thousand views
Viewed versus swiped away
Subscriber count
Comments per view
checks.expl: Usually the hook didn't get them.

checks.q: What is 'valued watch time'?
opts: An estimate, partly from surveys, of whether viewers valued their time
Watch time on paid content, which counts for more than free viewing
The time viewers spend choosing a short, measured before they watch it
The average length of all shorts a viewer watches in a single session
checks.expl: It goes beyond raw watch time.

checks.q: Why do Hoyos's shorts still get thumbnails?
opts: They still drive most of the feed views on Shorts
The algorithm requires a custom one for every upload
For the channel page and for showing past work to brands
To hide spoilers about the ending of each short in the feed
checks.expl: Feed viewers decide from the video itself.

spch100.12.3.takeaway: Paddy Galloway, interviewed by YouTube's creator liaison: the first thing he looks at is views over time and the top videos. What worked can be repeated, staircased or adapted — and almost nobody watches enough of your channel to notice.

beats.d: Which periods performed, and what about them led to it.
Brainstorm 10–30 ideas from what made the winners work.
A tiny share of viewers watch any significant portion of your videos.
Roughly 40 per cent the packaging, 60 per cent whether the video delivered.
Other channels your audience watches, and where suggested traffic comes from.

spch100.12.3.worked: A client spends perhaps 1 per cent of their time on the title and thumbnail when those may account for around 40 per cent of a video's performance. His suggestion isn't 40 per cent of the time — it's 10 or 15.
spch100.12.3.watch: Ticking an idea off as done. Galloway asks whether a winning idea can be repeated with a twist, or taken up a level, before moving on.

checks.q: What does Galloway look at first on a new client's channel?
opts: Views over time and the most-viewed videos
The comments, to see what the audience asks for
Thumbnail colours and how often they change
The upload schedule and how regular it is
checks.expl: Correlation spreadsheets come later.

checks.q: What does 'staircasing' an idea mean?
opts: Repeating it identically on a schedule
Taking a proven idea up another level
Splitting it into parts as a series
Posting it again at a different time
checks.expl: Alongside repeating with a twist and adapting to a new format.

checks.q: Why does he check the other channels your audience watches?
opts: To copy their most successful videos exactly, title and thumbnail included
To report channels that copy your content to your audience's feeds
To find the cluster you're really in, and ideas your audience already likes
To choose collaborators only, since overlap makes a partnership work
checks.expl: You may be in a different cluster than you thought.

spch100.13.0.takeaway: A TV director who has filmed thousands of presenters: talking to camera is ownership, not performance. Own the words, talk to one person, keep a natural eye rhythm, and run two or three notches higher than you would in a room.

beats.d: Coached, scripted executives at a launch in Berlin couldn't make sense of their own sentences; presenters who write their own mark up the prompter.
'Hey guys' flattens everything. Picture a video call with one friend.
A phone has no prompter glass. Read ahead, glance away, come back for the key line.
The camera strips texture out; a heightened version of yourself puts it back.
Script first, then off script; around video ten the lens starts to feel like a face.

spch100.13.0.worked: Kirsty Young recording the closing link for the Queen's funeral: weeks spent on every word, so that in front of the prompter the emotion still came through. She owned every syllable before she said it.
spch100.13.0.watch: A locked stare. Looking into the lens the whole time feels as unnatural to the viewer as it does to you — and notes off to one side make the viewer wonder who you're talking to. The video includes a plug for his paid course.

checks.q: What does the director say talking to camera mostly is?
opts: A performance skill — playing the part of a presenter well
An ownership skill — knowing and owning every word
A technical skill — framing, lighting and sound done right
A natural talent that some people simply have
checks.expl: He has never seen anyone fake their way through it.

checks.q: What is wrong with opening on 'hey guys'?
opts: It aims at everyone, so delivery goes vague and flat — pick one person
It is too casual for most brands, and it sounds as if you're talking to kids
It takes too long to say, and the first seconds are the ones that count
It sounds old-fashioned now, so viewers assume the video is out of date
checks.expl: You phrase things differently for someone you know.

checks.q: How should you handle eye contact without a teleprompter?
opts: Stare at the lens throughout, since any glance away reads as nervous or shifty
Read notes placed to one side, and look back at the lens at the end of each line
Read ahead, glance away naturally, and come back to the lens for key lines
Close your eyes briefly when thinking, so the viewer can see you working it out
checks.expl: A direct look lands harder by contrast.

spch100.13.1.takeaway: Eye contact through the lens is the basic piece-to-camera technique. The camera gives no feedback, so you stay on the lens anyway, and look away only at things the viewer can see.

beats.d: Looking into the lens is looking into the viewer's eyes.
We instinctively look for a face; the camera never gives one.
Assume it is landing as well as it possibly could.
Look down at the cup in your hand, not at something out of shot.

spch100.13.1.worked: Holding a cup, he looks down at it — fine, because the viewer can see what he is looking at. Look at something out of shot and the viewer is distracted; add the wrong movement and it all falls apart.
spch100.13.1.watch: Searching the room for approval. The TV director's glance away is a thinking beat inside a conversation; this trainer's rule is about where your attention goes. Neither lets you look for a reaction off-camera.

checks.q: Why keep your eyes on the lens?
opts: It reads as looking into the viewer's eyes; avoiding it looks shifty
It hides the notes, so the viewer doesn't realise you are reading at all
The camera focuses better on the eyes when they are aimed at the lens
It is a broadcasting rule that presenters are trained to follow strictly
checks.expl: The same as eye contact in person.

checks.q: When is it fine to look away from the lens?
opts: To check the floor manager's reaction to how it's going
To read notes off to the side when you lose the thread
When the viewer can see what you are looking at
Never, under any circumstances
checks.expl: Otherwise it is distracting.

checks.q: What does he suggest assuming about how your words are landing?
opts: That they are probably failing, so you push harder
That they are going down as well as possible
That nobody is listening, so nerves can't win
Nothing at all — just say the words clearly
checks.expl: Be a little presumptuous.

spch100.13.2.takeaway: A ninety-second demonstration: the same presenter and the same words, with energy drained and then nervous movement added — and how quickly the piece to camera stops working.

beats.d: Still, on the lens, energetic: nothing distracting.
Flatter voice, less expression — still natural, but less engaging.
Small wobbles, then rocking.
Uncomfortable with the lens, the eyes start to slide away.

spch100.13.2.worked: He keeps talking while his voice flattens, then begins to rock gently — 'like I'm on a boat' — and his eyes drift off the lens. Each change is small; together they make the piece hard to watch.
spch100.13.2.watch: Pacing that comforts you. Constant movement, like a caged animal, feels good to the presenter and does nothing for the person watching.

checks.q: Where does nervous energy go when you hold yourself rigid?
opts: Into your voice, which gets faster and higher
Into small movements like wobbling and rocking
Nowhere — keeping still makes it disappear
Into your hands, which start to fidget
checks.expl: It comes out somewhere else.

checks.q: What is his fix?
opts: Move around constantly, so the nerves have an outlet
Lower your energy until the wobble stops on its own
Pick up the energy, stay still, use your hands a little
Look away from the lens until you feel calm again
checks.expl: Occasional movement is fine.

checks.q: Why does constant movement fail?
opts: It feels good to the presenter but does nothing for the viewer
It breaks broadcasting rules about staying inside the frame
It blurs the picture, because the camera can't keep focus on you
It is too fast for the viewer to follow what you are saying
checks.expl: Like a caged lion.

spch100.13.3.takeaway: Ali Abdaal: camera confidence is a skill that spills into the rest of life. Pick a mode — coffee or presenter — lift your energy to make up for what the camera takes, smile, use your hands, warm up, and get reps.

beats.d: Remote interviews, sales, content — and it raised his confidence off camera too.
Coffee with a friend; a talk to three or four students.
Your own words and jokes beat a put-on presenter voice.
Speaking through a smile lifts voice and energy; relaxed gestures read as confident.
He sings along to music while setting up.

spch100.13.3.worked: He says a line flat, then the same line through a smile. The words don't change, but the second take sounds more confident and more engaged — and he says it lifts his own energy as well.
spch100.13.3.watch: The course pitch. The first three minutes are mostly about his paid course; the five tips start after that.

checks.q: Why does Abdaal suggest presenter-mode energy of about 7 out of 10?
opts: To sound like a TV host rather than a friend on a video call
To speak faster, so the whole video feels more energetic
Because the camera takes roughly two points off your charisma
To save time in the edit by needing fewer retakes of each line
checks.expl: A 5 comes across as a 3.

checks.q: When does he use coffee mode?
opts: For calls, negotiations, sales and heartfelt videos
For loud product launches and big announcements
Only on stage, where there is a real audience
Never — presenter mode is always the safer choice
checks.expl: The camera is a friend over coffee.

checks.q: What easy daily rep does he suggest?
opts: Reading the news aloud for ten minutes every morning
Sending video messages to friends instead of texts
Filming strangers in the street to get used to it
Rewatching old videos and listing what went wrong
checks.expl: Practice that costs nothing.

spch100.13.4.takeaway: Five practical tips from a course-video coach, and one drill worth keeping: record yourself way over the top first, then tone it down — because what feels natural reads as flat on camera.

beats.d: Repetition becomes the distraction.
Sit, stand or lean — whatever lets you act naturally.
If it feels over the top to you, it probably looks right.
Saying a line again and again is normal.
Be your best self, not someone else.

spch100.13.4.worked: Her rule of thumb: if it feels dramatic and over the top to you, it probably looks good on camera. So the first take is deliberately too much, and the review tells you how far to bring it back.
spch100.13.4.watch: Pop statistics. The '10,000 hours' and '37 times better in a year' lines are motivational figures, not research on camera skill.

checks.q: Why record an over-the-top take first?
opts: To use as a blooper reel at the end of the course video
Because toning down is easier than pushing energy up bit by bit
Because over the top is funnier, and viewers enjoy that more
To test the microphone levels before the real take begins
checks.expl: You've done the hard work already.

checks.q: What does she say about what feels natural to you?
opts: It will probably read as bored and unengaged on camera
It always looks best, so don't change it for the camera
It should never change, or viewers will sense it's fake
It is only right for experts who have done years of video
checks.expl: You need to dial it up.

checks.q: What should the tips not do?
opts: Change your energy level
Change your hand gestures
Turn you into someone else
Change where you sit or stand
checks.expl: Audiences see through it.

spch100.13.5.takeaway: A creator who worried about his accent records himself every day for 30 days, rates every take, and goes from no uploads in eleven months to talking to the lens like a friend on a video call. The method is incremental, not heroic.

beats.d: A journal entry predicted the worst case — zero uploads — and it came true.
Record daily, note weak and strong points, rate five things.
Far fewer 'uh's and silences — not perfection.
Imitate to enhance, hands, smile, consistency, no announcer voice.

spch100.13.5.worked: His 'British Airways mode' demonstration: a perfectly pleasant announcer voice cancelling your flight to Dubai and threatening to call security — polished, and completely fake. The fix is to sound like yourself, not like an announcement.
spch100.13.5.watch: Treating it as a course review. He credits a paid course for some tips; the part that worked first was free — thirty days of recording and rating himself.

checks.q: What did he rate after each recording?
opts: Views, likes and comments on each upload he made
Lighting, sound and framing quality of each take
Script accuracy, line by line, against what he wrote
Pace, pronunciation, engagement, energy and charisma
checks.expl: The goal was one small improvement a day.

checks.q: What is 'British Airways mode'?
opts: An over-polished, fake announcer voice
Speaking too fast, as if boarding is closing
Travel vlogging with an announcer's script
Reading from a teleprompter in a flat voice
checks.expl: Sounding perfect and not like a person.

checks.q: What does 'imitate to enhance' mean?
opts: Copy another creator's style in your published videos to grow faster
Imitate a speaker you admire in practice, to stretch your range
Use a voice changer until your own voice sounds more confident
Repeat your old videos line for line to see how far you've come
checks.expl: Practice only, not uploads.

spch100.14.0.takeaway: Austin Kleon's SXSW keynote on showing your work: forget being a genius; become part of a 'scenius' — a community of people sharing, crediting, teaching and learning in the open. Share your process, not just your product, and play the long game.

beats.d: People who drain you, and people who want your attention but never give theirs. Use the vampire test.
Brian Eno's word for communal genius: Florence for Da Vinci, Paris for Picasso.
He started by drawing panels at SXSW and posting them — sharing what he loved, with credit.
Like R.A. Dickey's fellow knuckleball pitchers, the few doing your odd thing share secrets rather than hoard them.

beats.t: Teach and work in the open
beats.d: Teaching drawing made more people draw — and added to his own work rather than competing with it.

spch100.14.0.worked: Steve Albini, asked by a former talent-show contestant to produce his record, answered that he had never had connections that weren't a natural outgrowth of doing the work — people waste energy making connections instead of getting good, and being good is the only thing that earns them.
spch100.14.0.watch: Watch to 37:30; the rest is audience questions. The pitfall he names: 'follow me back' — asking for attention instead of earning it.

checks.q: What does Kleon mean by 'scenius'?
opts: A lone genius's studio, where a single great artist works in private
Communal genius — good work coming out of a network of people sharing
A type of art school where students learn by copying their teachers' work
A social network for artists that rewards whoever shares the most often
checks.expl: It makes room for the rest of us.

checks.q: What does he say good credit includes?
opts: Just the creator's name, placed where people can see it clearly at the start
Context: what it is, who made it, how, why you're sharing it, where to find more
A link to buy it, so the creator benefits directly from every share you make
Nothing — sharing it at all is the credit, as long as you don't claim it as yours
checks.expl: Without it, your sharing makes no connection.

checks.q: According to Albini, where do real connections come from?
opts: Networking events where you meet the right people early on
Social media follows that build up over years of sharing
Doing good work — connections are a natural outgrowth of it
Asking famous people for favours until one of them says yes
checks.expl: Being good at things is what earns clout.

spch100.14.1.takeaway: A filmmaker's case that even a vlog needs a story: give it setup, a challenge, complications, a payoff and a change — and decide the goal before you film, because the complications will turn up on their own.

beats.d: Turn everyday reports into stories in conversation, and notice how people respond.
Setup, challenge, complications, payoff, change.
A sunset, three days on the Pony Express trail, a 24-hour challenge — a clock gives you a through-line.
Watch stories, not just tutorials, and write down their beats.
Show it — wides, close-ups, a beginning and an end.

spch100.14.1.worked: The hike, told twice. As a report: 'we went up this mountain and it had the best view.' As a story: five long studio days, a peak in the distance, one hour of daylight, 1,800 feet straight up, the summit just as the sun dips — and then doing a new trail every evening after that.
spch100.14.1.watch: Just filming whatever happens. Without a goal and an obstacle decided beforehand, a day of footage is a diary, not a video.

checks.q: Which is NOT one of his five story beats?
opts: Setup
Challenge
Sponsorship
Payoff and change
checks.expl: The others are complications and change.

checks.q: Why is a time limit useful in a vlog?
opts: It shortens the edit, because there's less footage to cut
It creates a challenge and a through-line the viewer wants resolved
It pleases the algorithm, which favours videos with a countdown
It saves battery, so you can film the whole day on one charge
checks.expl: Will they make it in time?

checks.q: What does he recommend consuming more of?
opts: Gear reviews, so the vlogs look better
Tutorials on editing and colour grading
Stories — and noting their beats
Analytics, to see what holds viewers
