checks.expl: Story matters more than cinematic B-roll.

spch100.14.2.takeaway: A game developer's guide to devlogs: choose technical (how) or design (why), record as you go, tell it as a straight line from goal to result, keep the struggle, script for confidence, and give every video a question worth searching for.

beats.d: Record your screen while you work; speed it up; show results and your thought process, not code.
The decisions and why — a video on what makes a good twin-stick shooter before the game is finished.
Summarising lets you come in with a conclusion and what you learned.
Unscripted he says 'like' and 'probably'; scripted and rehearsed he sounds sure.
Frame each video around something people might search for, like how to use playtest feedback.

spch100.14.2.worked: His own titles: graphics, level design, sound and music, player feedback — and 'that time I cancelled my game'. Each devlog takes one topic and explores it through the game he is making, so a playlist becomes a timeline of the build.
spch100.14.2.watch: Forced personality. If you are not funny, don't try to be; turn up the personality you already have instead — a confident monotone that shows impressive results works too.

checks.q: What does a design devlog focus on?
opts: The code, explained line by line
The editing software and how you use it
The decisions you made and why
Sales figures and wishlist numbers
checks.expl: Technical devlogs cover how.

checks.q: Why leave struggles in a devlog?
opts: They fill time in a devlog when there isn't enough finished work to show yet
Honest struggle plus what you learned shows competence and keeps you human
Viewers like failure for its own sake, so the more struggle shown the better
Platforms favour devlogs that show problems, so struggles help the video spread
checks.expl: Nothing ever goes that smoothly, and everyone knows it.

checks.q: How does he recommend recording technical work?
opts: Run a screen recorder while you work, then speed it up and show results
Recreate everything afterwards, once you know which steps actually mattered
Film the keyboard and your hands, so viewers can see the work being done
Only show the finished product, since the process bores most of the audience
checks.expl: Making it as you go is easier than assembling it backwards.

spch100.14.3.takeaway: An indie developer's warning: devlogs made for other developers reach only developers. Explain your systems simply, with visuals and a bit of fun, for the people who would actually use what you build — and make it look good first.

beats.d: Raycasts and state machines attract developers who may never play your game.
A harvesting system explained with visuals and funny scenes became the best-retained part of his videos.
Each devlog is a mini-trailer; ugly placeholders lose viewers.

spch100.14.3.worked: His harvesting system, explained without jargon: a component on any object checks whether you're using the right tool, how good the tool is, how much damage to apply, when to drop the resource — and then damages the tool that hit it. Complex logic, said as a little story of cause and effect.
spch100.14.3.watch: The sponsor segment at the end, and the jargon reflex. The video is short; the point is that the explanation, not the system, is what an outsider watches.

checks.q: Why does he warn against making devlogs for other developers?
opts: Developers don't watch YouTube, so those videos get almost no views at all
It limits your reach to peers, not the people who'd use what you make
Other developers are too critical, so the comments put off everyone else
Platforms count developer content as education, which limits its reach
checks.expl: Most of them won't play your genre.

checks.q: Which parts of his videos hold viewers best?
opts: The plain, visual, funny explanations of systems
The code walkthroughs that show how it works
The sponsor reads, which are short and punchy
The outros, where he shows what comes next
checks.expl: Builders and non-builders alike.

checks.q: Why make the work look good before filming?
opts: To win awards, which bring more viewers to the channel
Because each devlog acts as a mini-trailer and visuals come first
To hide bugs, which would distract from what you're explaining
To save editing time, since good footage needs fewer cuts
checks.expl: Even the best video flops if the game looks bad.

spch100.15.0.takeaway: Seth Godin: begin with the smallest viable audience — the people who share your taste — and get specific. Generic can't be the best at anything; specific is how the right person finds you.

beats.d: Develop taste, understand your genre, and ship even when it feels not quite ready.
A better question than 'if you couldn't fail': what is worth doing anyway?
One per cent of two billion English speakers is a lot of people.
'Niche down' sounds like shrinking; being specific is how you become the best at something.

spch100.15.0.worked: Cory Doctorow: 99 per cent of English speakers have never read a word he wrote — and the remaining one per cent is enough to make him a bestseller and a successful Kickstarter.
spch100.15.0.watch: Chasing the people who don't get it. You can spend your whole day persuading non-believers instead of serving the people who already want to go where you're going.

checks.q: What does Godin mean by the 'smallest viable audience'?
opts: The cheapest audience to buy ads for, so the work can grow without much spending
The smallest group who share your taste and want what you make — enough to sustain it
Your family and friends, who will support the work while it finds a wider audience
A small test audience you survey before you decide what to make for everyone else
checks.expl: They become fuel to be singular rather than generic.

checks.q: Why does he prefer 'specific up' to 'niche down'?
opts: It's shorter and easier to remember
Being specific is how you become the best at something and get found
It sounds more technical, which gives the work more weight and authority
It avoids competition entirely by finding an empty corner
checks.expl: Generic can't be the best because everyone does it.

checks.q: What question does he suggest instead of 'what would you do if you couldn't fail?'
opts: What would make the most money in the shortest time?
What would go viral if you only got one try?
What would be worth doing even if you knew it would fail?
What do your competitors do that you could do better?
checks.expl: Paradoxically, that leads to things that work.

spch100.15.1.takeaway: April Dunford: positioning is the foundation under all marketing — the context that makes your value obvious to the customers who care most. Choose it deliberately, starting from what customers would really do without you.

beats.d: Not messaging, a tagline, your 'why' or your brand. Those flow from it.
Say 'CRM' and people assume competitors, features, buyer and price before you've said anything else.
Email for lawyers became team collaboration for lawyers; robots became autonomous industrial vehicles.
Alternatives, capabilities, value, best-fit customers, market category.
CRM for investment banks went from about 1.5 million to nearly 80 million in revenue in around 18 months, and was acquired by the leader.

spch100.15.1.worked: A startup sold 'email for lawyers' — with no calendar, and not replacing anyone's email. Its loved feature was secure, context-aware document sharing with clients. Repositioned as team collaboration for lawyers, the competitors became Slack and Teams, the expected features matched, and customers expected to pay.
spch100.15.1.watch: Leaving customers to work it out. They grab the first clue ('there's an inbox, so it's email') and get stuck; the Segway, launched as 'a revolution in human transportation', confused everyone. Watch to about 34:00; questions follow.

checks.q: Where does Dunford say positioning work should start?
opts: The tagline, since everything else flows from it
Competitive alternatives — what customers would do if you didn't exist
The brand colours and the look, which set the tone for everything else
The founder's vision of what the product could become one day
checks.expl: Otherwise it sounds good in the office and loses in the market.

checks.q: Why does the market category matter so much?
opts: It sets off assumptions about competitors, features, buyers and price
It decides your logo and colours, which customers notice before anything else
Search engines require a category before they will list the product at all
It sets your tax rate and the regulations the business must follow
checks.expl: True assumptions save work; false ones create it.

checks.q: What was the 'email for lawyers' product better positioned as?
opts: A calendar app for law firms
A CRM for small practices
Team collaboration for lawyers
A law firm's internal tool
checks.expl: Same product, different context.

spch100.15.2.takeaway: Content pillars are broad topics within your niche that you want to be known for. A strategist draws hers from five sources — knowledge, experience, audience need, personal angle and values — so ideas never run dry and the content attracts the right people.

beats.d: 'Education' or 'inspiration' describe an outcome; 'five hair tips' and 'dog grooming' both qualify.
Her own: content systems.
Her winding career from corporate marketing to agency to personal brand.
'Content without the damage' — unlearning bad advice before her method can work.
'Against the status quo'; 'I have receipts' — no advice without proof.

spch100.15.2.worked: A curly-hair stylist's pillars: curl patterns and textures (knowledge), transformations (experience), a home hair-care routine (what clients need between appointments), putting down the flat iron (personal angle) — each one a topic she could post about for months.
spch100.15.2.watch: Picking pillars by post type. 'Educational, motivational, promotional' gives you nothing to search your memory with; topics do. (Strong language, and a course plug at the end.)

checks.q: Why does she reject 'education' and 'inspiration' as pillars?
opts: They're outdated categories from the early days of social media marketing
They describe what a post does, not what it's about, so they don't narrow it
They're too specific, so creators run out of ideas within a few weeks
Platforms penalise posts tagged as education or inspiration in their feeds
checks.expl: Pillars are topics you want to be known for.

checks.q: What does the 'audience need' pillar cover?
opts: What your audience likes to watch in their free time
What stands between them and the result you promise
Their demographics, so you can tailor the tone
Their budget, so the offer fits what they can pay
checks.expl: Teach what they must know before your offer can work.

checks.q: What is expected of the 'personal connections' pillar?
opts: To stay neutral, so nobody in the audience feels left out by your views
To be strictly professional, keeping your personal life out of the content
To be polarising — attracting the right people and repelling the wrong ones
To avoid personal stories and focus on values the whole audience shares
checks.expl: That's the point of it.

spch100.16.0.takeaway: Colin and Samir: the three-act structure is the most important thing to know before making a video. Set up the goal and the stakes, run rising tension through act two, and release it in act three — and spend the effort on act one.

beats.d: Context and a hook strong enough to carry the viewer to the end.
The meat: the adventure and transformation, with tension rising.
Everything ties together; the tension is released.
Music, location and style change to tell the viewer a new act has begun.
Think the idea through before picking up a camera.

spch100.16.0.worked: '24 hours to meet Yes Theory': act one declares the goal on screen with a building crescendo; act two runs through attempts under title cards to night-time, music gone, when it looks as if they'll fail; then a phone call — 'have you checked your Twitter?' — opens act three, with reflective music.
spch100.16.0.watch: Skipping the constraint. Meeting Yes Theory was the goal; the 24-hour limit is what gave act two its tension.

checks.q: What is act two for, in their structure?
opts: The conflict — where tension rises
The introduction of the characters
The sponsor read, placed mid-video
The credits and the call to action
checks.expl: Everything set up in act one plays out.

checks.q: How did they raise the stakes in act one?
opts: A bigger budget than usual
A 24-hour time limit
A celebrity guest star
A giveaway at the end
checks.expl: A constraint makes the journey worth following.

checks.q: How did they signal the start of act two?
opts: A title card saying 'Act Two' on screen
Silence, then a new voice-over
A fast drumbeat and a change of location
A sponsor read before the adventure
checks.expl: Act one had been voice-over and B-roll.

spch100.16.1.takeaway: One script order for long videos: packaging, outline, intro, body, outro — all driven by one principle, expectations against reality. When what they get beats what they expected, they stay.

beats.d: Like the relief after a speech you expected to bomb.
The title sets the expectation; the first lines confirm and ideally beat it.
If the points are common knowledge, research more before writing.
Topic, common belief, contrarian take, proof, plan.
Second-best point first, then build; re-hook between points; end on a high note.

spch100.16.1.worked: The intro of the video itself: 'Today we're talking about writing killer scripts' (topic); 'this is an art, one of the hardest things to learn' (common belief); 'but there is a right answer — they all run the same process' (contrarian); then the five-step plan and his credentials (plan and proof).
spch100.16.1.watch: Leading with your best point. He argues a rising pattern — strong, stronger — keeps people watching, the way albums rarely open with the hit. Three of his own plugs are deliberately 'native embedded' in the video.

checks.q: What principle does the guide say drives every scripting decision?
opts: Length versus budget
Expectations versus reality
Topic versus trend
Hook versus thumbnail design
checks.expl: Reality beating expectations keeps viewers.

checks.q: Which point does he put first in the body?
opts: The best one
The weakest one
The second-best
A random one
checks.expl: Then the best, so value seems to rise.

checks.q: What is 'click confirmation'?
opts: The first lines confirming what the title promised
A pop-up asking viewers to subscribe before they watch
A thumbnail test that confirms which version gets clicked
The end screen confirming what the next video will be
checks.expl: Ideally they beat the expectation too.

spch100.16.2.takeaway: Derek Muller of Veritasium: there's a difference between 'legitbait' — enticing and accurate — and the click trap. Packaging is at least half the job, because click-through decides how many people YouTube shows your video to at all.

beats.d: 'Strange Applications of the Magnus Effect' went nowhere on YouTube; a re-upload titled 'Basketball Dropped From Dam' got tens of millions.
YouTube moved from subscriptions to engagement, which raised the importance of packaging.
Legitbait versus click trap, mapped on sensationalism and withholding.
Real-time metrics let you change a title and watch for a bump in views.
Jack Conte's idea: keep the box uncompromised; change the wrapping.

spch100.16.2.worked: 'Are Negative Ions Good For You?' — a question nobody asked — became 'Do Salt Lamps Work?', and gained about one and a half million views. The new title was also clearer and more accurate.
spch100.16.2.watch: Treating all clickbait as the enemy. The dead zone ('Strange Applications of the Magnus Effect') fails too; the target is accurate and enticing. The last minute is a sponsor read.

checks.q: What is 'legitbait'?
opts: Packaging that is enticing and accurate
Misleading titles that still get the clicks
Titles with no curiosity, so nobody is misled
Paid promotion that looks like a normal video
checks.expl: As opposed to a click trap.

checks.q: Why does click-through matter beyond clicks?
opts: It sets the ad rates the channel earns per view
It largely decides how many impressions YouTube gives the video
It counts towards watch time, which is what the system ranks on
It sets your subscriber count, since clickers tend to subscribe
checks.expl: Limited real estate goes to what gets clicked.

checks.q: Why title a video 'The Simplest Math Problem No One Can Solve' rather than 'The Collatz Conjecture'?
opts: It's shorter than the technical name, so it fits on a thumbnail as well
It hides the topic completely, so viewers have to click to find out what it is
It tells far more people why they'd care, not just those who know the term
It's funnier, and humour gets more clicks than accuracy on a science channel
checks.expl: More people learn something new.

spch100.16.3.takeaway: Colin and Samir cut a documentary from more than fifty hours of footage: capture moments, show instead of announcing, count down rather than up, and let tension rise like a Jenga tower.

beats.d: An unguarded 'do you think I'm evil?' exchange became the soul of the piece.
A two-minute explanatory car scene became a visual cold open.
'Day one, day two' meant nothing; time running out did.
Each piece removed makes the tower shakier until the end.
How will two worlds come together? — with smaller curiosity gaps inside.

spch100.16.3.worked: Their first title cards counted production days up — day one, two, three. They realised that raised no stakes, so they counted down instead, and showed unfinished sets to make the audience feel the time running out.
spch100.16.3.watch: Over-explaining. On YouTube you're used to saying everything aloud so nobody's lost; in a documentary the picture can do it, and it's stronger.

checks.q: What's the difference between a moment and a shot?
opts: Shots can be recaptured later; moments can't
Moments are longer and need more coverage
Shots need a crew; moments need only a phone
There's no real difference once it's edited
checks.expl: Either you get the moment or you don't.

checks.q: Why did they switch from counting days up to counting down?
opts: To shorten the film by cutting the early days
Counting up meant nothing; counting down raised the stakes
For the sponsor, whose product had a countdown timer built in
It looked better on screen with the new graphics
checks.expl: Time running out builds tension.

checks.q: What is 'Jenga storytelling'?
opts: Stacking jokes until the whole thing topples over
Editing with blocks of colour to mark each section
Tension rising as the structure gets less stable
Telling the story backwards, piece by piece
checks.expl: By the end you're on the edge of your seat.

spch100.16.4.takeaway: Marques Brownlee asks Colin and Samir whether MrBeast's storytelling advice transfers to tech reviews. Their answer: storytelling does — set up something the viewer waits for — but not every retention tactic suits a niche, and packaging is best decided before you film.

beats.d: 'Two things I really like, one I really don't' sets up a wait.
The South Park rule applies to a phone launch too.
A review is tension in itself: what does Marques think?
Their audience wants long answers; cutting everything to six minutes would lose value.
If you're frantically changing titles, the mistake was earlier.

spch100.16.4.worked: A phone review told with 'but, therefore': this line of phones has been incredible — but this one is different — therefore you should think about it differently. The same causal chain a story uses, inside a product review.
spch100.16.4.watch: About half of this clip is podcast conversation (a MrBeast-challenge tangent, creators' complaints about thumbnails and AdSense). The structure points are in the first seven minutes and from about 11:40 to 13:30.

checks.q: How can a review open a narrative, according to Samir?
opts: By setting up something the viewer waits for, like the one thing he dislikes
By telling a childhood story about the first phone he ever owned and loved
By hiding the product until the end, so viewers stay to see what it looks like
By using music that builds, so the review feels like a trailer from the start
checks.expl: That's a story element.

checks.q: What does frantic title-swapping suggest, in their view?
opts: Good testing, done exactly the way the platform intends you to
A mistake earlier in the process — the idea wasn't packaged first
A broken algorithm that no longer rewards good titles the way it did
Too many uploads, so no single video gets enough attention
checks.expl: Good ideas make titles and thumbnails easy.

checks.q: Why don't they take every retention tip to the extreme?
opts: It's too expensive and slow to edit every video that tightly
YouTube forbids some of those tactics in its community guidelines
Their niche audience values depth that a very short cut would remove
They don't track retention closely enough to act on every tip they hear
checks.expl: Know your audience.

spch100.4.8.takeaway: Vinh Giang's system for the moments when everyone is watching, in three stages: before (rehearse to the stakes, out loud, at full energy, then without notes), during (nerves on three levels, connection before content, a balance of education, inspiration and entertainment), after (record and review, and build your own stage).

beats.d: Theatre's rule is two hours of rehearsal per minute on stage. He scales it: one to three runs for a weekly stand-up, ten when leaders attend, a hundred for an investor pitch.
Read the script aloud five to ten times with the energy, volume and pace of the real thing. Rehearse it mumbling while you pace, and you will pace on stage.
Go without notes; when you forget, pause and try for ten seconds before checking. The strain fixes the words and trains a pause instead of panic.
Think about who you are helping. Push-ups or star jumps backstage, then slow breathing. Call the feeling excitement — Mel Robbins told him the body cannot tell the two apart.
Open with a short origin story, not research or statistics. In an interview, answer 'tell me about yourself' with a story instead of adjectives.
Pure magic felt like a show; pure education put the room to sleep. Organisers wanted people to learn something useful, feel inspired and have fun — plus the one per cent that is yours.
Film every talk and meeting you reasonably can and watch the whole thing back. With no gigs, he built a stage in his backyard, then got a busking permit and spoke to strangers.

spch100.4.8.worked: At a dentists' conference in Sydney the organiser told him his talk was one of the best she had seen. An hour later he watched a flat, monotone speaker walk off and heard her say the same words to him. That is why he stopped trusting compliments and started filming: two GoPros taped together, one on him and one on the audience, so he could see what he was doing at the moment they reached for their phones.
spch100.4.8.watch: The seven-step rehearsal video he advertises is a sign-up for his own material, and a hundred rehearsals is his standard, not a rule. The first two steps — table reads at full energy and the ten-second recall — are the lesson.

checks.q: During an improv rehearsal you forget your next line. What does he tell you to do?
opts: Look at your notes straight away, so you keep the energy and momentum going
Pause, breathe and try to remember for at least ten seconds before checking
Skip to the next part you remember and come back to the gap at the end
Start again from the top, so the whole talk is rehearsed as one unbroken run
checks.expl: The strain fixes the material, and you are practising a calm pause instead of panic.

checks.q: Why does he insist table reads are done at full performance energy?
opts: Because you end up presenting the way you rehearsed
Because it tires the voice so it sits lower on the day
Because organisers expect it
Because it makes the script shorter
checks.expl: Higher effort in rehearsal also means better recall.

checks.q: What is the '33 / 33 / 33 / 1' formula?
opts: Thirty-three slides, thirty-three minutes, thirty-three questions, and one clear ask
A third preparation, a third rehearsal, a third delivery, and one percent luck on the day
A third education, a third inspiration, a third entertainment, plus your own X-factor
A third story, a third data, a third questions from the room, and one call to action
checks.expl: He arrived at it by asking organisers what they wanted their audience to take away.

checks.q: Why does he distrust the feedback people give right after a talk?
opts: Audiences are usually hostile right after a talk ends
People say 'amazing' to everyone, so it tells you nothing
Feedback forms are anonymous, so people say what they like
Only professional speakers know what to look for in a talk
checks.expl: They don't want to hurt you, and they wouldn't know what specific feedback to give anyway.

spch100.4.9.takeaway: David JP Phillips spent seven years analysing 5,000 speakers and found 110 learnable skills. His five favourites — open body language, no retreating, functional gestures, a calm pace, the pause instead of 'uh' — plus four tiny skills that change a room's state in five seconds.

beats.d: The more of the 110 you use, the better you are; nobody is born with a gene for the stage. Knowing what each move does is the difference between guessing and choosing.
Closed positions signal threat. His catalogue: the fig leaf, the double bunny, the forklift, the peacock, the prayer, the beggar, the British horse rider, the T-rex.
Hands are for showing better, worse, one-two-three. When they say the opposite of the words, the audience believes the hands.
A slow pace reads as importance — his 'utterly boring' sentence held the room because he slowed down. 'Uh' is the cheap compromise for a pause, and the biggest single loss of credibility.
Look up, inhale audibly, smile with the eyes, laugh at yourself. He spent six months learning the eye-reaching smile after finding it missing from years of holiday photos.

spch100.4.9.worked: His demonstration of contradiction: an upbeat paragraph about why everyone should learn public speaking, said warmly but with hands doing the opposite. Then he asks whether you were listening to what he said or watching what he did. The room had been watching.
spch100.4.9.watch: The list of 110 is his own taxonomy, and some claims (smiles and divorce rates) come without a source on screen. Trust the demonstrations, which you can test on your own recording, over the statistics.

checks.q: Of the 110 skills, which does Phillips say lowers your credibility most?
opts: Standing behind a lectern
Filling pauses with 'uh'
Speaking slowly
Using too many slides
checks.expl: It signals you don't know what you are saying or where you are going.

checks.q: When your gestures contradict your words, what does the audience do?
opts: Ignore the gestures
Average the two messages
Ask what you meant
Follow the gestures
checks.expl: Positive words with negative hands: the room watched the hands.

checks.q: What does a calm, slow pace signal, in his account?
opts: That what you are saying is important
That you are nervous and holding back
That you are unprepared and thinking
That you want the talk to be over soon
checks.expl: A high pace suggests you don't really want to be there.

spch100.4.10.takeaway: Caroline Goyder's three lessons, from a voice coach who once bombed: practise the instrument by singing daily, breathe low from the diaphragm because relaxed breathing is what power looks like, and remember that we breathe our thoughts — the in-breath, taken with the mouth closed, decides how the next sentence sounds.

beats.d: As a rookie she went too fast, lost her words, and when the microphone broke someone shouted 'speak up'. She concluded that confidence lives inside the body, not on the outside.
Demosthenes stammered and was jeered, then practised for months in a cellar and over the waves. Her version is easier: sing every day.
The most powerful person in a room has the most relaxed breathing, and the king stays still while everyone moves around him.
A yoga teacher put a gym weight on her stomach and said lift it with your breath. The thumb below the breastbone gives the same feeling standing up.
Inspiration and respiration share a root. Breathe in someone you love and the out-breath carries it; breathe in excitement and the voice has excitement in it.

spch100.4.10.worked: A client whose husband died on their honeymoon had to give the eulogy in the church where they had married. She wrote that the only way she got through it was what she had practised: breathing low and slow, taking her time, finding the control.
spch100.4.10.watch: Low breathing is for the moment before a phrase, not a reason to stop after every word. Pair it with thought groups from Unit VI so the breath lands at the end of a meaning.

checks.q: How do actors tell who is most powerful in a room, by her account?
opts: They speak first and the others fall quiet to listen
They have the most relaxed breathing and stay still
They stand nearest the door and watch everyone
They are the loudest, and move around the most
checks.expl: Everyone moves around the king; the king stays still.

checks.q: What is her simplest daily practice for the voice?
opts: Reading the news aloud for ten minutes each morning
Humming scales at a piano every morning
Singing — in the shower, in the car, anywhere
Recording voice notes and listening back
checks.expl: Practice is the way to a great instrument.

checks.q: What is the 'big secret' she ends on?
opts: Know when to shut your mouth — take the in-breath with it closed
Always smile before a sentence, so the warmth carries into the voice
Project to the back wall, so the voice never sounds small or thin
Breathe in through the mouth, deep and fast, before every sentence
checks.expl: All speech is out-breath; the in-breath is where the thought arrives.

spch100.9.17.takeaway: David JP Phillips's five rules for slides that don't kill the room: one message, no sentences you also speak (the redundancy effect), the important thing biggest, contrast and a dark background to steer the eye, and six objects at most — which means more slides, not fewer.

beats.d: Car five, seat 42: people check a train ticket about six times before they sit down. Slides draw on the same memory.
Two messages split attention, like hearing your name across a party and nodding along to the person in front of you.
Text on the slide while you speak leaves close to nothing remembered. Sentences go in the notes; the slide gets short phrases and an image.
Eyes go to moving, signal-coloured, high-contrast and big things. Shrink the headline so the eye falls to the content; reveal one item at a time.
On a white slide the screen out-contrasts and out-sizes you. Darken it and you become the visual aid.
A few balls are seen in about two-tenths of a second; more must be counted, about five times slower. Past six, the audience stops seeing.

spch100.9.17.worked: One deck he worked on went from 95 crowded slides to 135 sparse ones, with an immediate result for the project. Rules that cap the number of slides just make people cram 36 slides' worth into four.
spch100.9.17.watch: These rules are for slides that sit behind a speaker. A deck that will be read alone — a leave-behind after an audit — needs its sentences. Make two versions rather than one that does both badly.

checks.q: What is the 'redundancy effect' he warns about?
opts: Repeating your key point three times, so the audience tunes out the rest
Showing sentences on screen while you say them, so little is remembered
Using one template for every deck, so all the slides blur together
Two slides carrying the same message, which halves the attention each gets
checks.expl: Pull the text into the notes field and keep the slide for short phrases and an image.

checks.q: Why does he recommend a dark background?
opts: It prints better when people want handouts of the slides
It saves battery on laptops and on some kinds of projector
So you, not the screen, are the biggest high-contrast object
White backgrounds are hard to read in a bright room with windows
checks.expl: You are the presentation; the slide is the support.

checks.q: What is his limit for objects on one slide?
opts: Six
Three
Ten
Fifteen
checks.expl: Beyond six, people count instead of see.

spch100.9.18.takeaway: Chip Heath on Stanford's Think Fast, Talk Smart: untranslated numbers are like shouting a phrase in a language half the room doesn't speak. Translate every important number into a comparison, a human-scale timeline or a frequency, and make it emotional — the curse of knowledge hides how much the audience needs this.

beats.d: Experts can't imagine not knowing what they know — doctors, lawyers, an eleven-year-old explaining his favourite game. The cure is concrete language.
When a search result gave an area with a comparison ('about two Californias'), people remembered it much better a week and six weeks later.
His students sold a seven-year bulb by tying each change to a child's milestones: learning to walk, second grade, driver's ed.
Forty per cent skip handwashing becomes two of the last five people you shook hands with — and listeners reach for the sanitiser.
Florence Nightingale's charts showed hospitals killing far more soldiers than the enemy did. Emotion is what moves people to act.
After the analysis you are tired and two-thirds done; the translation is the extra third most people skip.

spch100.9.18.worked: In a budget meeting where you are not the numbers person: 'Let's imagine this table is the whole budget — how much of it does this line take up?' The analyst gets to calculate, and everyone else can now see whether it is trivial or huge.
spch100.9.18.watch: A translation has to keep the proportion honest. Dollar bills stacked to the moon are concrete, but nobody has a feel for that distance either — pick something from daily life.

checks.q: What does Heath mean by 'every number must be translated'?
opts: Convert it into another currency or unit
Round it to one decimal place so it's easy to say
Put it into terms people already have a feel for
Show it in a chart rather than reading it aloud
checks.expl: Comparisons, human-scale timelines and frequencies.

checks.q: Which version of '40% don't wash their hands' did he find most powerful?
opts: Two of the last five people you shook hands with
Four in ten adults don't wash their hands
Forty per cent of the whole population
Nearly half of everyone you will meet this week
checks.expl: We are bad at picturing probabilities and good at picturing people.

checks.q: Why, in his view, do analysts skip translating?
opts: They are not allowed to simplify numbers that will go into official reports
After the analysis they're tired, and translating takes another third of the effort
Audiences in their field prefer raw numbers, which feel more precise and honest
Translating makes the numbers less accurate, and accuracy is their whole job
checks.expl: Getting the answer feels like the finish line; communicating it is the rest of the job.

spch100.9.19.takeaway: Dan Pink's six pitches from To Sell Is Human — Pixar, subject line, rhyme, question, short post and one word — each a way to invite a conversation rather than throw a message at someone.

beats.d: Emma Coats's story spine used as a pitch: we see the world as episodes, not as logical propositions.
Utility or curiosity, not a muddle of both. A campaign's most-opened email said only 'Hey'.
Rhyme increases processing fluency. Johnnie Cochran's line from the O. J. Simpson trial is still remembered.
Questions are active and statements passive. Reagan asked instead of asserting, and voters supplied the reasons.
Useful information and questions do well in short posts. Own one word, the way 'Forward' carried a campaign.

spch100.9.19.worked: In 1980 Reagan could have said economic conditions had deteriorated over 48 months. He asked, 'Are you better off now than you were four years ago?' — and each listener did the persuading by thinking it through.
spch100.9.19.watch: A rhyme or one-word pitch that is clever but untrue is a slogan, not a pitch. Use the format to make a true point easier to hold.

checks.q: Which two kinds of subject line work, according to Pink?
opts: Long ones and short ones, used in turns
Useful ones and curiosity ones — not a mix
Questions and commands that get a reply
Personal ones and formal ones, by audience
checks.expl: Anything in between does poorly.

checks.q: Why is a question pitch more persuasive than a statement?
opts: Listeners start articulating their own reasons
It sounds more polite, so people listen longer
It is shorter, so it fits into a busy day
It hides the ask until the listener is ready
checks.expl: People believe the reasons they come up with themselves.

checks.q: What does Pink say a pitch really is?
opts: A performance
A throw you either catch or miss
An invitation to a conversation
A list of features
checks.expl: Pitching, done well, is collaborative.

spch100.9.20.takeaway: Andy Raskin, author of 'The Greatest Sales Deck I've Ever Seen': the story that cuts through a crowded market is not 'why us' but 'why you, now' — name the shift, show the winners and losers, tease the promised land, and make your product the weapon for getting there.

beats.d: A list of dishes, then reasons under 'why should I come in?' — the self-centred 'why us' most companies use.
It opens with a change in the world — we have moved to a subscription economy — and celebrates those who adapt. It is not about Zuora at all.
Obi-Wan's demo doesn't move Luke; a change in his world does, and then there are stakes. Most buyers aren't in pain — they assume life will stay okay.
Logikcull asked customers why it was more valuable now and heard 'now everything is discoverable'. Prospects say 'that's me' at that slide.
Zaius named the monster — marketing data and campaign tools in separate systems — and pointed every feature at it. The 'how are you different?' questions stopped.
A promised-land story is an invitation to join people heading somewhere. Even a pizza place can tell one.

spch100.9.20.worked: Logikcull, a legal-discovery platform: the shift was 'now everything is discoverable' — data from drones, cars, chats; deadlines haven't changed, so you either fail miserably or look like a star; the promised land is instant discovery. Raskin reports new reps' time to their first win fell from about sixty days to under thirty.
spch100.9.20.watch: A shift you can't evidence is a scare tactic. His teams interviewed real customers about what had changed before they wrote a slide.

checks.q: What is the first move in a 'why you, now' story?
opts: Show the product demo before anything else
List your differences from the competitors
Name an undeniable shift in the customer's world
Tell your founding story and why you started
checks.expl: The shift creates the urgency that a feature list can't.

checks.q: Which question did his clients put to their customers?
opts: What has changed so that having this is worth more now than a few years ago?
What do you dislike most about our competitors, and why did you leave them?
How much would you pay for this today, and how much would you have paid before?
Which feature should we build next to make this more valuable to your team?
checks.expl: The answers became the shift on the first slide.

checks.q: Why do people who copy the Zuora deck often fail, in his account?
opts: The deck is too long for most buyers, who stop reading after a few slides
They paste their logo into the template instead of following the principles
They pitch it to the wrong buyer, who doesn't feel the shift in the market
They leave out pricing, so the buyer can't act on the promised land at the end
checks.expl: Like a good film, a narrative has its own flow.

spch100.9.21.takeaway: Jonah Berger at Talks at Google on Magic Words: six kinds of language (similarity, questions, emotion, agency, confidence, concreteness), with depth on identity nouns, could versus should, hedges and how to state uncertainty without sounding unsure, and why asking for advice raises how competent you look.

beats.d: Asking young children to 'be a helper' rather than to 'help' raised helping by about thirty per cent; 'be a voter' raised turnout by about fifteen. We want to hold desirable identities.
A 'runner' runs more than someone who runs; a 'hard worker' sounds more consistent than 'hard-working'.
'Should' implies a single right answer; 'could' widens the options, and people produced more creative solutions.
People preferred a more certain financial advisor even when he was no more accurate. Habitual hedges undercut you.
'It's a great idea, but these three things need to happen' and 'it seems to me' keep you honest without sounding unsure. Pause instead of 'um'.
People who asked their partner for advice were rated as more competent — everyone thinks their own advice is good.
Certainty is a tool. In a small team meeting, or as the newest member, hedging signals openness — and certainty lands differently across cultures.

spch100.9.21.worked: Instead of telling a client 'I'm not sure this strategy will work', say 'I think this is a strong strategy — and for it to work, these three things need to happen.' Both admit uncertainty; only the second sounds like you have thought it through.
spch100.9.21.watch: One of his examples of confident speech is a politician; the point is the mechanism, not the politics. Certainty you don't have is overconfidence — name the conditions instead of faking it.

checks.q: Why did 'can you be a helper?' work better than 'can you help?'
opts: It is shorter, so children understand it
It frames the action as an identity people want to hold
It sounds more polite, so children feel respected and listen
Children prefer nouns to verbs at that age
checks.expl: Turning actions into identities makes them more appealing to take on.

checks.q: How does Berger suggest expressing real uncertainty without undermining yourself?
opts: Don't mention it, since any doubt undermines you
Add more hedges to be safe, so nobody can say you were wrong
Name the conditions it depends on and own it with 'I'
Speak more quickly, so the uncertainty doesn't linger
checks.expl: Calling out the hurdles shows you have thought about them.

checks.q: What happened to people who asked their partner for advice?
opts: They were seen as more competent
They were seen as less intelligent
Nothing changed
They were seen as lazy
checks.expl: The person asked thinks: they must be smart, they asked me.

spch100.9.22.takeaway: Vanessa Van Edwards at Talks at Google: her lab's coding of TED talks, inaugural addresses and Shark Tank pitches, then a crash course in five facial expressions to watch for during a pitch and what to say when you see each — plus pitching to the other person's personality.

beats.d: The most-viewed TED talks averaged about 465 hand gestures in eighteen minutes, the least-viewed about 272. Gestures work like bold type.
Mistakes with the numbers sank 64 per cent of failed pitches whatever the charisma. Past that, 45 per cent of successful entrepreneurs smiled walking in, against 21 per cent of unsuccessful ones.
Fear widens the eyes — reassure or explain. Anger draws two vertical lines; suspicion tightens the lower lids, a sign you are not done selling.
Contempt, a one-sided smirk, festers and needs addressing now. Disgust often appears when someone is hunting for a polite way to say no — give them permission to say it.
High-conscientiousness people want agendas and details; low want the big idea. Worriers take longer to recover from even small bad news.
After dinner with Gladstone a journalist thought him the cleverest person in England; after Disraeli, she thought she was.

spch100.9.22.worked: You see a flash of contempt when you mention the price. Instead of pushing on: 'Are we all good? Anything you'd like me to go back over?' Then go back over that part and watch whether the expression returns.
spch100.9.22.watch: These are her lab's findings and a popular reading of Paul Ekman's work; the claim that nonverbal signals carry about twelve times the weight of words is hers, and reading micro-expressions is contested by other researchers. Treat a face as a cue to check in, never as proof of what someone thinks.

checks.q: As you explain your price, someone's lower eyelids tighten. What does she say that signals?
opts: Boredom — move to your next point
Suspicion — you are not done explaining
Agreement — it's time to close the deal
Tiredness — offer a short break
checks.expl: Keep explaining; the sale isn't made yet.

checks.q: Why does she say contempt has to be addressed straight away?
opts: It is the one emotion that doesn't fade by itself
It means the deal is already lost, so stop pitching
It is the most common expression in a pitch meeting
It shows the person is lying about their interest
checks.expl: Fear and anger burst and pass; contempt sits and grows.

checks.q: What is the 'platinum rule'?
opts: Always pitch to the most senior person in the room
Treat others the way you want to be treated
Treat others the way they want to be treated
Mirror the other person's posture exactly
checks.expl: Meet people through the lens of their personality, not yours.

spch100.6.12.takeaway: Scott Dikkers, founder of The Onion, interviewed on how to write funny reliably: switch on purpose between the clown (generate) and the editor (judge), get neutral feedback on the whole shape before polishing, and in writing give readers what a club gives a comedian — a funny title and escalating beats.

beats.d: Brands build when something people like is produced consistently; a daily comic strip and a weekly print deadline kept him at it.
Eddie Murphy and Chris Farley looked like overnight talents but had been at it since childhood. The real development started when they met audiences who owed them nothing.
Children are all clown; many adults are all editor, which is writer's block. Professionals move between the two with precision.
He gets notes on a short treatment before drafting, and tells film outlines aloud — questions from the listener mean a broken outline.
Twenty to fifty readers, picked for variety, fill in a form: overall impression, five things that didn't work, a fix for each. Problems many of them mention get fixed.
No room to read, no control of timing, no club announcing comedy. So the title announces the joke and the beats are paced to escalate.

spch100.6.12.worked: His favourite character is the bumbling authority — Leslie Nielsen's doctors and detectives — and The Onion is that character: an important-sounding newspaper saying silly things. Casting a newsreader with a deep, perfect 'voice of authority' for its radio show made every line funnier.
spch100.6.12.watch: This is an interview, and after about 33:20 it turns to his views on satire and the state of the world rather than craft — stop there. The eleven filters themselves are in this unit's earlier lesson.

checks.q: What does Dikkers say writer's block usually is?
opts: A lack of talent that practice can only partly fix
Being stuck in editor mode, judging before anything is written
Not reading enough funny writing to know what works
Writing at the wrong time of day, when your energy is at its lowest
checks.expl: The editor cuts everything before it reaches the page.

checks.q: Why does a written funny piece need a funny title?
opts: The reader isn't in a comedy club, so the title must announce it's funny
Search engines rank funny titles higher, so more readers find the piece
Editors judge a piece by its title, so a dull one is never read at all
The title replaces the first joke, so the piece can start on the second
checks.expl: Most writers go from a dull title straight into a block of grey text and lose the reader.

checks.q: What does he ask beta readers for?
opts: A star rating for each joke, so the weakest can be cut first of all
What they liked best and least, so you can keep doing the good parts
An overall impression, five things that didn't work, and a fix for each
A line-by-line edit of the wording, so every sentence is as tight as it can be
checks.expl: Praise isn't actionable; problems and proposed fixes are.

spch100.6.13.takeaway: Bob Mankoff, The New Yorker's cartoon editor, on designing humour: incongruity fuses things that don't belong; context decides whether a violation is benign or malign; the target can be us rather than them; and it is all a numbers game of many ideas and a lot of rejection.

beats.d: No humour pleases everyone. An angry letter about 'jokes on old white males' and an animal lover who rated a cartoon two show how wide the spread is without a laughing room around you.
Entertainment needs a little danger with protection, like a zoo. Ask where the tiger is and how you will manage it.
His contract said 'idea drawings', not cartoons: work that needs thinking from the cartoonist and from the reader.
'No, Thursday's out. How about never — is never good for you?' fuses the syntax of politeness with the message of rudeness.
A crude line is perfect in a book of rejects and malign beside an article on the immune system. The week after 9/11 the magazine ran no cartoons at all.
'I started my vegetarianism for health reasons... now it's just to annoy people.' The humour reflects back on the reader.

spch100.6.13.worked: After 9/11 the magazine waited a week, then ran: 'I thought I'd never laugh again. Then I saw your jacket.' The joke isn't about the attackers; it is about us choosing to go on living — and the context made it a benign violation.
spch100.6.13.watch: Self-directed humour works for The New Yorker because its readers share the target. In a pitch, 'us' should mean you or your shared trade — never the client sitting in front of you.

checks.q: Why does 'How about never — is never good for you?' work, by his analysis?
opts: It is so short that the reader gets it before thinking about it twice
A polite form carries a rude message — two things that don't belong
It borrows a famous line, so the reader enjoys recognising it
It rhymes and repeats 'never', so the rhythm does the work
checks.expl: Incongruity: we hold both readings at once.

checks.q: Why would a cartoon that is perfect in The Rejection Collection fail in The New Yorker?
opts: Context turns a benign violation into a malign one
The drawing is worse than the magazine's standard
Its readers are older, and the joke is too modern
It is too long for the space under a cartoon
checks.expl: There is no such thing as funny in and of itself.

checks.q: Who is usually the target of New Yorker humour, as he describes it?
opts: Politicians, whose foibles everyone enjoys mocking
Other magazines, and their more earnest readers
The readers themselves — our obsessions and foibles
Outsiders, whose habits the readers find strange
checks.expl: Most humour is friends mocking enemies; theirs reflects back on us.

spch100.6.14.takeaway: John Cleese's 1991 talk on creativity: it is a way of operating, not a talent. You need the open mode to have ideas and the closed mode to carry them out, and you can set up the open mode with space, time, more time, confidence and humour.

beats.d: Donald MacKinnon's research found the most creative architects, scientists and writers no different in IQ; they could get themselves into a playful, almost childlike mood.
In the closed mode Fleming would have thrown away the dish where nothing grew; in the open mode he got curious about it. Hitchcock told stories when a writing session got tense.
Seal yourself off for a defined period. The first minutes fill with urgent trivia; sit through it and the mind quietens. Ninety minutes, then stop.
A Python colleague took the first solution and finished by five; Cleese sat with the discomfort for another hour and got something more original. Defer decisions until they are due.
While playing, nothing is a mistake. Humour gets you into the open mode fastest — serious subjects don't require solemnity.
A joke and an idea both connect two frames of reference. Random juxtapositions can start it; intuition picks which ones mean something.

spch100.6.14.worked: The airline pilot asked when he last had sex says '1958' — and, seeing the researcher's surprise, 'well, it's only 2110 now'. The laugh arrives the moment two frames, a year and the 24-hour clock, connect: the same click as a new idea.
spch100.6.14.watch: The talk was given to managers and ends with an ironic list of ways to stamp out creativity in your staff — it is satire, not advice. The light-bulb jokes in between are period filler, not models to copy.

checks.q: Why, in Cleese's telling, did Fleming notice what became penicillin?
opts: He was in the open mode, so a useless dish became a clue
He was working under pressure, which sharpened his attention
He had a higher IQ than colleagues working on the same dishes
He followed a strict protocol that told him to check every dish
checks.expl: In the closed mode an uncultured dish is an irrelevance; in the open mode it is a clue.

checks.q: What does he recommend when you face a decision?
opts: Decide at once, because looking decisive matters most to a team
Ask when it has to be taken, and keep pondering until then
Delegate it to the person who knows the most about the problem
Put it to a vote so that the whole group owns the outcome
checks.expl: The most creative people tolerate the discomfort of an unsolved problem for longer.

checks.q: What does he say a joke and a new idea have in common?
opts: Both need a punchline that arrives at the very end
Both work best when developed in a group
Both connect two frames of reference in a new way
Both should be short enough to say in a breath
checks.expl: The laugh, and the idea, come at the moment of connection.

spch100.7.9.takeaway: Second City's Anne Libera and Kelly Leonard run their classic exercise on a live conference audience — ideas met first by people told to negate them, then by people told to yes-and them — and add a tool from their work with Chicago behavioural scientists: 'thank you because', genuine gratitude before a genuine disagreement.

beats.d: Improv is loud group mindfulness and practice at being unpractised. It began as Viola Spolin's games for immigrant children at Hull House, many of them silent or in gibberish.
Pitching to people who deny everything was 'challenging' — one participant said it felt like being a woman in a meeting. The yes-and round was exhilarating for everyone.
The man in the suit who says he'd get no work done if he yes-anded everything misses the point: it is five minutes at the start of a brainstorm. And it can be used for evil.
Research shows gratitude makes people more open to negative feedback. It was the round people found hardest to stop talking in.
Stating the last word someone said before you answer forces you to listen to the end of the sentence.
Asked for ideas Second City would never stage, the cast produced scenes that mostly ended up in the show. An ensemble compensates for its weakest member — who could be anyone.

spch100.7.9.worked: Demonstrated live: 'Let's build a dome on the moon for the reunion.' 'Thank you, because there's such poetry in that idea — but the budget worries me.' 'Thank you — I appreciate that you're grounding me while looking for a way to make it happen.'
spch100.7.9.watch: 'Thank you because' works only if the 'because' is something you actually heard and valued; said by rote, it is the manipulation they warn about. The exercise rounds are crowd noise — follow along in the transcript.

checks.q: When is 'yes, and' meant to be used, according to Leonard?
opts: In every conversation, always, so nobody's idea is ever turned down at all
At the front end of ideas — a brainstorm's first minutes — to get abundance
Only on stage, where the rules are clear and agreed in advance by all
When closing a deal, so the other side feels heard before you decide
checks.expl: It is rapid prototyping for ideas, not a vow never to say no.

checks.q: What is 'thank you because'?
opts: Naming something you genuinely valued in what they said, before disagreeing
A polite way to end a meeting, thanking each person for one contribution
A way of avoiding disagreement by thanking people instead of answering
A thank-you note after a pitch that names why you chose to say no
checks.expl: Gratitude first makes the disagreement easier to hear.

checks.q: Why repeat the last word someone said before you reply?
opts: To sound agreeable while you go on to disagree with them
It buys you a few seconds to think of what you'll say back
It forces you to listen to the end instead of planning your answer
To mirror their accent and tone back to them, which builds trust
checks.expl: Most of us start composing a reply halfway through.

spch100.7.10.takeaway: Greg Dean on why crowd work is so popular and what it really is: joke-writing done live. Find the premise in someone's answer, connect it to something else, build a story with more questions, escalate, tag, take other points of view, and compare.

beats.d: Strong crowd work is applied joke writing under pressure; an unfunny answer is exactly where the skill shows.
In his system a premise is a negative opinion about a subject. Hear the subject in their answer and pick your position, or you loop on 'what's funny?' and stop being present.
Identify the assumption in what was said and reinterpret it instantly.
Make the consequences worse with each line; follow a punchline with more punchlines and no new setup.
Your honest opinions show your values; people may disagree but respect consistency. Speaking as the tree, the fire or the firefighter adds angles.

'I'm an accountant but I hate numbers' — 'that's like a lifeguard who hates water.' Or treat a relationship as an ice-hockey game: it starts with icing, fights break out, the counsellor is the referee.

spch100.7.10.worked: His tag chain: 'For Father's Day I took my father out.' 'It only took three shots.' 'I could always drink him under the table.' 'Not sure why we drank under the table.' 'Maybe because he was my priest.' Every tag rides on the first setup.
spch100.7.10.watch: It is a promotional 'blogcast' for his paid class, and on stage the target volunteered for it. Off stage, aim the negative opinion at the situation or at yourself, not at the person who just answered you.

checks.q: In Dean's system, what is a premise?
opts: The first line of a joke
A negative opinion about a subject
A funny fact about the subject
The assumption the audience makes
checks.expl: It is the engine for the jokes that follow.

checks.q: What is a tag?
opts: A punchline that follows a punchline without a new setup
A callback to an earlier joke, made near the end of a set
A follow-up question to the audience that sets up a joke
A short setup added to make a weak punchline stronger
checks.expl: Tags keep the laughter rolling.

checks.q: 'I'm an accountant who hates numbers.' Which reply uses his comparison technique?
opts: 'So why did you become one, then?'
'Numbers probably hate you too, mate.'
'That's like a lifeguard who hates water.'
'Me too — I've always hated numbers as well.'
checks.expl: Find another pair that shares the same contradiction.

spch100.7.11.takeaway: A London comedy MC's safe crowd-work technique: because the same names, jobs and places come up night after night, he pre-writes jokes for them and drops them in, so it looks spontaneous.

beats.d: Being quick with a crowd is a skill worth building, but much good MC work leans on material written in advance.
In London a handful of names — Dave, Rob, Phil, Helen, Sarah — and the same ten or twenty jobs and places keep coming up.
A line for each of those, kept for years, means he always seems quick when he meets Dave who works in IT.
People messing with you claim to be airline pilots or gynaecologists — expect them.

spch100.7.11.worked: At a networking event, 'So what do you do?' is certain. A prepared, true line about your work — written once, tried a few times — means you never freeze, and the conversation can go somewhere unplanned after it.
spch100.7.11.watch: It is a short clip from a course promotion. A prepared line opens the door; after it, listen and riff — the previous lesson.

checks.q: What is the MC's 'safe' crowd-work technique?
opts: Never talking to the audience, so nothing can go wrong
Pre-written jokes for the names, jobs and places that always come up
Asking only yes-or-no questions, so the answers stay short
Picking on latecomers, whom the rest of the audience enjoys teasing
checks.expl: It gives the impression of improvising.

checks.q: Why does it work?
opts: The same handful of answers come up again and again
Audiences never listen closely enough to notice
Every crowd is different, so each joke seems new
Comedians learn the audience's names in advance
checks.expl: Name, job and home town are predictable.

checks.q: Which job claims does he say often mean someone is messing with you?
opts: Teacher and nurse, the most common answers
Accountant and lawyer
Airline pilot and gynaecologist
IT and sales, which are too vague
checks.expl: Have a line ready for the liars too.

spch100.7.12.takeaway: English with Lucy on British banter: playful teasing and clever comebacks are a big part of the culture, built on irony, same-theme replies and self-deprecation — with a firm line between teasing and bullying, and a knack for ending it.

beats.t: Don't give up your day job
beats.d: Said to a friend after off-key karaoke: irony to ease an awkward moment, with no intent to offend.
It crosses the line when you mean to hurt. Someone can laugh on the outside and feel uncomfortable inside.
'You're having a laugh, aren't you?', 'you and me both, mate', 'you and your trusty pal Google' — doubt, shared self-deprecation and a sarcastic jab.
'I bet that sounded funnier in your head' and 'you know you love it' work between friends; with someone you've just met, they probably won't.
'Nice one, genius' after a wrong answer is met with 'all right, Einstein' — the volley stays on intelligence.
'I highly doubt that.' 'Me too.' Agreeing with the jab closes the exchange before anyone gets annoyed.

spch100.7.12.worked: Alex is sure the longest river in the UK is the Thames, bets the next two rounds on it, and it's the Severn. 'Nice one, genius.' 'All right, Einstein, let's see how you do.' 'Stick with me and you might learn a thing or two.' 'I highly doubt that.' 'Me too.'
spch100.7.12.watch: This is British friendship banter. In many workplaces and cultures — and in a first meeting with a client — the same lines read as rude. Listen to how a group teases each other before you join in. The lesson includes a sponsor segment and course plugs.

checks.q: When does teasing cross into bullying, according to Lucy?
opts: When it happens in public, in front of others
When you are purposely trying to hurt someone
When it's about someone's work or career
When the other person doesn't laugh at once
checks.expl: Consider the other person's feelings; err on the side of caution.

checks.q: After 'nice one, genius', which comeback stays on the same theme?
opts: 'All right, Einstein'
'Whatever you say'
'Your round, then'
'That's not fair, mate'
checks.expl: Both lines are about intelligence.

checks.q: How does the exchange end?
opts: With a harsher joke that tops theirs
By changing the subject to something else
By agreeing with the jab — 'me too'
By walking away laughing
checks.expl: A self-deprecating agreement signals the teasing is done.

spch100.2.8.takeaway: Pixar story artist Kristen Lester: structure is what you want the audience to know, and when. A mushroom joke told out of order dies, and Finding Nemo's audiences only warmed to Marlin once his loss moved from late flashbacks to the opening.

beats.d: Opening, build-up, punchline ('I'm a fungi'). Botch the opening or the middle, or let every lady say yes, and there's no joke.
Structure decides what the audience knows at each moment, and so what they feel.
Early versions wove Marlin and Coral's past through the film and revealed the barracuda attack near the end. Audiences didn't like Marlin.
Almost all the flashbacks went; the attack moved to the beginning. Knowing his loss from the start, audiences saw his protectiveness as love and his journey as brave.

spch100.2.8.worked: Same events, new order: once the audience sees Coral and all but one of the eggs taken in the opening minutes, 'I promise I will never let anything happen to you' explains every over-cautious thing Marlin does afterwards.
spch100.2.8.watch: This is the short opening video of a longer Khan Academy lesson; the exercises are on Khan Academy's Pixar in a Box pages.

checks.q: How does Lester define structure?
opts: The number of acts and where each one ends
What you want the audience to know, and when
The order in which the events really happened
How long each scene runs before the next
checks.expl: Get the order wrong and the effect changes, even with the same material.

checks.q: Why didn't early audiences like Marlin?
opts: They didn't learn why he was so protective until near the end
His fussing over Nemo made the film feel slow and repetitive
They saw the barracuda attack too early and found it upsetting
Dory was funnier, so audiences took her side against him
checks.expl: The flashback structure hid his reason until it was too late.

checks.q: What breaks the mushroom joke in her last failed attempt?
opts: A punchline given away too early
An opening that skips the setup
No conflict — everyone says yes
A build-up told much too fast
checks.expl: Without conflict, joke over.

spch100.2.9.takeaway: Pete Docter opens Pixar in a Box's storytelling season: stories connect on an emotional level, 'write what you know' means putting your own feelings into any plot, and stories only sparkle after many retellings.

beats.d: When Val asks Pete what happened, she is asking for a story. People have told them for as long as they could speak.
As a kid he wanted explosions and car chases, not suburban Minnesota. You can have both — put how you felt into the explosions.
'A monster who scares kids for a living' got smiles in a pitch but left audiences restless. It was really about a man becoming a father — what was happening to Docter.
Not even the greats get it right first time; Pixar's stories improve over retelling after retelling, up to the thirtieth and beyond.

spch100.2.9.worked: Monsters, Inc.: the clock-in, eat-donuts, talk-about-union-dues joke was funny for a minute. The film found its spine when Docter recognised his own life in it — someone suddenly responsible for a small child.
spch100.2.9.watch: Under three minutes of introduction; the rest of the season is on Khan Academy. Its value here is one move: name the feeling under your plot.

checks.q: What does 'write what you know' mean in Docter's telling?
opts: Write only about places and people you know well
Put something you have felt into whatever you write
Avoid fantasy and stick to events that really happened
Research every detail until you know it as an expert
checks.expl: Something from your own life makes the story come alive.

checks.q: What did Docter realise Monsters, Inc. was really about?
opts: A man becoming a father
Union politics
Fear of the dark
A friendship between monsters
checks.expl: That was what was happening to him at the time.

checks.q: What does he say about getting a story right?
opts: The best storytellers get it right first time
Two drafts are enough if the idea is strong
It takes many retellings before it sparkles
Test it once on an audience, then lock it
checks.expl: Up to the thirtieth time, and on.

spch100.5.12.takeaway: Rachel's English introduces stress: in American English certain syllables in a word, and certain words in a sentence, are higher in pitch and longer. That contrast is what lets the ear pick out meaning — and much of what makes an accent.

beats.d: Two syllables, the second stressed: higher in pitch and longer.
Embarrassment: primary stress on the second syllable, a secondary on the first, the last two unstressed.
In 'I saw her at the meeting', 'saw' and the first half of 'meeting' stand out.
Pitch-tracking software shows each stressed syllable as a scoop up in the voice.
'I got it for you' — 'for' becomes a short, low 'fr'. Stress and reduction together make up much of an accent.

spch100.5.12.worked: Embarrassment: em (secondary) – BAR (primary) – rass – ment. Say it once with every syllable equal and once with this pattern; the second is the one a listener recognises at once.
spch100.5.12.watch: The model is American English. Stress as pitch plus length holds for British English too, but some words differ, so check a dictionary for the variety you want.

checks.q: What makes a syllable stressed, in Rachel's explanation?
opts: It is louder, and nothing else changes
It is usually higher in pitch and longer
It is spoken faster than the syllables around it
It always comes first in the word
checks.expl: Pitch and length are what the ear picks up.

checks.q: In 'embarrassment', where is the primary stress?
opts: On the second syllable
On the first syllable
On the last syllable
Spread evenly over all four
checks.expl: The first syllable has a secondary stress.

checks.q: What happens to 'for' in 'I got it for you'?
opts: It is stressed, because it shows purpose
It disappears completely
It is reduced to a short, low 'fr'
It is lengthened to make the rhythm even
checks.expl: Unstressed words reduce.

spch100.5.13.takeaway: Rachel's English defines intonation as the pitch pattern across a phrase. American statements fall to their lowest point at the end, questions rise, and the melody alone can turn the same words into concern or judgement.

beats.d: Stressed syllables are higher; content words are stressed and function words not. Strung together, those pitches make a pattern.
'Today it's sunny.' 'I wish I'd been there.' Even long sentences with ups and downs reach their lowest point at the end.
'Me?' goes up; 'me.' goes down.
'I'm dropping out of school.' 'Are you serious?' — rising sounds open and concerned; falling sounds like disapproval.
The right sounds in another language's melody still sound foreign. Loop native speech until the melody is in your ear.

spch100.5.13.worked: 'I'm dropping out of school.' Reply A, rising: 'Are you serious?' — what happened, are you okay? Reply B, falling: 'Are you serious.' — that's a bad idea. The same three words set up opposite conversations.
spch100.5.13.watch: Unit V's coaches disagree about how a sentence should end on stage; this lesson describes everyday American statements. In a talk, a falling ending still signals that you mean it.

checks.q: How do American English statements usually move in pitch?
opts: They start higher and end lowest
They rise at the end, like a question
They stay level, then drop slightly
They start low and rise to a peak
checks.expl: The lowest point is at the end.

checks.q: After 'I'm dropping out of school', what does a falling 'Are you serious?' convey?
opts: Concern
Confusion about the words
A judgement — disapproval
Excitement
checks.expl: Rising would sound open and concerned.

checks.q: Why can correct sounds still sound foreign?
opts: The vocabulary is too formal for everyday speech
They are spoken with another language's melody
They are spoken too slowly, so they sound careful
The grammar follows the first language's word order
checks.expl: Intonation characterises a language as much as its sounds.

spch100.5.14.takeaway: A short lesson from an English teacher who also speaks Arabic, on the slips Arabic speakers most often make in English: p and b, a strongly rolled r, non-phonetic spelling and silent letters, capital letters, the missing 'a/an', and adjective order.

beats.d: Arabic has a B but no P, so 'people' can come out as 'bibble'. B vibrates in the throat; P is only air.
A rolled r is still understood; soften it so the tongue lifts toward the roof of the mouth without touching.
Arabic is read as it is written; English is not. 'Though' and 'through'; an initial 'kn' drops the k.
Arabic has none. English capitalises sentence starts, names, cities, countries and nationalities.
'I teacher' and 'I have pen' carry Arabic patterns straight across; English needs 'I'm a teacher' and 'I have a pen'.
English puts the adjective first and doesn't change it for gender: 'I have a red pen'.

spch100.5.14.worked: 'I have pen red' carries two Arabic patterns at once — no indefinite article, and the adjective after the noun. Fixed: 'I have a red pen.'
spch100.5.14.watch: Two of the six points (spelling and capitals) are about writing. The speaking ones — p and b, and the dropped 'a' — are what a listener notices in a pitch.

checks.q: Why do many Arabic speakers mix up p and b?
opts: Arabic has a B but no P
The letters look alike
English spelling is confusing
They are the same sound
checks.expl: The p sound simply doesn't exist in Arabic.

checks.q: How can you feel the difference between B and P?
opts: Hand in front of the mouth — P is quieter
Hand on the throat — B vibrates, P doesn't
Say both slowly — B is always the longer one
Watch your lips — B is made with the tongue
checks.expl: B is voiced; P is voiceless.

checks.q: Which sentence correctly fixes 'I have pen red'?
opts: I have red pen
I have the pen red
I have a red pen
I have pen a red
checks.expl: Indefinite article, then the adjective before the noun.

spch100.8.11.takeaway: Trial lawyer Jefferson Fisher at Talks at Google: assume what you said isn't what they heard, go in to learn rather than to prove, share struggle, speak in perspectives, replace 'does that make sense?' with a real question, use silence on purpose, and keep your answers short.

beats.d: We judge our own words badly because we also interpret them for the listener. Ask what they heard instead of insisting on what you said.
Telling someone they're wrong can mean telling them their grandparents were wrong; walls go up and facts bounce off. Ask how long they've felt that way and what led to it.
A newly promoted woman who didn't feel qualified could say: 'I know I have a way to go — and what excites me about that is…'
'I see things differently' and 'I have a different take' keep a conversation open where 'I don't agree' closes it.
It implies the listener is slow or that you're unsure, and nobody says no. Ask for their thoughts or questions instead.
A considered pause signals thinking; five to seven seconds after a rude remark lets it echo. 'I'm not ignoring you, I'm thinking' says it plainly.
His company keeps emails to three sentences or fewer. On video calls especially, answer briefly and trust people to ask.

spch100.8.11.worked: Someone says something belittling in a meeting. Instead of firing back, he lets five seconds of silence pass. Their words now sit out in the open; often they take them back or apologise, and if they double down you've lost nothing — 'silence can never be misquoted'.
spch100.8.11.watch: The first few minutes are host chat and the book's framing; the tools come thick from about the nine-minute mark. Using AI as a 'thought partner' is his personal habit, not part of the method.

checks.q: What does Fisher suggest asking instead of saying 'that's not what I said'?
opts: 'Let me repeat myself'
'What did you hear?'
'You misunderstood me'
'Calm down'
checks.expl: It gives you their perspective instead of a fight about the record.

checks.q: Why does he want people to drop 'does that make sense?'
opts: It suggests the listener is slow or you're unsure, and nobody says no
It is too informal for a work conversation with someone senior
It takes too long, and the listener has already moved on by then
It is a leading question about facts, so it invites an argument
checks.expl: Ask a real question that invites them to respond.

checks.q: What does 'be a well, not a waterfall' mean?
opts: Speak more slowly, so each idea has time to sink in
Ask more questions than you answer in a conversation
Give a short answer and let people ask for more
Repeat your point until the other person accepts it
checks.expl: Limit it to about three sentences; they have the agency to ask.

spch100.8.12.takeaway: Charles Duhigg, author of Supercommunicators, in a long interview: anyone can learn it. Find out which of three conversations you're in and match it, ask deep questions, loop for understanding, share something real back, see people's many identities, and in hard conversations look for what you can control together.

beats.d: He came home venting about work (emotional) while his wife offered solutions (practical), and neither could hear the other. Now she asks: solve it together, or just vent?
Supercommunicators ask ten to twenty times as many questions as average, about half of them deep — beliefs, values, experiences. Ask how someone feels about their life, not its facts.
Ask, repeat back in your own words, ask if you got it right. It proves you listened, and people become more willing to listen in return.
CIA officer Jim Lawler spent months failing to recruit a source; when he finally admitted his own disappointment in himself, matching hers, she agreed — and was a prized asset for twenty years.
Reducing someone to one identity stereotypes them. Name their others — parent, neighbour, lawyer — and find the tribe you share.
Don't try to control the other person. Control things together — the time, the place, the boundaries of the argument — say up front it may be awkward, and ask what each of you wants.

spch100.8.12.worked: A performance review that opens: 'This might be a tough conversation, and I really want to help you. What are you hoping to get out of it?' 'A raise.' Now both people know what the conversation is about, even if the answer is 'not yet — here's the path to one'.
spch100.8.12.watch: The three conversations are also in this unit's short Duhigg lesson (spch100.8.6); this interview adds looping, identities and hard conversations. Figures like 'ten to twenty times as many questions' are his summaries of studies, with no papers shown.

checks.q: What are the three steps of looping for understanding?
opts: Ask, agree, then advise once you're sure you understand the whole problem
Ask a question, repeat the answer in your own words, ask if you got it right
Listen without interrupting, nod along, and summarise everything at the end
Question their view, challenge the weakest part, and conclude together
checks.expl: The third step gives them the chance to say you heard them — or to correct you.

checks.q: Duhigg comes home venting and his wife offers solutions. What went wrong?
opts: He was in an emotional conversation and she in a practical one
She wasn't really listening, because she was busy with dinner
They were both too tired after work to have that conversation
He had asked for advice, then rejected it when she gave it to him
checks.expl: Different conversations, different parts of the brain.

checks.q: In a hard conversation, what does he say you should try to control?
opts: The other person's emotions, so things stay calm
The other person's conclusion, by preparing your case
Things you can control together, like the time and the boundaries
Nothing at all — let it run its course and see what happens next
checks.expl: Trying to control each other backfires; controlling things together builds cooperation.
